Target 2 analytic input. Proof draft, unaudited. This is an explicit
consequence of known Biane and Voiculescu results, not a novelty claim.
It does not by itself establish the observation law for the real matrix
model or prove the T287 MMSE comparison.

Let mu be a compactly supported probability law on R. Write
mu_t=mu free-plus sigma_t, where sigma_t is the centered semicircle law
of variance t>0, p_t its density, and

    E(t)=Sigma(mu_t)=double integral log|x-y| mu_t(dx)mu_t(dy).

Then E is C1 on (0,infinity), with

    Phi(t)=(4*pi^2/3) integral p_t(x)^3 dx,
    E'(t)=Phi(t)/2.                                  (1)

No density, non-atomicity or finite initial logarithmic energy of mu is
assumed. In particular finite-rank/zero-atom input laws are allowed.

## Primary inputs and normalization

1. Biane, *On the free convolution with a semi-circular distribution*,
   Indiana Univ. Math. J.46 (1997),705-718, DOI10.1512/iumj.1997.46.1467.
   Lemma2, journal p709, defines v_t and gives its positive-level equation.
   Corollaries1-3, journal p711, give the continuous Cauchy boundary,
   a continuous density, and p_t(psi_t(u))=v_t(u)/(pi*t).
   Proposition4, journal p714, gives
   |p_t(x)^2 p_t'(x)|<=1/(4*pi^3*t^2) where p_t>0.
2. Voiculescu, *Free Entropy*, arXiv:math/0103168, chi.4 (one variable),
   and Section3.5 definition and chi*.1. In one variable
   chi(mu)=Sigma(mu)+3/4+(1/2)log(2*pi)=chi*(mu), and

   chi*(mu_t)=(1/2)integral_0^infinity
                  [1/(1+u)-Phi*(mu_(t+u))]du+(1/2)log(2*pi*e).

   Section3.3, J.1 and J.3 identify the scalar conjugate variable and
   the score under a positive semicircular perturbation. The Phi*
   convention is its squared L2 norm, Section3.4. We verify the scalar
   density constant explicitly below rather than borrow a classical
   Fisher-information convention.

All source artifacts and SHA256 values are recorded in SOURCES.jsonl.
The hypotheses quoted here were checked in the original journal PDF
and the author's arXiv survey, not inferred from an unrelated classical
de Bruijn card.

## Uniform spatial regularity and continuity in heat time

The v_t equation gives v_t<=sqrt(t): if v_t>0,
1/t=integral[(u-x)^2+v_t^2]^-1 mu(dx)<=1/v_t^2.
At v_t=0 the bound is immediate. Therefore

    0<=p_t(x)<=1/(pi*sqrt(t)).                       (2)

Set q_t=p_t^3. Proposition4 gives |q_t'|<=3/(4*pi^3*t^2) on the open
positivity set. Since q_t is continuous and zero on its complement,
this is a global Lipschitz bound on R. To see the extension across zeros,
integrate within each positive component; if two points lie in different
components, the values at their adjacent boundary zeros bound the
absolute difference by the same constant times the distance.

Fix 0<a<b<infinity. Realize mu as the law of a bounded selfadjoint X,
free from a variance-one semicircular S. The norms of X+sqrt(t)S for
t in [a,b] are bounded by ||X||+2sqrt(b). Thus all p_t have a common
compact support. Norm continuity of X+sqrt(t)S gives weak continuity
of its laws (first for polynomials, then for continuous functions on
the common compact interval).

For any t_k->t in [a,b], the q_(t_k) are uniformly bounded by (2),
uniformly Lipschitz and have common compact support. Every subsequence
has an Arzela-Ascoli uniformly convergent further subsequence, say to q.
Taking cube roots gives uniform convergence p_(t_k)->q^(1/3). The
weak-continuity statement forces q^(1/3)=p_t, since continuous densities
of the same law agree everywhere. Every possible subsequential uniform
limit is therefore q_t. Hence q_(t_k)->q_t uniformly, and

    t -> integral p_t^3                             (3)

is continuous on [a,b]. This argument does not assume joint parameter
regularity beyond Biane's actual spatial estimates.

## The exact scalar Fisher constant

Fix t>0, abbreviate p=p_t and define
G(z)=integral(z-x)^-1 p(x)dx. By Biane Corollary1 its upper boundary is
continuous, with G(x+i0)=h(x)-i*pi*p(x), h=PV integral p(y)/(x-y)dy.
It is bounded on compact subsets of the closed upper half-plane and
decays as O(1/|x|) off the compact support. In particular the boundary
function lies in L3(R).

For epsilon>0, the contour integral of G(z+i*epsilon)^3 around an upper
half-disk vanishes: it is analytic there and its large arc is O(R^-2).
Thus integral_R G(x+i*epsilon)^3 dx=0. Let epsilon decrease to zero.
Continuous boundary values give a uniform compact bound; outside a
fixed interval |G(x+i*epsilon)|<=2/|x| for 0<epsilon<=1. Dominated
convergence justifies passing the cubic integral to the boundary.
Taking imaginary parts gives

    integral p(x) h(x)^2 dx=(pi^2/3) integral p(x)^3 dx.                (4)

The scalar conjugate variable is 2h(X_t). This is Voiculescu J.1 with
the Hilbert-transform normalization removed; it can also be checked
directly from its defining polynomial identity:

    double integral [f(x)-f(y)]/(x-y) p(x)p(y)dxdy
                           =2 integral f(x)h(x)p(x)dx.

The principal-value passage is valid here: q_t is Lipschitz, so p_t is
Holder1/3, compactly supported, and its symmetric principal-value
integrals converge; the subtracted polynomial numerator is nonsingular.
Polynomial uniqueness in L2 on compact support identifies the score.
Therefore Phi*(mu_t)=4 integral p h^2=(4*pi^2/3)integral p^3, as asserted.
By (3), Phi*(mu_t) is continuous at every positive time.

## From the defining heat integral to the derivative

J.3 writes the score as t^(-1/2) E[S|X+sqrt(t)S]. The conditional
expectation is an L2 contraction and E S^2=1, hence

    0<=Phi*(mu_t)<=1/t.                              (5)

The bounded continuous compact density at positive t gives finite
logarithmic energy; thus the one-variable chi*=chi identity is finite
there. Apply Section3.5 at times 0<t1<t2 and subtract its two defining
improper heat integrals with the same upper cutoff T. The reference
1/(1+u) terms cancel. The result is

    chi(mu_t2)-chi(mu_t1)
      =(1/2)integral_t1^t2 Phi*(mu_v)dv
         -(1/2)lim_(T->infinity) integral_(T+t1)^(T+t2) Phi*(mu_v)dv.

The last term vanishes by (5), bounded by
(1/2)log((T+t2)/(T+t1)). Subtracting the constant between chi and Sigma
therefore gives the integral identity for E. The continuity already
proved gives E'(t)=Phi*(mu_t)/2 at every t>0, proving (1).

## Consequence once the matrix spectral identity is attached

For a compact symmetric input law mu, suppose a square matrix channel
has limiting normalized MI

 i(s)=Sigma(dilation_sqrt(s)(mu) free-plus sigma_1)-Sigma(sigma_1).

Dilation and the heat semigroup give
i(s)=E(1/s)+(1/2)log(s)-Sigma(sigma_1). Consequently i is C1 for s>0 and

    i'(s)=1/(2s)-Phi*(mu_(1/s))/(2s^2).              (6)

This is a conditional matrix consequence. The real Gaussian-reference
spectral identification and transfer assumptions remain to be paid in

[Thm 12 (Bounding  star discrepancy discrepancy by $L^1$-Wasserstein distance) of arXiv:2605.03528, '\bf Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance and discrepancies {\em versus} Wasserstein distances'] Let $\nu $ be an absolutely  continuous distribution on $\R^d$
with density $g\!\in {\cal L}^{\frac{r}{r-1}}(\R^d, \lambda_d)$ for some $r\!\in (1,+\infty]$ and finite first moment. Then, for every probability distribution  $\mu$ on $\R^d$with  finite first moment,
\begin{equation}
D^\star(\mu,\nu)\le C_{r,d}{\cal W}^{\ell^\infty}_1(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{d}{r+d}} \big \| g\big\|^{\frac{r}{r+d}}_{{\cal L}^{\frac{r}{r-1}}(\lambda_d)}.
\end{equation}
with $C_{r,d} =  \begin{pmatrix}r+d \\ r \end{pmatrix}^{-\frac{1}{r+d}}\bigg( \Big(\frac dr\Big)^{\frac{r}{r+d}} + \Big(\frac rd\Big)^{\frac{d}{r+d}} \bigg)$ for $r\ge 1$.

If $g$ is bounded, one has:
\[
D^\star(\mu,\nu)\le C_{1,d}{\cal W}^{\ell^\infty}_1(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{d}{d+1}} \big\| g\big\|^{\frac{1}{d+1}}_{\infty}.

\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:GwithSeeds of arXiv:2606.24793, '\LARGE Random sequential nearest-neighbor coloring on trees'] Let $\mathcal G$ denote the genealogical graph of the coloring process on $\mathcal{T}$ without seeds. Write the decomposition of $\mathcal G$ into its connected components as:
$$
\mathcal G = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} \mathcal{C}_i.
$$
Fix $M\geq 1$ and vertices $\tilde{s}_1, \ldots \tilde{s}_M \in \mathcal{T}$ chosen as seeds. Let $\tilde{\mathcal{G}}$ denote the genealogical graph constructed\footnote{In this coupled construction of $\mathcal G$ and $ \tilde{\mathcal{G}}$, we also require ties (when there are multiple possible ancestors) to be broken in the same way, see Section (sec:constructionW of the paper) for more details.} with the same i.i.d.\ sequence of arrival times $(\tau_v,\, v\in \mathcal{T})$ except that now $\tau_{\tilde{s}_j}=0$ for all $1\le j\le M$. Then the decomposition of $\tilde{\mathcal{G}}$ into connected components satisfies
$$
\tilde{\mathcal G} = \bigsqcup_{i \in I} \tilde{\mathcal{C}}_i \sqcup \bigsqcup_{j = 1}^M\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j,
$$
where 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $i\in I$, $\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_i$ is an infinite oriented subtree of $\mathcal{C}_i$. In particular, we have $\mathop{dir} \tilde{\mathcal{C}}_i = \mathop{dir} \mathcal{C}_i$.

    \item For each $j\in \{1,\ldots, M\}$, $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$ is an oriented tree rooted at $\tilde{s}_j$. Moreover, 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For $v \in \tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$, $v \neq \tilde{s}_j$, the set $\tilde{D}(v)$ of descendants of $v$ in $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$ is finite with $\mathbb{E}[\sharp\tilde{D}(v) \mid \tau_v] < \infty$.
\item The component $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$ is infinite if and only if $\tilde{s}_j$ has infinite degree. Furthermore, we have 
$$
\mathbb{P}(\mbox{$\tilde{s}_j$ has infinite degree in $\tilde{\mathcal{U}}_j$})=
\begin{cases}
    1 & \mbox{if $\{v\in \mathcal{T}, d(v,\tilde{s}_j)=\min_{i\le M} d(v,\tilde{s}_i)\}$ is infinite}\\
    0 & \mbox{otherwise}
\end{cases}.
$$
\end{enumerate}    
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textbf{The genealogical graph with a finite number of seeds}

For a real continuous local martingale M starting at zero, quadratic variation [M] is characterized by: [M] starts at zero, is adapted, continuous and increasing, and M^2 - [M] is a continuous LOCAL martingale. Uniqueness is up to indistinguishability. For each finite T, squared-increment sums along deterministic partitions of [0,T] with mesh tending to zero converge in probability to [M]_T. If E([M]_T) is finite at every finite T, the compensated square is a true martingale; this condition is equivalent to M being a true martingale with E(M_T^2) finite at every finite T. Brownian motion has [B]_t=t. Merely assuming M is a true continuous martingale does not justify the compensated-square integrability upgrade.

        = \int_0^t p'(s)^{1/2}
        b_s\,ds
        +
        \int_0^t \Big[ (sp)'(s) \Big]^{1/2} \sigma_s\,dB(s)\,.
    \eeq
The \textbf{sets of achievable measures} 
for the Ising and spherical problems are defined to be 
    \begin{align*}
        \cM^{\Ising}(\alpha) 
        &= \Big\{
            \mu(b,\sigma,p) : p \in \sP, (b,\sigma,w) \in \Adm^{\Ising}(\alpha,p)
        \Big\}, \\
        \cM^{\sph}(\alpha) &= \Big\{
            \mu(b,\sigma,p) : p \in \sP, (b,\sigma) \in \Adm^{\sph}(\alpha,p)
        \Big\}.
    \end{align*}
Define $\cM^{\Ising, \concave}(\alpha)$ and $\cM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$ analogously, but with the additional restriction that $p\in\sP_c$. Let $\ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)$,
$\ocM^{\sph}(\alpha)$,
$\ocM^{\Ising, \concave}(\alpha)$, $\ocM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$
 be the closures of these sets in the 
    $\bbW_2$ metric.

[Theorem quadratic of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Quadratic Recursion]

Let $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequence of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{i,j}\}_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n}$ be a double sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define 
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) = \sum_{(i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n} {\bf A}_{i,j} x_{i}x_{j}.
$$
Suppose that ${\bf F}({\bf x})$ is also permutation symmetric, i.e.,\xspace ${\bf A}_{i,j} = {\bf A}_{j,i}$, $\forall (i,j) \in {\mathcal T}^2_n$. Then for $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $2 \leq t < \infty$,
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t} ~ \leq ~ 2 (32t)^{2} \cdot \left( \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\a+b+c=2 }} L^c \cdot \norm{ {\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t} \right).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Mordell-Weil theorem: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K. Then A(K), the group of K-rational points of A, is a finitely generated abelian group, called the Mordell-Weil group; equivalently A(K) is isomorphic to Z^r x T, where r >= 0 is the rank and T is the finite torsion subgroup. The special case in which A = E is an elliptic curve and K = Q is Mordell's theorem, which answers a question apparently posed by Henri Poincare around 1901 and was proved by Louis Mordell in 1922; the general case is due to Andre Weil (1928). It is a foundational theorem of Diophantine geometry and of the arithmetic of abelian varieties.

[Lemma 46 (Cofinality and exhaustion) of arXiv:2609.02267, 'Locally Conformally Flat Manifolds with Positive Scalar Curvature: Kleinian Groups, Moduli'] Put $E_j:=S^n\setminus V_j$ and
$C_j:=S^n\setminus\operatorname{int}V_j$.  Then:
\textup{(a)} every open $U\supset K$ contains some $V_j$; the $V_j$
are cofinal among compact neighborhoods of $K$;
\textup{(b)} the $E_j$ are open and increase to $M$, and every compact
$D\subset M$ satisfies $D\subset E_j\subset C_j$ for some $j$;
\textup{(c)} the $C_j$ are compact and nested, exhaust $M$, and
$C_j\subset E_{j+1}\subset\operatorname{int}_M C_{j+1}$.

body: Method for the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture. ||p_Q||_inf <= (1/2 pi) int |phi_Q|, so a bounded density follows from |phi_Q(t)| <= C min(1, |t|^{-1-kappa}). The decay per large eigen-direction is NOT uniform over amplitudes: for every t and lambda there is a density f <= 1 with Re int f(x) e^{i t lambda x^2} dx >= 1/2 (f the indicator of a unit-measure subset of {cos(t lambda x^2) >= 1/2}), so van der Corput, which needs an amplitude of bounded variation, does not apply to one rough coordinate. What is uniform over all laws is the decay along spread directions: for orthonormal v_1..v_k with sum_j v_ji^2 <= 1/2 for every coordinate i, the Fresnel identity e^{i eta lambda V^2} = (4 pi i eta lambda)^{-1/2} int e^{-i xi^2/(4 eta lambda) + i xi V} d xi and the geometric Brascamp-Lieb inequality (Hoelder with p_i >= 2 and int |psi_i|^p <= 4 pi/sqrt p) give |E e^{i eta (sum_j lambda_j V_j^2 + diagonal + linear)}| <= (4 pi)^{k/2} prod_j |eta lambda_j|^{-1/2} for every diagonal and every linear term, and three spread large directions give a bounded density. The conjecture is hard exactly where a coordinate carries a large part of an eigenvector (a pivot or a hub), where the one-coordinate obstruction returns.

[Proposition 15 of arXiv:2609.04153, '\vspace*{-3cm}Smooth autonomous fast dynamo action on the three-torus'] Let $T_N$ be the time-$1$ flow map in \eqref{eq:TN}, and let $g \in C^\infty(\TT^2)$ be any real-valued, smooth function so that 
$$
\int_{\TT^2} \e^{2 \pi i g(x,y)}f_1'(x)f_2'(y) \dd x \dd y \neq 0.
$$
Then, for all $N$ large enough, the SFS operator 
$$
\mathcal{M}_{N,g} b=\e^{2 \pi i g}(DT_N b)\circ T_N^{-1}
$$
admits an isolated, algebraically simple eigenvalue $\Lambda_N$ on $X$, with $|\Lambda_N|\geq c_0N^2$, for some $c_0>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

	a scale $D \geq 1$, $p \in (0,1)$, $N_0 \in {\mathbb N}$ and $C\geq 1$ such that 
	for any given direction $\xi$, 
	  the following hold for all $o_1, o_2 \in G$:
	\begin{enumerate}
	\item Let $c=c(o_1,o_2, \xi)$ denote a centroid of the ideal triangle with vertices $o_1,o_2, \xi$, and let $[c,\xi)$ be a geodesic ray from $c $
	to $\xi$. Let $c=c_0, c_1, c_2, \dots$ be points on
	$[c,\xi)$ such that $d(c_i, c_0) = Di$.
	Then the probability that $[o_1,\xi)_\omega$ and 
	$[o_2,\xi)_\omega$  coalesce after $N_k([c,c_n])$  
	(i.e.\ $[o_1,\xi)_\omega\cap [o_2,\xi)_\omega \cap N_k([c,c_n]) =\emptyset$) 
 is at most $Cp^n$

	\item 	{Let $H_i$ denote the hyperplane at $c_i$ perpendicular to $[c,\xi)$}. The probability that $[o_1,\xi)_\omega$ has 2 disjoint subpaths between hyperplane {$H_i$ and $H_{i+M}$} (i.e.\  $[o_1,\xi)_\omega$  as a parametrized path goes from $H_i$ to $H_{i+M}$ and then  backtracks   to $H_i$)  
	has probability  at most $Cp^M$ for $M \geq N_0$.
	\end{enumerate}

Let T be an arbitrary index set and suppose that for every finite subset {t_1, ..., t_n} of T a probability measure mu_{t_1, ..., t_n} on R^n (or on S^n for a Polish space S with its Borel sigma-algebra) is given. Suppose the family is CONSISTENT: (i) permuting the indices permutes the measure correspondingly, and (ii) the marginal of mu_{t_1, ..., t_n, t_{n+1}} on the first n coordinates is mu_{t_1, ..., t_n}. Then there is a probability measure P on the product space S^T equipped with the PRODUCT sigma-algebra whose finite-dimensional marginals are exactly the given family, and P is unique. TWO LIMITATIONS, both routinely forgotten. FIRST, the topological hypothesis is essential: for general measurable spaces the theorem is FALSE, and there are consistent families with no extension (Andersen and Jessen); what is really needed is that the marginals be inner regular in a suitable sense, which Polish spaces provide. SECOND, the resulting measure lives on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra, every member of which is determined by countably many coordinates. When T is uncountable, sets such as {the path is continuous}, {sup_t X_t <= c}, or {the path is bounded} are therefore NOT measurable for that sigma-algebra, so the theorem does not by itself construct Brownian motion as a continuous process; it constructs a process with the right finite-dimensional laws, and a separate regularity theorem - Kolmogorov's continuity criterion - is needed to produce a modification with continuous paths. [Kolmogorov (1933); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.21, and Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 36]

Consistency makes this well defined, since a given cylinder has many representations differing by adding dummy coordinates or permuting them, and the two consistency conditions say exactly that all representations give the same value. Finite additivity on the algebra follows from finite additivity of each mu. The whole content is COUNTABLE additivity on the algebra, equivalently continuity at the empty set: if cylinders A_1 containing A_2 containing ... have empty intersection then P_0(A_n) -> 0. Suppose instead P_0(A_n) >= eps > 0 for every n. Then P_0(K_n) >= eps/2 > 0, so each K_n is nonempty; picking a point from each and using compactness of the bases coordinate by coordinate, a diagonal argument produces a point lying in every K_n, hence in every A_n, contradicting that the intersection is empty. So P_0 is countably additive on the algebra, and Caratheodory's extension theorem extends it uniquely to the generated product sigma-algebra. Let (S, d) be a metric space. A sequence of Borel probability measures (\mu_n)_{n=1}^\infty on S converges weakly to a probability measure \mu (denoted \mu_n \Rightarrow \mu) if for every bounded continuous function f: S \to \mathbb{R}, \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_S f d\mu_n = \int_S f d\mu.

body: [Lemma l.Tisometry of arXiv:2606.11043, 'Thick points under Gaussian free field dynamics'] For each $\varphi \in  C_c^\infty (\mathbb R)$, define $T(\varphi)(t) = (k* \varphi)(t)$, where $k(s)= \exp(-|s|/2)$. Then, we have $a(\varphi, \varphi) = \mathcal{E} (T\varphi)$. Hence, $a$ is actually an inner product and the operator $T$ defines an isometry between $(C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb R), a)$ and $(H_0^1(\mathbb R), \mathcal{E})$.

[Proposition prop:comb-estimates of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Under the setup above, the following hold.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
			\item \textup{(Continuation resistance)}\; For every $0\leq j\leq n{-}1$, one has $R_j\leq 2\,L_{j+1}$, and hence $V_j\leq 2\,I_{j+1}\,L_{j+1}$.
			\item \textup{(Trunk currents)}\; The trunk currents satisfy $I_1\geq 1/(4B)$ and $I_{j+1}\geq I_j/(2B)$ for every $1\leq j\leq n{-}1$. Consequently, $I_n\geq(4B)^{-n}$.
			\item \textup{(Total voltage mass)}\; There exists $C_{\mathrm{comb}}>0$ depending only on $B$ and~$\alpha$ such that
			\[
			\sum_{u\in D_{w,n}}g(u)\leq C_{\mathrm{comb}}\,I_n\,L_n^2\,.
			\]
			\item \textup{(Spike contribution)}\; Let $a\colon D_{w,n}\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $a(u)\geq -b$ for all~$u$, for some finite $b\geq 0$, and set $K\coloneqq 2+2b\,(C_{\mathrm{comb}}+1)$. If a vertex~$v$ in the first half of the terminal pipe~$P_w$ (at distance at least $L_n/2$ from the boundary) satisfies $a(v)\geq K\,L_n-b$, then
			\[
			\sum_{u\in D_{w,n}}g(u)\,a(u)\geq I_n\,L_n^2\,.
			\]
			\item \textup{(Exponential growth)}\; $I_n\,L_n^2\geq\lambda^n/4$.
		\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 1 (Exact deletion dynamics) of arXiv:2608.30261, 'Estimating Population-Risk Curves Along Nonconvex Gradient Flows from the Training Sample'] \label[proposition]{prop:exact-deletion}
Fix $i\in[n]$, $\lambda\in\Lambda$, and $T'\in[0,T]$, and suppose both
flows exist on $[0,T']$.  Suppose $F_{P_{-i},\lambda}$ is twice continuously
differentiable on the line segments joining $\theta_t^\lambda$ to
$\theta_{-i,t}^\lambda$ for every $t\in[0,T']$.  Then, for $0\leq t\leq T'$,
\begin{equation}
 \dot\Delta_{i,t}^\lambda
 =-\overline B_{i,t}^\lambda\Delta_{i,t}^\lambda
   +\frac{c_{i,t}^\lambda}{n-1},
 \qquad \Delta_{i,0}^\lambda=0,
\end{equation}
where the secant operator $\overline B_{i,t}^\lambda:\Theta\to\Theta$ is
\begin{equation}
 \overline B_{i,t}^\lambda
 =\int_0^1
   \nabla^2F_{P_{-i},\lambda}
      (\theta_t^\lambda+u\Delta_{i,t}^\lambda)\,\dd u.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Exact deletion dynamics

\[ \mathbb{E} \left( W_{\mathbb{T},2}^2 (\mu_N, \lambda) \right) \sim \frac{L^2 c_1(L \alpha)}{\sigma^2} \cdot \frac{\log N}{N} \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathrm{Var} \left( W_{\mathbb{T},2}^2 (\mu_N, \lambda) \right) \sim \frac{L^4 c_2(L \alpha)}{\sigma^4} \cdot \frac{\log N}{N^2} \]
with $L = \mathrm{gcd} (\mathrm{supp} (X_1))$, $\sigma^2 = \mathbb{E} (X_1^2)$ and explicit positive constants $c_1(L \alpha)$, $c_2(L \alpha)$. If in addition $\mathbb{E} (|X_1|^p) <\infty$ with some real constant $p>2$, then

body: For two probability measures mu and nu on a measurable space (S, A), the total variation distance is d_TV(mu, nu) = sup over A in A of |mu(A) - nu(A)|, a number in [0, 1]. If mu and nu have densities f and g with respect to a common reference measure lambda (which always exists, for instance lambda = mu + nu), then d_TV(mu, nu) = (1/2) integral |f - g| d lambda = 1 - integral min(f, g) d lambda, and the supremum is attained at A = { f > g }. Equivalent characterisations: d_TV is half the supremum of |integral h d mu - integral h d nu| over measurable h with |h| <= 1; and by the coupling characterisation, d_TV(mu, nu) = min P(X not equal to Y) over all couplings (X, Y) with X distributed as mu and Y as nu, the minimum being attained by the maximal coupling. Convergence in total variation is strictly stronger than weak convergence (point masses at 1/n converge weakly to the point mass at 0 but stay at total variation distance 1). The normalisation matters: some texts use the un-halved integral |f - g| d lambda, which lies in [0, 2].

body:
Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with C^1 boundary (or any bounded extension domain, for instance a bounded Lipschitz domain), let 1 <= p < n and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. Then the embedding of W^{1,p}(Omega) into L^q(Omega) is COMPACT for every q strictly less than p*. At the endpoint q = p* the embedding is continuous but NOT compact. For p = n the embedding into L^q is compact for every finite q, and for p > n the embedding into C^{0,gamma}(closure of Omega) is compact for gamma < 1 - n/p. For the space W_0^{1,p}(Omega) no boundary regularity is needed: boundedness of Omega suffices.
Boundedness of Omega is essential (the embedding is never compact on R^n, by translating a fixed bump), and for W^{1,p} rather than W_0^{1,p} some boundary regularity is needed so that an extension operator exists.
Compactness FAILS at the critical exponent q = p*, which is exactly the loss of compactness behind concentration phenomena in critical problems.

[Proposition pr:tracking of arXiv:2504.11107, 'An Invariance Principle for some\\% Reaction-Diffusion Equations with a Multiplicative Ran'] For every $T>0$ let $u=u^{(T)}$ denote the solution to the parabolic Anderson model,
	\begin{equation*}\left[\begin{split}
		&\partial_t u = \partial^2_x u + \mu u  + \sigma u\dot{W}
			\hskip.95in\text{on $(T\,,\infty)\times\mathbb{T}$},\\
		&\text{subject to }u(0)=w(T)\hskip.9in\text{on $\mathbb{T}$}.
	\end{split}\right.\end{equation*}
	Then, for every $k \in (6\,,\infty)$ there exist non-random numbers
	$L=L(k\,,f\,,g)>0$ and 
	$\Delta_0=\Delta_0(k\,,f\,,g)\in(0\,,1)$ such that, independently of
	the value of $T$ and uniformly for all $\Delta(T)\in(0\,,\Delta_0)$,
	\[
		\mathrm{E}_{\mathscr{F}(T)}\left(\|w_T-u_T\|_{C([T,T+\Delta(T)]\times\mathbb{T})}^k
		\right)
		\leqslant L \left[\mathscr{E}\left({\rm e}^{-\gamma T}\right)\right]^k\|w(T)\|_{C(\mathbb{T})}^k,
	\]
	almost surely on the event $\{\tau(T)>T\}$, where
	$\mathscr{E}$ was defined in (equation R:star of the paper), and
	\[
		w_T(t\,,x) = w(t\wedge\tau(T)\,,x),\
		u_T(t\,,x) = u(t\wedge\tau(T)\,,x)\quad\forall t\geqslant T,\ x\in\mathbb{T}.
	\]
title: Proposition pr:tracking of arXiv:2504.11107

[Theorem thm: homo connected of arXiv:2411.02898, '\vspace{-1.5cm}The connectivity and phase transition in inhomogeneous random graphs of fin'] Consider $\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}:=\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}_{n, c\log n / n}$ where $c>0$ is a constant.

Given a Young function psi (e.g., psi_q(x) = exp(x^q) - 1 or psi(x) = x^q), the Orlicz norm of the maximal envelope of a random vector is ||max_{1 <= i <= p, 1 <= t <= n} |x_{i,t}|||_{psi} = inf{C > 0 : E[psi(max_{i,t} |x_{i,t}| / C)] <= 1}.
psi is a convex non-decreasing function with psi(0) = 0

body:
[Lemma le:tightness_bdry_fl_refl of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] There exists $\zeta > 0$ such that the following is true. 
Fix $M >0$, $a_1>0$. Let $\delta^{1-a_1} \le r \le 1$, and let $h$ be a GFF on $r\mathbf{D}$ with some boundary values that are bounded by $M$ and so that the flow line $\eta_1$ from $-ir$ to $ir$ and the flow line $\overline{\eta}_2$ from $ir$ to $-ir$ in the components of $\mathbf{D} \setminus \eta_1$ to the right of $\eta_1$ (and reflected off $\eta_1$) are defined. Given $\eta_1,\overline{\eta}_2$, sample a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}${} and the internal metric in the region bounded between them. Let $E_\delta$ be the event that there exist $x,y \in \eta_1 \cap \overline{\eta}_2$ such that if $U$ denotes the region bounded between the segments of $\eta_1$ and $\overline{\eta}_2$ from $x$ to $y$, then $U \subseteq B(0,3r/4)$, $\mathrm{diam}(U) \le \delta$, and
\[ D_\epsilon^{\partial U} \ge \delta^\zeta+\epsilon^{a_0} . \]
Then $\mathbf{P}[E_\delta] = o^\infty(\delta)$ as $\delta\searrow 0$.

The same is true when $\overline{\eta}_2$ is the (reflected) flow line in the components to the left of $\eta_1$.

[Prop restriction of arXiv:2509.16541, 'Two-stage Bootstrap Percolation'] Fix an integer $m \geq 1$, a configuration $\xi_0 \in \{0,1,2\}^{{\mathbb Z}^2}$, and a finite nonempty set $Z \subset {\mathbb Z}^2$.
    Run two modified bootstrap percolation dynamics:  the first is $\xi_t$, and the second $\xi_t^Z$. 
    Suppose that $Z$ and $\xi_0$ satisfy conditions (PR1)--(PR3).
    Then for every $t \geq 0$ and every $u \in Z$, if $\xi_t(u) = 2$, then $\xi_t^Z(u) = 2$.

body:
[Definition def:triangular-solution of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] A \emph{triangular weak solution} of
(equation eq:limit1 of the paper)--(equation eq:limit2 of the paper) consists of a standard stochastic
basis $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathbb F_t)_{t\in[0,1]},\mathbb P)$,
continuous non-negative adapted processes $(V^1,V^2)$ with
\[
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sup_{t\le1}\bigl(V_t^1+V_t^2\bigr)\Bigr]<\infty,
\]
and $\mathbb F$-Brownian motions $\beta^1,\beta^2$ satisfying
(equation eq:limit1 of the paper)--(equation eq:limit2 of the paper) almost surely, such that $\beta^2$ is
a Brownian motion with respect to the initially enlarged filtration
\[
\mathbb F_t':=\sigma\bigl(V_s^1,\beta_s^1:0\le s\le1\bigr)\vee\mathbb F_t,
\qquad t\in[0,1].
\]
In particular
$\beta^2\perp\!\!\!\perp\sigma(V_s^1,\beta_s^1:0\le s\le1)$.
Proposition~(prop:limit-triangular of the paper) below shows that every limit point
of the renormalized Hawkes system is of this type.
title: Triangular weak solution

  $\ensuremath{\mathcal{A}}$.  Then for all $\alpha, \beta \in \real$, we have the
  sandwich relation
\begin{align}
  
  \frac{1}{2} e^{-|\beta - \alpha|} \mathsf J_\alpha(p, q) & \leq
  \mathsf J_\beta(p, q) \leq 2 e^{|\beta - \alpha|} \mathsf
  J_\alpha(p, q).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work target-partial result C008 v1, proof (unaudited); novelty unestablished. Let n>=2, m,d>=1, labels y_i in {-1,1}, z_i=y_i*x_i, ||x_i||<=1, rank{z_i}>=2, z_i dot z_l>=kappa>0 for all pairs, and a unit u satisfy u dot z_i>=gamma>0. With literal leaky ReLU phi(v)=max(v,lambda*v), 0<lambda<1, f_i=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j dot x_i), train both layers simultaneously by step m*eta on average logistic loss, any eta>0. Assume for each neuron a_j(0) and every w_j(0) dot z_i have the same strict sign. Put r_j=min_i|w_j(0) dot z_i|, H=eta*lambda^2*m^-1 sum_j r_j^2, c=H/(4+2H). This open cone is invariant: all sample branches stay fixed, neuron products increase, and every margin grows by at least H*G_t, G_t the average logistic weight. Consequently L_t<=1/(1/L_0+c*t). With epsilon_s=min(log(2)/2,1/H) and s=ceil(max(0,1/epsilon_s-1/L_0)/c), one has L_t<=8/[H*(t-s)] for every integer t>s. Under independent Gaussian initialization a_j~N(0,sigma^2), w_j~N(0,sigma^2 I_d), sigma>0, consider for each neuron the union of {a_j>0,w_j/sigma in B(u,gamma/2)} and its simultaneous negative. Independence across initial neurons gives event probability at least b^m, where b=(gamma/sqrt(2*pi*d))^d*exp(-(1+gamma/2)^2/2). On this event H>=H0=eta*lambda^2*sigma^2*gamma^2/4. Set c0=H0/(4+2H0), epsilon0=min(log(2)/2,1/H0), s0=ceil(max(0,1/epsilon0-1/log(2))/c0). Then simultaneously L_t<=1/(1/log(2)+c0*t) for t>=0 and L_t<=32/[eta*lambda^2*sigma^2*gamma^2*(t-s0)] for t>s0. The Gaussian lower bound is positive mass and decays with width: no high-probability or almost-sure generic cone-entry conclusion is claimed. Sharp Cai-type burn-in and the full target remain open. 25965 finite rational checks support selected algebra only; independent mathematical audit, analytic certification and novelty comparison remain pending.
Strictly positive signed Gram entries, rank>=2, bounded separable data and positive leakage.
Aligned initial neuron cone for deterministic theorem; explicitly specified Gaussian ball/sign event for the probability corollary.
Both layers trained simultaneously with actual step m*eta; no output-layer freezing.
Proof (unaudited), C008 v1; Gaussian positive-mass statement only, no general Gaussian entry or novelty claim.
title: T368 leaky-ReLU logistic GD: acute signed data, aligned cone and Gaussian positive mass (unaudited)

body: [Prop 123084 of arXiv:2606.29143, 'Comonotonic and moment matching approximations for sums of lognormal random variables'] Let $A = (a_1, ..., a_m)^{'}$ and $Q = (q_1, ..., q_m)^{'}$ be two numerical vectors with $\min(a_1, ..., a_m) \geq 0, \max(a_1, ..., a_m) > 0$ and $0 = q_0 < q_1 < q_2 < ... < q_m = 1$. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable and $\omega_{A, Q}$ the step-weight function of $X$. Then it holds that $$0 < E[\omega_{A, Q}(X)] = \sum^m_{i = 1}a_i(q_{i} - q_{i - 1}) < \infty.$$ In particular, the expectation $E[\omega_{A, Q}(X)]$ is independent of the distribution of $X$.

body: [Lemma cor: parity is recoverable of arXiv:2512.18435, 'Indistinguishability for recurrent clusters'] If $q\neq 1/2$, and we say that the positive direction in a cluster is the one in which the first coordinate goes to $+\infty$, then for every even vertex $v$ that belongs to an infinite cluster, the edge going in the positive direction out of $v$ is almost surely horizontal if $q>1/2$ and almost surely vertical if $q<1/2$.
title: Lemma cor: parity is recoverable of arXiv:2512.18435

[Definition def:qRacah_tilings of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] We put a probability measure on the set of all
	nonintersecting path ensembles. The measure depends on the
	geometry of the hexagon (parametrized by $(T,S,N)$), and
	on two parameters $q>0$ and $\kappa\in
	\mathbf{i}\mathbb{R}$.
	The
	probability weight of a nonintersecting path ensemble is
	proportional to
	\begin{equation}
		
		\prod_{\textnormal{holes in the path ensemble}} \mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}\bigl( x-\tfrac t2+1\bigr),
		\qquad
		\mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}(j) \coloneqq \kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}-\frac{1}{\kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}}.
	\end{equation}
	Here the holes are points $(t,x)$ such that $x\notin X(t)$,
	but $x$ satisfies the inequalities
	(equation eq:hexagon_constraints of the paper). In other words,
	holes are lozenges of the type
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding box.south),scale=.25]
		\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.
	For example, in (fig:tiling_and_path_picture of the paper), right, the holes are $(1,2),(2,1),(2,4),(3,0),(3,2),(3,5),(4,2),(4,3),(5,3)$.
	The probability weights are normalized so that the total probability of all path ensembles is $1$.
	We call the resulting probability measure the \emph{$q$-Racah measure} on nonintersecting path ensembles
	(equivalently, on lozenge tilings of the hexagon).
title: $q$-Racah measure on nonintersecting path ensembles

[Proposition 4 (Qin) of arXiv:2609.03238, 'Representation Defects and Cassels Pairings for Congruent Number Curves'] Let $n$ be a positive squarefree integer.  Define $\Delta_Q(n)$ and $\sigma_Q(n)$ by
\eqref{eq:defect}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $L(E_n,1)\ne0$, then
\[
|\Sha(E_n)|_{\mathrm{an}}
 =\left(\frac{\Delta_Q(n)}{2\sigma_Q(n)}\right)^2.
\]
If $L(E_n,1)=0$, then $\Delta_Q(n)=0$.
\item If $m$ is odd and $m\equiv1\pmod8$, then
\[
r_f(m)+r_g(m)=4h(-m),
\qquad
\frac{r_f(m)-r_g(m)}2=r_a(m)-h(-m).
\]
\item If $m$ is odd and $m\equiv1\pmod4$, then
\[
r_s(m)+r_t(m)=2h(-2m).
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2605.27713, 'Lower path regularity in all dimensions'] Let $\mu$ be a finite Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $0<s\leq d$, and let $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be such that

body:
[Deffr Divisors of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] A divisor on $\mathbf{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{C} \cup \{\infty\}$ is a finite formal expression of the form $\sum n_a[a]$ where each $n_a \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $a$ ranges over elements of $\mathbf{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$. The support of a divisor is the finite set of all $a$ such that $n_a \neq 0$. The divisor $\operatorname{div}(f)$ of a rational function $f \in \mathbb{C}(z)^*$ is defined as
\[
\operatorname{div}(f) := \sum_a \operatorname{ord}_a(f)[a]
\]
where $\operatorname{ord}_a(f)$ denotes the order of $f$ at the point $a$, and the sum is taken over all $a \in \mathbf{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ and is in fact finite.
title: Divisors

body: For any ordinal \alpha, addition of an ordinal \beta is defined by transfinite recursion on \beta: \alpha + 0 = \alpha; \alpha + (\beta + 1) = (\alpha + \beta) + 1; and for a limit ordinal \lambda, \alpha + \lambda = \bigcup_{\beta < \lambda} (\alpha + \beta).
title: Ordinal Addition

body: [Definition def:disint1 of arXiv:2507.01236, 'Disintegration theorem for multifunctions, \\ with applications to empirical Wasserstein d'] Given $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\epsilon > 0$, and $r > 0$, we declare a metric Polish probability space $(\mathfrak{X},d,\mu)$ to be $(n,\epsilon,r)$\emph{-disintegrable} if, whenever $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are i.i.d.\ with distribution $\mu$ on a probability space $(\Psi,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$, there exists a disintegration of $\mu$ along $F_{r, X_{[n]}}$ with respect to the uniform measure on $[n]$ with $\mathbb{P}$-probability at least $1-\epsilon$.

body:
[Lemma tensorization-cut-distance of arXiv:2606.21556, 'Mean field limit of non-exchangeable interacting diffusions on co-evolutionary networks'] For any \(\mu,\bar{\mu} \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu}(\mathcal{X}\times [0,1])\) 
	and \(q,\bar{q} \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu \otimes \nu}(\mathcal{Y}\times [0,1]^2)\), define the probability-graphon 
	\(\mu\otimes \mu \otimes q \in \mathcal{P}_{\nu\otimes \nu}((\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})\times [0,1]^2)\) as 
	\[
		(\mu\otimes \mu \otimes q)^{\xi,\xi'}= \mu^{\xi} \otimes \mu^{\xi'} \otimes q^{\xi,\xi'}, \quad (\xi,\xi') \in [0,1]^2,
	\]    
	and similarly for \(\bar{\mu}\otimes \bar{\mu} \otimes \bar{q}\). Then, for every \(\varepsilon >0\) there exists
	\(\tilde{\kappa}(\varepsilon)\in \mathbb{N}\) such that 
	\[
		d_{\text{BL},\square}(\mu\otimes \mu \otimes q,\bar{\mu}\otimes \bar{\mu} \otimes \bar{q}) \leq 2 d_{\text{BL},1}(\mu,\bar{\mu}) +  \tilde{\kappa}(\varepsilon)^2 d_{\text{BL},\square}(q,\bar{q}) + \varepsilon.
	\]
title: Lemma tensorization-cut-distance of arXiv:2606.21556

\begin{enumerate}
\item If either ($\infty$-PD) or ($\alpha$-PD) is satisfied with $\alpha > 1$, and if also $\int K(x) \,dx \neq 0$, then there exists $\zeta > 0$ such that
\[ \theta(r) \sim \zeta r  \ , \quad \text{as } r \to \infty . \]
\item If ($\alpha$-PD) is satisfied with $\alpha \in (0,1)$, then there exists $\zeta > 0$ such that
\[ \theta(r) \sim \zeta r^\alpha (\log r)  \ , \quad \text{as } r \to \infty . \]

[Lemma lem2 of arXiv:2608.30848, '\huge \bf Limit Laws of the Iterated Logarithm Under Sub-linear Expectations'] Let $X\in \mathscr{H}$.
\begin{description}
  \item[\rm (i)]
 For any $\delta>0$, we have
$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbb V\big(|X|\ge \delta \sqrt{n\log\log n} \big)<\infty \;\; \Longleftrightarrow C_{\mathbb V}\bigg[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\bigg]<\infty.
$$
 \item[\rm (ii)]
   If $C_{\mathbb V}\bigg[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\bigg]<\infty$, then for any $\delta>0$ and $p>2$, we have
$$ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\widehat{\mathbb E}\big[\big(|X|\wedge (\delta \sqrt{n\log\log n})\big)^p\big]}{(n\log\log n)^{p/2}}<\infty. $$
 \item[\rm (iii)] If $C_{\mathbb V}\bigg[\frac{X^2}{\log\log|X|}\bigg]<\infty$, then for any $\delta>0$, we have
 $$ \widehat{\mathbb E}[X^2\wedge (2\delta n\log\log n)]=o(\log \log n), $$
  $$ \breve{\mathbb E}[(|X|-\delta \sqrt{2 n\log\log n})^+]=o(\sqrt{\log\log n/n}). $$
\end{description} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:spatial of arXiv:2602.14617, 'Stochastic Burgers equation driven by multiplicative Rosenblatt noise: local existence, un'] Let $u \in \mathcal{Y}_{T_0}$ be the unique local mild solution. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, $p \ge 2$, and $\gamma < 1/2$, there exists $C_{p,\varepsilon,\gamma} > 0$ such that for all $t \in [\varepsilon, T_0]$ and $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[|u(t,x)-u(t,y)|^p] \le C_{p,\varepsilon,\gamma} |x-y|^{p\gamma}.
\]
Consequently, for any $\gamma < 1/2$, $u(t,\cdot)$ admits a modification that is $\gamma$-Hölder continuous in the $L^p$-sense, and by Kolmogorov's criterion, also pathwise Hölder continuous of any order $\gamma' < \gamma - 1/p$.

[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2608.30551, 'Critical Discrete Hardy Inequalities in $L^p$'] Let \(\sigma\in(0,1/2)\), \(\alpha\in(\sigma,1/2)\), and
\(a\in(0,1]\). Put
\[
    \gamma=\frac{1-a(1-2\alpha)}{2}.
\]
Then \(\gamma\in[\alpha,1/2)\), and, as \(|x|\to\infty\),
\begin{equation}
    \frac{1}{\mathcal A_\alpha^a}k_{-\alpha}(x)^a
    =
    \frac{1}{\mathcal A_\gamma}k_{-\gamma}(x)
    +
    O\left(|x|^{2\gamma-2}\right),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
    \frac{1}{\mathcal A_\alpha^a}
    \Delta^\sigma k_{-\alpha}^a(x)
    =
    \frac{1}{\mathcal A_\gamma}
    \Delta^\sigma k_{-\gamma}(x)
    +
    O\left(
        |x|^{-1-\min\{2\sigma,1-2\gamma\}}
    \right).
\end{equation}

[Definition 12 (Second derivative / Hessian matrix) of arXiv:2605.18198, 'Large deviations of crowding in finite $\beta$-ensembles'] If the second partial derivatives exist, the \emph{Hessian matrix} of $Q$
	is the matrix-valued function
	
	\[
	D^2 Q(x)
	=
	\begin{pmatrix}
		\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial x_1^2}(x)
		&
		\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial x_1 \partial x_2}(x)
		\\[6pt]
		\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial x_2 \partial x_1}(x)
		&
		\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial x_2^2}(x)
	\end{pmatrix}.
	\]

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2608.17562, '2608.17562'] Let $(X_{n})_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of \iid random variables whose tail distribution function $\widebar{F}$ belongs to $\SRV{-\alpha}{\rho}$ with auxiliary function~$A$, for some $\alpha > 0$ and $\rho < 0$, and set
\[
U_n \coloneq \big\lb \exists i \in \lbra 1,n \rbra,\ \forall j \in \lbra 1,n \rbra \bs \lb i \rb,\ X_{i} > X_j \big\rb.
\]
Then, for some constant $C > 0$ we have 
\[
\prob(U_{n}^{c}) \leq C\Big(\frac{1}{n} + A(a_n)\Big),
\quad n \geq 1, 
\]
where $a_n \coloneq F^{\leftarrow}(1 - n^{-1})$.

body: FIRES WHEN a balls-in-boxes argument reaches for the tilted i.i.d. representation and the local limit theorem behind Janson's (18.14). THE ROUTE: write P(Y_1 = k) = w_k Z(m - k, n - 1)/Z(m, n) and union bound over the n boxes. WHERE IT BREAKS: Lemma 13.1, the local limit theorem that (18.14) rests on, is proved for FIXED lambda in (0, nu). When lambda_n = m/n -> 0 the tilted laws degenerate - the mass at 0 tends to 1 and the variance to 0 - so the Gaussian local limit theorem has to be replaced by a Poisson-regime one and glued to the Gaussian regime when m is comparable to n. That uniform statement does not appear to exist in the literature, and without it the union bound has no input at all. CONDITION OF FAILURE: m/n -> 0, which is exactly the regime the conjecture is about. The heuristic the route does give is still useful as a target: P(Y_1 >= k) is about w_k tau_n^k / Phi(tau_n) with tau_n = tau(m/n) -> 0, so n P(Y_1 >= k) -> 0 once k >= (1 + eps) log n / log(1/tau_n), and that threshold is o(log n) precisely because tau_n -> 0.

body:
In the binomial random graph G(n,p) with p = (log n + c)/n for a fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with mean e^{-c} (the method of moments: the factorial moments of the count converge to those of the Poisson law), and the probability that G(n,p) is connected tends to exp(-e^{-c}) (Erdos and Renyi 1959, 1960). The obstruction to connectivity in this window is isolated vertices alone: P(G connected) - P(G has no isolated vertex) tends to 0. Consequently p = log n / n is a sharp threshold: for p = (1 - epsilon) log n / n the graph is disconnected with probability tending to 1 (with a growing number of isolated vertices), and for p = (1 + epsilon) log n / n it is connected with probability tending to 1. Below the threshold at p = c'/n with c' > 1 the graph already has a unique giant component but is disconnected.
edges are present independently with the same probability p (the binomial model; the uniform model G(n,m) has the analogous statement with m = (n/2)(log n + c))
the statement is about the window p = (log n + c)/n with c fixed as n grows
the Poisson approximation is for the count of isolated vertices; other small components are negligible in this window
title: Erdos-Renyi connectivity threshold of G(n,p) and the Poisson paradigm for isolated vertices

body:
[Defn \cite{JamneshanMachado} of arXiv:2605.16921, '${\ASL_n}(\mathbb Z)$ invariant random subsets of $\mathbb Z^n$'] We call a \emph{bundle of nilsystems (of dimension $\leq k$) over $\Omega$} any $\mathbb{Z}^d$-system constructed from the following data:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item a standard Borel probability space $(\Omega, \nu)$;
    \item a countable Borel partition $(\Omega_n)_{n \geq 0}$ of $\Omega$ and a countable family of nilmanifolds $(N_n/\Gamma_n)_{n \geq 0}$ of dimension $\leq k$;
    \item Borel maps $\rho_n: \Omega_n \to \Hom(\mathbb{Z}^d, N_n)$ such that for $\nu$-a.e. $\omega \in \Omega_n$, the action of $\rho_n(\omega)$ on $N_n/\Gamma_n$ is ergodic.
\end{enumerate}
The space
$$ X := \bigsqcup_{n \geq 0} \Omega_n \times N_n/\Gamma_n,$$
equipped with the measure
$$\sum_{n \geq 0} \nu_{|\Omega_n} \otimes \mu_{N_n/\Gamma_n}$$
and the $\mathbb{Z}^d$-action defined for $(\omega, \overline{n}) \in \Omega_n \times (N_n/\Gamma_n)$ and $t \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ by
$$ t \cdot (\omega, \overline{n}) = (\omega, \rho_n(\omega)(t) \cdot \overline{n}),$$
is denoted
$$ \bigsqcup_{n \geq 0} \Omega_n \rtimes_{\rho_n} N_n/\Gamma_n.$$
The natural map $\bigsqcup_{n \geq 0} \Omega_n \rtimes_{\rho_n} N_n/\Gamma_n \to \Omega$ is called the \emph{bundle projection}.

[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2608.03575, '2608.03575'] (\cite[Lemma 4.1]{IIP2026})
Let $D_1, \dots, D_n$ be disks with centers $O_1, \dots, O_n$ and radii $r_1, \dots, r_n$. Assume that $O_1, \dots, O_n$ forms a polygon. $D_i$ and $D_{i+1}$ intersect with an angle $\Theta_i$ (where $1 \le i \le n$ and $D_{n+1} = D_1$). Suppose that:

$$\sum_{i} (\pi - \Theta_i) > 2\pi + \varepsilon_0 .$$

Let $E$ be a set inside the polygon that intersects with all $D_i's$. Then there exists a constant $C = C(\varepsilon_0)$ such that:

$$(\textrm{diam}(E))^{-1/2} < C \sum_{i} r_i^{-1/2}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 30 of arXiv:2608.03575

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-FRAC v1; no novelty claim]. For the cycle C_8, with perfect matchings restricted to new edges, the maximum lambda_2(L_C8+L_M) over individual matchings is exactly 2. Maximizing lambda_2 over probability mixtures of those matching Laplacians instead has value at least (16-4sqrt(2))/5>2. Consequently minimizing the density-matrix/max-weight-matching upper bound cannot always certify the integral optimum. Divide by three to obtain the corresponding ordinary SRW gaps. This is a strict-gap example, not a determination of the exact fractional optimum or of total-variation mixing time.

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.06576, 'The Resultant Distribution Method: Universality for $p$-adic Random Matrices and Polynomia'] Fix a finite set $S\subseteq\Z_{>0}$. For every $n\geq 1$, let
$A_n^{\Haar}\in\Mat_n(\Z_p)$ be additive Haar distributed. Then there
exists a random polynomial
$$
Q_{\infty}^{\Haar,S}\in\mathcal P^S
$$
such that
$$
P_{A_n^{\Haar}}^S
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
Q_{\infty}^{\Haar,S},
\qquad n\to\infty.
$$
Moreover, the limiting polynomial is almost surely squarefree:
$$
\mathbf{P}\left(
Q_{\infty}^{\Haar,S}\text{ is squarefree}
\right)=1.
$$

[Lemma 4 (One-excursion structure) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Let $K_n$ be the number of standard-coupon draws before the next reset.  Then
\[
        \Pbb(K_n=k)=\rho_n q_n^k,
        \qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]
A reset-free excursion succeeds precisely when
\[
        C_n\le K_n.
\]
Consequently the one-excursion success probability is
\[
        s_n:=\Pbb(C_n\le K_n)=\Ebb q_n^{C_n}=\phi_n(q_n).
\]

[Lemma lem:uniformboundFOU of arXiv:2601.21762, 'Navier-Stokes with a fractional transport noise as a limit of multi-scale dynamics'] Let $w$ be the stationary solution of $dw_t = -Mw_t dt + Q^{\frac 12}dB^H_t$. Then:
\begin{equ}
      \sup_{t>0} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\|w_t\right\|_{H^\sigma}^2\right] = C_H \tr{M^{-2H}Q}, \qquad 
       \sup_{t>0} \mathbb{E}\left[\norm{M^{-1}w_{t}}_{H^{\sigma}}^{2}\right] = C_H\tr{M^{-2-2H}Q}.
\end{equ}
Furthermore $w$ satisfies the bounds: 
$$\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|w_{s,t}\right\|_{H^\sigma}^2\right]  \lesssim  \left(\tr{M^{2-2H}Q} +\ensuremath\trace[Q] + \tr{M^{-2H}Q} \right) |t-s|^{2H},$$
$$\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|M^{-1} w_{s,t}\right\|_{H^\sigma}^2\right]  \lesssim  
\left(\tr{M^{-2H}Q} +\tr{M^{-2}Q} + \tr{M^{-2-2H}Q}\right) |t-s|^{2H},$$
where the constants indicated by $\lesssim$ depend only on $H$.
title: Lemma lem:uniformboundFOU of arXiv:2601.21762

[Definition of arXiv:2608.28505, 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests'] Given two cardinals $\kappa < \lambda$, a $(\kappa, \lambda)$-forest\footnote{In Eskew's more general notation, this is a $(\kappa, \lambda, 2)$-forest [MR3326048].} is a collection $F$ of functions satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every $f \in F$, $\mathrm{ran}(f) \subseteq \{0,1\}$,
\item $\{\mathrm{dom}(f) : f \in F\} = [\lambda]^{< \kappa}$,
\item for every $x,y \in [\lambda]^{< \kappa}$ with $x \subseteq y$,
\[
\{f \in F : \mathrm{dom}(f) = x\} = \{f \upharpoonright x : f \in F \text{ and } \mathrm{dom}(f) = y\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.28505, 'Quagmires and large Suslin forests'

[Theorem thm:maincgce of arXiv:2607.05671, 'Bi-infinite systems of singularly interacting Brownian particles and the KPZ equation'] As $\varepsilon \to 0$, $\tilde \mathcal{E}^{\varepsilon}_{\theta}$ converges to $u$, in distribution, in $C([0, \infty); \mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}))$.
Furthermore, for any $r \ge 1$, $T<\infty$ and compact $K\subset \mathbb{R}$,
\begin{equation}
   \left\|\sup_{t \in [0,T], x \in K} \left|\tilde \mathcal{E}_{\theta}^\varepsilon(t,x) - \mathcal{G}^\varepsilon(t,x) \right| \right\|_r \to 0 \text{ as } \varepsilon \to 0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\{\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(t,x), (t,x) \in \mathbb{R}_+\times \mathbb{R}\}$ converges, uniformly on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}$, in distribution to the random field
$\{u(t,x), (t,x) \in \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:maincgce of arXiv:2607.05671

[Proposition 7 (cf.~\cite{Kobayashi96}) of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $G$ be a locally compact Hausdorff group, $L$ and $H$ closed subgroups of $G$.
    The following six conditions are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The natural $L$-action on the homogeneous space $G/H$ is proper.
        \item The natural $H$-action on the homogeneous space $G/L$ is proper.
        \item The diagonal $G$-action on the space $G/H\times G/L$ is proper.
        \item The intersection $L\cap CHC^{-1}$ is relatively compact in $G$ for any compact subset $C$ of $G$.
        \item The intersection $CLC^{-1}\cap H$ is relatively compact in $G$ for any compact subset $C$ of $G$.
        \item The intersection $CHC^{-1}\cap CLC^{-1}$ is relatively compact in $G$ for any compact subset $C$ of $G$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: cf.~\cite{Kobayashi96}

[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2605.18198, 'Large deviations of crowding in finite $\beta$-ensembles'] Let $(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$  be distributed according to the law $\P_{n,\beta}^{\mathbb F}$, and $L_n$ be as defined in \eqref{eqn:defLn}.  Then the family of random measures $\{L_n\}$ satisfies  the large deviation principle in $M_1^*(\mathbb{F})$ equipped with the weak topology  with speed $n^2$ and good rate  $I_\beta$ as defined in \eqref{eqn:defIbeta}.
	In  other words,
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item for any open set $\mathcal O \subset M_1^*(\mathbb{F})$,
		\[
		\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n^2} \log \P^{\mathbb F}_{n,\beta} (L_n \in \mathcal O) \geq -\inf_{\mu\in \mathcal O} I_\beta(\mu),
		\]
		\item for any closed set $\mathcal F \subset M_1^*(\mathbb{F})$,
		\[
		\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n^2} \log \P^{\mathbb F}_{n,\beta}(L_n \in \mathcal F) \leq -\inf_{\mu\in \mathcal F} I_\beta(\mu).
		\]
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Audit of w417-L1: for a Boolean event on a common finite cell skeleton, two product laws mu and nu obey |E_nu f-E_mu f| <= sum_i TV(mu_i,nu_i) P_Hi(S_i), where H_i has nu_j for j<i and mu_j for j>i on the exterior, and S_i means the section in cell i is nonconstant. The finite inequality follows by telescoping and conditioning on each actual exterior; it does not require independence between the S_i events. To use it as a square-bond/triangular-site bridge, one must construct faithful full connectivity-state laws on a common skeleton and prove their summed weighted error vanishes uniformly over all intermediate laws, including boundary cells. The endpoint-majority counterexample blocks automatic substitution of homogeneous-model influences. None of these missing percolation premises is asserted here.

such that if $u$ is an admissible solution 
to \eqref{SNS2}--\eqref{bin2} satisfying

$$
\E e^{-\phi_{t}}|u_t-v_t|^2_{\cH}
\leq \E |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}^2\quad\text{for $t\in[0,T]$}

for any admissible solution $v$ to \eqref{SNS2}--\eqref{bin2} 
on $[0,T]$ with an $\cH$-valued initial condition

\quad

$$
and $N=N(d,r,\delta)$ is a constant. In particular, if $u_0=v_0$ 
then almost surely $u_t=v_t$ for all $t\in[0,T]$ for the $H$-valued c\`adl\`ag

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C007 v1). Let 1<=d<=m. A spherical R^m law whose first d-coordinate projection is Unif(B_d) must have m<=d+2. Its coordinate second and fourth moments are 1/(d+2) and 3/((d+2)(d+4)), so E||Y||^2=m/(d+2) and E||Y||^4=m(m+2)/((d+2)(d+4)). Nonnegative variance of ||Y||^2 implies the ceiling. At m=d+2 the radius is one almost surely. This is a restriction on spherical extensions, not on arbitrary nonspherical constant-sum couplings. It warns against assuming the matrix-generator extension in Yin's elliptical theorem without checking it.

First d-coordinate projection exactly uniform on unit ball

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{no_atoms_bigger_than_p}
Let $f \in \Sym$ with $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f)} \ge 3$. 
For all $y \ne 0$, $f(y) < p$. 
\begin{proof}
We separate the proof into two cases, when $y=1$ and when $y \ne 1$. 
In the case where $y \ne 1$, 
\begin{align*}
q f(-y+2) + p f(-y)
&=  f_{X+Y}(-y+1) \\
&= f_{X+Y}(y-1) = q f(y) + p f(y-2) 
\ge qf(y). 
\end{align*}
Dividing both sides by $p$ and adding $f(y)$, 
\[
f(y) + \frac{q}{p} f(-y+2) + f(-y) \ge \frac{q}{p}f(y) + f(y) = \frac{1}{p}f(y) .
\]
Since $\frac{q}{p} < 1$ and the values $y$, $-y+2$, and $-y$ are distinct, the left-hand side of the preceding equation is strictly bounded above by $1$. 

Similarly, when $y=1$, we have 
\[
qf(-1) + pf(-3) 
= f_{X+Y}(-2) 
= f_{X+Y}(2)
= qf(3) + pf(1) 
\ge pf(1) 
\]
so that
\[
f(-1) + f(-3) \ge \frac{q}{p} f(-1) + f(-3) \ge f(1) . 
\]
Adding $f(1)$ to both sides, we see that 
\(
1 \ge f(1) + f(-1) + f(-3) \ge 2f(1)
\);
in particular $f(1) \le \frac{1}{2} < p$. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'

Status: proof (unaudited), owner campaign claim T410-w739-C003 version 2; independent review pending. Fix an oracle O and laws P_L on binary length-L strings. Assume (A) a uniform oracle algorithm with known polynomial running time and fair random tape bound in L and 1/tau produces a law within TV tau of P_L for each inverse-polynomial rational tau; and (B) every uniform polynomial-time deterministic oracle map family F_L on a known polynomial number d(L) of uniform bits has polynomial-time, polynomial-randomness inverters I to every inverse-polynomial rational accuracy rho, with TV(law(F_L(U),I(L,rho,F_L(U))),law(F_L(U),U))<=rho eventually at all lengths. body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, let $\mu$ be its 
Haar probability measure and $Y$ be a random variable on $G$ with 
density $f_Y$. Let $S$ be a set of positive Haar measure 
and $g_S = \frac{1}{\mu(S)}\mathbb{I}_S$ be the density of a uniform 
random variable $U_S$ on $S$. For $t>0$, also define
    \begin{equation*} 
    g^t(y) = \frac{t+f_Y(y)}{1+t}, \quad y \in G.
    \end{equation*}
    Then, for all $t > 0 $
\begin{equation*} 
    \chi^2(f_Y \ast g_S \| g^t  \ast g_S) \leq \eta_S\frac{t+\|f_Y\|_{\infty}}{t}\chi^2(f_Y\|g^t),
\end{equation*}
where
$$\eta_S = \left(\frac{\sin(\pi \mu(S))}{\pi \mu(S)}\right)^2.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.22534

body:
[Lem 22 (Decomposition of $\TLis{k}$ at the root) of arXiv:2506.19123, 'The longest increasing subsequence of Brownian separable permutons'] Let $k \geq 1$. Then the law of $\left( \lis(\TLis{k}_{\lfa}), \lis(\TLis{k}_{\rga}), D \right)$ is described as follows:
    \begin{enumerate}
		\item  With probability $\frac{1}{2 q(1)} \mathds{1}_{k=1}$, the tree $\TLis{k}$ consists of a single vertex, which is a leaf.
		\item  For all $1\leq i < k$, with probability $\frac 1 2 (1-p) q(i)$, the root $\rho_k$ is negative, $\lis(\TLis{k}_{\lfa})=i$ and $\lis(\TLis{k}_{\rga})=k$. 
        Moreover, in this case $D=\rga$. 
		\item  For all $1\leq i \leq k$, with probability $ \frac 1 2 (1-p) q(i)$, the root $\rho_k$ is negative, $\lis(\TLis{k}_{\lfa})=k$ and $\lis(\TLis{k}_{\rga})=i$. Moreover, in this case $D=\lfa$.
		\item  For all $1 \leq i \leq k-1$, with probability $ \frac p 2  \frac{q(i) q(k-i)}{q(k)}$, the root $\rho_k$ is positive, $\lis(\TLis{k}_{\lfa})=i$ and $\lis(\TLis{k}_{\rga})=k-i$. Moreover, conditionally on this, the direction $D$ is $\lfa$ with probability $\frac{i}{k}$ and $\rga$ with probability $\frac{k-i}{k}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, conditionally on $\{( \lis(\TLis{k}_{\lfa}), \lis(\TLis{k}_{\rga}), D )=(k_1, k_2, d)\}$, the trees $\TLis{k}_{\lfa}$ and $\TLis{k}_{\rga}$ are independent trees with respective laws $\TLis{k_1}$ and $\TLis{k_2}$, and $L^k$ is a uniform leaf of $(\TLis{k}_{d})^{\lmax}$.
title: Decomposition of $\TLis{k}$ at the root

body:
Let $S$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \times M$ matrix (a sample covariance) and consider the long-only minimum-variance problem $\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ and $w \ge 0$. Let $w^+$ be a solution and $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^M$, $\delta \ge 0$, the Lagrange multipliers of the nonnegativity constraints ($\delta_m > 0$ only where $w^+_m = 0$). THEOREM (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003). $w^+$ is also the UNCONSTRAINED minimum-variance solution (subject only to $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$) for the modified covariance $$\tilde S = S - \delta \mathbf{1}^T - \mathbf{1}\delta^T,$$ which is symmetric, positive semidefinite on the relevant set, and differs from $S$ by lowering the covariances of the constrained (excluded) assets with every other asset by $\delta_m$ and their variances by $2\delta_m$. Imposing the no-short constraint is therefore equivalent to shrinking the large entries of the sample covariance toward zero by data-determined amounts - which is why the constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when the true covariance would not call for it ("why imposing the wrong constraints helps"): it acts as a covariance-shrinkage estimator whose amount is chosen implicitly by the optimisation, without cross-validation.
S symmetric positive semidefinite
the feasible set is nonempty (it always is: the simplex)

body: A random variable X is sub-Gaussian with proxy sigma^2 if E exp(t(X - EX)) <= exp(sigma^2 t^2 / 2) for all real t. Equivalently, its tails satisfy P(|X - EX| > s) <= 2 exp(-s^2 / (2 sigma^2)) up to constants; bounded random variables are sub-Gaussian by Hoeffding's lemma with sigma = (b - a)/2.

\[
  \inf_{y\in S^{m-1}}\|D^{-1}Uy\|_2\ge a
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad

$\dim(E)\ge m/2$ such that
\[

  \ge
  \frac{a\sqrt m}{\sqrt2\,H}.
\]

[Theorem T:selfsim of arXiv:2412.09655, 'The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree III: The exchangeable partition representation and'] Let $t\ge0$ be fixed and let $n$ grow from $1$ to $\infty$. 
At each increase of $n$, either one of the trees in $F^{(n)}_t$ gets a new leaf,
or a new tree consisting only of a root is added to $F^{(n)}_t$; in either case
all other trees in $F^{(n)}_t$ remain unchanged.

increases in size, grows as a copy of the process $\operatorname{CTCS}(n)$,
and different trees grow as  independent copies. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition McKean--Vlasov approximation of type 2 of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] Let \(p^\star\in[0,1]\) be a solution of the fixed-point equation
\[
p^\star=\mathbb P(q^{p^\star}>0),
\]
where \(q^p\) denotes the stationary random-environment queue defined above.

For each \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\), let \(D_i^p\) be a Poisson random measure on
\[
\mathbb R_+\times \mathbb R_+\times \{0,1\}^{N-1}
\]
with intensity
\[
\mathrm du\,\mathrm dz\,\nu_{
p}(\mathrm d\theta),
\]
where \(\nu_{p}\) is the product measure of \(N-1\) independent Bernoulli random
variables with parameter \(p\).

For \(\theta=(\theta_m)_{m\neq i}\in\{0,1\}^{N-1}\), define
\[
\mu_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(\theta)
=
B\log_2\left(
1+
\frac{1}{1+\sum_{m\neq i}\theta_m l(d(i,m))}
\right).
\]
The McKean--Vlasov approximation of type 2 is defined by
\begin{equation}
q_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(t)
=
q_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(0)
+
A_i[0,t]
-
\int_{\{0,1\}^{N-1}}\int_{\mathbb R_+}\int_0^t
\mathbf 1_{\{u\leq \mu_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(\theta)\}}
\mathbf 1_{\{q_i^{\mathrm{MF2}}(z^-)>0\}}
\,D_i^{p^\star}(\mathrm du,\mathrm dz,\mathrm d\theta).
\end{equation}
title: McKean--Vlasov approximation of type 2

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2606.21394, 'McKean-Vlasov Equations for Large Networks of Neurons with Adaptive Asymmetric Edges'] For any  $b \geq T^{1/4}$, there is a constant $C_b > 0$ such that the following holds.  For any $u,\tilde{u} \in \mathcal{C}\big([0,T], \mathbb{R}^c\big)$ and $z,\tilde{z} \in \mathcal{C}\big([0,T], \mathbb{R}^d\big)$ such that 
 \begin{align}
    \sup_{h\leq 1} \sup_{0\leq t \leq T-h} \big\lbrace h^{-1/4} \norm{\tilde{u}_{t+h} - \tilde{u}_t} \big\rbrace &= b < \infty \\
   \sup_{h\leq 1} \sup_{0\leq t \leq T-h} \big\lbrace h^{-1/4} \norm{z_{t+h} - \tilde{z}_t} \big\rbrace &= b < \infty \\
 \norm{u_0}^2 &\leq b \\
  \norm{\tilde{u}_0}^2 &\leq b \\
  \norm{z_0}^2 &\leq b  \\
    \norm{\tilde{z}_0}^2 &\leq b,
 \end{align}
 it holds that
\begin{align}
\sup_{t\leq T}\big\| u(t) - \tilde{u}(t) \big\|^2 &\leq C_b\int_0^T \big\| u(t) - \tilde{u}(t) \big\|^2  dt  \\
\sup_{t\leq T}\big\| z(t) - \tilde{z}(t) \big\|^2 &\leq C_b\int_0^T \big\| z(t) - \tilde{z}(t) \big\|^2  dt  
\end{align}

[Theorem teoScaleFnBV of arXiv:2604.08889, 'Matrix Representations for Scale Functions of Spectrally Negative Lévy Processes with Rati'] Let $X$ be a L\'evy process as in (equation eqnXTrajectories of the paper), with $\sigma=0$ and $d>0$. Then, for any $x\geq 0$ and $q\geq 0$ such that $\psi'(\Phi_q)>0$ we have
\begin{equation}
W^{(q)}(x) = \frac{1}{\psi'(\Phi_q)} \Big( \mathrm{e}^{\Phi_q x} - \bm{\Psi}\, e^{\bm{G}x}\,\bm{\nu} \Big), \qquad x \ge 0,
\end{equation}where $\bm{G}: = \bm{T} + \bm{t}\,\bm{\Psi}$, $\bm{\nu}:=(\Phi_q \bm I - \bm{T})^{-1}\bm{t}$ with $\bm I$ the identity matrix.
The matrix $\bm{\Psi}$ is a solution to 
\begin{equation}
\bm{\Psi} \big( (\lambda + q)\bm{I} - d\bm{T} - d\,\bm{t}\,\bm{\Psi} \big) = \lambda\, \bm{\alpha}.
\end{equation}Finally, $\bm{\Psi}$ can be obtained as the limit of the recursive equation
\begin{equation}

[Proposition 6 of arXiv:2608.22693, 'Uniformity of extremal behaviour along geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\Phi \in (0,1/10)$ and $p_1 \in (0,1)$. There exists a translation and scale invariant family of deterministic points $\{u_-,u_+,v_-,v_+\}_{z \in \CC, r>0}$ satisfying $u_+,u_- \in B_{\Phi r}(z-r)$ and $v_+,v_- \in B_{\Phi r}(z+r)$ such that with $P_+,P_-$ defined by $P_+=\Gamma_{u_+,v_+}, P_-=\Gamma_{v_-,v_+}$, suppose we have a translation and scale invariant family of events $\{H_r(z)\}_{z\in \CC, r>0}$ which are measurable with respect to $\sigma(P_-\cup P_+, \cap_{\varepsilon>0}\sigma( \pi(h)\lvert_{B_{\varepsilon}(P_-\cup P_+)}))$ viewed modulo an additive constant and satisfy $\PP(H_r(z))\geq p_1$, then there exist constants $A > 1, \rho \in (0,1)$ depending only on $p_1$ and constants $c_1,c_2$ depending only on $\gamma$ such the following is true.

Let $U \subseteq \CC$ be a bounded open set. Set $\varepsilon_n = 2^{-n}$ for all $n \in \NN$. With $\mathcal{H}_n = ((\varepsilon_n / 2)^{1/c_1} \ZZ^2) \cap U$, for all $\beta >0$, there exist (random) $0<\varphi < \psi < \beta /20$ depending only on $U$ and $\beta$ such that we have the following for all $n \in \NN$ large enough. For all $\bz \in \mathcal{H}_n$ and all $w \in U$ satisfying $D_h(\bz,w) \geq \beta$, and every $D_h$-geodesic $\Gamma_{\bz,w}$ from $\bz$ to $w$, there exists $(z,r) \in \CC \times [\varepsilon_n^{1/(2c_2)} , \varepsilon_n^{1/(4c_2)}]$ satisfying the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There exists $z' \in \partial B_r(z)$ such that for the points $u_-,u_+,v_-,v_+$ corresponding to $z'$ and the radius $\rho r/A^2$, the event $\scX^{u_+,v_+}_{u_-,v_-} \cap H_{\rho r/A^2}(z')$ occurs.
    \item With $P_+ = \Gamma_{u_+,v_+}, P_- = \Gamma_{u_-,v_-}$ being the unique $D_h$-geodesics corresponding to the points $u_-,u_+,v_-,v_+$ associated to the point $z'$ and the radius $\rho r/A^2$, we have $P_-\cup P_+\subseteq B_{\rho r/(4A)}(z')$ and further there exists $\varphi<\tau^- < \tau^+<\psi$ such that $P_- \cap P_+ = \Gamma_{\bz,w}|_{[\tau^-,\tau^+]}$.
\item $P_+$ (resp.\ $P_-$) intersects $\Gamma_{\bz,w}$ on its left (resp.\ right) side.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\gamma_L=(L-1)/\ell$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label={\normalfont(\arabic*)}]
\item The discrete in space processes DITP (resp. DFTP) converge, with quantitative control,  when $L$ tends to infinity, in Skorohod topology towards the continuous-space piecewise deterministic Markov process CITP (resp. CFTP).
\item The processes DITP and DFTP are exponentially ergodic with invariant measures converging as $L$ tends to infinity to the unique invariant measures of the CITP and CFTP.
\item The invariant measures of CITP and CFTP have a positive mass at $\{0\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$ and  $\{\ell\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$.
\item Let us define for a Markov process with semigroup $P_t$ and invariant measure $\pi$ its mixing time as
$t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)=\inf\left\{t\ge0\,;\, sup_\mu\|\mu P_t-\pi\|_{TV}\le \epsilon\right\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\normalfont (a)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CITP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)\frac 1\omega(1+\omega^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\item[\normalfont (b)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CFTP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)(\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta)(1+\alpha^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964

body: In computational complexity theory, a branch of computer science, bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time (BPP) is the class of decision problems solvable by a probabilistic Turing machine in polynomial time with an error probability bounded by 1/3 for all instances. BPP is one of the largest practical classes of problems, meaning most problems of interest in BPP have efficient probabilistic algorithms that can be run quickly on real modern machines. BPP also contains P, the class of problems solvable in polynomial time with a deterministic machine, since a deterministic algorithm is a special case of a probabilistic algorithm.
title: BPP (complexity)

    The family

[Proposition 139 (Boundary generation versus evolutionary value compression) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Put
\[
 \mathscr S_T:=\overline{\mathcal G_T^0(\mathscr T_0)}
 ^{\,\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}}
\]
and assume that this closed terminal solver range is invariant under the
first-jet truncations.  Terminal generation and evolutionary value compression
are different requirements:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.5em]
\item terminal generation asks whether
$\mathcal G_T^0:\mathscr T_0\to\mathscr S_T$ is Cauchy-continuous for the
terminal-data topology;
\item evolutionary compression asks whether
$\pi_Y|_{\mathscr S_T}$ is injective and has a stable-causal inverse
for the inherited $\mathbb S_{\cP}^2$ value topology.
\end{enumerate}
These conditions concern different maps, and neither implication is assumed
without additional comparison hypotheses.  The following comparison is
sufficient for boundary generation to
imply evolutionary compression.  Suppose
\eqref{eq:terminal-to-jet} holds and there is a nondecreasing modulus
$\chi$ with $\chi(0)=0$ and $\lim_{r\downarrow0}\chi(r)=0$ such that
\begin{equation}
 d_{\mathscr T}(\xi,\eta)
 \le\chi\bigl(\|Y^\xi-Y^\eta\|_{\mathbb S_{\cP}^2}\bigr),
 \qquad \xi,\eta\in\mathscr T_0.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|Z^\xi-Z^\eta\|_{\mathbb H_{\cP}^2}
 \le(\omega\circ\chi)
       \bigl(\|Y^\xi-Y^\eta\|_{\mathbb S_{\cP}^2}\bigr),
\end{equation}
and the induced closed terminal solver range is value-process compressible by
\Cref{prop:nonlinear-solver-range-compression}.

[Lem 33 of arXiv:2506.20146, 'Parabolic Anderson Model in the Hyperbolic Space. Part I: Annealed Asymptotics'] Let $X$ be a locally convex, Hausdorff topological
(real) vector space and let $X^{*}$ be its topological dual. Suppose
that $F:X\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]$ is a lower semi-continuous,
convex function. Define $G:X^{*}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]$ by 
\begin{equation}
G(\lambda)\triangleq\sup\big\{_{X^{*}}\langle\lambda,x\rangle_{X}-F(x):x\in X\big\},\ \ \ \lambda\in X^{*}.
\end{equation}
If $F$ is not identically equal to $\infty,$ then one has 
\[
F(x)=\sup\big\{_{X^{*}}\langle\lambda,x\rangle_{X}-G(\lambda):\lambda\in X^{*}\big\},\ \ \ x\in X.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 5 (Random environment) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary ergodic sequence.
Assume that
\[
\E[|\ell_0|]<\infty \qquad\text{and}\qquad
\E\!\Big[\bigl|\log\bigl(\p(\xi_{1,0}>0\mid\mathcal E_0)\bigr)\bigr|\Big]<+\infty,
\]
where $\xi_{1,0}$ denotes the number of offspring colonies of a single
colony given the environment $\mathcal E_0$ (see
Section~\ref{sec:branching-structure}).
Set $\Lambda=\E[\ell_0]$. Then:
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(a)] If $\Lambda>0$, survival has positive probability.
  \item[(b)] If $\Lambda<0$, extinction is almost sure.
  \item[(c)] If $\Lambda=0$ and the offspring law is non‑degenerate,
        extinction is almost sure.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:general of arXiv:2609.02123, 'Groups of Transverse Stratifications and the Hierarchy of Configuration Spaces'] Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a moduli space with a transversely nice stratification. Then there exists a natural homomorphism
\[
\pi_1(\mathcal{M}, *) \longrightarrow G(\Gamma),
\]
where $\Gamma$ is the hypergraph associated with the stratification.

In particular, for the configuration space of points on the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$, the stratification by projective constraints (collinearity, conics, etc.) yields a natural homomorphism from the spherical braid group to the corresponding group $G(\Gamma)$.

[Lem lem_meet_reduction of arXiv:2608.29914, 'Fixed points in abstract provability structures'] Let $S$ be a meet APS satisfying \textup{(C3*)} and let $x \in L$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every one-variable APS term $\triangle v$ with $d(\triangle) \geq 1$, we have $\boxtimes \triangle x = \boxtimes \Box \triangle x$. 

    \item For every one-variable APS term $\triangle v$ with $d(\triangle) \geq 1$, we have $\boxtimes \triangle x \leq \boxtimes^3 \triangle x$. 

    \item For every $k\geq 0$, we have $\boxtimes\Box^k\boxtimes x=\boxtimes^2x$.

    \item For every one-variable APS term $\triangle v$ which is of the form $\boxtimes \triangle_0 v$, we have $\triangle \boxtimes x=\boxtimes^{d(\triangle) + 1} x$.

\end{enumerate}

[Proposition l:covasymstatfindiffsobolev of arXiv:2411.08848, 'Stationary random measures: Covariance asymptotics, variance bounds and central limit theo'] Let ${\mathcal X}$ be a stationary random measure and let ${\mathcal X}_L$ denote the scaled random measure defined by ${\mathcal X}_L(A)={\mathcal X}(LA)$ for $L \geq 1$. Assume that $\int |z^{\gamma}||{\bf K}|(\mathrm{d} z) < \infty$ for $|\gamma|\le 2k+1$. Let $f,g\in L^1\cap H^k$ functions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ for some $k\ge 0$ (with the convention that $H^0=L^2$).  Then,
\begin{enumerate}
\item $L^{-d} \mathrm{Cov}({\mathcal X}_L(f),{\mathcal X}_L(g))  \to Q_0^{{\bf K}}(f,g)$ as $L\to \infty$.

\item If $\lambda_D + I(0) = 0$ and $I(\alpha)=0$ for  $1\le |\alpha|< 2k$, then
$L^{-d+2k} \mathrm{Cov}({\mathcal X}_L(f),{\mathcal X}_L(g)) \to Q_{2k}^{{\bf K}}(f,g)$.

\item If $\lambda_D + I(0)= 0$ and $I(\alpha)=0$ for  $1\le |\alpha|\le 2k$, then $\mathrm{Cov}({\mathcal X}_L(f),{\mathcal X}_L(g))=O(L^{d-2k-1})$  if one of  $f$ or $g$ is in $C_b^{2k+1}$  (functions with bounded, continuous partial derivatives of order $2k+1$).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition l:covasymstatfindiffsobolev of arXiv:2411.08848

For real Gaussian phase retrieval, rotate the fixed unit signal to e_1, so y_i=a_{i1}^2. The leave-one-out trajectory deletes observation l from the loss while retaining the denominator m and uses an initialization independent of all observations. It is independent of a_l. In a second trajectory replace each first coordinate a_{i1} by xi_i |a_{i1}| with fresh independent Rademacher signs xi_i; retain the other coordinates and labels. This random-sign trajectory is independent of the original first-coordinate signs. A third auxiliary trajectory combines both changes and has both independence properties. Bounds comparing these three trajectories with the original trajectory transfer concentration estimates to the original dependent iterates. The comparison bounds, not exact independence of the original iterates, are the essential step. Sections 4.4–4.6 establish these comparisons in the polylogarithmically oversampled setting of the main theorem.

[Definition $\Theta$-Martingales of arXiv:2507.22577, 'A Mean-Field Theory of $\Theta$-Expectations'] An $\mathbb{F}$-adapted process $M = (M_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is called a \textbf{$\Theta$-martingale} if $M \in \mathcal{S}^2([0,T])$ and for all $0 \le s \le t \le T$, it satisfies
\[ M_s = \mathfrak{E}[M_t | \mathcal{F}_s]. \]
The process is a \textbf{$\Theta$-supermartingale} if $M_s \ge \mathfrak{E}[M_t | \mathcal{F}_s]$ and a \textbf{$\Theta$-submartingale} if $M_s \le \mathfrak{E}[M_t | \mathcal{F}_s]$.

For a measure space (X, mu) and measurable sets A, B, d_mu(A, B) = mu(A symmetric difference B), possibly infinite. For an increasing sequence E_1 in E_2 in ... with increments D_k = E_{k+1} minus E_k and union E, d_mu(E_m, E_n) = sum_{k=m}^{n-1} mu(D_k) for m <= n and d_mu(E_m, E) = sum_{k >= m} mu(D_k). Hence the following are equivalent: the sequence is d_mu-Cauchy; sum_{k >= m} mu(D_k) < infinity for some m; d_mu(E_m, E) < infinity for some m; d_mu(E_n, E) -> 0. Consecutive distances tending to zero are not enough: under the measure with weight 1/k at the point k, the chain E_n = {1, ..., n} has d(E_n, E_{n+1}) = 1/(n+1) -> 0 but is not Cauchy.

\begin{equation*}
S_{N} \to 
1\quad \text{a.s. in }C(K),\quad \text{i.e.}\quad
\sup_{z\in K}|S_{N}(z)-1| 
\to 
0 \quad \text{a.s.} \qquad (N\rightarrow
\infty). 
\end{equation*}
Here $C(K)$ is the space of continuous functions on $K$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2605.02713, '2605.02713'] Let $(X_k)_{k \in \N_0}$ be a stationary Gaussian Markov process. Then after centering with $\E X_0=\mu$, the process is either constant in time or satisfies the recursion
		$$
		X_{k} - \mu = \alpha (  X_{k-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_k,\quad k\geq 1,
		$$
		with $\varepsilon_k \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}\big(0, \mathrm{Var}(X_0) (1 - \alpha^2)\big)$ and $|\alpha|<1$.

body:
[Thm 14 of arXiv:2609.03468, 'Almost-invariant half-spaces of operators on $\omega$'] Let $T \in L(\omega)$. If there exists $k \geqslant 0$ such that the set 
\[\{n \ne k \  ; \  P_k T^{l}e_n \neq 0 \ \text{for some $l$}\} \ \text{is infinite,}\]
then either $T$ possesses a closed invariant half-space or there exist $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ and an operator $R \in L(\omega)$ of finite rank such that $T$ is conjugate to $B+ \lambda \operatorname{Id}  + R$.

body: Let M be a compact, oriented, boundaryless smooth surface with Gaussian curvature K and area element dA. The Gauss-Bonnet theorem states that the integral over M of K dA equals 2 pi chi(M), where chi(M) is the Euler characteristic of M; for instance a topological sphere always has total curvature 4 pi, whatever its metric. If M has a piecewise-smooth boundary with geodesic curvature k_g and exterior angles theta_i at its corners, the formula generalizes to: integral of K dA over M, plus integral of k_g ds over the boundary, plus the sum of the theta_i, equals 2 pi chi(M). Due to Carl Friedrich Gauss and Pierre Ossian Bonnet.
title: Gauss-Bonnet theorem

body:
[Lemdef 9 of arXiv:2605.31088, 'On couplings for kinetic Langevin diffusions'] Let $z,\tilde z\in\R^{2d}$, $n\in\N_{>0}$, and let
$y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\in\R^{2dn}$ satisfy $y_n=0$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:finite-time-coalescence-map}). 
 There exists a unique
coalescence map $\Psi^n_{z,\tilde z}\colon\R^{2dn}\to\R^{2dn}$ such that,
for every $\xi=(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n)\in\R^{2dn}$, the vector
$\tilde\zeta=(\tilde\zeta_1,\dots,\tilde\zeta_n):=\Psi^n_{z,\tilde z}(\xi)$
satisfies
\begin{equation}

    \Psi^k_{\tilde z}(\tilde\zeta_1,\dots\tilde\zeta_k)=\Psi^k_z(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_k)+y_k, \qquad k\in\{1,\dots n\}.
\end{equation}
The map $\Psi_{z,\tilde{z}}^{n}$ is called the \emph{coalescence map defined by the trajectory $y$}.

[Theorem thm:oriented of arXiv:2609.02820, 'Sharpness and critical scaling of parking'] Let $\eta=(\eta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ be i.i.d.\ with mean zero, and let $\vec u_n$
	obey (equation eq:oriented-divisible of the paper). The following bounds hold for $n\geq1$.
	If $d=2$ and $\mathbb{E}|\eta(0)|^r<\infty$ for some $r>4$, then
	\[
		\mathbb{E} \vec u_n(0)\leq Cn^{1/4}.
	\]
	If $d\geq3$ and $\mathbb{E} e^{\theta|\eta(0)|}<\infty$ for some $\theta>0$, then
	\[
		\mathbb{E} \vec u_n(0)\leq C\log(n+1).
	\]
	If $\eta(0)$ has positive finite variance, then
	$\mathbb{E} \vec u_n(0)\geq c\sqrt{\vec\kappa_d(n)}$.
