body:
[Corollary 16 (The separatrix is the cone of square roots) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Suppose, as in Remark~\ref{rem:pi-mu}, that the underlying chain
is $(\sigma,\kappa)$-reversible with reversible measure
$\mu\propto\kappa^{-1}$. Then
\[
\Sigma\cap\Delta_{m-1}
=\Bigl\{\pi:\ \pi|_O\propto\sqrt{\mu}\,\bigl|_O\ \text{on each
orbit }O,\ \text{neutral weights free}\Bigr\},
\]
and the per-orbit constants (together with the neutral weights,
modulo normalisation) are global coordinates on $\Sigma$. Note that
the two pictures are of different kinds: in the $\pi$-coordinates
$\Sigma$ is an affine slice of the simplex, not a cone; it is in the
coordinates $x=2\sqrt\pi$ that it becomes a genuine cone, and the
name is to be read there. On the sphere, correspondingly,
\[
\Phi\bigl(\Sigma^\circ\bigr)
=\operatorname{cone}_{+}\bigl\{\mu^{1/4}\big|_O,\ \text{neutral
axes}\bigr\}\cap S^{m-1}_+(2),
\]
the \emph{positive} cone --- positivity and normalisation are part
of the statement, not decoration. The spectral square root
$\mu\mapsto\sqrt\mu$ and the geometric square root $\Phi$ thus
compose, and the separatrix is generated, in spherical coordinates,
by the fourth roots of the reversible measure.

[Theorem 240 (Existence and continuation criteria for the characteristic initial value problem; \cite{speckyucharacteristicIVP}) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Local existence for the characteristic IVP}}. 
Recall that the classical solution is $C^{\infty}$ on $\twoargMrough{[\timefunction_0,0],[- \rightu,\leftu]}{0}$
and therefore induces $C^{\infty}$ data on the characteristic surfaces
$\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\leftubar}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}, \, \outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\moreinterestingu_1}{[\leftubar,0]}$; see Appendix~\ref{A:DATASSUMPTIONS}.
Then there exists a  
$\ubarlocal \in (\leftubar,0)$, depending on the data, such the characteristic data launch a unique $C^{\infty}$ solution
on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$,
and the change of variables map $(u,\ubar,x^2,x^3) \rightarrow (t,x^1,x^2,x^3)$
is a diffeomorphism from $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$
onto its image in Cartesian coordinate space.

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Continuation criteria for the characteristic IVP}}.

Assume the following: 
\begin{itemize}
	\item The assumptions of Theorem\,\ref{T:EXISTENCEUPTOCAUCHYHORIZONBYCONTINUATIONCRITERIA} hold.
	\item $\ubarboot < 0$.
	\item The ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the wave variables $\wavearray$, and the acoustic geometry variables $u, \, \chi$, etc. are classical solutions on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$. 
	\item The bootstrap assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold for $(\ubar,u) \in [\leftubar,\ubarboot)\times[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]$. 
\end{itemize}

Then there exists a $\Delta \in (0,|\ubarboot|)$ such that the ingoing eikonal function $\ubar$, the solution variables $\wavearray, \, u$, and all of the other geometric quantities defined throughout the article can be uniquely extended to a strictly larger region of the form $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot + \Delta)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$ on which all of the bootstrap
assumptions of Sects.\,\ref{S:BOOTSTRAPEVERYTHINGEXCEPTENERGIES} and\,\ref{SS:BOOTSTRAPASSUMPTIONSFORTHEWAVEENERGIES} hold.

The linear arboricity la(G) of a graph G is the minimum number of linear forests (disjoint unions of paths) into which the edges of G can be partitioned. Akiyama, Exoo, and Harary (1980) conjectured that every d-regular graph G satisfies la(G) = \lceil (d + 1) / 2 \rceil. Alon (1988) proved using the Lovasz Local Lemma that la(G) <= d/2 + O(d^{2/3 - c}).
G is a d-regular graph

[Prop 12 of arXiv:2608.23450, 'The Oldest Allele in a Moran Model'] Let $g_0$ be the unique $C([0,1]) \cap C^2((0,1])$ solution of the differential equation $\hat Gg_0 = -1$ with boundary conditions $g_0(0) = 0$, and $g_0'(1)$ finite. Then $\mathbb{E}_x[\tau] = g_0(x)$ for all $x \in [0,1]$. Consequently, the expected hitting time is explicitly given by:
\[ \mathbb{E}_x[\tau] = \int_0^x (1-u)^{-\theta} \left[ \int_u^1 \frac{(1-y)^{\theta-1}}{y} \,dy \right] du. \]

mollified approximation of the tuple

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.25772, 'Propagation of Chaos and Gaussian Fluctuations for Mean-field Coupled Maps'] Fix $T\in\N$. Under the assumptions \textup{\textbf{(A1.3)}}, \textup{\textbf{(A2)}} and \textup{\textbf{(A3)}}, assume further $\eta_0$ in the assumption \textup{\textbf{(A3)}} is characterized by
    $$\langle\varphi,\eta_0\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\langle\varphi^2,\bar{\rho}_0\rangle-\langle\varphi,\bar{\rho}_0\rangle^2\right),\quad\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\T),$$
    and let $\eta=(\eta_t)_{0\leq t\leq T}$ be the solution to \eqref{eq:etat} with initial datum $\eta_0$. If $\Delta<\Delta_0$, where $\Delta_0$ is the constant in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, then the sequence $\eta_N=(\eta_t^N)_{0\leq t\leq T}$ converges in distribution to $\eta$ in the space $(H^{-\alpha}(\T))^{T+1}$ as $N\to\infty$ for every $\alpha>1/2$. Furthermore, the process $\eta$ is a Gaussian field satisfying
    $$\langle\varphi,\eta_t\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\langle|Q_{0,t}\varphi|^2,\bar{\rho}_0\rangle-\langle Q_{0,t}\varphi,\bar{\rho}_0\rangle^2\right),$$
    for each test function $\varphi$ and $0\leq t\leq T$. Here the time evolution operator $\{Q_{0,t}\}_{0\leq t\leq T}$ is given by $Q_{0,t}:=Q_{0,1}\circ\cdots\circ Q_{t-1,t},\ t\geq 0$, with
\begin{equation}
    (Q_{t,t+1}\varphi)(y):=(\varphi\circ F_{\bar{\rho}_t})(y)+\Delta\int_{\T}(\varphi\circ F)'(\phi_{\bar{\rho}_t}(x))\bar{\rho}_t(x)h(x,y)\dd x,\quad y\in\T,\ t\geq 0.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 15 (One-stratum relative-entropy net) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] Let $H_P=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in P}H_\alpha$
be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space equipped with a fixed block decomposition. Write
\[
b_\alpha:=\dim H_\alpha,
\qquad
m:=\sum_{\alpha\in P}b_\alpha,
\qquad
h:=\max_{\alpha\in P}b_\alpha.
\]
Let
\[
\Delta_P
:=
\left\{
X\succeq 0:
\operatorname{tr}X=1,\
X=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in P}X_\alpha
\text{ with }X_\alpha\in B(H_\alpha)
\right\}
\]
be the block-diagonal spectraplex associated with this decomposition. Then for every \(\tau>0\), there exists a finite relative-entropy net $T_P(\tau)\subseteq \Delta_P$ of the spectraplex $\Delta_P$ with $|T_P(\tau)|\le \exp(C\tau)$ such that  for every \(X\in\Delta_P\) there is \(Y\in T_P(\tau)\) satisfying
\[
S(X||Y)
\le
C\log\left(e+\frac{hm}{\tau}\right).
\]
Here \(C>0\) is a universal constant.

body: In mathematical analysis, the intermediate value theorem states that if f is a continuous real-valued function whose domain contains the interval [a, b] and u is a number such that min(f(a), f(b)) <= u <= max(f(a), f(b)), then there exists some c between a and b (that is, c in [a, b]) such that f(c) = u. That is, the image of a continuous function over an interval is itself an interval, and it contains every value between f(a) and f(b).

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open with $\lambda_1=\inf\{\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2/\|v\|_{L^2}^2:v\in H^1_0(U),v\ne0\}>0$; this positivity holds in particular when $U$ is bounded, when $U$ is merely bounded in one direction, and when $U$ has finite measure. Let $u$ be the weak solution of $u_t=\Delta u$ in $U\times(0,\infty)$, $u=0$ on $\partial U\times(0,\infty)$, $u(0)=g\in L^2(U)$. Then $\|u(t)\|_{L^2(U)}\le e^{-\lambda_1t}\|g\|_{L^2(U)}$ for all $t\ge0$. The rate is optimal: no larger exponent works, and when $U$ is bounded the infimum defining $\lambda_1$ is attained by a first Dirichlet eigenfunction $\phi_1$, for which equality holds with $g=\phi_1$ (on an unbounded $U$ with $\lambda_1>0$ the infimum need not be attained, and then no datum realizes equality). Moreover $t\mapsto\|u(t)\|_{L^2}$ and (for $g\in H^1_0(U)$) $t\mapsto\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^2}$ are nonincreasing.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2609.02850, 'Canonical-row Chern flow on Bott--Samelson towers:\\ realizable-volume models for Schubert'] Let \(\kk\) be any field.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every partition \(\lambda\) and every \(w\in S_n\),
\[
 \Nrm_{x,z}\bigl(H_{w,\lambda}\bigr)\in\RV.
\]
Consequently, the minimal homogeneous Lascoux packet, every homogeneous
Lascoux excess layer, and every normalized key polynomial are
realizable-volume polynomials over \(\kk\).  The support of every ordinary
Lascoux polynomial is \(M^\natural\)-convex and is exactly the lattice-point
set of its integral generalized-polymatroid Newton polytope.

\item For every partition \(\lambda\) and every \(w\in S_n\),
\[
 \Nrm_{x,z}\bigl(\overline H_{w,\lambda}\bigr)\in\RV.
\]
Consequently, every homogeneous Lascoux-atom layer and every normalized
Demazure atom \(\Nrm(\mathcal A_\alpha)\) are realizable-volume polynomials
over \(\kk\).  The support of every ordinary Lascoux atom is
\(M^\natural\)-convex and is exactly the lattice-point set of its integral
generalized-polymatroid Newton polytope.

\item For every \(w\in S_n\),
\[
 \Nrm_{x,z}(F_w),\qquad
 \Nrm_{x,z}(\widetilde G_w),\qquad
 \Nrm(A_{w,k})\ (0\le k\le r_w),\qquad
 \Nrm(\Sch_w)
 \quad\text{belong to }\RV.
\]
The support of every ordinary Grothendieck polynomial is
\(M^\natural\)-convex and is exactly the lattice-point set of its integral
generalized-polymatroid Newton polytope.
\end{enumerate}
Every nonzero homogeneous polynomial occurring in \textup{(i)}--\textup{(iii)}
has support equal to the integral base set of a polymatroid algebraic over
\(\kk\).  If \(\operatorname{char}(\kk)=0\), each such polynomial admits a
smooth integral projective realization by semiample Cartier divisor
classes.  Over \(\CC\), each is Lorentzian. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:ensemble of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] Let $A_1,\dots,A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ be sketches applied to the same data.
\begin{romannum}
\item \emph{Converse.} Stacking gives one linear map of rank at most
$p=\min\{km,d\}$. For any joint decoder, the recoverable centered-distance
variance is at most $\alpha_p(\Sigma)$. In the isotropic case,
$\rho_{\mathrm{HGR}}\le\sqrt{p/d}$, with equality for independent Gaussian blocks and the
optimal joint decoder.
\item \emph{Explicit averaging decoder.} If the $A_i$ are independent
Gaussian maps and we average the $k$ rescaled squared distances they produce,
then the correlation, jointly over the maps and data, is
\[
\sqrt{\frac{km}{km+d+2}}.
\]
The ratio of this correlation to the HGR ceiling is
\[
\gamma_{k,m,d}
=\sqrt{\frac{km\,d}{(km+d+2)\min\{km,d\}}}
=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{d/(km+d+2)}, & km\le d,\\
\sqrt{km/(km+d+2)}, & km\ge d.
\end{cases}
\]
\end{romannum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Ensemble ceiling and averaging

[Theorem 4 (Mod-$\phi$ convergence for number of inversions) of arXiv:2608.14143, 'Mod-$\phi$ convergence for random variables with cyclotomic generating functions'] For each $N\in\N$ let $X_N$ be the number of inversions of a uniform random permutation of size $N$. Then the sequence of random variables $X_N/N$ converges mod-$\phi$ to the limiting function
	\[
	\psi(z) := \sqrt{\frac{e^z-1}{z}}e^{-z/2}
	\]
	with parameters $w_N=N$ and normalization function
	\[
	\phi(z) := \int_0^1 \log\Bigl(\frac{e^{tz}-1}{{tz}}\Bigr)dt
	\]
	on the domain $\mathscr{D} = \{z\in \C: \frac{e^{tz}-1}{{tz}}\not\in (-\infty, 0] \text{ for all } t\in [0,1]\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Mod-$\phi$ convergence for number of inversions

body:
[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.04168, 'Error analysis for learning fractional stochastic differential equations with applications'] Suppose that the assumptions of Section \ref{sec:assumptions} hold, in particular, \ref{H0} holds for both $H$ and $\HeM$, with $\hat{H}_M$ an estimator of the Hurst parameter. Let $\epsilon,\epsilon_0>0$, $s,s_2,\tilde{\delta}\in(0,1)$ with $\tilde{\delta}<\HeM$, and denote $\tilde\sigma = \sigma - \sigma_n$ and $\tilde b = b - b_n$. Then, for any 
$q>\frac{d}{1-s}$, $q_2>\frac{1}{1-s_2}, \rho > \frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ such that $q\ge\rho$, and any $\alpha \in (1-H\wedge\HeM, \, \min(1/2,s\tilde{\delta},s_2))$, we have for almost all realisations:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal{E}_{\texttt{appr},\alpha}(n) &\leq  C_\omega\left[ \Vert\partial_t\nabla_z\tilde\sigma\Vert_{(q_2,q)} +\Vert\nabla_z\tilde\sigma\Vert_{(q_2,q)} + \Vert\partial_t\tilde\sigma\Vert_{(q_2,q)} + \Vert\tilde\sigma\Vert_{(q_2,q)}\right.  \\
    &+\left.\Vert \nabla_z \tilde b\Vert_{(\rho,q)}  + \Vert  \tilde b\Vert_{(\rho,q)}\right]\\
        \mathcal{E}_{\texttt{fit},\alpha}(M) &\leq C_\omega|\HeM-H|^{\frac12}.
    \end{align*}

    Furthermore, for any $\eta>0$ there exists $\Delta_0 >0$ and $\Omega_0\subseteq \Omega$ such that $\P(\Omega_0)>1-\eta$ and, for any $\Delta t\leq \Delta_0$:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal{E}_{\texttt{time},\alpha}(\Delta t) & \leq C_{\epsilon_0}\,  \Delta t^{2\hat{H}_M-1-\epsilon_0}.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.04168

[Theorem Fubini of arXiv:2604.24914, 'SPDEs with time-independent\\ L\'evy colored noise'] Let $\Phi :[0,T] \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be such that:
\\
a) $\Phi(t,\cdot) \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for any $t \in [0,T]$, and the map $t \mapsto \Phi(t,\cdot)$ is continuous in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$;\\
b)  $\Phi  \in L^2([0,T] \times \mathbb{R}^d)$.

Then the process $\{Z(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\Phi(t,x)L(dx)\}_{t \in [0,T] }$ has a jointly measurable modification denoted by $\{\widetilde{Z}(t)\}_{t \in [0,T]}$, 
\[
\int_0^T |\widetilde{Z}(t)|dt<\infty \ \mbox{a.s.},  \quad \int_0^T|\Phi(t,x)|dt<\infty \ \mbox{for almost all $x\in \mathbb{R}^d$,}
\]
 the function $x\mapsto \int_0^T\Phi(t,x)dt$ belongs to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$, and
\begin{equation}

\int_0^T \widetilde{Z}(t) dt=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left( \int_0^T\Phi(t,x)dt \right) L(dx) \quad \mbox{in $L^2(\Omega)$}.
\end{equation}

body:
[Theorem thm.salem.func.gen.functional of arXiv:2609.01007, 'Global universality of the expected number \\of zeros of non-analytic random signals'] Suppose that the base function $f$ satisfies the condition $\mathbf{(H1)}$ and that the common law of the $(a_k)$ admits a finite third moment. Then, $\mathbb{P}-$almost surely, as $n$ goes to infinity, the finite dimensional marginals of process $(g_{n}(t))_{t\in[0,2\pi]}$ converge in distribution  to the ones of the stationary Gaussian process $(g_{\infty}(t))_{t\in[0,2\pi]}$ with covariance function
$$\mathbb{E}_X[g_{\infty}(t)g_{\infty}(s)] = \rho(t-s),~~\text{with}~\left\{\begin{array}{l}\displaystyle \rho(u):=\frac{1}{u}\int_0^{u}(f\ast \widetilde{f})(x)dx,~u\neq 0 \\\rho(0)=\langle f,f \rangle\end{array}\right.,$$
where $\widetilde{f}(x):=f(-x)$ for all $x\in {\rm I\kern-0.16em R}$. Moreover, if the function $f$ is of class $\mathcal C^2$, the process $(g_{n}(t))_{t\in[0,2\pi]}$ converges is distribution in the $\mathcal{C}^1$ topology towards $(g_{\infty}(t))_{t\in[0,2\pi]}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm.salem.func.gen.functional of arXiv:2609.01007

[Theorem 24 of arXiv:2506.17045, '\LARGE{On bivariate Archimax copulas: Level sets, mass distributions and related results}'] Let $\gamma \in \mathcal{P}_\mathcal{W}$, $\vartheta \in \mathcal{P}_\mathcal{A}$ and $C$ be the corresponding Archimax copula. Then the following assertions hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[$(i)$] If $\gamma$ and $\vartheta$ are absolutely continuous, then $C\in\mathcal{C}_{am}^{abs}$.
        \item[$(ii)$] If $\gamma$ is discrete and $\vartheta$ is discrete with $\vartheta(\{0\}) = 0 = \vartheta(\{1\})$, then $C\in\mathcal{C}_{am}^{dis}$.
        \item[$(iii)$] If $\gamma$ and $\vartheta$ are singular, then $C\in\mathcal{C}_{am}^{sing}$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:limit_correlation_function of arXiv:2603.27906, 'Marked GUE-corners process in doubly periodic dimer models'] Let~$K_{\operatorname{Int}}$ be the correlation kernel given in Theorem~(thm:correlation_kernel of the paper), then,  with the notation introduced above,  for $\mu_1\not=\mu_2$, 
\begin{multline}
\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{g(\ell x_1+i_1,2y_1+j_1)}{g(\ell x_2+i_2,2y_2+j_2)}N^{\frac{1}{2}}K_{\operatorname{Int}}\left(\ell x_1+i_1,2y_1+j_1;\ell x_2+i_2,2y_2+j_2\right) \\
=\nu(t_2,j_2)\sigma^{-1}K_{\operatorname{GUE}}(t_1,\sigma^{-1}\mu_1;t_2,\sigma^{-1}\mu_2),
\end{multline}
where
\begin{equation}
K_{\operatorname{GUE}}(t_1,\mu_1;t_2,\mu_2)=\frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^2}\int_{\gamma_s'}\int_{\gamma_l'}\mathrm{e}^{\frac{1}{2}(z_2^2-z_1^2)}\mathrm{e}^{\mu_1 z_1-\mu_2z_2}\frac{z_2^{t_2}}{z_1^{t_1}}\frac{\,\mathrm{d} z_1\,\mathrm{d} z_2}{z_2-z_1},
\end{equation}
and the sequence on the left-hand side is uniformly bounded in $N$
 on compact subsets of 
$\Lambda_{\{0,1\}}^2$ with respect to the embedding given by $(t_p, \mu_p, j_p)\in \Lambda_{\{0,1\}}$ for $p=1,2$.
Here~$\gamma_s'$ is a counterclockwise oriented contour around the origin and~$\gamma_{\ell}'$ is a contour connection of $-i\infty$ and $+i\infty$ and 

 is at the right of $\gamma_s$ if $\mu_1<\mu_2$ and at the left if $\mu_1> \mu_2$, see Figure (fig:contours_gue_corners of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition p:bella of arXiv:2510.00748, '\bf On irreducible central limit theorems'] Consider a sequence $G^0_n = (V_n^0, {\ensuremath{\mathcal E}} _n^0)$, $n\geq 1$, of connected graphs, with normalized Laplace spectra given by
$$
0 = \mu_1^{(0,n)} < \mu_2^{(0,n)}\leq \cdots \leq \mu_{|V^0_n|}^{(0,n)}\leq 2, \quad n\geq 1.
$$
 Assume that {\rm (i)} $G^0_n$ is $d_n$-regular for some $d_n\geq 1$, {\rm (ii)} $|V^0_n|\to\infty$, and {\rm (iii)} $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \mu_2^{(0,n)}  >0 $. Then, for any fixed integer $m\geq 2$, the sequence of product graphs
$$
G_n := \left(G^0_n\right)^{\mathord{\raisebox{-0.15ex}{\scalebox{1.15}{$\square$}}} m}, \quad n\geq 1,
$$
generates an irreducible CLT, in the sense of Definition (def:irreducibilegraphs of the paper).

[Theorem thm:upper_lower_simple of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\alpha \in (0,2)\setminus\{1\}$, and suppose $\bm{Z}$ is $\alpha$-stable and $\bm{X}$ is in the domain of normal attraction of $\bm{Z}$.\\
{\normalfont{(a)}} Let Assumption~(\nameref{asm:T}) hold for $p\geqslant 1\vee 2(\alpha-1)$. Then, for any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^q]<\infty$, as $t \downarrow 0$, 
\[
\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z}\big)
=\begin{dcases}
    \mathcal{O}\big(t^{1-q/\alpha}\big), 
   & \alpha<1,\\
   \mathcal{O}\big(t^{q(1-1/\alpha)}\big), 
   & \alpha>1.
\end{dcases}
\]
{\normalfont{(b)}} If $\bm{X}$ does not have the law of $\bm{Z}$, then for any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ there exists some $C_q>0$ satisfying 
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})
    \geqslant\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}_1^t,\bm{Z}_1) 
    \geqslant C_q t^{1-q/\alpha},
\quad \text{for all sufficiently small }t>0. 
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:upper_lower_simple of arXiv:2411.03609

body:
[Ppn 71 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For fixed $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $f \in L^\infty([q_0,1];[0,1/\alpha])$, the mapping $p \mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$, viewed as a function from $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ to  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)\Big)^2
        \le 6(1+\|f\|_\infty) \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1\,.
    \]
Here $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is metrized by  $\mathsf{dist}(p,\tilde p) = \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1$, and we recall that  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. 

\begin{proof}
Let $p,\tilde p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 = \delta$.
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows by integrating that $|p(t) - \tilde p(t)| \le \delta$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$, and so certainly we have $\|p-\tilde{p}\|_1\le\delta$. Recalling the notation of Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, let $(b,\sigma)\in \Adm(q_0;p,f)$. We will construct modified controls $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma) \in \Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$ such that the corresponding solutions to \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} approximate each other. Recall $s(t)\equiv (tp)'(t)^{1/2}$, and similarly denote
$\tilde{s}(t)\equiv (t\tilde{p})'(t)^{1/2}$.
We set $\tilde{b}=b$, and let $\hat \sigma$ be defined by the relation
	\[\hat{\sigma}_t-1
	= a(t) 
	(\sigma_t-1)\,,\quad
	a(t)
	\equiv 
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	\frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{\tilde{s}(t)}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$. We note that 
	\[
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	= \frac{[p(t) + tp'(t)]^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}} \ge 1\,,
	\]
so the ratio $a(t)$ can only be large if $p'(t)$ is very large, which occurs on a set of times of small measure. It is clear from the construction that $(\tilde b,\hat{\sigma})$ satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{e:budget-f} defining $\Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$, with the exception that $\hat{\sigma}$ is not necessarily non-negative. Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$, and $\hat X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(\tilde b, \hat \sigma)$. We couple these processes with the same initialization $X(q_0) = \hat{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. We will first show the endpoint laws of $X(1)$ and $\hat{X}(1)$ are close, then address the issue of $\hat{\sigma}$ being possibly negative. To this end, we recall from \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} that
  \[
        X(1) = \int_{q_0}^1 p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t)\,dB(t)
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t) (\sigma_t-1)\,dB(t)
        \,,
    \]
and similarly for $\hat{X}(1)$. This gives us a decomposition
$X(1)-\hat{X}(1) = \textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}+\textup{(c)}$, and we proceed to bound each of the three terms:
    \begin{align*}\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E \bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big) b_t\,dt\bigg)^2\bigg]
    \le \bigg(
     \int_{q_0}^1\Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg( \int_{q_0}^1 \E[(b_t)^2]\,dt\bigg) \\
    &\le\bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 |p'(t)-\tilde{p}'(t)|\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 f(t)\,dt\bigg) 
    =  \delta \|f\|_1 \,,
    \end{align*}
having used the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality along with the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f}. Next,
    \[\E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    = \int_{q_0}^1 \Big( s(t)-\tilde{s}(t) \Big)^2\,dt
    \le \int_{q_0}^1 \Big|s(t)^2 - \tilde{s}(t)^2\Big|\,dt
    \le \|p-p\|_1+\|p'-p'\|_1 \le 2\delta\,.\]
Lastly, using the above definition of $\hat\sigma$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\E[\textup{(c)}^2]
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \Big( s(t) (\sigma_t-1)-\tilde{s}(t)(\hat{\sigma}_t
    -1)\Big)^2\,dt\\
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}
    \E[(\sigma_t-1)^2]
    \cdot p(t)
    \bigg( 1- 
    	\frac{\tilde{s}(t)}{s(t)} a(t)
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt\\
	&\le
	\|f\|_\infty
	\int_{q_0}^1
	p(t)
    \bigg( 1- \frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}}
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt 
	\le \|f\|_\infty \delta\,,
	\end{align*}
having used the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f} along with the calculation from the bound on (a) above. Collec (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\begin{itemize}
\item For $x \in \mathbb T_N^L$ and a percolation configuration $\omega$ in $\mathbb T_N$, introduce the function 
\[f^L_{z,x}(\omega) \coloneqq  \big\{ \prod_{e\in E(\Lambda_L(x))} \alpha_z^{\omega(e)} \big\} - 1 .\] 

\item  For any polymer $\gamma \in \mathsf{P}_N^L$, define the activity function
\[
\mathsf{w}_z(\gamma) \coloneqq  \sum_{A\subset \gamma} \mathbb P[ \prod_{x\in A} f_{z,x}(\omega)\mathds{1}_{\{\mathcal C_A = \gamma\}} ].
\]

\item For any family $\{\bar\gamma\}$ of polymers, define the \emph{non-intersecting} activity function as, for $\gamma \in \mathsf{P}_N^L$:
\[
\mathsf{w}_z^{\{\bar\gamma\}}(\gamma)\coloneqq  \ind{\gamma \cap \mathsf{Tr}(\{\bar\gamma\}) = \emptyset} \mathsf{w}_z(\gamma).
\]

\item Finally, for any \emph{non-intersecting} family of polymers $\{\bar\gamma\}$, define the function:
\[
G_z(\{\bar\gamma\}) \coloneqq  \sum_{A\subset \mathsf{Tr}(\{\bar\gamma\}) } \mathbb P[F(\omega) \prod_{x\in A} f_{z,x}(\omega)\ind{\mathcal C_{A \cup \Delta} = \mathsf{Tr}(\{\bar\gamma\})}].
\]
\end{itemize}

body: A random variable X (or its distribution) is called lattice if there exist real numbers a and h > 0 such that \mathbb{P}(X \in a + h\mathbb{Z}) = 1. The largest such number h is called the maximal span (or span) of the lattice distribution. If no such a and h exist, the distribution is called non-lattice. A distribution is lattice with span h if and only if |\phi_X(2\pi / h)| = 1 and |\phi_X(t)| < 1 for 0 < t < 2\pi / h.
title: Lattice Distribution and Span

[Definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] We say that a variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is uniform if its law has a density, taking only 2 values. That is, the law must be of the following type,
$$\mu=\frac{1}{\lambda(E)}\,\chi_E(x)dx$$
for a certain subset $E\subset\mathbb R$, with $\lambda$ being the Lebesgue measure. In the case of an interval $E=[a,b]$, the corresponding law must be given by the following formula,
$$\mu=\frac{1}{b-a}\,\chi_{[a,b]}(x)dx$$
with the $\chi$ symbols standing in all this, as usual, for characteristic functions.
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'

[Proposition 100 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a variational datum satisfying Assumptions~\ref{Assumption_A}, \ref{Assumption_B} and \ref{Assumption_C} with segment filling fractions $\boldsymbol{n}^{0}$, such that each segment contains a single band of the equilibrium measure. [Corollary cor: boolean_vs_grg of arXiv:2411.02917, '\hspace*{2mm}\\[-16mm] Stein's Method for Spatial Random Graphs'] Consider a determinantal point process on $\R^d$ with kernel $K$ fulfilling the above assumptions and intensity $\mu = K(x,x)$. Let $\Xi$ be the restriction of the point process to $\mathcal{X}_{1/q}$. For a strictly increasing function $\psi$ with $\psi(0)=0$, consider the edge process where $r_*=\hat{r}_*$ satisfies $\Prob(R \geq r_{*}) > 0$ and $\hat{R}_i = r_{*} + \psi(R_i - r_*)$. Denote by $P_{r_*,q} \otimes Q_{r_*,q}$ the distribution of the percolation graph $(\Xi_{r_*,q}, \Sigma_{r_*,q})$ of the Boolean model based on $\hat{R}_i$ after thinning and rescaling. \\
Let furthermore $\lambda = \lambda_{r_*,q} = \mu \tfrac{p(r_*)}{q}$, $t = q^{1/d}r_*$. Denote by $P^{\lambda}$ the homogeneous Poisson process distribution with intensity $\lambda$ and set $\kappa_t(x,y) = \1_{\{\norm{x-y} \leq 2t\}}$.\\
Then
\begin{align*}
W_{\mathbb{G},i} \bigl(&P_{r_*,q} \otimes Q_{r_*,q} \hspace*{1.5pt} , \, P^{\lambda} \otimes Q^{\kappa_{t}}\bigr) \\[1mm]
&\leq 2 c_V(\lambda_{r_*,q}) \,\lambda_{r_*,q} \abs{\mathcal{X}} \frac{q}{1-q} \\[-0.5mm]
&\hspace*{6mm} {} + c_E(\lambda_{r_*,q}) \, \lambda_{r_*,q}\, c_d\, \mu \abs{\mathcal{X}}
    d \, 2^{d} \E \bigl[ \psi(R-r_*) \bigl(r_* + \psi(R-r_*) \bigr)^{d-1} \, \1\{R \geq r_*\} \bigr] \\[1mm]
&\leq \mathrm{const} \Bigl(\min \bigl\{ \lambda_{r_*,q} \abs{\mathcal{X}}, 1 + \log^{+}(\lambda_{r_*,q} \abs{\mathcal{X}}) \bigr\} \frac{q}{1-q}  \\[-0.5mm]
&\hspace*{6mm} {} + \min \bigl\{ \lambda_{r_*,q} \abs{\mathcal{X}}, 1 \bigr\} \mu \E \bigl[ \psi(R-r_*) \bigl(r_* + \psi(R-r_*) \bigr)^{d-1} \, \1\{R \geq r_*\} \bigr] \Bigr),
\end{align*}
where $c_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2 +1)}$ is the volume of the unit ball in $\R^d$ and $c_V(\lambda)$, $c_E(\lambda)$ are defined in Equations~(equation eq: SteinPoissonV of the paper) and~(equation eq: SteinPoissonE of the paper).

Let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset of R^n and let lambda be Lebesgue measure. Then lambda(E) = inf { lambda(U) : U open, U contains E } (outer regularity) and lambda(E) = sup { lambda(K) : K compact, K contained in E } (inner regularity). Equivalently, for every eps > 0 there are an open U containing E and a closed F contained in E with lambda(U - F) < eps. Lebesgue measure is complete, and every Lebesgue measurable set differs from a Borel set by a null set.
E Lebesgue measurable.
Inner regularity by COMPACT sets holds for every measurable set here because R^n is sigma-compact;
on a general locally compact space inner regularity by compacta is usually stated for open sets and for sets of finite measure.

Let pi(dx)=Z^{-1}exp(-V(x))dx be a smooth positive probability density on R, with V in C2(R) and bounded V_second. Let k:R-by-R->R be continuous, symmetric, positive definite and integrally strictly positive definite: its double integral against any finite nonzero signed Borel measure is strictly positive whenever that integral is defined. Assume integral k(x,x) pi(dx)<infinity. Let H_k be its RKHS and assume the embedding H_k into H1(pi) is continuous and dense. Define T f(x)=integral k(x,y)f(y)pi(dy). For phi in H_k set Q(phi)=integral [V_second(x)phi(x)^2+phi_prime(x)^2]pi(dx). Fix lambda>0. The local Stein Hessian lower bound (36) holds for every smooth compactly supported potential Psi if and only if Q(phi)>=lambda ||phi||_{H_k}^2 for every phi in H_k. Explicitly, in one dimension the former condition is Q(T Psi_prime)>=lambda ||T Psi_prime||_{H_k}^2 for every Psi in C_c^infinity(R); the right side also equals lambda times integral integral Psi_prime(y)k(y,z)Psi_prime(z)pi(dy)pi(dz). This concerns the local curvature criterion at equilibrium, as defined in Definition 32, rather than a global nonlinear convergence rate for every initial distribution.
d=1
smooth positive normalized pi proportional to exp(-V), V in C2 with bounded second derivative
continuous symmetric positive-definite ISPD kernel k
finite diagonal integral under pi
continuous dense embedding H_k into H1(pi)
lambda>0

body: [Prop 120367 of arXiv:2606.29143, 'Comonotonic and moment matching approximations for sums of lognormal random variables'] Let $A = (a_1, ..., a_m)^{'}$ and $Q = (q_1, ..., q_m)^{'}$ be two numerical vectors with $\min(a_1, ..., a_m) \geq 0, \max(a_1, ..., a_m) > 0$ and $0 = q_0 < q_1 < q_2 < ... < q_m = 1$. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable and $X_{A, Q}$ the step-weighted version of $X$ associated with the numerical vectors $A$ and $Q$. Then for any $p \in (0, 1)$ it holds that $$\text{VaR}_p[X_{A, Q}] = \text{VaR}_{G_{A, Q}^{-1}(p)}[X].$$

Let S be a separable metric space, and let \mu_n, \mu be Borel probability measures on S such that \mu_n \Rightarrow \mu weakly. Then there exists a single probability space (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) and S-valued random variables X_n, X defined on \Omega such that the law of X_n is \mu_n for all n, the law of X is \mu, and X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega) as n \to \infty for \mathbb{P}-almost every \omega \in \Omega.

Let P be locally finite, R a commutative ring with 1 and Q any subset with the induced order. Extending h in I_R(Q) by 0 on comparable pairs of P not lying in Q gives an injective, R-linear, multiplicative map j_Q: I_R(Q) -> I_R(P) whose image is e_Q I_R(P) e_Q, where e_Q is the indicator of the diagonal pairs (x, x) with x in Q. The corner has identity e_Q, so j_Q is unital into I_R(P) only when Q = P. The corner embedding exists for every Q, while restriction I_R(P) -> I_R(Q) is multiplicative only for order-convex Q, so an arbitrary induced subposet cannot be handled by restriction.

Let A be a uniformly random n-element subset of {1, ..., N}, with N >= 2 and 1 <= n <= N, and I_i = 1{i in A}. Then E I_i = n/N, Var(I_i) = n(N-n)/N^2 and, for i != j, Cov(I_i, I_j) = -n(N-n)/(N^2(N-1)). For real a_1, ..., a_N with mean a_bar, the sample total satisfies Var(sum_{i in A} a_i) = n(N-n)/(N(N-1)) sum_i (a_i - a_bar)^2. If X_1, ..., X_n is an ordered sample drawn without replacement from a_1, ..., a_N, sigma^2 = (1/N) sum_i (a_i - a_bar)^2 and X_bar = (1/n) sum_k X_k, then Var(X_bar) = ((N-n)/(N-1)) sigma^2 / n: n independent uniform draws would give sigma^2 / n, so the finite-population correction is exactly (N-n)/(N-1), equal to 1 at n = 1 and to 0 at the full census n = N.

[Theorem Entropic symmetrization resistance of Bernoulli of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[theorem]{thm:HY_exceeds_HX}
Let $X \sim \Bern(p,a,b)$ with $p \ne \frac{1}{2}$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}(X=b) = p$ and $\mathbb{P}(X=a) = 1-p$. 
Then, any independent symmetrizer $Y$ of $X$ satisfies $H(Y) \ge H(X)$, with equality if and only if $f_Y = f_{-X}$. 
\begin{proof}
By (lem:affine_invariance,cor:psymmetry of the paper) it is sufficient to consider $X \sim \Bern(p,-1,1)$ 

with $p > \frac{1}{2}$. 

Equality is attained when $f_Y=f_{-X}$ by (lem:support_size_one_or_two of the paper); therefore we only need to show that $H(Y) > H(X)$ when $f_Y \ne f_{-X}$, i.e., $\@ifstar{\oldabs}{\oldabs*}{\supp(f_Y)} \ge 3$. 

In this case, by (calYzero_sufficient of the paper) either $H(f_Y) > H(X)$ or projecting $f_Y$ onto $\Sym^0$ does not decrease its entropy; therefore it suffices to consider 
$f_Y \in \Sym^0$. 
By (lem:calYzero_representation of the paper), we write $f_Y = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \hat{f}_i^0$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 = 1$. 
Then, 
$ f(0) = \alpha_1^0 \hat{f}_1^0(0) = \frac{\alpha_1^0}{2}$, 
so that $\alpha_1^0 > 2p > 1$. 
Note that $\alpha_1^0 = 1 - \sum_{i=2}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0$. 
But, by (lem:calYzero_negative_coefficient_control of the paper), $\sum_{i=2}^{\infty} \alpha_i^0 \ge 0$, so $\alpha_1^0 \le 1$, a contradiction. 

\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Entropic symmetrization resistance of Bernoulli

body: In abstract algebra and number theory, Kummer theory provides a description of certain types of field extensions involving the adjunction of nth roots of elements of the base field. The theory was originally developed by Ernst Eduard Kummer around the 1840s in his pioneering work on Fermat's Last Theorem. The main statements do not depend on the nature of the field – apart from its characteristic, which should not divide the integer n – and therefore belong to abstract algebra. The theory of cyclic extensions of the field K when the characteristic of K does divide n is called Artin–Schreier theory.
title: Kummer theory

The probability of the event that none of the paths $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$ reaches its continuation threshold and that each of them intersects $\partial B_{\varepsilon}(0)$ is at most $C \varepsilon ^2$. body: [Theorem thm:trees-vertex-ramsey of arXiv:2609.00636, 'Forcing monochromatic subdivisions'] The family of trees is vertex-$R_\Delta$-bounded. More precisely, for every integers $d \ge 1$ and $s\ge2$ there is an integer $D$, depending only on $d$ and $s$, such that for every tree $T$ with $\Delta(T) \le d$ there is a graph $H$ with $\Delta(H) \le D$ in which every $s$-coloring of $V(H)$ contains a monochromatic copy of~$T$.

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2609.02065, '\textbf{From Bowditch's question to Goldman's conjecture for type-preserving representatio'] \cite[Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.8]{ryu} 
        Let $\Sigma = \Sigma_{g, p}$ with $g\geqslant 1$ and $p\geqslant 1$. Let $n\in \mathbb{Z}$ and $s\in \{+1,0, -1\}^p$. Then the space $\HP_n^s(\Sigma)$ is non-empty if and only if the pair $(n,s)$ satisfies the generalized Milnor-Wood inequality: 
        $$\chi(\Sigma) + p_+(s)\leqslant n\leqslant -\chi(\Sigma) - p_-(s).$$
        Each non-empty  $\HP_n^s(\Sigma)$ above is connected. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 29 (Pointwise lower bound under sparsity, edge-density control, and log-convexity) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\). Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph
with \(|V|=n\), and assume that for some \(\eta,\varepsilon>0\),
\[
e_G(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)|S|
\qquad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ with }|S|\le \eta n.
\]
Assume moreover that
\[
\frac{|E|}{n}\in [m_-,m_+]
\]
for some \(m_-,m_+>0\), and that
\[
m_->c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon).
\]
Then, for every
\[
t>
\frac{\theta\log\theta}{(\theta-1)\bigl(m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)\bigr)},
\]
one has
\[
\Pbb^G_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)
\ge
\frac{
m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)-\frac{\theta\log\theta}{(\theta-1)t}
}{
(1+\theta)m_+ - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)
}.
\]
title: Pointwise lower bound under sparsity, edge-density control, and log-convexity

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:46de0bb07cb8f702a4ba19ca39de48f71b4dd047b5ad0fb56b5b2501572fbba8","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/46/46de0bb07cb8f702a4ba19ca39de48f71b4dd047b5ad0fb56b5b2501572fbba8.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d95d8426b02f7b99f3c510421bdf82d04486a5f840319b624090deac8e2ec234","bundle_entry_key":"t336-w727-c010","bundle_id":"population.w727-t336-newton-gp-005","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"Transformers; finite-rank Gaussian-process Bayesian prediction","draft":"w727/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.transformers:draft-t336-w727-c010-newton-gp-mean-variance","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C010: explicit Newton GP transformer with matrix-token storage

Claim T336-w727-C010 v1. Target: 1. Kind: bound.
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty or independent audit is claimed.
This is a resource-explicit adaptation of known attention/Newton constructions
to the noisy GP mean and variance together. The additional p fixed tokens are
part of the stated model; no equality with C002's token budget is asserted.

## 1. Statement and model

Let p>=1, n>=0 be integers, s>0, B>=0, R>=0, eps>0. A zero-mean GP has
kernel k(x,x')=<phi(x),phi(x')>, with supplied features phi in R^p and
||phi(x)||_2<=R. Observation noises are independent N(0,s). The context
has l<=n observations, |y_i|<=B, and the query feature is q=phi(x_*).
No distributional assumption on the locations is needed for this pointwise
approximation theorem. For the context/query posterior, inputs are treated
as the fixed design of this GP regression model.

Put L=s+nR^2, kappa=L/s, M=nR^2 B/s. If R>0 and kappa>1, define

    delta=min(1/2, sqrt(s eps)/(1+M), s sqrt(2eps)/R^2),
    T=max(0,ceil(log_2(kappa log(1/delta)))).

If R=0 or kappa=1 use T=0 instead. There is a bidirectional residual
normalized ReLU-attention transformer with

    N=n+p+1 tokens, D=9p+4 coordinates per token,
    depth d=2T+3, at most four heads per layer,
    at most 12d D^2+2D dense attention/readout scalar parameters,

whose two outputs (mhat,vhat) define a Gaussian with vhat>=s and

    KL(N(m,v) || N(mhat,vhat)) <= eps

uniformly over the stated contexts and query features. Fixed token encoding
and selection of the output token are specified below. If every fixed
anchor/query positional constant is counted as a dense embedding table,
add at most (p+1)D scalars. No trainable encoder, MLP, softmax, layernorm,
causal mask, finite-precision model, or training guarantee is asserted.

The attention layer is precisely

    h_i^+=h_i+(1/N) sum_heads sum_j
                   ReLU(<Q h_i,K h_j>) V h_j.          (1)

All Q,K,V are D-by-D real matrices, fixed independently of the context.
The same transformer handles every l<=n by zero padding context slots.
For a GP weight-prior covariance tau^2 I, absorb tau into the supplied
feature map and its bound R before applying this statement.

## 2. Registers, input encoding and two head primitives

Each token has nine vector registers of length p, in this fixed order,

    E, F, q, G, X, Z, b, W, U,

followed by scalar registers y,c,a,v. Thus D=9p+4. Names here denote
coordinate projections, never a nonlinear operation within an encoding.

There are n context tokens, p anchor tokens and one query token. All
unmentioned registers start at zero.

* Context slot i<=l: F=phi(x_i), y=y_i. Slots i>l are all zero.
* Anchor j=1,...,p: E=e_j, G=s e_j, X=L^{-1}e_j.
* Query: q=phi(x_*), c=1, v=s.

This is a fixed linear embedding of the supplied features and labels plus
known positional constants. In particular feature-label products and the
context Gram matrix are not supplied as input.

For linear maps u,w from token space into the same R^r (r<=D) and a
linear map C from token space to itself, write Pair(u,w;C) for two heads:

    Q_+=pad(u), Q_-=-pad(u), K_+=K_-=pad(w),
    V_+=N C, V_-=-N C.

Pad means put the r outputs into the first r of D coordinates and zero
the rest. The combined residual increment from this pair at token i is
exactly

    sum_j <u(h_i),w(h_j)> C h_j.                        (2)

Indeed ReLU(t)-ReLU(-t)=t, and the V factors cancel 1/N. This holds
for signed inputs and labels without a positivity premise. Whenever C is
described as "F -> G", its only nonzero block copies source register F
into destination G; a coefficient or multiple blocks are stated explicitly.
Consequently every head below specifies concrete dense Q,K,V matrices.

One additional primitive, AnchorSelf(C), is a single head with
Q=K=pad(E), V=N C. Since E is e_j on anchor j and zero elsewhere, its
score is 1 exactly for equal anchor indices and 0 otherwise. It therefore
adds C h_i to anchor i only. This primitive uses the actual nonnegative
scores delta_ij, not an approximation to softmax selection.

No layer below writes E,F,q,y,c. Thus these fixed supports remain true
throughout all layers, which justifies every use of AnchorSelf and the
support arguments in the construction.

## 3. Initial Gram and right-hand-side layer: four heads

Use these two pairs in the SAME layer:

    Pair(E,F; F -> G),
    Pair(c,y; F -> b).

The first pair acts only on anchors, and only context sources contribute.
At anchor j, the new G is

    s e_j+sum_i <e_j,phi_i> phi_i=A e_j,
    A=s I_p+sum_i phi_i phi_i^T.

The second pair acts only on the query, where c=1. Its b becomes

    b=sum_i y_i phi_i.

G remains zero off the anchors; b remains zero off the query. X is still
X_0=L^{-1}I_p, stored column by column on the anchors. Z,W,U,a remain
zero and v is still s on the query. The two pairs read the old state and
write disjoint G and b registers, so their simultaneous implementation
does not use within-layer sequential updates.

## 4. Each Newton round: two layers, at most three heads

Suppose the columns of a matrix X_t are stored in anchor X registers,
G stores columns of A, and Z is zero. First apply

    Pair(X,E; G -> Z).                                (3)

At anchor i this adds sum_j (X_t)_{ji} A e_j=A X_t e_i
to Z. All other token Z registers remain zero, since their X is zero.

In the SECOND layer use both

    Pair(Z,E; -X -> X),
    AnchorSelf(C), where C sends X -> X and Z -> -Z.   (4)

All heads in (4) read the same state AFTER (3). At anchor i the pair
adds -sum_j (A X_t)_{ji} X_t e_j=-X_t A X_t e_i to X.
AnchorSelf adds the old X_t e_i to X and subtracts the old Z from Z.
Including the residual in (1), the resulting state is

    X_{t+1}=2X_t-X_t A X_t, Z=0.

No other registers are changed. Off-anchor X and Z stay zero. This
proves the round invariant by induction, without assuming exact inverses
or using a context-dependent head matrix. Repeating (3)-(4) T times
costs 2T layers. Three p-by-p working matrices G,X,Z occupy the p anchor
columns; embedding width remains linear in p while this matrix storage
uses O(p^2) scalar coordinates across tokens.

## 5. Two readout layers: four heads each

First use

    Pair(b,E; X -> W), Pair(q,E; X -> U).

Only the query has nonzero b or q. Its resulting registers are

    W=X_T b, U=X_T q,

and W,U remain zero on all other tokens. Then apply

    Pair(q,W; c -> a), Pair(q,U; s c -> v).

In these pairs only the query is a nonzero key source with c=1, and
only the query is a nonzero q target. Hence the query outputs are

    a=q^T X_T b, v=s+s q^T X_T q.

This second layer reads the W,U produced by the preceding layer; the
construction does not combine those dependent operations in one layer.
The final linear readout selects a and v of the fixed query token.

There is one initialization layer, 2T Newton layers and two readout
layers. Each uses at most four heads; pad unused heads by zero matrices.
The dense Q,K,V count is at most 3*4*d*D^2 and the two-output linear
readout adds 2D. All N, s and L factors in the displayed blocks are fixed
problem parameters. In particular the normalization factor is not hidden
in the input data or in a learned embedding.

More explicitly, every attention/readout matrix entry has absolute value
at most Wmax=N max(1,s): selectors have entries 0,+1,-1, and value
blocks have entries 0,+N,-N,+Ns,-Ns. Fixed input coordinates are bounded
by K0=max(1,R,B,s,1/L). These bounds can be used directly in the
parameter-cover recurrences of C006/C007, without an unspecified maximum
over an implemented solver's entries. Those statistical claims retain
their own task-law hypotheses and unaudited status.

## 6. Uniform Gaussian error budget

For a fixed context A is symmetric with sI<=A<=LI. Its exact noisy-GP
mean and variance are m=q^T A^{-1}b and v=s+s q^T A^{-1}q.
Let E_t=I-A X_t. Direct expansion gives E_{t+1}=E_t^2. Every X_t
is a polynomial in A, so on an eigenvalue lambda in [s,L],

    1-lambda X_t(lambda)=(1-lambda/L)^(2^t),
    0<=X_t<=A^{-1}.

For kappa>1 the operator norm of E_T is at most
(1-1/kappa)^(2^T)<=exp(-2^T/kappa)<=delta. The last inequality follows
from the choice of T even if kappa log(1/delta)<1, because then T=0
and 2^T=1>=kappa log(1/delta). For kappa=1, A=sI and X_0=A^{-1}
exactly. For R=0, all features vanish and all outputs are exact with T=0.

Consequently vhat>=s, vhat<=v, and for the nontrivial branch

    |m-mhat|<=||q|| ||A^{-1}-X_T|| ||b||<=M delta,
    0<=v-vhat<=R^2 delta,

where ||b||<=nRB and ||A^{-1}-X_T||<=delta/s. Put
z=(v-vhat)/vhat>=0. The exact forward Gaussian KL formula and
z-log(1+z)<=z^2/2 for z>=0 give

    KL=(z-log(1+z))/2+(m-mhat)^2/(2vhat)
       <= R^4 delta^2/(4s^2)+M^2 delta^2/(2s)
       <= eps/2+eps/2=eps.

The scalar inequality follows because the derivative of
z^2/2-z+log(1+z) is z^2/(1+z)>=0 and its value at zero is zero.
All reciprocal bounds use vhat>=s>0; delta is positive and its two
accuracy bounds apply simultaneously. There is no tail-probability or
independence multiplication in this deterministic error calculation.

For n=0, b=0, A=sI and the construction outputs N(0,s+||q||^2)
exactly. This explicitly checks that the query's latent prior variance
is retained even with empty context. Signed labels and features are
handled by (2), and all-zero padded slots contribute nothing.

[Definition 1 (Multispecies mixed Ising model) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let $N\geq 1$, $D\geq 1$ and $\Sigma_N=\{\pm 1\}^N$.
For all $\bmx\in\mathbb R^D$, define the covariance function
\[
    \xi(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \xi_k(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \sum_{\substack{\bm p\in\mathsf P_k}}
    \Delta_{\bmp}^2\prod_{d=1}^D x_d^{p_d}.
\]
where $\bmDelta=(\Delta_{\bmp}^2:\bmp\in\mathsf P_k,\, k\geq 1)$ is a family of nonnegative coefficients and
where
\[
    \mathsf P_k
    =
    \{\bmp=(p_1,\ldots,p_D)\in\mathbb Z_+^D:
      |\bmp|:=p_1+\cdots+p_D=k\}.
\]
We also assume that $\xi((1+\varepsilon)\bm{1})<\infty$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

For \(\sigma,\tau\in\SigN\), define the species overlap vector by
\[
    R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau)
    =
    \frac1N\sum_{i\in I_{N,d}}\sigma_i\tau_i,
    \qquad
    \bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)=(R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau))_{d=1}^D,
\]
where \(\bmI_N=\{I_{N,1},\ldots,I_{N,D}\}\) is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

The Hamiltonian of the \emph{multispecies mixed Ising model} is a centered Gaussian process
 \(H_N=(H_N(\sigma))_{\sigma\in\SigN}\)
with covariance
\[
    \mathbb E H_N(\sigma)H_N(\tau)
    =
    N\xi(\bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)),
    \qquad \sigma,\tau\in\SigN.
\]
title: Multispecies mixed Ising model

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2607.23401, 'Limit Theorems for the Pitman-Yor Frequency Spectrum'] For the two-parameter  Pitman-Yor model  
 we have the following limits as $n\to\infty$.
 First, 
 \be
 n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor x n^\alpha\rfloor} 
 \wh X_{in}^{(\nu f)}
 \todr Y_x^{(\nu,f)},
 \ee
where the $ \wh X_{in}^{(\nu f)}$ are i.i.d. with the distribution in \eqref{HM8} and $Y_x^{(\nu,f)}$ is  infinitely divisible with 
 characteristic function
\be
\EE\big(e^{\rmi \tau Y_x^{(\nu,f)}}\big)
=
\exp\Big(\frac{\alpha x}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}
  \int_{0}^1
 (e^{ \rmi\tau  y} -1 ) e^{\nu f(y)} y^{-\alpha-1} \rmd y\Big). 
\ee
This integral  is absolutely convergent, so each rv $Y_x^{(\nu,f)}$ has a continuous density.  Each $Y_x^{(\nu,f)}$  has support $(0,\infty)$.
A second limit is 
    \be
    \lim_{n\to\infty}
n\PP\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{\lf xn^\alpha\rf} \wh X_{in}^{(\nu f)}=n\Big)
=
 \frac{1}{2\pi } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\rmi \tau}
 \EE (e^{\rmi \tau Y_x^{(\nu,f)}}) \rmd \tau = f_{Y_x^{(\nu,f)}} (1),
 \ee
 where the RHS 
 is finite  and positive for each $\nu$, $f$ and $x$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 28 of arXiv:2607.13849, 'Rearranged Stochastic Heat Equation with an Entropy Gradient Structure'] Given a probabilistic set-up $(\Omega,\mathfrak{F},{\mathbb F}= \{\mathfrak{F}_t\}_{t\geq 0},\mathbb{P},(W_t)_{t\geq 0})$ as defined in Subsection \ref{Notations}, and an ${\mathcal F}_0-$measurable initial condition $X_0$ with values in ${\mathcal U}^2({\mathbb S})$ satisfying ${\mathbb E}[\| X_0\|^p_2] < + \infty$ for all $p \geq 1$, there exists a unique solution $(X_t,{\eta}_t)_{t\geq 0}$ to the RSHE~\eqref{RHSE2}  in the sense of Definition \ref{Defi 317}.
For every $T>0$, the law of $(X_t,W_t)_{0 \le t \le T}$ over $\mathcal{C}([0,T],\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{Sym}}^{-1}(\mathbb{S})\times L^2_{\rm Sym}(\mathbb{S}))$  is equal to the limit of the laws of the processes  $\{(X_t^{(h)},W_t)_{0 \le t \le T}\}_{{h \in T/{\mathbb N}^*}}$ given by \eqref{scheme0}, the space $\mathcal{C}([0,T],\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{Sym}}^{-1}(\mathbb{S})\times L^2_{\rm Sym}(\mathbb{S}))$  being equipped with the topology of uniform convergence. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

	\(t>0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^d\),
	\[
	c_1\left(t^{-\beta d/\alpha}\wedge \frac{t^\beta}{|x|^{d+\alpha}}\right)
	\leq G_t(x)\leq

	Equivalently,
	\[

	\qquad t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R^d .
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), T421-W706-029 version2. For separately bias-corrected deterministic Adam on a positive two-eigenvalue diagonal quadratic, with beta1=9/10,beta2=999/1000,epsilon=eta>0 outside sqrt,zero initial moments,and both initial positions nonzero, put r=sqrt(9/10),theta_-=(1-r)^2/(1/10),theta_+=(1+r)^2/(1/10). If both eigenvalues lambda_i are strictly between theta_- and theta_+, define omega_i in(0,pi) by cos(omega_i)=(19/10-lambda_i/10)/(2r). If 1,omega_1/pi,omega_2/pi are Q-linearly independent, the accumulation set of eta*C_active,t is exactly[min(lambda_1,lambda_2),max(lambda_1,lambda_2)] and eta*S_t tends to max(lambda_1,lambda_2)<38. Here P_i,t=sqrt(v_i,t+1/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon, C_active,t=sum(lambda_i*g_i,t^2/P_i,t^2)/sum(g_i,t^2/P_i,t), S_t=max(lambda_i/P_i,t), and g_i,t=lambda_i*x_i,t; active limits are along defined times. This applies to every eta>0 and every such start. The frequency hypothesis holds off countably many null curves in the open two-cap region. Proof uses the still-unaudited strict-subcritical global decay claim012v2. No p>1 asymptotic conclusion or exhaustive literature novelty claim follows.
Ordinary separate bias corrections; epsilon outside sqrt
Standard zero moments and nonzero positions in both coordinates
Both caps in the strict complex-root interval
Rational independence of 1,omega_1/pi,omega_2/pi

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4ea04c80416ecbc35e4576f1eef8894f5cd0011387c72495e3928e1ef02967ca","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4e/4ea04c80416ecbc35e4576f1eef8894f5cd0011387c72495e3928e1ef02967ca.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:db64c3208644752512103a70da7f0e06f668217bb42f82cd2926f3a22bdb238b","bundle_entry_key":"adam-oscillation-interval","bundle_id":"population.adam-subcritical-oscillation-018","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization and discrete dynamical systems","draft":"w706/bundle_018.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adaptive:adam-subcritical-two-frequency-active-curvature-accumulation-interval","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-029 v2; kind narrowed; target 1; proof (unaudited).

STATEMENT AND SCOPE
Run deterministic, separately bias-corrected Adam on
f(x)=(lambda_1*x_1^2+lambda_2*x_2^2)/2, lambda_i>0,
eta>0, epsilon=eta, b=9/10, d=999/1000, epsilon outside sqrt,
m_0=v_0=0, and both initial coordinates nonzero. Set
r=sqrt(b), theta_i=lambda_i, theta_-=(1-r)^2/(1-b),
theta_+=(1+r)^2/(1-b), and assume theta_-<theta_i<theta_+.
Define omega_i in (0,pi) by
cos(omega_i)=[1+b-(1-b)*theta_i]/(2*r).
Assume 1,omega_1/pi,omega_2/pi are linearly independent over Q.

Use P_i,t=sqrt(v_i,t+1/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon, g_i,t=lambda_i*x_i,t,
A_t=eta*sum(lambda_i*g_i,t^2/P_i,t^2)/sum(g_i,t^2/P_i,t),
S_t=eta*max(lambda_i/P_i,t). A is defined when the gradient is nonzero.
Then the accumulation set of A, along defined times tending to infinity,
is exactly [min(lambda_1,lambda_2),max(lambda_1,lambda_2)], and
S_t -> max(lambda_1,lambda_2). In particular A has no limit and
limsup A=max(lambda_1,lambda_2)<theta_+<38.
The assertion holds for every eta>0 and every specified nonzero start.

The same proof holds for arbitrary fixed positive eta,epsilon after
replacing theta_i by eta*lambda_i/epsilon throughout the conclusion and
the hypotheses. The epsilon=eta specialization addresses target 1 on
a full-measure subset of this open two-cap parameter region, not just
an isolated example. It does not address fixed-eigenvalue p>1 as eta->0.
No exhaustive novelty claim or independent verification is made.

HARDEST STEP AND DEPENDENCIES
The substantive prerequisite is strict-subcritical global geometric
decay in claim 012 v2, proofs/015_global_subcritical_critical.md. That
claim remains unaudited. The proof below supplies the previously unpaid
nonzero-amplitude argument; geometric coefficient convergence alone
must not be confused with a nonzero leading oscillation coefficient.
Torus density uses Beck--Chen--Yang, arXiv:2404.00077v1, Theorem 2,
printed p3, on the single-square torus; the definition of a Kronecker
vector is in Section 1, printed p1. Fong--Yang 2608.20638v2, Theorem
3.4, printed p7, assumes all caps >38 and does not state this result.

1. EXACT RECURRENCE AND GEOMETRIC ERROR
Write the corrected scalar update as
 m_(t+1)=b*m_t+(1-b)*lambda*x_t,
 v_(t+1)=d*v_t+(1-d)*lambda^2*x_t^2,
 x_(t+1)=x_t-a_t*m_(t+1),
 a_t=eta/[(1-b^(t+1))*(sqrt(v_(t+1)/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon)].
All a_t are strictly positive. Since theta_+<38, claim 012 gives
|x_t|+|m_t|<=C*q^t for some q<1 in each channel. The variance convolution
then obeys v_t<=C*kappa^(2t), for a possibly enlarged kappa<1:
choose kappa^2>max(d,q^2), which absorbs any resonance factor t.
The bias clocks decay geometrically as well. Hence, enlarging kappa
again if needed, a_t=eta/epsilon+O(kappa^t) and
a_t/a_(t-1)=1+O(kappa^t). Constants may depend on the fixed start.

For t>=1 eliminate m_t using m_t=(x_(t-1)-x_t)/a_(t-1):
 Y_(t+1)=A_t*Y_t, Y_t=(x_t,x_(t-1))^T,
 A_t=[[1+b*a_t/a_(t-1)-(1-b)*lambda*a_t, -b*a_t/a_(t-1)],
      [1,0]].
Thus A_t=A+O(kappa^t), where
 A=[[2*r*cos(omega),-b],[1,0]], det(A_t)=b*a_t/a_(t-1)>0.
Y_1 is nonzero since its second component is x_0!=0; invertibility
therefore makes every Y_t nonzero.

2. BALANCED POWERS AND A NONZERO LIMIT
Set S=[[r*cos(omega),r*sin(omega)],[1,0]]. Its determinant is
-r*sin(omega)!=0, and direct multiplication gives
 A*S=S*r*R, R=[[cos(omega),sin(omega)],[-sin(omega),cos(omega)]].
Consequently ||A^t||<=K*r^t and ||A^(-t)||<=K*r^(-t) for all t>=0.
Define Z_t=A^(-t)*Y_t. Then
 Z_(t+1)=(I+E_t)*Z_t,
 E_t=A^(-t-1)*(A_t-A)*A^t, ||E_t||<=C*kappa^t.
Every I+E_t is invertible. To spell out the infinite-product issue,
let Q_1=I and Q_t=(I+E_(t-1))*...*(I+E_1). The product norm is bounded
by product(1+||E_j||)<infinity. Its increments are summably bounded,
so Q_t converges. On a tail ||E_t||<=1/2, the Neumann-series bound
||(I+E_t)^(-1)-I||<=2||E_t|| implies bounded inverse products and
summably bounded increments of Q_t^(-1). The finite prefix is invertible.
Thus Q_t^(-1) converges too; multiplying the limits gives Q_infinity
invertible. In particular Z_infinity=Q_infinity*Z_1 is nonzero.
The tail sum gives Z_t=Z_infinity+O(kappa^t).

Since Y_t=A^t*Z_t, the first component is
 x_t=r^t*[B*cos(t*omega+phi)+O(kappa^t)], B>0.
Indeed, S^(-1)*Z_infinity is a nonzero real vector, and the first row
of S has norm r>0; its product with a rotating nonzero vector has
strictly positive sinusoidal amplitude. This establishes both channels'
nonzero leading coefficients without assuming a ratio x_(t+1)/x_t exists.

3. ALL AND ONLY THE INTERVAL
Write h_i(t)=B_i*cos(t*omega_i+phi_i)+O(kappa_i^t), so
g_i,t^2=b^t*lambda_i^2*h_i(t)^2. Also P_i,t -> epsilon.
The exact A_t is a convex combination of eta*lambda_i/P_i,t with
nonnegative weights g_i,t^2/P_i,t. Therefore every accumulation value
belongs to [min(theta_i),max(theta_i)], even on subsequences where the
two leading cosines simultaneously become small. The quotient is always
bounded at its defined times, so no other finite or infinite limits occur.

For the reverse inclusion, rational independence makes
(t*omega_1+phi_1,t*omega_2+phi_2) modulo pi dense, with arbitrarily late
visits to every open set. Kronecker--Weyl on the single-square torus
gives this for every phase offset. Given u between theta_1 and theta_2,
choose nonnegative weights w_1,w_2, w_1+w_2=1, with
u=theta_1*w_1+theta_2*w_2. Choose a sufficiently small constant L>0 so
L*w_i<=lambda_i^2*B_i^2 for each i, and phases alpha_i satisfying
lambda_i^2*B_i^2*cos(alpha_i)^2=L*w_i. At least one is nonzero.
There is an increasing sequence t_n with the two phases tending to
alpha_i modulo pi. Along it the scaled squared-gradient sum tends to
L>0. Thus A_tn is defined eventually, errors may safely be divided out,
and A_tn -> u. Endpoints are included by taking one weight zero.
No assertion of uniform division near simultaneous zero cosines is used.
Finally P_i,t -> epsilon directly gives S_t -> max(theta_i).

4. SIZE OF THE PARAMETER FAMILY AND LIMITS
Each nontrivial integer relation k_0+k_1*omega_1/pi+k_2*omega_2/pi=0
defines a null curve in the open square: omega'(theta)=(1-b)/
[2*r*sin(omega)]>0, and at least one of k_1,k_2 is nonzero.
The union is countable. Its complement has full two-dimensional measure
and is dense. Independence excludes equal caps, so the interval is
nondegenerate. These conclusions impose no Diophantine rate condition.
All nonzero starts are included, but no uniform quantitative attraction
rate over starts or frequency pairs is asserted. Rationally dependent
frequencies and endpoint/double-root caps require separate treatment.

body:
[Definition 11 (Regular feature) of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Fix $K_{\rm feat}>0$ and $\tau\ge0$.  A random vector
	$Z\in\R^N$ is called a
	$(K_{\rm feat},\tau)$-regular feature, if $\E[Z]=0$, $\Cov(Z)=\Sigma$ with
	$\lambda_{\Sigma}=\|\Sigma\|_{\op}>0$, and the following holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
		\item[$\mathrm{(F1)}$] For every fixed $\theta\in\R^N$,
		\[
		\|\langle Z,\theta\rangle\|_{L^4}^2
		\le K_{\rm feat}^2\lambda_{\Sigma}\|\theta\|_2^2.
		\]
		\item[$\mathrm{(F2)}$] For every fixed symmetric matrix
		$T\in\R^{N\times N}$,
		\[
		\Var\left(Z^\top TZ\right)
		\le \tau^2\|T\|_F^2.
		\]
	\end{enumerate}

[Lemma weakvsmera1 of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] We keep the previous notation. 
Let $\mu, \mu_n\! \in \!  \mathcal{M}^{\mathtt{era}}_f(T)$, $n\! \in \!  \mathbb{N}$. 

\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$] If $\mu_n \! \to \! \mu$ weakly in $\mathcal{M}_f(T^*)$, then $\mu_n \! \to \! \mu$ in the sense of mass erasure. The converse is not true in general (even if $\mu \! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_f(T)$: see Example (dilutestar of the paper)). 

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] If $\mu_n \! \to \! \mu$ in the sense of mass erasure, if $h_n \! \to h \! \in \!  \mathbb{R}^*_+$ and if $h'\! \mapsto T_{\! \mu, h'}$ is $d_{\mathtt{Haus}}$-continuous at $h$, then $d_{\mathtt{Haus}} (T_{\! \mu_n, h_n} , T_{\! \mu, h})\! \to \! 0$ and $\mathtt{P}_{T_{\! \mu_n, h_n}} \mu_n \! \to \! \mathtt{P}_{T_{\! \mu, h}} \mu $ weakly in $\mathcal{M}_f(T)$. 

\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma weakvsmera1 of arXiv:2608.09856

body:
[Corollary 5 (KL sampling guarantee for kTULA under LSI) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Assume \hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}--\hyperref[ass:LSI]{\textup{(A6)}}, and let $\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{\max}^{\mathrm{kTULA}}]$.
Then there exist constants $C_1,C>0$ such that, for all $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\R^d)$ and all $N\ge3$,
\begin{equation}
\KL\!\bigl(\mu\widehat P^N\,\big\|\,\pi_\beta\bigr)
\le
\KL\!\bigl(\mu\widehat P^N\,\big\|\,\mu P^N\bigr)
+
R_2\!\bigl(\mu P^N\,\big\|\,\pi_\beta\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $R_2(\cdot\|\cdot)$ denotes the R\'enyi divergence of order $2$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\KL\!\bigl(\mu\widehat P^N\,\big\|\,\pi_\beta\bigr)
\le
C\,\bigl((N\lambda)\vee\log N\bigr)\lambda^2
+
e^{-2C_{\mathrm{LSI}}N\lambda}\,R_2\!\bigl(\mu\,\big\|\,\pi_\beta\bigr).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm: main uninformative of arXiv:2605.19894, 'Sharp Spectral Thresholds for Multi-View Spiked Wigner Models'] Suppose that Assumptions~(assump:Gaussian Wigner of the paper)--(assump:irreducible-normalized-B of the paper)
    hold, and recall that $\sigma_+$ is the upper edge of the limiting bulk
    spectrum defined in~(equation eq:sigma-plus-def of the paper). Then $\sigma_+<1$ whenever
    $\mathsf{SNR}(\lambda,B)\neq1$, and the top eigenvalue of $H$ undergoes the
    following phase transition.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(i)] If $\mathsf{SNR}\rbr{\lambda,B}<1$, then no eigenvalue separates
        from the right edge of the bulk:
        \[
            \sigma_1(H)\xrightarrow{\mathbb P} \sigma_+ .
        \]

        \item[(ii)] If $\mathsf{SNR}\rbr{\lambda,B}>1$, then an outlier emerges at
        the point $1$:
        \[
            \sigma_1(H)\xrightarrow{\mathbb P} 1 .
        \]
        Moreover, with high probability as $n \to \infty$, this top eigenvalue is
        simple and separated from the rest of the spectrum: there exists
        $\rho\in[\sigma_+,1)$ such that $\sigma_2(H)\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}\rho$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm: main uninformative of arXiv:2605.19894

[Proposition of arXiv:2411.17109, 'On the maximal correlation of some stochastic processes'] Let $X$ and $Z$ be independent copies of $\alpha$-stable random variables with $0<\alpha<2$. Then the L\'{e}vy measure $\nu_{X}(x)\mathrm{d}x$ of $X$ has the following form:
\[\nu_{X}(x)\mathrm{d}x=\frac{c_{-}}{|x|^{1+\alpha}}1_{x<0}\,\mathrm{d}x+\frac{c_{+}}{|x|^{1+\alpha}}1_{x>0}\,\mathrm{d}x.\]
For all $\lambda<0$, we have
\begin{equation}
R(X,X+\lambda Z)=1/\sqrt{1+\frac{\min(c_{-},c_{+})}{\max(c_{-},c_{+})}|\lambda|^{\alpha}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:fourier-rep-fs of arXiv:2512.04371, 'Constructive Approximation under Carleman's Condition, \\ with Applications to Smoothed An'] Let 
\[ f(z) = \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} (iz)^{\alpha} f_{\alpha} \]
where each $f_{\alpha} \in B(\mathbb{R}^d)$, so $f_{\alpha}(z) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n} \int e^{i \xi \cdot z} d\rho_{\alpha}$ and $\rho_{\alpha}$ is a complex Radon measure. Let $r$ be the $L_2(\mu)$ orthogonal projection of $f$ onto any closed subspace and let
\[ \varphi(\xi) = \int e^{i \xi \cdot z} \bar r(z) \, d\mu(z). \] 
Then
\[ \|r\|_{\mu}^2 = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^n}  \sum_{|\alpha| \le k} \int  \partial^{\alpha} \varphi(\xi)\, d\rho_{\alpha}(\xi) \]

[Thm 5 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] Let $d$ be fixed. Suppose the base vector $\mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc, X_n)$ \begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
        \item has independent isotropic components with $\sup_n \max_{1\leq \alpha \leq n} \E X_\alpha^4 < \infty$ (as in \cref{thm:indep-tensor}); or 
        \item is an exchangeable and unconditional vector that satisfies the three conditions in \cref{thm:main}.
    \end{enumerate}
    Assume in addition that we have a real-valued random variable $R$, independent of $\mathbf X$.
    
    Consider $\mathbf x^{(1)},\dotsc,\mathbf x^{(m)} \in \R^p$ sampled independently from $\PrincipalT(n,d, R\cdot \mathbf X)$, and suppose $p / m \to c$ for some fixed $c > 0$. Then with probability $1$, the sample covariance matrix $K = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^m \mathbf x^{(k)} {\mathbf x^{(k)}}^\trp$ converges weakly to a weighted MP law $\mu$, which is uniquely determined by its Stieltjes transform \[
      s(z) = \frac{1}{\int_0^\infty \frac{x}{1 + c x s(z)}\,d\tau(x) - z},
    \] where $R^{2d} \sim \tau$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 5 of arXiv:2607.21759

[Lemma appendix lemma proof of asymptotic variance formula of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] Consider a strongly continuous Markov semigroup $(P_t)_{t \geq 0}$ on 
a measurable space with an invariant probability measure $\mu$.
Let \(K\subset L_0^2(\mu)\) be a closed \(P_t\)-invariant subspace, and
let \(L_K\) denote the generator of the restricted semigroup
\((P_t \vert_K)_{t\ge0}\).
Fix \(g\in K\). Suppose there exists \(f\in \operatorname{Dom}(L_K)\) such
that
\[
        -L_K f=g.
\]
Then the asymptotic variance of \(g\) exists and is given by
\[
        \sigma_g^2
        :=
        \lim_{t\to\infty}
        t\,\operatorname{Var}_\mu(\mu_tg)
        =
        2\operatorname{Re}\langle g,f\rangle .
\]
In particular, if the local gap defined in (equation gap definition invariant subspace of the paper)
satisfies $\gamma_K > 0$, then
\[
        \sigma_g^2
        =
        2\operatorname{Re}\langle g,-L_K^{-1}g\rangle .
\]

[Definition 9 ($S$-partite graph) of arXiv:2604.05138, 'Convergence rate of $H$-property for step-graphons'] Let $S$ be an undirected graph on $q$ nodes, possibly with self-loops.
A simple, undirected graph $G$ is {\bf $S$-partite} if there exists a graph homomorphism
$\pi :G \to S$. 
Further, $G$ is a \emph{complete $S$-partite graph} if
\[
(v_i, v_j) \in E(G)
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
(\pi(v_i), \pi(v_j)) \in E(S).
\]

body: Brouwer fixed-point theorem: Let K be a nonempty compact convex subset of R^n (n >= 1), and let f : K -> K be a continuous map. Then f has a fixed point, i.e. there exists x_0 in K with f(x_0) = x_0. The simplest cases are K = [a, b], a closed interval of real numbers, and K = D^n = {x in R^n : |x| <= 1}, the closed unit ball. Both hypotheses are needed: a rotation of the circle S^1 (compact but not convex) and a nonzero translation of R^n (convex but not compact) have no fixed points.
title: Brouwer fixed-point theorem

[Proposition 5 (Varadhan upper bound) of arXiv:2606.16083, 'Eyring--Kramers asymptotics for infinite-dimensional stochastic gradient systems'] For each $\beta>0$, let $\sigma_\beta$ be a probability measure on a separable
Banach space $B$,  let $h_\beta:B\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be measurable and  let
$J:B\to[0,\infty]$ have compact sublevel sets. 
Assume that $ \widetilde h_\alpha:=\inf_{\beta\ge\alpha} h_\beta $
is lower semicontinuous for every $\alpha>0$
and that
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]  $
   \varlimsup_{\beta\to\infty}
   \frac1\beta\log\sigma_\beta(C)
   \le
   -\inf_{x\in C}J(x) $   for every closed set $C\subset B$;
\item[(ii)] $h_\beta\to h$ uniformly on compact sets;
\item[(iii)]
$   \varliminf_{\beta\to\infty}\inf_{x\in B}h_\beta(x)>-\infty  $.
\end{itemize}
Then, for every closed set $C\subset B$,
\[
   \varlimsup_{\beta\to\infty}
   \frac1\beta
   \log\int_C e^{-\beta h_\beta}\,d\sigma_\beta
   \le
   -\inf_{x\in C}\bigl[h(x)+J(x)\bigr].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 18 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {}{}
    Let \(\{X_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) be a (time-homogeneous) Itô diffusion in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).  
The (infinitesimal) generator \(\mathcal{A}\) of \(X_t\) is defined by
\[
\mathcal{A} f(x) = \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\mathbb{E}^x[f(X_t)] - f(x)}{t}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}^d.
\]
The set of functions \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) such that the limit exists at \(x\) is denoted by \(D_{\mathcal{A}}(x)\), while \(D_{\mathcal{A}}\) denotes the set of functions for which the limit exists for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\).

    for some functions $T_i : \mathcal{X}_i \times \mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{pa}_{i}} \to \mathcal{Y}_i$. We call $T$ \emph{$G$-biadapted} if it is $G$-adapted, bijective, and its inverse is itself $G$-adapted.\\

body:
[Lemma lem:convergence of arXiv:2607.05671, 'Bi-infinite systems of singularly interacting Brownian particles and the KPZ equation'] Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Let $T > 0$, and suppose $f \in C([0,T) \times \mathbb{R})$ is such that for all $c \in (0,\infty)$ and $T' \in (0,T)$, 
\begin{equation} 
\sup_{(s,y) \in [0,T'] \times \mathbb{R}} e^{cy^+} |f(s,y)| < \infty.
\end{equation}
Then for all $m \in (0,\infty)$, 
$r \in [1,\infty)$ and $T' \in [0,T)$,
\begin{equation} 
\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} e^{m i}\mathbb{E}[\sup_{0 \leq s \leq T'}|f(s,X_i^\varepsilon(s))|^r]^{1/r} <\infty.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for all $m \in (0,\infty)$,
the sum 
\[
\sum_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} e^{m i} f(s,X_i^\varepsilon(s)), \quad s \in [0,T),
\]
converges uniformly on compact subsets of $[0,T)$, in $L^r(\mathbb{P})$, for all $r \in [1,\infty)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:convergence of arXiv:2607.05671

body:
[Definition def:local-direction of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Fix an integer $\ell\in\{2,\dots,n\}$.  
A random direction $\rho\in S_n$ with law $q_\ell$ is generated as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Sample a starting index $i$ uniformly from $[n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}$.
  \item For $r=0,1,\dots,\ell-1$, define
  \[
    i_r \;:=\; 1 + \bigl((i-1+r)\bmod n\bigr)\ \in\ [n].
  \]
  \item Let $\rho$ be the $\ell$--cycle on these indices,
  \[
    \rho \;:=\; (i_0\ i_1\ \cdots\ i_{\ell-1}),
  \]
  i.e.\ $\rho(i_r)=i_{r+1}$ for $r=0,\dots,\ell-2$, $\rho(i_{\ell-1})=i_0$, and
  $\rho(k)=k$ for all $k\notin\{i_0,\dots,i_{\ell-1}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
We write $\rho\sim q_\ell$. The law $q_\ell$ is state independent (i.e.,
$q(\cdot\mid\sigma)\equiv q_\ell$ for all $\sigma\in S_n$) and is orbit--equivariant
in the sense of Definition~(def:direction-law of the paper).
title: Local direction law $q_\ell$

[Prop prop_verification of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] Fix \(x\ge0\). 
    Let \(\widehat U:I_x\to\mathbb R\) be continuous on \(I_x\) and \(C^1\) on \((-x,\infty)\). Assume that \(\widehat U'\) extends to \(I_x\) and is absolutely continuous on every compact interval \([-x,r]\), \(r>-x\). Suppose that \(\widehat U\) satisfies (var_ineq_1 of the paper)--(var_ineq_3 of the paper) of subsection (subsec_var_ineqaulities of the paper) on \(I_x\), wherever \(\widehat U''\) exists. Suppose also that the candidate continuation region
    \[
        \widehat{\mathcal C}
        \coloneqq
        \{y\in I_x:\widehat U(y)<k_x(y)\}
    \]
    is contained in \((-x,R)\) for some \(R<\infty\). Then
    \(
        \widehat U(y)=U_x(y),\ y\in I_x,
    \)
    and an optimal stopping time is given by 
    \[
        \tau^*
        \coloneqq
        \inf\{t\ge0:Y_y(t)\notin\widehat{\mathcal C}\}.
    \]
title: Prop prop_verification of arXiv:2606.23648

[Proposition 13 (Explicit Poisson domination) of arXiv:2607.16833, 'Dynamical Equations for Poisson Galton--Watson Trees and Component Densities of Sparse Inh'] If $\lambda=uD<1$, then $T_u$ is stochastically dominated, uniformly in the root
type, by the total progeny $T^{(\lambda)}$ of a one-type Galton--Watson process
with $\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$ offspring.  Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_x\bE_{x,u}e^{\theta T_u}<\infty
 \quad\text{for every}\quad
 0\leq\theta<\lambda-1-\log\lambda.
\end{equation}
For $\lambda=0$ all exponential moments are finite.

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.28307, 'Rigidity of closed $\lambda$-self-expanders'] \cite{AncariCheng}
Let $x:M^n\to R^{n+1}$ be a smooth immersed closed $\lambda$-self-expander. Then,\\
(i)~ $\lambda\geq \sqrt{2n}$. Moreover, the sphere $\mathbb{S}^n(\sqrt{2n})$ is the only closed $\lambda$-self-expander with $\lambda=\sqrt{2n}$.\\
(ii)~ If $$S\leq -\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\lambda(\lambda-\sqrt{\lambda^2-2n})}{2n},$$ then $x$ is a sphere $\mathbb{S}^n(r)$ with $r=\lambda+\sqrt{\lambda^2-2n}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 6 of arXiv:2608.28307

[Lemma lem:uniform_bound of arXiv:2609.01984, 'Instantaneous shrinking of supports for stochastic PDEs\footnote{JY was supported by a KIA'] Let $\tau\le T$ be a bounded stopping time. Recall the parameters $\gamma$ and $p$ from Assumption (asp:sigma of the paper) and (equation eq:asp_initial_regularity of the paper), respectively. Assume in addition that one of the following conditions holds:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm (a)]
$p\gamma\ge1$ and
\[
    \mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{R}}u_0(x)\,\mathrm{d} x<\infty;
\]

\item[\rm (b)]
$p\gamma<1$, and for some $q>0$,
\[
    p\gamma>\frac1{q+1},
    \qquad
    \mathbb{E}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+x^2)^{q/2}u_0(x)\,\mathrm{d} x<\infty .
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists a constant $N>0$, independent of $n$, such that
\[
\sup_{n\ge1}
\mathbb{E}\left[
\sup_{\substack{0\le t\le\tau\\x\in\mathbb{R}}}v_n(t,x)
+
\sup_{\substack{0\le t\le\tau\\x\in\mathbb{R}}}w_n(t,x)
\right]
\le N .
\]

body:
[Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.30089, 'On the Coefficients of Hurwitz-Type Matrix Polynomials'] Let \(\kappa\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}\), and let
\((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\) be a sequence of complex
\(q\times q\) matrices. For each \(n\in\mathbb N_0\), define the
block Hankel matrix
\[
H_n^{(\widetilde s)}
:=
(\widetilde s_{j+k})_{j,k=0}^{n}.
\]

The sequence
\((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\)
is called \emph{Hankel positive definite} if
\(H_n^{(\widetilde s)}\) is Hermitian positive definite for every
\(n\le\kappa\).

A sequence \((P_k)_{k=0}^{\kappa}\) of complex
\(q\times q\) matrix polynomials is called a
\emph{monic left orthogonal system of matrix polynomials with respect
to \((\widetilde s_j)_{j=0}^{2\kappa}\)} if the following conditions
are fulfilled:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(I)]
\(\deg P_k=k\) for all \(k\in\mathbb Z_{0,\kappa}\).
\item[(II)]
The leading coefficient of \(P_k\) is \(I_q\).
\item[(III)]
\[
Z_n^{[P_j]}
H_n^{(\widetilde s)}
\bigl(Z_n^{[P_k]}\bigr)^*
=
0_{q\times q},
\]
for all \(j\neq k\), where
\(n=\max\{j,k\}\).
\end{itemize}
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2608.30089

[Defi kesten of arXiv:2607.01877, 'Coupling some conditioned L\'evy trees with the Kesten tree'] Let  $\psi$   be  a   branching  mechanism  satisfying~(equation eq:hyp-param of the paper)-(equation eq:grey of the paper).   Let
  $(h_i, {\mathcal T}_i)_{i\in  I}$ be the  atoms of  a Poisson point  measure on
  $\llbracket 0, \infty  \rrparenthesis \times  {\mathbb T}$ with intensity  ${\rm d} h \, {\mathbf N}^\psi[{\rm d}  {\mathcal T}]$ (and
  ${\mathbf N}^\psi$ given in~(equation eq:def-bN of the paper)).  The  Kesten tree ${\mathcal K}$, whose
  distribution is  denoted ${\mathbb P}^\psi$,  is a ${\mathbb T}$-valued  random variable
  defined as the infinite branch (or  spine) $\llbracket 0, \infty  \rrparenthesis$, on which the ${\mathcal T}_i$ are
  grafted at height $h_i$, that is:
\[
  {\mathcal K}= \llbracket 0, \infty  \rrparenthesis  \circledast_{i\in
    I}( {\mathcal T}_i,h_i).
\]

[Lemma lm:predual and ideal of arXiv:2609.00970, 'The unique predual problem for Lipschitz spaces, revisited'] Let $Y\subset\Lip_0(M)^*$ be a predual of $\Lip_0(M)$. Let $N\subset M$ be such that $0\in N$ and suppose that
\begin{enumerate}[label={\upshape{(\roman*)}}]
\item $\mathcal{I}({N})$ is closed in the weak topology $\sigma(\Lip_0(M),Y)$ induced by $Y$, and
\item $\mathcal{F}({N})$ is the strongly unique predual of $\Lip_0(N)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathcal{F}_M(N)\subset Y$.

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The all-one, or flat matrix, diagonalizes according to
$$\frac{1}{N}\begin{pmatrix}
1&\ldots&1\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
1&\ldots&1\end{pmatrix}=\frac{1}{N}\,F_N
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
&0\\
&&\ddots\\
&&&0\end{pmatrix}
F_N^*$$
where $F_N=(w^{ij})_{ij}$ with $w=e^{2\pi i/N}$ is the Fourier matrix, and $F_N^*=(w^{-ij})_{ij}$.
