body: [Lemma 11 of arXiv:2609.02701, 'Circuit Decompositions for Triangulations of Surfaces'] Let $S$ be a 3-divisible surface with weak labeling $\lambda$. Let $\sigma$ be one of its triangles. Then $S$ carries a unique (up to reversal) 2-circuit $v_0v_1\ldots v_n$ containing $\sigma$ such that $\lambda\{ v_i, v_{i+1}\}\ne 0$ for all $i$.

body:
[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved special case of Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution, the distribution of a sum of freely independent self-adjoint variables with the indicated laws, and * for classical convolution of independent real variables. Call lambda freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal probability measure nu. For every t>0 the centered Cauchy distribution C_t with density t/[pi(t^2+x^2)] is not freely strongly unimodal: some unimodal nu makes nu boxplus C_t nonunimodal. The proof combines the Cauchy convolution identity with Ibragimov's characterization of classical strong unimodality by log-concavity of the density; the Cauchy density is not log-concave. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
t>0.
The classical Ibragimov characterization for nondegenerate absolutely continuous laws.
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:19376a1848339d8e997d8383134fea49a30cedf22bc4dd49fd8f0af4f093ffb1","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/19/19376a1848339d8e997d8383134fea49a30cedf22bc4dd49fd8f0af4f093ffb1.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9d13417b75738e2fc15d10e3322f651494c6abbbfcb1c6c7d810fcc69a74ead5","bundle_entry_key":"hasebe-ueda-problem-3-11-cauchy-not-freely-strongly-unimodal","bundle_id":"population.probability-campaign-results-20260914-001","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-prob1000-nodes-1010/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.free:hasebe-ueda-problem-3-11-cauchy-not-freely-strongly-unimodal","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Write $C_t$ for the Cauchy law of scale $t$, with density $t/(\pi(t^2+x^2))$.

The whole point is an identity that is special to the Cauchy family. Its Cauchy transform is
$G_{C_t}(z) = 1/(z+it)$ on the upper half plane, so $K_{C_t}(w) = 1/w - it$ and the $R$-transform is the
constant $R_{C_t}(w) = -it$. Free convolution adds $R$-transforms, so for any $\mu$,
$$K_{\mu\boxplus C_t}(w) = K_\mu(w) - it \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_{\mu\boxplus C_t}(z) = G_\mu(z+it).$$
On the other side, the density of $\mu * C_t$ at $x$ is the Poisson integral
$\tfrac1\pi\int t\,d\mu(y)/((x-y)^2+t^2) = -\tfrac1\pi\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(x+it)$, so
$G_{\mu*C_t}(z) = G_\mu(z+it)$ as well. Hence
$$\mu \boxplus C_t \ = \ \mu * C_t \qquad\text{for every } \mu \text{ and every } t>0,$$
the free and classical convolutions with a Cauchy law coinciding.

Now the Proposition. The Cauchy density is not log-concave, so by Ibragimov's characterisation of
classically strongly unimodal laws, $C_t$ is not strongly unimodal: there is a unimodal $\nu$ with
$\nu * C_t$ not unimodal. By the identity, $\nu \boxplus C_t = \nu * C_t$ is not unimodal either, and

body:
[Corollary 108 (All-order generation from the least state) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $\tau=(\eta;\mathcal S_2,\mathcal S_1)$ be accessible, write
$\operatorname{ch}_\tau(z)=(x(z),A(z),q(z))$, and put
\[
 \mathsf Q_\eta
 :=C_0^{0,2\eta}\bigl([0,T];\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa}\bigr)
\]
with its natural truncations.  The projective
families
\[
 \mathbf S^{S,\infty}:=(\mathbf S^{S,N})_{N\ge2},
 \qquad
 \mathbf S^{I,\infty}:=(\mathbf S^{I,N})_{N\ge2},
\]
endowed with the projective-limit topologies generated by their finite-degree
Hilbert-tensor projections, are stable-causal readouts of $Z_\tau$.

\textup{(i) Geometric quotient.}
Let $\pi_{\rm geom}(z):=(x(z),A(z))$, with the image topology and induced
truncations.  The geometric tower factors through $\pi_{\rm geom}$ and is a
lossless representation of precisely this quotient.  Its degree-one and
degree-two coordinates give the stable-causal decoder
\[
 x=\pi_1\mathbf S^{S,\infty},
 \qquad
 A=\Anti\pi_2\mathbf S^{S,\infty}.
\]
Consequently a causal source state $S$ realizes the geometric tower if and only
if $\pi_{\rm geom}(Z_\tau)\preceqsc S$.  The covariance path is not determined
by this tower.

\textup{(ii) Lossless augmented towers.}
For $\bullet\in\{S,I\}$, define
\[
 \mathcal T^\bullet(z)
 :=\bigl(\mathbf S^{\bullet,\infty}(z),q(z)\bigr)
\]
and equip its image with the topology inherited from the product of the
projective tower space and $\mathsf Q_\eta$.  Then $\mathcal T^\bullet$ is a
stable-causal homeomorphism onto its image.  A stable-causal decoder is
\[
 \mathcal D^\bullet(\mathbf s,q)
 :=\operatorname{ch}_\tau^{-1}
   \bigl(\pi_1\mathbf s,\Anti\pi_2\mathbf s,q\bigr),
 \qquad
 \mathcal D^\bullet\mathcal T^\bullet=I.
\]
Thus both augmented towers are lossless representations of the complete
state.

\textup{(iii) Algebraic recovery from the It\^o tower.}
The unaugmented It\^o tower determines $q$ algebraically through
\[
 q=x^{\otimes2}-\pi_2\mathbf S^{I,\infty}
   -\bigl(\pi_2\mathbf S^{I,\infty}\bigr)^*.
\]
In infinite dimension this formula does not in general define a continuous
decoder from the standard projective Hilbert-tensor topology to the
$\mathcal S_1$ state topology.  The explicit $q$ coordinate in
$\mathcal T^I$ retains this trace-class topology.  It may be omitted when the
declared covariance range has equivalent $\mathcal S_2$ and $\mathcal S_1$
topologies, in particular when $H$ is finite dimensional.

\textup{(iv) Least-state consequence.}
For every causal source state $S$ and either $\bullet\in\{S,I\}$,
\[
 S\text{ jointly realizes }\mathcal T^\bullet(Z_\tau)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 Z_\tau\preceqsc S.
\]
Hence $Z_\tau$ remains the unique least sufficient state for every response
program containing either augmented tower and whose remaining responses are
stable-causal readouts of $Z_\tau$.

body: Let f be in L^1(R^n) and let f-hat(xi) = integral over R^n of f(x) exp(-2 pi i x . xi) dx be its Fourier transform. Then f-hat(xi) tends to 0 as |xi| tends to infinity. The same conclusion holds for the Fourier coefficients of an L^1 function on the circle: the coefficients tend to 0 as the frequency tends to infinity. [standard, e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Fourier Analysis]

Suppose that its transition tensor $\cal P$ is regular. \lim_{k \rightarrow \infty} {\cal P}^{(k)}=\pi \otimes \underbrace{e \otimes \cdots \otimes e}_{m-1}.

[Theorem thm:markovian-2bsde of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Let $w$ be a regular weight of order $\alpha$, where $0\leq\alpha<1$.  Assume
Assumptions~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper),
(ass:drift-multiplier of the paper), (ass:lipschitz-driver of the paper), and
(ass:differentiable-driver of the paper) at the same order $\alpha$.  Suppose
$C_w(X)<\infty$, $\delta_{\mathrm{sg}}>0$, $\psi\in H^2(\mu_T)$, and
$f_0\in L_0^2$.  Then the unique order-$\alpha$ weighted Sobolev solution
$u^*$ and its source $F^*=F_{u^*}$ determine a unique regular fixed-reference
Markovian 2BSDE solution in the sense of
Definition~(def:regular-markovian-2bsde of the paper), namely
\begin{equation*}
 u=u^*,\qquad p=D_xu^*,\qquad H=D_x^2u^*,\qquad
 \mathfrak A_t=-\int_0^t\mathfrak g[u^*,F^*](s,X_s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation*}
Thus the derivative identities and absolute continuity of $\mathfrak A$ are
consequences of the two dynamics.
title: Theorem thm:markovian-2bsde of arXiv:2608.16119

[Thm main-order-m of arXiv:2607.17048, 'Concentration Inequalities for Incomplete U-statistics over Arbitrary Sampling Graphs'] Suppose for every $e=(i_1, i_2,\ldots,i_m)\in E$, there exists $\sigma_e>0$ such that 
\begin{equation} 
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[e^{\lambda \{h_e(X_{i_1}, \ldots, X_{i_m})-\mathbb{E}h_e(X_{i_1}, \ldots, X_{i_m})\}}\Bigr]\leq e^{\lambda^2\sigma_e^2/2}, \qquad\mbox{for all $\lambda>0$}. 
\end{equation}
If there exists a proper $K$-edge-coloring of $G$, then for all $t>0$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}(U-\mathbb{E}U>t)\leq \exp\biggl\{ - \frac{t^2}{2K\sum_{e\in E}\sigma_e^2}\biggr\}. 
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary cor:spectral-sandwich of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] Combining Theorems~(thm:spectral-upper of the paper) and~(thm:spectral-lower of the paper),
for any reversible chain:
\[
  \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2
  - \frac{1}{6}\sum_x\pi(x)\,T_3(x)
  \;\le\;
  I(X_0;X_1)
  \;\le\;
  \sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2.
\]
When $\max_{x,y}|g(x,y)|\le C$ for a constant $C$ independent of $n$, one
has $\sum_x\pi(x)T_3(x) \le C\sum_{i\ge 2}\lambda_i^2$, so the lower bound
simplifies to
$I(X_0;X_1) \ge (1/2 - C/6)\sum_{i\ge 2}\lambda_i^2$,
which is positive when $C < 3$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Two-sided spectral bounds

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2506.17470, 'The coalescent of a sample from a linear-fractional branching process'] Let $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and $y\in (0,1)$. Denote by $\{H_{k,i}, 0\le i < k\}$ and $\{H_{y,i}, 0\leq i< K\}$ the node depths of \textnormal{$\textbf{T}_{k}$} and \textnormal{$\textbf{T}_y$}, respectively. Let $x_0=T$ and $x_1,\dots, x_{k-1}\in\{1,2,\dots, T\}$. Then
$$\mathbb{P}(H_{k,0}=x_0,\dots, H_{k,k-1}=x_{k-1} \mid N_T \ge k)= \int_0^1 \mu_k(\mathrm{d}y) \mathbb{P}(H_{y,0}=x_0, \dots, H_{y,k-1}=x_{k-1}\mid K=k).$$

body:
[Definition def:gamma of arXiv:2606.06612, 'The limit shape and emergence of the \ Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $\phi$ be any $\mathbb Z$-valued height function on a domain $V \subset \mathbb Z^2$. Associate to each bond $e\in (\mathbb Z^2)^*$, dual to some edge $(x,y)\in\mathbb Z^2$, the gradient $(
abla \phi)_e := \phi_x - \phi_y$, where $x$ is taken to be the 	extsc{north} vertex if $(x,y)$ is vertical and the 	extsc{west} vertex if $(x,y)$ is horizontal. Call $e$ a \emph{disagreement bond} of $\phi$ if $(
abla\phi)_e
eq 0$. A \emph{disagreement polymer}~$\gamma$ is a (maximal) connected component of the disagreement bonds of $\phi$. For such a polymer, let $D_i$ be the connected components of $V \setminus \gamma$. By construction, within each $D_i$, all the vertices that are $*$-adjacent to $V\setminus D_i$ must have the same height $h_i$ in~$\phi$. Hence, we can view each $\gamma$ as a triple $(\gamma, \{D_i\}, \{h_i\})$, and it makes sense to talk about the components $D_i$ of $\gamma$ and their corresponding heights $h_i$.
title: Disagreement polymer

[Lemma lem:neumann-ground-state-mixing of arXiv:2607.04264, 'Macroscopic Feynman Cycles and Poisson--Kingman Universality in Bose Condensation'] Let \(\varepsilon_2^N>0\) be the first positive Neumann eigenvalue of
\(-\Delta_Q^N\).  Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item For every \(t_0>0\), there exists \(C<\infty\) such that, for all
\(t\ge t_0\) and \(r,s\in\overline Q\),
\[
  \left|
    p_t^{Q,N}(r,s)-1
  \right|
  \le
  C e^{-\varepsilon_2^N t}.
\]

\item Let \(F,G\) be bounded measurable functionals depending only on time
windows of length at most \(2T\).  Then there exist constants
\(C_{F,G},c_{F,G}>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(S\),
\[
\left|
  \operatorname{Cov}_{S}^{N,\mathrm{loop}}
  \bigl(
    F(\theta_uY),
    G(\theta_vY)
  \bigr)
\right|
\le
  C_{F,G}
  \exp\{-c_{F,G}(d_S(u,v)-4T)_+\},
\]
where
\[
  d_S(u,v)=\min\{|u-v|,S-|u-v|\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:92dc99dd38187032ea54bae2ceacb02d5e5898e7136f2355e14dcdba298baf54","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/92/92dc99dd38187032ea54bae2ceacb02d5e5898e7136f2355e14dcdba298baf54.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e46b93d5bf149b2fff836bcc7c52bd70b1d1130f4c72842e2b881bd3fbe0cbc1","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c04","bundle_id":"population.t309-equilateral-ddpm-symmetry-breaking-drafts","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability, score matching, Gaussian mixture learning","draft":"w721/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:known-plane-equilateral-gaussian-empirical-ddpm-orbit-augmentation","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T309: empirical DDPM GD for a restricted equilateral family

T309-w721-C04 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. This is a restricted instance of Target 2, not its general solution.

## Precise statement and extra information used

Fix an absolute R>=1, which may be chosen as a large constant. In a known two-dimensional plane P in R^d, consider the equal-weight mixtures

    q_phi = (1/3) sum_{j=0}^2 N(R R_phi u_j,I_d),

where u_j are unit equilateral vectors and phi is unknown. The centroid is known to be zero; the plane, radius, equal weights, and component covariance are known. The component separation is sqrt(3) R. The orientation is the only unknown geometric parameter of this family.

There is a fixed absolute noise level t>0 (depending on the fixed R) and a procedure using full ordinary GD on the three means in the Shah--Chen--Klivans Eq. (9) student, on an orbit-augmented empirical DDPM objective, such that for every d>=2 and 0<epsilon<1 it returns a mixture within TV epsilon of q_phi with probability at least 2/3. Its sample size and real-arithmetic runtime are polynomial in d and 1/epsilon. A complete bit-complexity implementation is not asserted. The initialization is an equilateral triple of noisy radius a=R exp(-t) with a uniform random angle in P. It is independent of phi and of the samples, and it need not be a componentwise warm start.

This theorem does NOT cover an arbitrary i.i.d. Gaussian initialization, unknown plane or radius, unequal weights, nonequilateral centers, or unaugmented empirical DDPM GD. The use of a finite symmetry orbit of each sample is part of the stated training procedure.

## 1. The algorithm and exact empirical invariance

Choose a fixed positive absolute a small enough for C03, with a<R, and set t=log(R/a). Put sigma=sqrt(1-exp(-2t))>0. Given independent pairs (X_i,Z_i), where X_i~q_phi and Z_i~N(0,I_d), let Y_i=exp(-t) X_i+sigma Z_i.

Let Q rotate P by 2pi/3 and fix P-perpendicular. Let S fix P and negate P-perpendicular. The finite orthogonal group G generated by Q and S has order at most six (for d=2, S is the identity and the order is three). Define the empirical objective

    Lhat(m)=(1/(n |G|)) sum_i sum_{g in G}
               ||s_m(g Y_i)+g Z_i/sigma||^2.                     (1)

Initialize m_j=a R_Theta u_j in P, with Theta uniform, independently of all data and noise. Perform equal-step Euclidean GD on all three m_j using (1), for the deterministic number of steps specified below. Divide the final means by exp(-t), and return their equal-weight identity-covariance Gaussian mixture.

Because the augmented sample multiset is exactly invariant under G, (1) has the same rotation and perpendicular-reflection invariances as the population objective. Label-permutation invariance also holds. The fixed-point argument of C02 therefore shows that every empirical GD iterate is exactly of the form

    m_j=Q^j z,   z in P.                                          (2)

This is a conclusion about ordinary updates in the unrestricted mean space. No projection or constrained optimizer is inserted. The dependence among augmented samples within one orbit causes no problem: the n underlying pairs remain independent, and the orbit average is one function of each independent pair.

Every g preserves the joint law of (X_i,Z_i), because the teacher has the specified symmetry and the denoising noise is isotropic and independent. Thus E Lhat=Lpop. In particular the expected augmented objective is exactly the original DDPM population objective, up to the same score-risk constant as before.

## 2. A uniform gradient estimate with polynomial sample complexity

On the invariant space (2), regard the loss as a function of the two planar coordinates z, and write ell(z,W_i) for the orbit-averaged single-pair loss. Parameter-independent terms may be subtracted. Let the parameter domain D be the planar ball ||z||<=2a. Its population gradient is the gradient of the loss studied in C03, including the threefold parameterization factor.

There is a nonnegative random envelope M(W) with finite second moment, whose distribution and moments are independent of d, satisfying

    sup_{z in D} (||grad_z ell(z,W)||+||Hess_z ell(z,W)||) <= M(W). (3)

To see this explicitly, for planar means the perpendicular part of every student score is -Y_perpendicular. Its contribution to the restricted loss is independent of z. The only derivatives are those of

    b_z(y)=sum_j softmax_j(y dot Q^j z-||z||^2/2) Q^j z,

where y=projection_P Y. The common norm term cancels; differentiating softmax once or twice gives polynomials in y and bounded means, multiplied by products of weights in [0,1]. The planar residual in the DDPM loss is bounded by C(1+||y||+||projection_P Z||/sigma). Consequently (3) holds, for example, with

    M(W)=C(1+||projection_P Y||+||projection_P Z||)^6,

where C depends only on fixed a,t. The projected variables are a two-dimensional Gaussian mixture and a two-dimensional Gaussian, jointly correlated but with every fixed polynomial moment finite. In particular E M^2<infinity independently of d. No concentration statement here requires those two projections to be independent.

Here is an elementary quantitative uniform law, avoiding an unproved concentration assertion. Choose a deterministic constant K>1+E M. Chebyshev's inequality makes (1/n)sum_i M(W_i)<=2K with probability at least 1-1/48 for all sufficiently large n bounded by an absolute constant. On this event the empirical gradient is 2K-Lipschitz, while the population gradient is K-Lipschitz by (3). For 0<tau<1, choose a net of D of mesh tau/(12K); its cardinality is at most C tau^(-2), since D is a ball in two dimensions. At each net point and for each of the two gradient coordinates, Chebyshev's inequality, using (3), gives

    P(|empirical coordinate-population coordinate|>tau/4)
         <= C/(n tau^2).

The union bound over the net and both coordinates is at most C/(n tau^4). Take n>=C_0 tau^(-4) with C_0 large enough that this is at most 1/48 and also the envelope-average failure is at most 1/48. At every net point the Euclidean gradient error is at most sqrt(2) tau/4<tau/2. Moving to the nearest net point changes the error by at most 3K tau/(12K)=tau/4. Therefore, with probability at least 23/24,

    sup_{z in D} ||grad_z Lhat-grad_z Lpop|| <= tau.                (4)

The loose failure bound 23/24 includes both failures. The estimate requires n polynomial in 1/tau and is uniform in d. It is stated for a fixed training set reused at all GD steps, so it already handles adaptive iterates; no false multiplication of conditional probabilities is involved.

## 3. Finite-horizon coupling is polynomial at a fixed high-noise radius

Use a fixed step h>0 meeting C03, for instance h=h_0/(2a^2). Because a is fixed, h is an absolute constant for this family. Let delta=pi/36<1/10. Under a uniform angle, the population initialization lies at least delta from all three unstable angles with probability 11/12.

For those angles, C03 supplies a deterministic horizon

    T<=C_1(1+log(1/epsilon))                                      (5)

at which the population noisy means are within a epsilon/(10R) of the corresponding teacher means. Constants absorb the prescribed fixed R and a. If necessary increase T to at least one and choose the population accuracy slightly smaller than the displayed tolerance.

The population iterates remain within 1/10 of radius a. On the whole ball D the restricted population gradient has a finite Lipschitz constant L, independent of d. This follows either directly by the envelope (3) or by smoothness and the exact two-dimensional reduction. No sharp a-dependent Hessian estimate is needed here since a is fixed.

Under the tied parameterization (2), a full mean GD step is a z-update of size h/3: the metric is sum_j ||d(Q^j z)||^2=3||dz||^2. Put B=1+(h/3)L>=1, and choose

    tau=min(1/2, a epsilon/(100 R h T B^T)).                       (6)

On event (4), a population iterate z_k and an empirical iterate zhat_k with the same initialization obey, as long as both stay in D,

    ||zhat_{k+1}-z_{k+1}||
       <= B||zhat_k-z_k||+(h/3)tau.

Starting with difference zero, induction bounds every difference through T by

    (h/3) tau T B^T <= a epsilon/(300R).                          (7)

This also proves the domain condition in the induction: population radii are in [0.9a,1.1a] and the bound in (7) is less than a/100. Thus every empirical iterate is strictly inside D. Since D is convex, the Lipschitz estimate applies to the segment between the two iterates. The induction is not assuming its own conclusion.

Although B^T is exponential in T, (5) implies

    B^T <= C_2 epsilon^(-C_1 log B).

The exponent is an absolute constant for this fixed family. Hence tau^(-1), the sample size n>=C_0 tau^(-4), and the number of arithmetic operations are all polynomial in 1/epsilon and d. Factors of T contribute only powers of 1+log(1/epsilon). This argument does not give a polynomial joint bound when a is an additional vanishing parameter; fixing a before epsilon is essential.

Combining (7) with the population endpoint gives matched noisy-mean error less than a epsilon/(2R). Rescaling by R/a gives matched original-mean error less than epsilon/2.

## 4. Success probability and TV conversion

The good initial-angle event has probability 11/12, and (4) has probability at least 23/24. Their simultaneous probability is at least 7/8 by the union bound, exceeding 2/3. This does not depend on assuming independence between a sample-dependent iterate and its training set.

For matching means mu_j and muhat_j with identity covariance, convexity of TV under mixtures and Pinsker's inequality give

    TV((1/3)sum_j N(mu_j,I),(1/3)sum_j N(muhat_j,I))
       <= (1/3)sum_j ||mu_j-muhat_j||/2.

The last inequality uses KL(N(mu,I)||N(muhat,I))=||mu-muhat||^2/2. Thus the mean-error endpoint is more than enough for TV epsilon. No diffusion sampling-discretization guarantee is needed: the returned law is an explicit three-Gaussian mixture.

## 5. Arithmetic and implementation model

This is a real-arithmetic statement with exponential evaluations, as in the population gradient formulas. A finite-precision implementation would need to evaluate the two-coordinate equivariant gradient with an error budget no larger than tau/2 and preserve the known symmetry through its representation. The same finite-horizon coupling would control that error. A complete bit-complexity implementation and its exact symmetry representation are not supplied here; no bounded-precision SQ conclusion follows from this result as written.

## What remains unpaid

The theorem is deliberately confined to a family whose symmetry is known before looking at the samples. It does not estimate the plane or radius. An approximate plane or a generic three-vector initialization no longer lies in the exact fixed-point subspace; the resulting extra directions need a new stability argument. Finite orbit augmentation has also changed the empirical training procedure and must be retained in the claim. The general Target 2 asks for more than this result supplies.

body:
Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) U(t) is unitary for every t ∈ ℝ and satisfies the group law on all of ℝ; (ii) t ↦ U(t)x is continuous (weak continuity or, on a separable space, weak measurability suffices, but some regularity is required); (iii) the generator is self-adjoint. What fails. Without any continuity: pick a discontinuous additive function φ: ℝ → ℝ (a Hamel basis construction) and set H = ℂ, U(t) = e^{iφ(t)}. This is a one-parameter group of unitaries with U(0) = 1, but φ is non-measurable and unbounded on every interval, so U(t) is not of the form e^{ita} for any real a; no generator exists. Hence 'one-parameter unitary group' without a continuity hypothesis carries no spectral information. Overshooting in the other direction: if one assumes t ↦ U(t) is continuous in operator norm, then the generator is necessarily bounded, so norm continuity is the wrong hypothesis for Schrodinger evolutions, where A is unbounded. With a symmetric but not self-adjoint generator: on L²(0, ∞) the right translation semigroup (T(t)f)(x) = f(x − t) for x > t, 0 for x ≤ t, is a C_0-semigroup of isometries that is not a group (T(t) is not surjective), and its generator is A = −d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0}, i.e. A = −iS with S = −i d/dx closed and symmetric with deficiency indices (1, 0). There is no unitary group whose generator extends S, so exponentiating a symmetric operator to 'e^{itS}' is not legitimate: only self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness followed by taking the closure) licenses the unitary group. Audit rule: in quantum dynamics arguments, check that the Hamiltonian has been shown self-adjoint on a stated domain before using e^{itH}, unitarity, conservation of norm, or invariance of D(H).

[Proposition malliavin-estimate of arXiv:2412.04013, 'Rate estimates for total variation distance with applications\thanks{The author gratefully'] Let $I$ be an arbitrary
index set. Let $q\geq 1$ be an integer and
let $F_{i}\in (\mathbb{D}^{q+2,\infty})^{d}$, $i\in I$ be a family of functionals
with corresponding Malliavin matrices $\sigma_{i}$.
Let 
$$
C_{r}^{\sigma}:=\sup_{i\in I}E[|\mathrm{det}(\sigma_{i})|^{-r}]<\infty,
$$
as well as
$$
C_{r}^{F}:=\sup_{i\in I}\Vert F_{i}\Vert_{q+2,r}<\infty,
$$
hold for all $r\geq 1$. Then $F_{i}$ has a continuous density $f_{i}$
with respect to the $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure,
and for all $l\geq 1$ we have
\begin{equation}
\max_{|\alpha|\leq q}\sup_{i\in I}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\partial_{\alpha} f_{i}(x)|(1+|x|)^{l}\leq \bar{C}_{q,l}
\end{equation}
for some finite $\bar{C}_{q,l}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition malliavin-estimate of arXiv:2412.04013

[Cor topo of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $z_1, \dots, z_n$ be distinct points in $D$. Let $A \subseteq D$ be a closed connected set not containing any of the $z_j$, such that $D \setminus A$ has countably many connected components,  the boundary of each connected component is a Jordan curve, and for every $\varepsilon > 0$ only finitely many of these curves have diameter more than 
$\varepsilon$. 
Let $(A_m)_{m \geq 1}$ be closed sets that converge to $A$ in the sense that $A_m$ converges to $A$ in the Hausdorff distance, as do the outer boundary and all boundaries of the connected components of $z_1, \dots, z_n$ in $D\setminus A_m$. 

Then there exists a closed path $\gamma \subseteq A$ with $\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\gamma}(z_j) \text{ odd}$ and $\gamma \cap \bigcup_{j=1}^n\mathbb{D}(z_j, \varepsilon_j) = \emptyset$ if for all $m \geq m_0$ the same holds for some $\gamma \in A_m$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Cor topo of arXiv:2604.15146

[Dfn 222 (Lipschitz algorithms) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\cA$ as in \eqref{eq:algorithms-as-maps},
we say that $\cA$ is an \textbf{$L$-Lipschitz algorithm} if it satisfies the following two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]\item 
$\cA$ defines an $L$-Lipschitz mapping, that is,
    \[
        \Big\|\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})-\cA(\bG',(\bg')^{\aux})\Big\| 
        \le L \Big\|(\bG,\bg^{\aux}) - (\bG',(\bg')^{\aux})\Big\|\,,
    \]
where $\|\cdot\|$ always refers to Euclidean norm unless specifically indicated otherwise.
    \item 
    We have 
    $\bbE[\|\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})\|^2] = N$.
\end{enumerate} We say $\cA$ is a \textbf{deterministic $L$-Lipschitz algorithm} if it satisfies the above conditions with $\cA=\cA(\bG)$, i.e., without dependence on any auxiliary randomness $\bg^\aux$.
title: Lipschitz algorithms

body: In statistics, the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem provides sufficient conditions for the existence of a best unbiased estimator in a statistical model. The theorem states that any unbiased estimator for a quantity that depends on the data only through a complete, sufficient statistic is the unique uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator (UMVUE) of that quantity. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem is named after Erich Leo Lehmann and Henry Scheffé, given their two early papers.
title: Lehmann–Scheffé theorem

[Defi def_indivGraph of arXiv:2411.16464, 'Generating social networks with static and dynamic utility-maximization approaches'] For a given individuals space $\mathcal{I}$ and a given individuals set $\mathscr{I} \in \mathcal{I}^I$, an \textbf{individual graph} is a 3-tuple $\mathcal{G}(\mathscr{I} , \alpha, C)$ with $\alpha, C$ two vectors of $(\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+})^{n_I}$ and $(\mathbb{R}_{+})^{n_I}$) with $n_I=\binom{I}{2} = \frac{I^2-I}{2}$ :
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\alpha$ is a \textbf{weight list}. $$\alpha = (\alpha_{1,2}, \hdots, \alpha_{1,I},  \alpha_{2,3}, \hdots, \alpha_{2,I}, \hdots,\alpha_{I-1,I} )^T$$
    with $\alpha_{i,j}$ the edge weight between agent i and j
    \item $\chi(i,j) = \innerproduct{P_i}{P_j}\mathbbm{1}(i\neq j)$ is the \textbf{compatibility function}, with $(i,j)\in \mathscr{I}^2$ and $P_i$ the first component of i (in $\mathcal{E}$).
    \item $C$ is a \textbf{compatibility list} $$C = (c_{1,2}, \hdots, c_{1,I},  c_{2,3}, \hdots, c_{2,I}, \hdots,c_{I-1,I} )^T$$ with $c_{i,j} = \chi(i,j) = \innerproduct{P_i}{P_j}$.
    
\end{itemize}

On each graph is defined $d : \mathcal{I}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{N}$ the distance between agents $i$ and $j$: the smallest number of intermediary nonnull edges it takes to reach a vertex from another.
title: Individuals graph

[Theorem Bivariate density of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] We have
$$\pi(u,v) =  C \sum_{n\geqslant 0} c_n e^{-a_n u-b_n v}+ C' \sum_{n\geqslant 0} c_n' e^{-a_n' u-b_n' v} . $$
All constants are made explicit in [franceschi_ichiba_karatzas_raschel_degenerate_2024]:
\begin{itemize}
   \item There is a recursive computation of the constants;
   \item $a_n,b_n,a_n',b_n'$ are quadratic polynomials in $n$, see Figure~(fig:parabolecomp of the paper);
   \item $c_n=P_8(n)+(-1)^nQ_8(n)$
   and $c_n'=P_8'(n)+(-1)^nQ_8'(n),$
   \\ where $P_8$, $Q_8$, $P_8'$ and $Q_8'$ are polynomials of degree 8 in the symmetric case, and in the general case $$
c_n\underset{n\to\infty}{\sim} n^{2({-\gamma}+1)} .
$$
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Bivariate density

[Thm 18 of arXiv:2607.06745, 'Regularization and asymptotic behaviour of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck evolution operators in infin'] Let the system satisfy Assumptions
$\text{\ref{assu: periodicita}}$ and $\text{\ref{ass: U* ha autov di mod max}}$,
and assume that all the eigenvalues of $U\left(T,0\right)^{*}$ of
maximum modulus $e^{\omega_{0}T}$ are semisimple for $U\left(T,0\right)^{*}$.
Then, there exists a constant $C>0$, depending only on the problem's
data, and a positive integer $N_{0}$, such that:
\[
\left\Vert P_{0,T\mid Im\Pi_{0}}^{N}\right\Vert _{\mathcal{L}\left(L^{p}\left(X,\mu_{0}\right)\right)}\leq Ce^{\omega_{0}NT}\quad\forall N\geq N_{0}.
\]

Consequently, there exists $C_{T}>0$ such that:
\begin{align*}
\left\Vert P_{s,t}f-\int_{X}f\left(y\right)\mu_{t}\left(dy\right)\right\Vert _{L^{p}\left(X,\mu_{s}\right)}\leq C_{T}e^{\omega_{0}\left(t-s\right)}\left\Vert f\right\Vert _{L^{p}\left(X,\mu_{t}\right)}\\
\forall s<t,\ f\in L^{p}\left(X,\mu_{t}\right).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 18 of arXiv:2607.06745

body:
Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x), the multiplicities dim E_i(x), and the subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere. The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.
M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M
mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)
the exponents, multiplicities and subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; constant a.e. when mu is ergodic
the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant
title: Lyapunov exponents, the Oseledets splitting, and Pesin blocks

[Proposition 99 (Cutoff convergence in probability) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Suppose $(\Xi_\Lambda,y_\Lambda)\to(\Xi,y)$ in probability in
$d_{T_0}$.  For every fixed $A\in\mathbb N$, $T$, and every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{align}
 \Pp\Bigl(&\mathcal G_{A,T}\cap
 \Bigl(\mathcal A_T(\Xi_\Lambda,y_\Lambda)^c
 \cup\Bigl(\mathcal A_T(\Xi_\Lambda,y_\Lambda)\cap
 \bigl\{\|\mathscr S_T(\Xi_\Lambda,y_\Lambda)-Z\|_{\mathcal Z_T}>\varepsilon\bigr\}\Bigr)\Bigr)\Bigr)
 \longrightarrow0.
 
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{T\downarrow0}\Pp(\mathcal G_{A,T})
 =\Pp\{M_{T_0}^{\mathrm{bd}}(\Xi,y)\le A\},
 \qquad
 \lim_{A\to\infty}\lim_{T\downarrow0}\Pp(\mathcal G_{A,T})=1.
\end{equation}
This gives local convergence in probability for arbitrary admissible cofinal
families, without choosing a cutoff-dependent lifespan.

[Lemma 8 (Growth of the Fourier coefficients $\frac{1}{3}<\gamma<1$ and $\varepsilon>0$) of arXiv:2603.29473, '$\chi^2$--cut-off phenomenon for Galerkin projections of Fokker--Planck equations with mon'] \hfill

	\noindent
	Let $\frac{1}{3}  < \gamma < 1$ and let $\delta = \varepsilon^{\frac{1-\gamma}{\gamma+1}}$, and let $\psi_{k,\varepsilon}$ be the $k$-th non-constant eigenfunction of the operator $-\mathcal{L}_\varepsilon$ with eigenvalue $\lambda_{k,\varepsilon} = \lambda_k \varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}}$, where $\lambda_k$ is the $k$-th eigenvalue of the operator $-\mathcal{L}_1$.
	For $x_0\neq 0$
	and small enough $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(k,\gamma,x_0)>0$ it holds
	\begin{equation}
		\left\lvert \int \varrho_{\varepsilon,0}(x) \psi_{k,\varepsilon}(x) \dx \right\rvert \approx \fint_{B_{\delta}(x_0)} e^{\lambda_{k} \frac{|x \varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{\gamma+1}}|^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}} \dx \approx e^{\lambda_{k} \varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}} \frac{|x_0|^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}},
	\end{equation}
	where the implied constant is independent of $\varepsilon$.

	For  $x_0 = 0$ and $\psi_{k}(0) \neq 0$ we have that $\psi_k$ is an even function and hence
	\begin{equation*}
		\left\lvert \int \varrho_{\varepsilon,0}(x) \psi_{k,\varepsilon}(x) \dx \right\lvert  \approx \varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma(1-\gamma)}{1+\gamma}} e^{\frac{\lambda_{k}}{1-\gamma} \varepsilon^{\frac{\gamma(\gamma-1)}{\gamma+1}} },
	\end{equation*}
	while  for $x_0 = 0$ and  $\psi_{k}(0) = 0$ we have that $\psi_k$ is an odd function and hence
	\begin{equation*}
		\int \varrho_{\varepsilon,0}(x) \psi_{k,\varepsilon}(x) \dx = 0.
	\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

DRAFT AUDIT CONCEPT; independent referee pending. For real t and z in C, set r=|z| and F_t(z)=-t*r^2+r^(5/2)-Re(z^3)+r^4. Rotation by 2pi/3 and conjugation preserve F_t, giving the standard S3 action. The cubic polynomial term has a fixed nonzero coefficient. Put c=1-2/(3sqrt(3))>0; 1-s+s^3>=c for s>=0 gives F_t>=-t*r^2+c*r^(5/2). Thus zero is the unique global minimizer for t<=0. For t>0, small positive real z has negative value, and coercivity gives nonzero minimizers with radius at most (t/c)^2. All minimizers approach zero as t decreases to zero. This is a toy variational counterexample to the bare invariant-cubic criterion, not a lattice Potts model. The fractional term prevents a uniform quartic Taylor remainder.

[Prop 91 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] $\Perm$ is a quasitopological $*$-monoid\footnote{This notion does not seem to exist in the literature. However, it is a natural generalization of a quasitopological group, which is a well-known concept.}, which means the following properties hold true, for all permutons $\mu,\nu,\xi$
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item $(\xi \circ \nu)\circ \mu = \xi \circ (\nu \circ \mu)$ (Associativity),
		\item $I \circ \mu = \mu \circ I = \mu$ (Identity),
		\item $\mu^{**} = \mu$ (Involution), 
		\item $(\nu\circ \mu)^* = \mu^* \circ \nu^*$ (Anti-Homomorphism),
		\item The operations $*, \mu \circ \blnk, \blnk \circ \nu$ are continuous with respect to weak convergence.
	\end{enumerate}
	Moreover, we have
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\setcounter{enumi}{6}
		\item $\mu \circ \Leb = \Leb \circ \mu = \Leb$, (Absorbing element),
		\item $W \circ W = I$ (Square root of identity),
	\end{enumerate} 
	where $\Leb$ is the Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]^2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A graph G = (V, E) is bipartite if the vertex set V can be partitioned into two disjoint sets X and Y, V = X union Y, X intersect Y = empty set, such that every edge in E has one endpoint in X and one endpoint in Y; no edge lies entirely within X or entirely within Y. Equivalently, G is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length. [standard, e.g. Diestel, Graph Theory]

Method: Explicit model calculation and hypothesis obstruction Result: For a single-particle eigenfunction phi of the underlying graph Laplacian with mean zero, F(eta)=sum_x eta_x*phi(x) is an exclusion eigenfunction with the same eigenvalue. On a uniform m-particle configuration among N sites, direct sampling-without-replacement gives Var_pi F = m*(N-m)/(N*(N-1))*sum_x phi(x)^2. The initial mean decays exactly exponentially. This yields the natural lower-bound scale by comparing the initial eigenfunction amplitude with its equilibrium standard deviation. Check: The variance formula follows from E eta_x=m/N and Cov(eta_x,eta_y)=-m*(N-m)/(N^2*(N-1)) for x different from y, using sum phi=0. All times must use a single rate convention; multiplying the generator by N changes the location but not cutoff. Obstruction: This spectral observable only proves a lower obstruction to mixing; it gives no matching total-variation upper bound. The one-dimensional height monotonicity argument fails on higher-dimensional tori. Salez2022 reservoir cutoff and Tran2023 Glauber-exclusion are different processes.

body: [Defn Fine slope of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] A \textbf{(finite) fine slope} is a pair $(s,\heartsuit)$ (usually written $s^\heartsuit$), where $s\in \mathbb{R}$ and $\heartsuit \in \{\sharp,\flat,\natural,\dagger\}$. We say that $s$ is the underlying \textbf{coarse slope} of $s^\heartsuit$. If $\mathcal{F}$ is a foliation on $M$, its \textbf{fine (boundary) multislope} is the tuple $$\bm{\fineslope}(\mathcal{F}):=(\fineslope(\partial_1\mathcal{F}),\dots,\fineslope(\partial_n\mathcal{F})).$$

[Thm Result1 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m>1$ and let $c_1,c_2,c_3,\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}$. Then
\[
  f_1(x)=x+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\!\bigl(c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3+x^{q+2}\bigr)
\]
is a permutation polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$ if and only if one of the following
holds:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $\gamma=0$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*}$, $c_3=1$, ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)\neq0$ and ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)=\gamma^{-1}$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*}$, $c_3=1$, ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)=0$ and ${\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)\neq\gamma^{-1}$;
  \item $\gamma\in\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_q$, $m$ is odd, and, with
        $A:={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_3\gamma^3+\gamma^{q+2})$,
        \[
          A\neq0,\qquad
          {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma^2)+(c_3\gamma+\gamma^{q})^{q+1}=0,\qquad
          A\bigl(1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)\bigr)+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2^2\gamma^4)=0 .
        \]
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:addparallel of arXiv:2608.30973, 'Pseudo-Anosov flow and dynamics on guts'] Let \((N,N_{+},N_{-},\gamma_{N})\) be a sutured manifold and let \(\psi\) be a tight semiflow on \(N\).
Let \(K\) be a connected component of \(N_{+}\), and endow \(K\times I\) with the product sutured structure and product flow.
Then attaching \(K\times \{0\}\) to \(N_{+}\) gives a semiflow on \(N\cup_{N_{+}} K\times I\)  which is orbit equivalent to \(N\).
Similar result holds for components of \(N_{-}\).

Let \(T\) be a product sutured manifold and homeomorphic to a solid torus.
Endow \(T\) with the product flow. Choose a glue map \(f:\mu\to \gamma\) which maps a suture \(\mu\) of \(T\) to a sutured annulus \(\gamma\) of \(N\) homeomorphically and preserving flow segments.
Then gluing \(T\) to \(N\) by \(f\) gives a semiflow on \(N\cup_{f}T\) which is orbit equivalent to \(N\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:addparallel of arXiv:2608.30973

body:
[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\textbf{Geometric interpolation of two equivalent Gaussian measures on Hilbert space}]
		
		Let $\mu_i = \Ncal(m_i, C_i) \in \Gauss(\Hcal, \mu_{*})$, $i=0,1$, where
		$C_i = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_i)C_{*}^{1/2}$, $S_i \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{<I}$. Let the corresponding 
		Radon-Nikodym densities with respect to $\mu_{*}$ be denoted by $p_i = \frac{d\mu_i}{d\mu_{*}}$. Then
		for $\alpha \in [0,1]$,
		\begin{align}
			(p_0p_1)^{G}_{\alpha}(x) = \frac{d\mu_{\alpha}}{d\mu_{*}},
			
			
		\end{align}
		where $\mu_{\alpha} = \Ncal(m_{\alpha}, C_{\alpha}) \in \Gauss(\Hcal,\mu_{*})$, $C_{\alpha} = C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\alpha})C_{*}^{1/2}$, with
		\begin{align}
			S_{\alpha} &= I - [(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1} + \alpha (I-S_1)^{-1}]^{-1} \in \SymHS(\Hcal)_{< I},
			
			\\
			C_{\alpha} &= C_{*}^{1/2} [(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1} + \alpha (I-S_1)^{-1}]^{-1}C_{*}^{1/2},
			
			\\
			m_{\alpha} &= m_{*} + C_{*}^{1/2}(I-S_{\alpha})[(1-\alpha)(I-S_0)^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*}) 
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad \quad + \alpha(I-S_1)^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})].
			
		\end{align}
	The normalizing factor is given by
	\begin{align}
		&Z_{\alpha}^G(p_0:p_1)
		\nonumber
		= 
		\int_{\Hcal}p_0^{1-\alpha}(x)p_1^{\alpha}(x) d\mu_{*}(x)
		\\
		&=\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}]^{-1/2}
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1-\alpha}{2}||(I-S_0)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_0 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times 
		\exp\left[-\frac{\alpha}{2}||(I-S_1)^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_1 - m_{*})||^2\right]
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times \exp\left(\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right).
		
	\end{align}
		Here $I + A = (I-S_1)^{-1/2}(I-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} > 0$, with $A =(I-S_1)^{-1/2}(S_1-S_0)(I-S_1)^{-1/2} \in \Sym(\Hcal)\cap \HS(\Hcal).$
		In particular, for $S_0, S_1 \in \SymTr(\Hcal)_{< I}$,
		\begin{align}
			(p_0p_1)^{G}_{\alpha}(x) &	=[\det(I-S_{\alpha})]^{-1/2}
			\nonumber
			\\
			& \quad \times \exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*})\ra \right\}
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \times \exp(\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), (I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})\ra)
			\nonumber
			\\
			&\quad \times \exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}||(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1/2}C_{*}^{-1/2}(m_{\alpha} - m_{*})||^2\right].
			
		\end{align}
Let $P_N = \sum_{k=1}^Ne_k \otimes e_k$, $N \in \Nbb$, be the orthogonal projection onto the $N$-dimensional subspace of $\Hcal$ spanned
by $\{e_k\}_{k=1}^N$, where $\{e_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}$ are the orthonormal eigenvectors of $C_{*}$.
In the expression in Eq.\eqref{equation:geometric-interpolation-Gaussian-S-Tr},
\begin{align}
	&\la C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}(x-m_{*})\ra 
	\nonumber
	\\
	& \doteq \lim_{N \approach \infty} \la C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*}), S_{\alpha}(I-S_{\alpha})^{-1}C_{*}^{-1/2}P_N(x-m_{*})\ra 
	\\
	&

[Coro 27 of arXiv:2609.03188, 'Some generalizations of Oort's conjecture'] Let $\lambda^{(k)}$ be as above.
If $g$ is even, then
$$
\Pi(\lambda^{(k)})=
\begin{cases}
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_{\frac{g}{2}}\}&\text{if $1\leq k<\frac{g}{2}$},\\
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_0,\alpha_g\}&\text{if $k=\frac{g}{2}$}.
\end{cases}
$$
If $g$ is odd, then
$$
\Pi(\lambda^{(k)})=
\begin{cases}
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_0,\alpha_g\}&\text{if $1\leq k<\frac{g-1}{2}$},\\
\Pi\setminus\{\alpha_{\frac{g-1}{2}},\alpha_{\frac{g+1}{2}}\}&\text{if $k=\frac{g-1}{2}$}.
\end{cases}
$$
In either case, we have
$$\Irr\bigl(X_\mu(\tau)'\bigr)=\bigl\{j\overline{X_\mu^{\lambda^{(k)}}(\tau)}\mid 1\leq k\leq\left\lfloor\tfrac{g}{2}\right\rfloor,\ j\in\J/(\J\cap P_{\Pi(\lambda^{(k)})})\bigr\}.$$

On the environment $ \sigma_l^a\sigma_m^b(\omega)$ there is a geodesic such that $K_1$ is before $K_2$; while on the environment 
$ \sigma_l^b\sigma_m^a(\omega)$ there is a geodesic such that $K_2$ is before $K_1$.

[Lemma CIL of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] \cite [Lemma A.1]{TVuniversality}  Let $1\leq m\leq n$. 
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix and $A'$ be the sub-matrix formed by the first $n-m$ rows of $A$. Let $s_1(A) \geq \cdots \geq s_n(A) \geq 0$ and $s_1(A') \geq \cdots \geq s_{n}(A') \geq 0$ be the singular values of $A$ and $A'$, respectively. Then we have 
\[
s_{i+m}(A) \leq   s_i(A') \leq  s_i(A),
\]
 for $1 \leq i \leq n-m$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition Polymers from $A$ to $B$ of arXiv:2606.06612, 'The limit shape and emergence of the \\ Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $V \subset \mathbb Z^2$ be finite and simply connected, with two marked points $A, B$ on $\partial V$. Assuming without loss of generality that $A$ is left of $B$, let $\xi$ be boundary conditions of $h$ along the upper\footnote{The choice of which arc is upper can be made precise via a conformal map sending $\partial V$ to the unit circle, $A$ to $(0, -1)$, and $B$ to $(0, 1)$, and selecting the arc which maps to the upper half plane.} arc of $\partial V$ from $A$ to $B$ and $h-1$ along the lower arc. For every $\mathbb Z$-height function on $V$ with boundary condition $\xi$, there is a unique disagreement polymer $\gamma$ which contains the boundary disagreements. Define $\ensuremath{\mathcal P}_V(A, B)$ as the set of all such possible disagreement polymers in this setting.\footnote{Note that the choice of $h$ is irrelevant here, all that matters here is that the boundary heights differ by 1.} If $V$ is an infinite volume domain, then define $\ensuremath{\mathcal P}_V(A, B) = \bigcup_{V' \subset V} \ensuremath{\mathcal P}_{V'}(A, B)$, where the union is over all simply connected $V' \subset V$ which have finite volume.
title: Polymers from $A$ to $B$

body:
[Theorem thm:stexist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] There exists a stochastic process 
\begin{align}
    \bigl(B^{h{\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,y) : x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\, h \in \mathcal{H},\, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{+,-\}\bigr)
\end{align}
on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}  [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}]   \itemsep=3pt
\item \textup{(}No $\pm$ distinction at fixed $h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\{B^{h-}= B^{h+}\}=1.
\]
When $B^{h-}(\omega) = B^{h+}(\omega)$, call the common cocycle $B^h(\omega)$.
\item \textup{(}Forward measurable Busemann function\textup{)} For each $h\in \mathcal{H}, B^h \in \mathcal K_c^+$.
\item \textup{(}Mean $-h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$, $\mathbb{E}[B^h(0,e_i)] = -h \cdot e_i.$
\item \textup{(}Monotonicity\textup{)} For $h,h'\in \mathcal{H}$ with $h \cdot e_1 \leq h' \cdot e_1$, all $x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, and $\mathbb{P}$ almost every $\omega$
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1)  
\]
and
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2).
\]
\item \textup{(}Left-/right-continuity\textup{)} For $\mathbb{P}$-almost all $\omega$, all $h\in \mathcal{H}$, and all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$,
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \nearrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y) \,\text{ and }\, B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \searrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y).
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, this process is unique in the sense that any two processes satisfying the above conditions are equal almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:stexist of arXiv:2507.08757

body:
[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Assuming that a random variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ has as law 
$$\mu=\sum_i\lambda_i\delta_{x_i}\quad,\quad x_1<\ldots<x_N\quad,\quad\lambda_i>0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1$$
its cumulative distribution function is the following step function:
$$F(x)=\begin{cases}
0&:\ x\in(-\infty,x_1]\\
\lambda_1&:\ x\in(x_1,x_2]\\
\lambda_1+\lambda_2&:\ x\in(x_2,x_3]\\
\vdots&\\
\lambda_1+\ldots+\lambda_{N-1}&:\ x\in(x_{N-1},x_N]\\
1&:\ x\in(x_N,\infty)
\end{cases}$$
Conversely, any such step function $F$ produces a law $\mu$, in the obvious way.

[Theorem thm:laguerre of arXiv:2609.02155, 'Exact Limits of Random Projections for Preserving Geometry:\\ Distance Recovery, Nearest-N'] The conditional-expectation operator
$f(\mathcal T)\mapsto\E[f(\mathcal T)\mid U]$ has generalized Laguerre
singular functions and singular values
\[
\ell_k=\left(\frac{(r/2)_k}{(d/2)_k}\right)^{1/2},
\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots,
\]
where $(a)_k$ is the rising factorial [griffiths1969canonical]. If
$f(\mathcal T)-\E f(\mathcal T)=\sum_{k\ge1}c_k\phi_k(\mathcal T)$ is the
orthonormal Laguerre expansion, then
\[
\Var(\E[f(\mathcal T)\mid\mathcal{O}])=\sum_{k\ge1}\ell_k^2c_k^2.
\]
For fixed $k$, as $r\to\infty$ and $d-r\to\infty$,
\[
\ell_k=\left(\frac rd\right)^{k/2}
\left[1+O_k\!\left(\frac1r+\frac1d\right)\right].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Laguerre spectrum

body: [Lem instability_sharpspiraling of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a foliation of an annulus $S^1 \times [0,1]$ which is positively transverse to $S^1 \times \{0\}$ and $S^1 \times \{1\}$. Suppose $\mathcal{G}$ has no closed leaf of $\flat$-type (resp $\sharp$-type) spiraling. If $\mathcal{G}'$ is another foliation of the annulus which is similarly transverse to the boundary and has pointwise higher (resp.~lower) slope than $\mathcal{G}$, then $\mathcal{G}'$ has no closed leaf of degree $+1$ (resp.~$-1$) in the annulus. See \zcref{fig:instability}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2605.22146, 'Poisson approximation of the largest gaps between zeros of a stationary Gaussian process'] Let $f$ be a $C^1$-smooth SGP satisfying $|K(x)| \le c_0 |x|^{-\alpha}$ for some $c_0 > 0$ and $\alpha > 1$. Then for every $\eps > 0$ there exists a $c_1 > 0$ such that, for sufficiently large $r$ 
\[ \phi_r \le 4 \P\big[ f(x) > -\eps : x \in [0,(1-\eps)r] \big]^2  + e^{-  c_1 r^{(\alpha-1)/2} }  .\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: For an adapted process H with E integral of H_s^2 ds finite, the Ito integral of H against Brownian motion is defined as the L^2 limit of sums H_{t_i} (W_{t_{i+1}} - W_{t_i}) over refining partitions, with the integrand evaluated at the LEFT endpoint (non-anticipating). The result is a continuous martingale; left-endpoint evaluation is what distinguishes Ito from Stratonovich calculus and gives the martingale property at the cost of the chain-rule correction.
title: Ito Integral

body:
[Definition Metric Entropy of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $(X,\rho)$ be a metric space and let $\varepsilon>0$.  A set
    $\mathcal X_\varepsilon\subseteq X$ is called an $\varepsilon$-net of $X$ if
    $
    X
    \subseteq
    \bigcup_{x\in\mathcal X_\varepsilon}
        B(x,\varepsilon).
    $
    The $\varepsilon$-covering number of $X$ is
    \[
        \mathcal N(X,\rho,\varepsilon)
        \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
        \inf
        \left\{
            |\mathcal X_\varepsilon|
            :
            \mathcal X_\varepsilon\subseteq X
            \text{ is an } \varepsilon\text{-net of }X
        \right\}.
    \]
    The metric entropy of $(X,\rho)$ is defined as 
    \[
        \log_2
        \mathcal N(X,\rho,\varepsilon)
        .
    \]
title: Metric Entropy

Let mu be a nonnegative Borel measure on R such that every polynomial is absolutely integrable and integral q(t)^2 dmu(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial q. Let p_k be its degree-k monic orthogonal polynomials, with p_0=1. Fix n>=1 and alpha in R, and write r_1<...<r_n for the n distinct real roots of p_n+alpha p_(n-1). For an integer 0<=j<=n-1, define the signed measure dmu_j(t)=product_(s=0)^(j-1)(r_(n-s)-t)dmu(t), with the empty product1. Then integral f(t)^2 dmu_j(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial f of degree<=n-j-1. Thus mu_j is positive definite up to degree n-j-1 in Definition3.4. The weight has factors r_(n-s)-t, with this sign, and mu_j need not be a nonnegative measure. No assertion at j=n is included. This is Lemma3.7 of Cohn-Kumar.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02743, 'Sharp mean-field estimates for diffusive log/Riesz gases in the Hilbert--Schmidt regime'] \begingroup We study fixed-temperature logarithmic and Riesz gases after subtracting the leading mean-field contribution relative to a prescribed background law. For repulsive interactions in the Hilbert--Schmidt regime, we prove $N$-uniform bounds and quantitative convergence of the resulting modulated partition function to a normalization expressed by the Carleman--Fredholm determinant of the centered interaction operator. We show that the Hilbert--Schmidt threshold is sharp and obtain explicit lower bounds on the rate of divergence at and above it; these rates are expected to be nonoptimal. The proof combines positive-definite truncations and a low/high-frequency decomposition with exponential inequalities and Gaussian-chaos asymptotics for canonical degree-two $U$-statistics. As consequences, we establish entropic commutator estimates with the sharp $O(N^{-1})$ additive scale in the modulated-free-energy method, a static joint linear-statistics central limit theorem, and a dynamical central limit theorem for joint linear statistics at finitely many times. This extends the logarithmic partition-function estimates of the first two authors to the full Riesz Hilbert--Schmidt range and identifies the limiting determinant normalization. For the attractive logarithmic interaction at sufficiently small inverse temperature, we also prove analogous results. \endgroup
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02743: Sharp mean-field estimates for diffusive log/Riesz gases in the Hilbert--Schmidt regime

body:
[Theorem 48 (Fock energy and free-capacity balance) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Assume in this theorem that \(M\) is continuous and that \(V_T\leq K\)
almost surely for a deterministic \(K<\infty\).  Let \(Z^\lambda\) and
\(Z^{\lambda,N}=P_{\leq N}Z^\lambda\) be the exterior lifts above, and put
\[
 T_t^N=Z_t^{\lambda,N}\otimes Z_t^{\lambda,N},
 \qquad T_t=Z_t^\lambda\otimes Z_t^\lambda.
\]
The finite-level bracket is \eqref{cc:eq-exterior-Fock-bracket}, and its
trace-class limit is the equality of positive
\(\mathcal S_1(\mathcal F_{\wedge}(H))\)-valued measures
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm d\langle Z^\lambda\rangle_t
 =\lambda^2\mathcal B_{\mathrm dR_t}(T_t).
 
\end{equation}
More explicitly, write
\(
 \mathrm dR_t=r_t\,\mathrm dV_t
\), where \(r_t\succeq0\) and
\(\operatorname{Tr}r_t=1\) for \(\mathrm dV\)-almost every \(t\), and set
\[
 Y_t=\|Z_t^\lambda\|^2,
 \qquad
 L_t=2\int_0^t
      \langle Z_s^\lambda,\mathrm dZ_s^\lambda\rangle.
\]
Then \(L\) is a real continuous local martingale and
\begin{align}
 \mathrm dY_t
 &=\mathrm dL_t
   +\lambda^2\operatorname{Cap}^{\mathrm{free}}_{r_t}(T_t)
      \,\mathrm dV_t \notag\\
 &=\mathrm dL_t
   +\lambda^2\left(
      Y_t-\operatorname{Tr}(\mathrm d\Gamma(r_t)T_t)
     \right)\mathrm dV_t,
 \\
 \mathrm d[L]_t
 &\leq4\lambda^2Y_t
   \operatorname{Cap}^{\mathrm{free}}_{r_t}(T_t)
   \,\mathrm dV_t.
 
\end{align}
Thus the predictable growth of Fock energy is exactly the free capacity;
the occupied part is removed, rather than estimated away.

[Lemma lem:circular of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] A continuous one-periodic $U$ is the rank Hill potential of a
			circular law if and only if the Hill equation
			$\psi'' + \tfrac12 U\psi = 0$ has a positive one-periodic solution,
			if and only if zero is the lowest periodic eigenvalue of the
			operator $-\,d^{2}/dz^{2} - \tfrac12 U$ on the rank circle. The
			circumference is recovered as $\ell = \int_{0}^{1}\psi^{-2}$ once
			the scale of $\psi$ is fixed, the
			law as $f = \psi^{2}\circ F$, and unit mass is automatic as in the
			identity~(equation eq:automatic-mass of the paper).

Own-work draft. Status: proof (unaudited); independent review and novelty assessment outstanding. Gaussian population input X~N(0,I_d), unit teacher u, student integral sigma(w.X)rho(dw) on the unit sphere, fixed +1 outer coefficients, uniform initialization, and risk E[(student-sigma(u.X))^2]. For every d>=6 and arbitrarily small positive cubic squared coefficient B relative to the quadratic coefficient A in the normalized He2/He3 activation, the zero-temperature population sphere flow from uniform initialization has b prime(0)=6B(d-5)/(d(d+2)(d+4))>0, where b=E[m(1-m^2)]/(d-1). Thus for all sufficiently small positive times a positive-overlap interval has (m^2) prime<0. No positive pointwise He2-type squared-overlap drift lower bound holds at every overlap. Small weighted odd-tail upper bounds alone cannot justify that particular comparison; this does not refute polynomial learning or averaged comparisons.

A,B>0, A+B=1
sigma=sqrt(A)He2/sqrt2+sqrt(B)He3/sqrt6

body:
[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2603.13798, 'Iterated Graph Systems (I): random walks and diffusion limits'] Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $v\in V_k(\Xi^n)$.
Fix an integer $m$ with $1\le m\le n-k$ and set $t:=n-m$.
Let $E_{\Xi^{t}}(v)$ be the set of edges of $\Xi^{t}$ incident to $v$.

For each $e=\{v,w_e\}\in E_{\Xi^{t}}(v)$, let $H_e^{(m)}\subseteq \Xi^n$ be the $m$-step substituted copy that replaces $e$ from level $t$ to level $n$.
Set
\[
S_{v}^{(n,m)}:=\{w_e:\ e\in E_{\Xi^{t}}(v)\}\subseteq V(\Xi^n),
\qquad
\tau_{v}^{(n,m)}:=\inf\{j\ge 0:\ X_j^{\Xi^n}\in S_{v}^{(n,m)}\}.
\]
Then there exist constants $c_{\star},C_{\star}>0$, depending only on the birth data of $v$, such that for all admissible $n,m$,
\[
c_{\star} \rho(\mathbf M)^m\rho(\Psi)^m
\le
\mathbb E^v\big[\tau_{v}^{(n,m)}\big]
\le
C_{\star} \rho(\mathbf M)^m\rho(\Psi)^m.
\]

[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] Let $m \in \{1,\dots,n-1\}$, $T \in\cT_m$, $r_0,\dots,r_m \in \N$. Then
\[
\int_{(\R^d)^m} \1_{\eqref{Fn:pas_loin}} \d x_1 \cdots \d x_m \le \prod_{0 \le i \le m} \overline v_d^M(r_i+1)^{dM}
\]

[Lem 21 (Lemma~5.3 of~\cite{Baik-Cordaro-Tripathi25}) of arXiv:2608.20552, 'One-point fluctuations for exponential last passage percolation under upper-tail condition'] Let $(\ff_L)_{L>0}$ be a Gaussian family.
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item
In Cases~\textnormal{(a)} and~\textnormal{(c)}, for every $b\in\R$, set 
\beqq
	\Gamma_-:=\cont^L_-(\cp^-+bL^{-1/2}).
\eeqq
There exist $c,C,L_0>0$ such that, for all $L\ge L_0$ and every $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$,
\beqq
	|\ff_L(z)|
	\le Ce^{-cL^{2\epsilon/3}}|\ff_L(\cp^-)|
	\qquad
	\text{if $z\in\Gamma_-$ and $|z-\cp^-|\ge L^{-1/2+\epsilon/3}$,}
\eeqq
and
\beqq
	\|\ff_L\|_{L^1(\Gamma_-)}
	\le \frac{C}{L^{1/2}}|\ff_L(\cp^-)|. 
\eeqq

\item
In Cases~\textnormal{(a)} and~\textnormal{(b)}, for every $b\in\R$, set
\beqq
	\Gamma_+:=\cont^L_+(\cp^++bL^{-1/2}).
\eeqq
There exist $c,C,L_0>0$ such that, for all $L\ge L_0$ and every $\epsilon\in(0,1/2)$,
\beqq
	\frac{1}{|\ff_L(z)|}
	\le Ce^{-cL^{2\epsilon/3}}\frac{1}{|\ff_L(\cp^+)|}
	\qquad
	\text{if $z\in\Gamma_+$ and $|z-\cp^+|\ge L^{-1/2+\epsilon/3}$,}
\eeqq
and
\beqq
	\left\|\frac{1}{\ff_L}\right\|_{L^1(\Gamma_+)}
	\le \frac{C}{L^{1/2}|\ff_L(\cp^+)|}.
\eeqq
\end{enumerate}
The constants may be chosen uniformly when $b$ ranges over a fixed bounded set. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma~5.3 of~\cite{Baik-Cordaro-Tripathi25}

body:
[Theorem thm:first-order-interval-correspondence of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Suppose that Assumption~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) holds.  For every $\alpha\geq0$,
every regular weight $w$ of order $\alpha$, every interval $I=(r_0,r_1)$,
every integer $m\geq1$, and
\begin{equation*}
 F\in L_w^2(I;\mathbb R^m),\qquad \eta\in L^2(\mu_{r_1};\mathbb R^m),
\end{equation*}
there is a unique first-order occupation-energy solution in the sense of
Definition~(def:first-order-occupation-solution of the paper), denoted by
$\mathcal U_I^w(F,\eta)$.  In the following BSDE, $D_xu$ is the $m\times d$
Jacobian and
\begin{equation*}
 \mathsf Z u:=(D_xu)\sigma\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}.
\end{equation*}
For $m=1$, its single row is identified with the column vector
$\sigma D_xu$ in (equation eq:reference-operators of the paper).  For every
$s\in(r_0,r_1)$, the composition of $u$ has a continuous version on
$[s,r_1]$ and
\begin{equation}
 u(t,X_t)=\eta(X_{r_1})+\int_t^{r_1}F(r,X_r)\,\mathrm d r
 -\int_t^{r_1}\mathsf Z u(r,X_r)\,\mathrm d W_r.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, for $\kappa\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 +\left\lVert \mathsf Z u\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 \leq e^{\operatorname{osc}_{\alpha,I}(w)}\left(
  \kappa^{-1}\left\lVert F\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
  +w_\kappa(r_1)\norm\eta_{L^2(\mu_{r_1})}^2\right).
 
\end{equation}
The construction is independent of the weight: if the same data belong to
the spaces associated with two regular weights $w_1,w_2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U_I^{w_1}(F,\eta)=\mathcal U_I^{w_2}(F,\eta)
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(I\times\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^m).
 
\end{equation}
Thus the superscript may be omitted and the solution written as
$\mathcal U_I(F,\eta)$; the full-interval notation is $\mathcal U(F,\eta)$.

[Proposition prop:doublecurrent-loop of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph and fix     $A\subset V$ with $|A|$ even, $\Omega:=\{0,1\}^E$ and $\Sigma:=\{F\subset E \mid \partial F=A\}$ be the set of subgraphs of $G$ with sources $A$. Let $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ be defined by $f(\omega)=\{F\subset \omega \mid \partial F=A\}$ and
	\[\rho[\omega]\propto 1\! \!1[\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A] (\ell^{A \triangle B} \cup \mathbb{P}_{t^2})[\omega],~\forall \omega\in \Omega, ~\gamma[\eta]\propto 1, ~\forall \eta\in \Sigma.\]
	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\ell^{A}$. For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A \cap \mathcal{F}_B$, the conditional measure is given by  $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega] = \mathtt{UG}^A[\omega]$, the uniform $\omega$-subgraph with sources $A$.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\mathbf{P}^{A,B}$.  For each $\eta\in\Sigma$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta]$ is $\ell^B \cup \mathbb{P}_{t^2} \cup \delta_{\eta}$ where $\delta_{\eta}$ is the Dirac measure concentrated at $\eta$.
	\end{enumerate}
In particular, the uniform graph with sources $A$ of the double random current measure with sources $A$ and $B$ is the loop $\mathrm{O}(1)$ model with sources $A$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop main2_2 of arXiv:2607.10105, 'The four-dimensional Anderson model: a case study for critical SPDEs'] Let $(\mathcal T,N_\mathfrak n,m_\mathfrak l)$ be a fixed marked Hepp tree with multiplicities $m_\mathfrak l\geq 2$, and with both simple and compound leaves (Definition (def.mul of the paper)). Let $(y_1,\cdots,y_m)$ be a fixed vector (where $m=\sum_\mathfrak l m_\mathfrak l$), such that the multiset $\{y_1,\cdots,y_m\}=\cup_\mathfrak l \{\textrm{$m_\mathfrak l$ copies of $z_\mathfrak l$}\}$, where $(z_\mathfrak l)$ satisfies Definition (def.hepp_3 of the paper) (a); moreover, instead of Definition (def.hepp_3 of the paper) (b), we assume that for each $\mathfrak n\in\mathcal B$ and two leaves $\mathfrak l,\mathfrak l'\in\mathcal L_\mathfrak n$, we have \begin{equation}|z_{\mathfrak l}-z_{\mathfrak l'}|\leq\sum_{\mathfrak m\leq\mathfrak n}\gamma_\mathfrak m^\infty\cdot N_\mathfrak m.
\end{equation}

Fix absolute constants $C_0>1000$ and $D=\exp(C_0^{10})$. Then, for any $(\mathcal T,N_\mathfrak n,m_\mathfrak l)$, and under all the above assumptions, we have
\begin{multline}\sum_{\pi}^{(*)}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1}{\langle y_{\pi(j)}-y_{\pi(j+1)}\rangle^2}\leq C_0^mD^{|\mathcal B|}\sum_{W\subseteq\mathcal B\backslash\{\mathfrak r\}}((m-2|W|)!)^{1/2}\\\times\prod_{\mathfrak l\in\mathcal L^S}(m_\mathfrak l!)^{1/2}\prod_{\mathfrak l\in\mathcal L^C}(m_\mathfrak l!)^{3/4}\prod_{\mathfrak n\in\mathcal B} N_\mathfrak n^{-2(\gamma_\mathfrak n^2-1)}\prod_{\mathfrak n\in\mathcal B\backslash\{\mathfrak r\}}\bigg(\frac{N_\mathfrak n}{N_{\mathfrak n^+}}\bigg)^2\prod_{\mathfrak n\not\in W}\frac{N_\mathfrak n}{N_{\mathfrak n^+}}.
\end{multline} Here $\pi\in S_m$ in ((eq.vol_3_2 of the paper)) (which is identified with a permutation of $m_\mathfrak l$ distinct copies of each leaf $\mathfrak l$) and satisfies the primitivity condition in Proposition (prop.main_3 of the paper). In addition, we restrict that there is no $j$ such that $\pi(j)$ and $\pi(j+1)$ are two copies of \emph{the same leaf}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.27093, 'Soliton Solutions to the Curvature Flow on the 2-dimensional De Sitter Space and Applicati'] Let $\Phi:S\rightarrow TS\subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the differential vector field given by
	$$\Phi(\alpha,\tau,\eta)=(\tau,\alpha+a\tau\eta,a\tau^2)$$
	where $a > 0$. Then $P = (0, 0, 1)$ and $-P = (0, 0,-1)$ are the singular points of $\Phi$ and the eigenvalues of $d\Phi_P$ and $d\Phi_{-P}$ are given respectively by
	$$\lambda_P=\frac{a\pm\sqrt{a^2+4}}{2},\;\;\lambda_{-P}=\frac{-a\pm\sqrt{a^2+4}}{2}.$$

\ADEUX\hspace{1cm} \forall \,t\!\in  [0, +\infty),\;\forall\, f \!\in\mathbb{L}^2(\nu),\quad {\rm Var}_{\nu}(P_t f)\le \ee(t) {\rm Var}_{\nu}(f).
 \end{equation}
When $X_0\sim{\nu}$, \emph{i.e.} when  $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is under its stationary regime, for every $\tzero>0$, Assumption   $(\mathbf{A}_{\frac{1}{2},q,\frac{1}{2}})$ holds true with $\proba_t=\nu$,  ${\Mpiq}=M_{\nu}(q)$.

[Lemma 46 (Stability of shifted hypoelliptic Green kernels) of arXiv:2607.20882, 'An Eyring--Kramers Law for the Hypoelliptic Third-Order\\ Langevin Diffusion'] Let $\mathscr U\subset\R^N$ be a fixed smooth bounded domain.  For some
$\nu_\star<\infty$, let
\[
\mathscr P_\nu=\sum_{j=1}^dX_{j,\nu}^2+Y_\nu,
\qquad \nu\in[\nu_\star,\infty),
\]
be diffusion generators whose coefficients converge in
$C^\infty(\overline{\mathscr U})$ to those of $\mathscr P_0$ as
$\nu\to\infty$.  Assume that a
fixed finite bracket family has least singular value bounded below on
$\overline{\mathscr U}$, uniformly for $\nu\ge\nu_\star$.  Assume also that,
for every $\nu\ge\nu_\star$,
$\mathscr U$ is regular for the Dirichlet problems of
$\mathscr P_\nu-\beta$ and its formal adjoint, with forward and adjoint
barrier inequalities having a common strictly positive margin, where
$\beta>0$ is fixed and larger than a uniform upper bound
$\kappa_\dagger$ for the zero-order coefficient of the formal adjoints.
Then, for every compact
$K\subset(\mathscr U\times\mathscr U)\setminus\{(x,x):x\in\mathscr U\}$,
the Dirichlet Green kernels $G_{\nu,\beta}^{\mathscr U}(x,y)$ of
$\beta-\mathscr P_\nu$ satisfy
\begin{equation}

G_{\nu,\beta}^{\mathscr U}\longrightarrow
G_{0,\beta}^{\mathscr U}
\qquad\text{in }C^\infty(K)\qquad\text{as $\nu\to\infty$}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $G_{0,\beta}^{\mathscr U}\ge c_0>0$ on $K$, then
$G_{\nu,\beta}^{\mathscr U}\ge c_0/2$ there for all sufficiently large
$\nu$.

    and for \(K > 0\) let
    \[\Lip_K([0,1]) = \left\{f \in \mathcal{H}^+([0,1]); \begin{array}{c}
        \sup_{x,y \in [0,1], x \neq y}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|}\leq K,  \\[6pt]
        \sup_{x,y \in [0,1], x \neq y}\frac{|f^{-1}(x)-f^{-1}(y)|}{|x-y|} \leq K
    \end{array} \right\}.\] 
 For \(f \in \Lip([0,1])\), we will denote by \(\Lip(f)\) the Lipschitz constant of \(f\).

    Let \[\Dif([0,1]) =\{f \in \mathcal{H}^+([0,1]); f' \in \mathcal{C}([0,1]), (f^{-1})' \in \mathcal{C}([0,1])\}.\] We will consider the space \(\Dif([0,1])\) with the following metric \[d_{\Dif}(f,g) = \sup_{t \in [0,1]}|f(t)-g(t)|+\sup_{t \in [0,1]}|f'(t)-g'(t)|,\] for \(f,g \in \Dif([0,1])\).

    We will consider the space \(\AC([0,1])\) with the following metric

For a finite irreducible rational n-state transition matrix P, set V_full=0. For each nonempty proper visited set S, solve (I-P_SS)V_S=1+(sum_(v outside S)P_uv V_(S union {v})(v))_(u in S), in descending size of S. The killed matrix has spectral radius less than one. V_{ {u} }(u) is the exact cover time from u, and their maximum is the worst-start cover time. The method uses O(2^n*n^3) rational arithmetic operations and does not give a polynomial-time approximation algorithm.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This is an exact finite-instance oracle, not a deterministic polynomial-time (1+epsilon) algorithm.

Let P be a finite irreducible rational transition matrix on n states. For a nonempty visited set S and current state u in S, let V_S(u) be the expected remaining number of steps until every state has been visited. Set V_full=0. For every proper S solve

    (I-P_SS)*V_S = 1 + [sum_{v outside S} P_uv*V_(S union {v})(v)]_(u in S).

Evaluate visited sets in descending cardinality. The exact answer starting at u is V_{ {u} }(u), and the worst-start cover time is their maximum. This takes O(2^n*n^3) rational arithmetic operations; no polynomial bit-complexity bound is claimed.

Proof: the right-hand values concern larger visited sets and are already known. First-step conditioning gives the equation. The killed matrix P_SS has spectral radius less than one: from each state in S, irreducibility provides an at-most-n-step positive-probability path to the complement; taking the minimum of finitely many such probabilities yields a geometric exit bound. Therefore I-P_SS is invertible and its inverse is sum_{k>=0}P_SS^k. This proves existence, uniqueness and the recursion by descending induction. Rational elimination gives exact rational expectations.

Independent controls for simple random walks:

* Complete graph K_n, n>=2: (n-1)*H_(n-1) from every start, because with k visited vertices the probability of a new one is (n-k)/(n-1).
* A path of L edges: expected cover time from i is L^2+i(L-i), by first hitting an endpoint and then the other. Hence worst-start cover time L^2+floor(L^2/4).
* Star with k leaves, k>=2: 2k*H_k-1 from the center and 2k*H_(k-1) from a leaf. Coupon trials are center-to-leaf excursions of length two except the final step. For k=1 both starts have cover time one; that boundary case must be handled separately.

The cached earlier attempt's GFF asymptotic discussion gives no effective finite-instance error bound or deterministic Gaussian-maximum algorithm. This oracle permits exact checks of proposed approximations on small graphs while keeping that unresolved requirement explicit. Its computational approach is classical and no novelty claim is made.

Checks: exact Fraction arithmetic against the three controls, and Bellman residuals on all connected labeled graphs up to four vertices. [Definition 8 (Localization pairs) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] A pair $(\chi,\rho)\in C_c^\infty(\R^3)^2$ is adapted to $(K,T_0)$ if
\begin{equation}
  0\le\chi,\rho\le1,
  \qquad
  \chi\equiv1\ \text{on }K^{[\speedmax T_0+3]},
  \qquad
  \rho\equiv1\ \text{on }(\supp\chi)^{[2]}.
\end{equation}
We call $(\chi,\rho)$ an adapted localization pair and write
$\chi\triangleleft\rho$.  Constants may depend on finitely many seminorms of
this fixed pair.

[Definition def:local_solutions_NSE of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Suppose that (equation eq:ass_caccioppoli1 of the paper) and (equation eq:ass_caccioppoli4 of the paper) are satisfied.
Let $Q=I\times B$ be a parabolic cylinder with center $(t_0,x_0)$ and radius $\varrho>0$, i.e., 
$$
Q_{\varrho}(t_0,x_0)=(t_0-\varrho^2,t_0)\times B_{\varrho}(x_0).
$$ 
We say that $(v,\pi,(\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n)$ is a local solution to (equation eq:turbulent_stokes_caccioppoli of the paper) if the following are satisfied.
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm(1)}]
\item The processes 
$$
v:I \times \Omega\to H^1(B;{\mathbb R}^d), \quad \pi:I \times \Omega\to L^2(B) \ \ \text{ and }\ \  (\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n:I \times \Omega\to H^1(B;\ell^2), 
$$
are progressively measurable, and a.s.,
\begin{align*}
v&\in C(\overline{I};L^2(B;{\mathbb R}^d))\cap L^2(I;H^1(B;{\mathbb R}^d)) \\
\pi&\in L^2(Q),\quad \text{ and }\quad  (\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n \in L^2(I;H^1(B;\ell^2)).
\end{align*}

\item The following conditions hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item a.s.\ for all $t\in I$, and all $\phi\in C^\infty_{{\rm c}}(B;{\mathbb R}^d)$:
\begin{align*}
\int_{B} v(t)\cdot \phi
&=
\int_{B} v(t_0-\varrho^2)\cdot \phi\\
&+\int_{t_0-\varrho^2}^t  \int_{B} \Big[ 
\pi\,\nabla \cdot \phi+ \Big(-F -\nu \nabla v+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{n} (\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_{n}\otimes \zeta_n)\Big):\nabla \phi\Big]\\
&+\int_{t_0-\varrho^2}^t \Big(\int_{B} \big[(-\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_n + (\zeta_n\cdot \nabla) v) +G_n\big]\cdot \phi \Big)_{n} \, \mathrm{d} \mathcal{W}_{\ell^2},
\end{align*}
\item a.e.\ on $I\times \Omega$, 
in $\mathscr{D}'(B)$,
\begin{align*}
\nabla \cdot v&=0,\\
\Delta \pi
&= \nabla^2 :F - \frac{1}{2} \nabla \cdot \sum_{n}\nabla \cdot(\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_{n}\otimes \zeta_n )  ,\\
\Delta \widetilde{\pi}_n
&= \nabla \cdot [(\zeta_{n}\cdot \nabla)v]+\nabla \cdot G_n.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 5 (Theorem 3.1 in \cite{ZhangLiShangGuo2018}) of arXiv:2609.03243, 'Weighted Ces\`aro type operators on the weighted Bergman spaces in the unit ball'] Suppose $b\geq 0$, $c\geq 0$ and $\delta>-1$. Let 
\[
    J_{b,c,\delta}(z,w)=\int_{\mathbb{B}_n}\frac{(1-|u|^2)^{\delta}}{|1-\langle z,u\rangle|^{b}|1-\langle w,u\rangle|^c}{\rm d}v(u),\quad z,w\in\mathbb{B}_n.
\]
Then the following asymptotic properties hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] If $b+c<n+1+\delta$, then $J_{b,c,\delta}$ is bounded.
\item[(2)] If $b+c>n+1+\delta$, $b<n+1+\delta$ and $c<n+1+\delta$, then 
\[
    J_{b,c,\delta}(z,w)\simeq \frac{1}{|1-\langle z,w\rangle|^{b+c-n-1-\delta}}.
\]
\item[(3)] If $b>n+1+\delta>c$, then 
\[
    J_{b,c,\delta}(z,w)\simeq \frac{1}{(1-|z|^2)^{b-n-1-\delta}|1-\langle z,w\rangle|^c}.
\]
\item[(4)] If $b>n+1+\delta$ and $c>n+1+\delta$, then
\begin{align*}
J_{b,c,\delta}(z,w)\simeq \frac{1}{(1-|z|^2)^{b-n-1-\delta}|1-\langle z,w\rangle|^c}+\frac{1}{(1-|w|^2)^{c-n-1-\delta}|1-\langle z,w\rangle|^{b}}.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3.1 in \cite{ZhangLiShangGuo2018}

body:
[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [Type characterisation lemma]}

Consider a Galton--Watson tree with the offspring law $(p_k)_{k\in\N_0}$ satisfying $p_1 =p\in (0,1)$ and $p_2= 1 -p$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[\rm{(a)}] 
The root can only be either positive or neutral. It is neutral if and only if it is a branching point and its two children are branching-linear points.
\item[\rm{(b)}] 
A linear point is negative if and only if it is the child of the root and is not the parent of a branching point. It is positive if and only if it is the parent of a branching point and is not the child of the root.
\item[\rm{(c)}] 
A branching-linear point is neutral if and only if its parent is the root and its child is a linear point, otherwise, it is positive.
\item[\rm{(d)}] 
A branching point that is not the root is either negative or neutral. It is neutral if and only if its parent and both of its children are also non-root branching points.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 2 of arXiv:2606.17381
