body:
[Lem 182 (quenched second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In addition to Lemma~\ref{l:barD.II.second} we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[\max\bigg\{
	\frac{\bE[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{p(q_d)}
	: 0\le d\le \dmax-1\bigg\}
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\RomII)^2 \BUCKETS \delta}{M}\,,\]
where $\SMAX_N(\RomII)$ is a random variable satisfying the bound
	\[\P\Big(\SMAX_N(\RomII) \ge \log N\Big)
	\le\exp\bigg(-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}\bigg)\,.\]
The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.

\begin{proof} Recall that
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}{(p_d)^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
If we define the random variable
	\[
	\SMAX_N(\RomII)
	\equiv\max
	\bigg\{
	\bigg|
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)
	\bigg|
	: 
	0\le d\le \dmax-1,
	B\in \mathcal{B}(q_d)
	\bigg\}\,,
	\]
then we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\frac{\bE[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{p_d}
	= \frac{\delta_d}{M}\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by \bigg)^2
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\RomII)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{M}\,,
	\]
Note that for any $B\subseteq[M]$ we have
$\bar{\bg}^B= \bar{\bG}^\st \be_B$, so $\|\bar{\bg}^B\| \le\|\bar{\bG}\|_\textup{op}$. It then follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart} that for $C(\alpha)$ large enough, we have 
	\beq
	\P\Big(\|\bar{\bg}^B\|^2 \ge 
	C(\alpha) N \textup{ for any }B\subseteq[M]\Big)
	\le \frac{1}{2^N}\,.
	\eeq
The vectors $(\bar{\bg}^B : B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d))$ are measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$, so applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\P\Big(\SMAX_N(\RomII) \ge \log N\Big)
	=\P\bigg(
	\bigg|
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)
	\bigg|
		\ge \log N
	\textup{ for any } 0\le d\le \dmax- 1, B \in \mathcal{B}(q_d)
	\bigg)\\
	&\qquad\le
	\dmax\BUCKETS
	\bigg\{ \frac{1}{2^N}
	+ \exp\bigg(-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}\bigg)
	\bigg\}
	\le\exp\bigg(-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}\bigg)
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the $1/2^N$ in the second line comes from \eqref{e:II.union.bound}, and the final simplification uses Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

HS(v):=\mathrm{HStar}\!(v;\{u_i\}_{i\le \lceil n^{\varepsilon}\rceil};\{w_{i,j}\}_{i\le \lceil n^{\varepsilon}\rceil,\,j\le \lceil n^{\varepsilon_1}\rceil})
$

If $\sigma_v(0)=I$, then for all sufficiently large $n$, there exists an event $C^{(v)}_{I\to \mathrm{HSlit}}\in \mathcal{G}(HS(v))$ such that
\[
\mathbb{P}(C^{(v)}_{I\to \mathrm{HSlit}})\ge 1-n^{-\varepsilon/4},
\]
and on $C^{(v)}_{I\to \mathrm{HSlit}}$ the vertex $v$ is $(n^{\varepsilon_3}, n^{\varepsilon_1/24})$-HS-lit with respect to $HS(v)$ at time $1$, where $\varepsilon_2=\tfrac{1}{200}\min\{\rho,\lambda,1\}\varepsilon_1$ and $\varepsilon_3=\tfrac14\varepsilon_2$.

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2505.21774, 'The friendship paradox for trees'] {\bf [Finite trees are significant]}

For all finite trees $\mathcal{T}_n$,  the following statements hold:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] 
If there is an $u\in V(\Tt_n)$ such that $d_u\ge 3$, then
\begin{equation}

N_n^+ - N_n^- \geq 2 + \sum_{u \in V(\Tt_n)} (d_u-3) \ind{d_u \geq 3} > 0.
\end{equation}
\item[(b)] 
If $\Tt_n$ is a path of size $n$, then
\[
N_n^+-N_n^-=\ind{n=3}.
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2505.21774

body:
[Openproblem op:mather-measures of arXiv:2609.01557, '$L^\infty$ Variational Approximation of the Aubry Set'] Conceptually, (equation eq:AtoM of the paper) shows that the Mather set can, in principle, be recovered from the projected Aubry set $\mathcal A$ together with the limiting function $u_\infty$. However, this characterization is not particularly convenient from a numerical point of view. It is therefore natural to ask whether Evans' variational approximation also provides a more direct way to recover the projected Mather set $\mathcal M$, or equivalently the full Mather set $\widetilde{\mathcal M}$.

Let
\[
\sigma_k(x)
:=
\frac{e^{kH(Du_k(x),x)}}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb T^n}
e^{kH(Du_k(y),y)}\,dy}.
\]
The pair \((u_k,\sigma_k)\) is also the logarithmically coupled stationary mean-field game associated with Evans' variational approximation; see [GY20].
Thanks to [Evans03, Evans04], along a subsequence,
\[
\sigma_{k_j}\rightharpoonup \sigma
\qquad\text{weakly in the sense of measures},
\]
where \(\sigma\) is a projected Mather measure. In dimension one, under a
suitable nondegeneracy condition, \(\operatorname{spt}(\sigma)\) coincides
with the whole projected Mather set (i.e., $\operatorname{spt}(\sigma)=\mathcal M$),  whereas degeneracy may lead to further
selection ([GISMY10]). What is the corresponding picture in higher dimensions? In
particular, under what conditions does
\[
\operatorname{spt}(\sigma)=\mathcal M,
\]
and what determines the subset of \(\mathcal M\) selected when this equality
fails? (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

body:
[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Fix \(0<\theta_*<\pi\), and let \(K\subset S_{\theta_*}\) be compact. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item There exists \(\delta_K>0\) such that
\[
        \operatorname{dist}\bigl(\sigma_\theta(\xi),(-\infty,0]\bigr)
        \ge \delta_K,
        \qquad \theta\in K,\quad \xi\in\mathbb R.
\]

\item The family \(\{\psi_\theta:\theta\in K\}\) is bounded in
\(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R)\).

\item For every compact \(\Omega\subset\mathbb C\), the families
\[
        \{e^{\lambda\psi_\theta}-1:\theta\in K,\lambda\in\Omega\},
        \qquad
        \{(e^{\lambda\psi_\theta}-1)\psi_\theta:\theta\in K,\lambda\in\Omega\}
\]
are bounded in \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R)\).

\item If
\(
        \tau_\theta(x):=(2\pi)^{-1}
        \int_{\mathbb R}\psi_\theta(\xi)e^{ix\xi}\,\mathrm d\xi,
\)
then
\[
        \mathcal C^{\operatorname{WH}}_{a,\theta_*}(\theta)
        :=
        \int_0^\infty x\tau_\theta(x)\tau_\theta(-x)\,\mathrm dx
\]
defines a holomorphic function on \(S_{\theta_*}\).
\end{enumerate}

Let  $x_0,s_0,\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.

Then there exists a sequence $(z_n,r_n)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $r_n\to\infty$, $z_n/r_n\to\theta$, such that, as $n\to\infty$,

STATUS: independently checked proof, C006 version1 exact reviewer PASS. Proposed functional angle limit: for a zero-bias Gaussian width-n ReLU network with fixed initial input angle theta_0 in (0,pi), U_n(s)=1/(n theta_floor(ns)) converges on finite time intervals to dU=(2U+1/(3pi))ds-sqrt(2)*U dB from U(0)=0, with arbitrary finite conventions on exponentially unlikely degeneracy events. For L/n->t>0, L*theta_L converges in law to 3pi/A_t and L^2*(1-cos(theta_L)) to 9pi^2/(2*A_t^2), where A_t=(1/t)*integral_0^t exp(s+sqrt(2)*W_s)ds. The version2 boundary-generator assembly is a separate unaudited proof, not covered by this PASS.
Independent Gaussian zero-bias width-n ReLU layers; fixed initial angle theta0 in (0,pi); finite T; finite absorbing cemetery embedding; reviewer-PASS C004,C005,C015,C016,C017 version 1.
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:5c0235d208da01b3354156fd03a2788cb4e2628c45d2d23332cb75f9489216fd","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/5c/5c0235d208da01b3354156fd03a2788cb4e2628c45d2d23332cb75f9489216fd.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:7e185a76f632fc458b19fe969e975e29336e6a75bb44e60aea49001f47687453","bundle_entry_key":"functional-angle-limit","bundle_id":"population.t244-relu-entrance-and-radial-drafts-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:gaussian-relu-functional-reciprocal-angle-limit","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Proposed proof of the two-input ReLU angle law

Status: proof draft (unaudited), relying on the explicit estimates in compact_generator.md and uniform_small_angle.md. This is the dossier's existing conjectured law, with its zero-angle and infinite-moment issues repaired. This file does not assert literature novelty, independent verification, a finite-n convergence rate, or the joint output-scale law.

Let two nonzero initial vectors have fixed angle theta_0 in (0,pi). Apply independent zero-bias Gaussian ReLU layers of width n. The Gaussian variance can be 2/n (critical initialization); angular transition probabilities do not depend on this common positive variance. Let theta_l be the angle between the two hidden vectors after l layers. Extinction or exact collinearity can be sent to a cemetery state. For any fixed T, the probability of such an event by layer floor(nT) is at most floor(nT)(n+1)2^-n by localization.md, so any convention there gives the same limiting distributions.

The candidate result is functional convergence of U_n(s)=1/(n theta_floor(ns)), for 0<=s<=T, to the continuous solution

    dU=(2U+a) ds-sqrt(2)U dB, U(0)=0, a=1/(3 pi).

The value U_n at a cemetery state may be set to zero for this convergence assertion. In particular, for L/n->t>0,

    L theta_L => 3 pi/A_t,
    L^2(1-cos(theta_L)) => 9 pi^2/(2 A_t^2),
    A_t=(1/t) integral_0^t exp(s+sqrt(2)W_s) ds.

Thus the correlation defect has stochastic order n^-2 at every fixed positive depth-to-width ratio, with the displayed positive limiting coefficient. No quantitative bound on the distance to this limit is asserted.

## Regularization and the finite initial phase

Fix K and a sufficiently small epsilon from uniform_small_angle.md. Use the self-loop kernel on failure of G while theta lies in [1/(nK),epsilon], and stop on exiting that interval. Before that exit and up to nT steps it can be coupled with the exact chain with disagreement probability at most CnT exp(-cn). We only use this regularization on the specified stopped interval.

For each fixed eta>0 smaller than epsilon, finitely many deterministic iterations of the infinite-width angle map

    F(theta)=arccos((sin(theta)+(pi-theta)cos(theta))/pi)

take theta_0 into (0,eta/2). This follows from F(theta)<theta for theta>0, continuity and F(0)=0. The exact chain follows these finitely many positive deterministic angles in probability by the law of large numbers for the bivariate Gaussian ReLU sample covariance. Consequently, after a deterministic number M(eta) of layers, with probability tending to one, theta is in [c_eta,eta] for some c_eta>0. At this time U_n tends to zero; M(eta)/n tends to zero. During the finitely many preceding layers, their positive limiting angles imply sup U_n tends to zero in probability.

Condition on this high-probability initial event. All estimates below are uniform over its possible starting states. The initial reciprocal angle is at most 1/(n c_eta).

## Stopped bounds

The uniform lemma proves that theta, stopped while theta is in [1/(nK),epsilon], is a nonnegative supermartingale. Therefore its probability of hitting theta>=epsilon before the upper reciprocal-angle exit U>=K is at most eta/epsilon. This is optional stopping at the first boundary exit, applied first with a deterministic time cutoff and then letting it grow. The stopped angle is integrable and bounded; the one-step supermartingale inequality is used only at interior states.

Fix a small delta<K/C, where C bounds the multiplicative reciprocal jump on G. Before U>=delta or theta>=epsilon, the uniform lemma gives E[Delta U|past]>=a/(2n). At the first such exit, U is at most C delta, since an upper reciprocal exit has bounded multiplicative overshoot and a large-angle exit decreases U. Applying the drift bound to the exit time stopped at a deterministic cutoff yields

    E[exit time]/n <= C' delta.

Hence, for any h>0, the probability of failing to enter U>=delta by s-time h, apart from the large-angle exit, is at most C'delta/h. Take h=sqrt(delta). All constants here can be chosen independent of delta after the uniform lemma's K and epsilon are fixed. The total large-angle failure is bounded by eta/epsilon.

At the entrance time sigma_delta, U>=delta. Its overshoot tends to zero in probability for fixed delta: on G, the preceding U must be in [delta/C,delta]. C004 bounds the third absolute jump moment there by C_delta n^-3/2. A union bound over nT possible steps gives probability O_delta(n^-1/2) of an overshoot larger than any fixed positive value, up to s-time T. The entrance-time bound controls later entrance. Thus U(sigma_delta)=delta+o_probability(1).

After entrance, apply the stopped theta supermartingale between U=delta^2 and U=K. Its probability of reaching U<=delta^2 before U>=K is at most delta, since the starting angle is at most 1/(n delta) and the lower-U exit has angle at least 1/(n delta^2). The same bound holds with a time cutoff. Overshoot in the favorable starting direction does not increase this probability.

For upper exits, the uniform reciprocal drift bound, applied to the process stopped at either boundary, gives by discrete Gronwall

    E U_stopped(T) <= (U_initial+(a+C_K epsilon+o_K(1))T) exp(2T).

The probability of an exit through U>=K is bounded by this quantity divided by K. For each fixed K, take n->infinity and then epsilon->0. The resulting bound is C_T/K with a constant independent of K. The K-dependent error is removed before taking K->infinity; it is not treated as uniform. The preceding small initial event and coupling errors are added separately.

## Identification and removal of the stopping

On every fixed compact interval [delta^2,K] in (0,infinity), C004 supplies local generator convergence for bounded C^3 test functions, conditional second moments O(1/n), and conditional third absolute moments O(n^-3/2). Taylor's formula for the martingale increments and the third-moment union bound imply vanishing jumps and identify all stopped subsequential limits with

    Af(u)=(2u+a) f'(u)+u^2 f''(u).

The corresponding one-dimensional diffusion has locally Lipschitz coefficients, and on this compact its noise coefficient is bounded away from zero. Its stopped martingale problem is unique. Standard localized Markov-chain diffusion convergence therefore gives the stopped SDE from initial value delta, after the strong-Markov entrance time. The random initial overshoot tends to zero as just proved.

To remove the stops, fix K and delta first, let n->infinity, then let eta->0 and epsilon->0, then K->infinity and delta->0. The error bounds are eta/epsilon, O(sqrt(delta)), delta, and C_T/K, plus terms vanishing with n for fixed parameters. Equivalently choose epsilon first for each K, eta arbitrarily smaller than epsilon, and subsequently send the other parameters to their limits; no simultaneous uniform-in-K assertion is needed. Before entrance the reciprocal path is at most delta, and the entrance time vanishes in probability as delta->0. The limiting SDE is globally Lipschitz and nonexplosive. Its solutions from delta and zero differ pathwise by

    delta exp(s-sqrt(2)B_s),

which tends uniformly to zero on [0,T] almost surely as delta->0. This also controls the vanishing entrance-time shift by continuity. The preceding bounds therefore give functional convergence to the SDE from zero.

## Marginal angle and correlation limits

Variation of constants gives

    U_t=a integral_0^t exp((t-s)-sqrt(2)(B_t-B_s)) ds>0, t>0.

For one fixed t, Brownian time reversal and symmetry give the equality in law U_t = a integral_0^t exp(s+sqrt(2)W_s) ds. This equality in law is used only at a fixed time; it is not a joint path time-reversal identity. Since L theta_L=(L/n)/U_n(L/n), the angle limit follows by continuity. Also 1-cos(theta)=theta^2/2+O(theta^4), and n theta_L is tight and converges to a positive finite variable. This proves the correlation limit.

## Limits and review priorities

This draft must be checked together with C004 and uniform_small_angle.md. The weakest point is the uniform remainder control in the latter, not the formal linear-SDE solution. The primary-source log-angle formula cannot replace that check because its unqualified raw expectation is infinite at finite n. The two-input output-law problem additionally requires a joint scale/alignment argument; this proof does not supply it.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:b4ac67267699b9f29c9c1ba26a8877b762dfa8a59e6e3dcf03491d54bc24557c","revision_digest":"sha256:e350aa2a411c389469a8a7dfee7030835c95296fc2ffa7d8580195c80e44a6e3","source_id":"own-work:T244-w691-C006:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-reviewer-PASS","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 12 (Upper Bound on Cumulative Expected Error over a Finite Horizon) of arXiv:2608.28198, 'Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility'] For a finite operational timeline $T$ and an initial population $N_0$, let $C_t(\gamma) > 1$ denote the strictly positive expected per-round demographic growth factor for all $t$. Under mean field-approximation of $N_t$, the cumulative expected Mahalanobis error aggregated across all $T$ rounds, defined as $\mathcal{E}_{\text{total}}(\gamma) \triangleq \sum_{t=1}^T \mathcal{E}_t(\gamma)$ is upper bounded by $\mathcal{E}_{\text{total}}(\gamma) \leq \hat{\mathcal{E}}_{\text{total}}(\gamma)$, where:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{\mathcal{E}}_{total}(\gamma) \triangleq
    \frac{\gamma^2 \mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma^{-1}) + d}{N_0 (C_1(\gamma) - 1)} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{[C_1(\gamma)]^T} \right)
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Upper Bound on Cumulative Expected Error over a Finite Horizon

[Lemma lem:Garsia of arXiv:2510.00214, 'On the local well-posedness of randomly forced reaction-diffusion equations with $\bm{L^2}'] For every pairs of real numbers $\tau,\mu\in(0\,,1)$, 
	and for all closed intervals $I\subset(0\,,\infty)$ of length $\le1$, let us
	define
	\begin{equation}
		\varrho( (s\,,y)\,,(t\,,x) ) = |t-s|^{\tau} \vee |x-y|^\mu
		\quad\text{for all $(t\,,x), (s\,,y)\in I\times[0\,,1]$}.
	\end{equation}
	Then, for every $f\in C( I\times[0\,,1])$ and $k\ge 4(\tau^{-1}+\mu^{-1})$,
	\[\displaystyle
		\sup_{y\in I\times[0,1]}|f(y)| - \inf_{y\in I\times[0,1]}|f(y)| \le 640
		\left(\int_{I\times[0,1]}\mathrm{d} a\int_{I\times[0,1]}\mathrm{d} a'\
		\left| \frac{f(a)-f(a')}{\varrho(a\,,a')}\right|^k\right)^{1/k}.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let A be an n x n real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues lambda_1 <= lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n, counted with multiplicity, and for nonzero x let R(x) = (x^* A x)/(x^* x) be its Rayleigh quotient. The Courant-Fischer theorem states lambda_k = min over k-dimensional subspaces U of (max over nonzero x in U of R(x)), which also equals max over (n-k+1)-dimensional subspaces U of (min over nonzero x in U of R(x)). In particular lambda_1 = min_x R(x) and lambda_n = max_x R(x). Also called the min-max theorem or Courant-Fischer-Weyl principle.
title: Courant-Fischer minimax principle

body:
[Lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The lax symmetrix monoidal ${\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}$-right adjoint ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}^\otimes|_{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}\to{\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}^\otimes|_{\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}$ of the inclusion is strong symmetric monoidal. Moreover, it is ${\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}$-cocontinuous.
    \begin{proof}
        Let us begin by showing that the right adjoint $r$ is strong symmetric monoidal. By Lemma~(lemma:equiv-spectra-vs-gl-spectra of the paper), $r$ is given in each degree by a localization at the $G$-equivariant weak equivalences. Thus, the Beck--Chevalley condition for the unit is automatic, while the Beck--Chevalley condition for the tensor product amounts to saying that a tensor product of $G$-equivariant weak equivalences is a $G$-equivariant weak equivalence. Plugging in the definition of the tensor product on ${\mathpalette\ulhelper{\mathfrak S\kern-.5pt\mathfrak p}}\hbox{\rule[-2pt]{0pt}{0pt}}_\textup{gl}^\otimes$ as the derived smash product of flat $G$-orthogonal spectra, this is then a direct consequence of Theorem~(thm:equiv-flatness of the paper).
        
        It remains to show ${\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}$-cocontinuity. By [schwede2018global]*{Corollary 3.1.37} equivariant weak equivalences are stable under wedge sum, so the same argument as above shows that $r$ preserves fiberwise coproducts. As it moreover preserves fiberwise finite colimits by stability, this shows that $f$ is fiberwise cocontinuous. Finally, Proposition~(prop:i!-left-Quillen-equiv-sp of the paper) implies by the same kind of argument that $r$ satisfies the Beck--Chevalley condition for the left adjoints to restrictions along injective homomorphisms, so that $r$ is ${\vphantom{\textup{t}}\smash{\textup{Orb}}}$-cocontinuous by Lemma~(lm:continuouity-clefts of the paper).
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Unnumbered lemma of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'

Passage time is precisely graph distance in this random quotient graph, counting the fewest positive edges needed to reach the target. body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2605.13512, '2605.13512'] Fix $(x,t)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R_+$ and define
\[
F_{x,t}(q):=v_0(q)-g^q(x-q,t),
\qquad q\in [r_L(x,t),r_U(x,t)],
\]
where $r_L(x,t),r_U(x,t)$ are as in Corollary \ref{cor: restriction to compact interval}. Define the two contact sets
\[
A_0(x,t):=\{q\in [r_L,r_U]: q\le x,\ g^q(x-q,t)=0\},
\]
and
\[
A_1(x,t):=\{q\in [r_L,r_U]: q\ge x,\ g^q(x-q,t)=q-x\}.
\]
Then
\[
\max_{q\in[r_L,r_U]}F_{x,t}(q)
=
\max_{q\in [r_L,r_U]\setminus (\operatorname{int}A_0(x,t)\cup \operatorname{int}A_1(x,t))}F_{x,t}(q).
\]
In particular, there exists a maximiser $q^*$ such that either
\[
g^{q^*}(x-q^*,t)>\max\{0,q^*-x\},
\]
or $q^*$ is an endpoint of a connected component of $A_0(x,t)$ or of $A_1(x,t)$.

[Theo 39 (Blowing-up is preserved by finitary coding) of arXiv:2602.14618, 'Finitary coding and Gaussian concentration\\ for random fields'] \leavevmode\\
Let $Y=(Y_i)_{i\in\Zd}$ be a finitary coding of $X=(X_i)_{i\in\Zd}$, and assume that $X$ is ergodic.
If $X$ has the blowing-up property, then $Y$ has the blowing-up property as well.
In particular, if $X$ is an i.i.d. random field, then $Y$ has the blowing-up property. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Blowing-up is preserved by finitary coding

[Corollary cor:general_order of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] For any functions $f^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$, if
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\delta\in O(1)$
    \item $\forall \vb*{y} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta}$ such that $ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta} iy_i \leq \delta$ and $ \|\vb*{y}\|_0\geq 2:$
    $$\mathds{E}\big[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta} (f^{(i)}(U))^{y_i}\big] \in o(n)$$
    \item $\forall k \in [\delta]:$
    $$\mathds{E}[(f^{(k)}(U))^{\lfloor \frac{\delta}{k} \rfloor}] \in o(n)$$
    \item $\forall k \in [\delta]$ s.t. $\exists v \in V$ with $f_1^{(k)}(v) > 0:$
    $$\exists c>0 \textnormal{ s.t. }  \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathds{P}(f^{(k)}(U) \geq 1) \geq c$$
\end{enumerate}
then
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta} ia_i = \delta}} \sum_{\alpha(\cdot) \in R(\vb*{a})} H( \vb*{a},\alpha(\cdot)) &= \delta!^w (n\mathds{E}[f^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta} + \Big( -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\delta!^{1+w}}{(\delta-2)!}(n\mathds{E}[f^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta-2} n\mathds{E}[(f^{(1)}(U))^2] \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{0.5cm} + \frac{1}{2^{1+w}} \frac{\delta!^{1+w}}{(\delta-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta-2} n\mathds{E}[f^{(2)}(U)] \Big) (1+o(1))\nonumber \\
   &= \delta!^w (n\mathds{E}[f^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta}(1+o(1)).
\end{align*}

body:
[Theorem 34 of arXiv:2609.02785, 'Characterization of Stanley-Reisner varieties by their automorphism group'] Let $\Delta$ be a fully hidden simplicial complex on $[n]$. Then
$$
\Aut(X_\Delta)\ =\ T_0\ \rtimes\ S(\Delta),
$$
a linear algebraic group of dimension~$n$ whose identity component is $T_0$.\rchange{\footnote{
For \emph{irreducible} rigid affine varieties, \cite[Theorem~1]{AG17} produces a subtorus of
$\Aut(X)$ containing every other subtorus, which is therefore normal. That statement does not
cover the present case: a fully hidden $\Delta$ on $n\geq2$ vertices has at least two facets;
a single facet would be all of $[n]$, every vertex of which is private, so $X_\Delta$ is
reducible. Their Proposition~1 does give a finite extension of the torus when the canonical
grading is pointed, a hypothesis $\KK[\Delta]$ satisfies (its weight cone is $\ZZ^n_{\geq0}$
and its degree-zero part is $\KK$), but only for an integral graded algebra, and the extension
is not asserted to split. Whether $\Aut(X)$ is a finite extension of a torus for a general rigid
$X$ is open even under strong hypotheses \cite[Remark~6.5]{BGa25}. The proof below is self-contained and gives more: the
extension splits, with finite complement $S(\Delta)$.}}

 M_{\mathcal D}=M\cap\mathcal D,\qquad

\[
 \lim_{X\to\infty}\frac1{N_{\mathcal D}(X)}
 \sum_{\substack{m,n\in M_{\mathcal D}\;m\ne n\\
                  \lambda_m,\lambda_n\leq X}}
 f(\lambda_m-\lambda_n)
 =D\int_\R f(t)\,dt.
\]

body:
[Proposition 11 (Isometry relation) of arXiv:2608.12225, 'Higher-order variation and\\ pathwise It\^o calculus on manifolds'] Let $p\geq 2$ be an even integer, let $X\in V_p(M,\pi)$, and assume
that the tensor measure $[X]_\pi^{(p)}$ has no atoms. Let $\nabla$ be
an affine connection on $M$ and let $f\in C^p(M,\mathbb R)$. Let
\[
    I_t^\nabla(f,X)
    :=
    \int_0^t
    \left\langle
        T_\nabla^{p-1}f(X_s),
        d_\pi^{p-1}X_s
    \right\rangle,
    \qquad 0\leq t\leq T.
\]
be the integral defined in \eqref{eq:pathwiseintegral}. Then
$I^\nabla(f,X)\in V_p(\mathbb R,\pi),$
and its $p$-th variation along $\pi$ is given by
\begin{equation}
    d[I^\nabla(f,X)]_{\pi,t}^{(p)}
    =
    \left\langle
        (df_{X_t})^{\otimes p},
        d[X]_{\pi,t}^{(p)}
    \right\rangle.   
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for every $t\in[0,T]$,
\begin{equation}
    [I^\nabla(f,X)]_\pi^{(p)}([0,t])
    =
    \int_{[0,t]}
    \left\langle
        (df_{X_s})^{\otimes p},
        d[X]_{\pi,s}^{(p)}
    \right\rangle.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Isometry relation

body:
[Theorem 2 (Convergence in path space) of arXiv:2606.27117, 'Occupation-Time Fluctuations of an Age-Dependent Branching System Driven by Poisson Immigr'] Let $F$ be an absolutely continuous lifetime distribution such that
\[
F(0)=0,\quad F(x)<1 \ \textit{\ for \ all } \ x\ge 0,\quad \textit{and}\quad
1-F(t)\sim\frac{1}{t^{\gamma}\Gamma(1-\gamma)}\quad\mbox{with}\quad\gamma<1.
\]

Let $0<\alpha<d<(1+\gamma)\alpha$, and $F_T^2 = T^{3+\gamma-\frac{d}{\alpha}}.$
Then $\X_T$ converges weakly to $\X$ in $C([0,\Upsilon],{\cal S}'(\mathbb{R}^d))$ as $T\to\infty$ for any $\Upsilon>0$, where $\X:=\{\X(t),\ t\ge 0\}$ is a centered Gaussian process with covariance functional given by
$$
\mathrm{Cov}\big(\langle \X(s),\varphi\rangle,\langle \X(t),\psi\rangle\big)
=
\frac{\gamma\Gamma(1/\alpha)\langle\lambda,\varphi\rangle\langle\lambda,\psi\rangle}
{2(\frac{d}{\alpha}-1)(2-\frac{d}{\alpha})(3-\frac{d}{\alpha})
\pi\alpha\Gamma(1+\gamma)} C(s,t),
$$
where
\begin{align}
\nonumber
C(s,t)
&=
\int_0^s w^{\gamma-1}\Bigg[
3(s-w)^{\b} + (t-w)^{\b}

+\frac{\b}{\gamma}w\Big(
(t-w)^{2-\frac{d}{\alpha}} - (s-w)^{2-\frac{d}{\alpha}}
\Big)
-(t+s-2w)^{\b}
\Bigg]\,dw,
\\ 
&\qquad 0\le s\le t,\quad \varphi,\psi\in\E.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Janson's Problem 20.2 (Probability Surveys 2012, Section 20.2) asks whether the outdegree counts N_d of a conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree are asymptotically normal. (a) nu = 1 with finite variance: yes, jointly with the covariances (Janson, Random Structures Algorithms 48 (2016), Theorem 1.13 with Example 2.2 and Section 8). (b) nu = 1 with infinite variance and (c) nu < 1: yes when the offspring law is regularly varying (Thevenin, Electron. J. Probab. 25 (2020), Theorems 6.2 and 6.7, variance pi_d(1 - pi_d)), but not in general. A subcritical law whose bulk sits on {0, 1}, with two rare atoms at (1 - q - c) n_r +/- A sqrt(n_r), each of probability n_r^{-4}, makes the conditioned tree carry exactly one of the two with probability tending to 1/2 each, so N_1 = n pi_1 -/+ A sqrt(n) up to smaller terms, a near two-point law (Theorem A, full proof); the critical infinite-variance case is the same construction with the pair straddling the missing mass of an absent rarer atom (Theorem B, a sketch that still needs a lattice local moderate-deviation expansion). Thevenin's conjecture that normality holds for every such law is therefore false. The regularly varying case survives because the giant's law is locally flat at scale sqrt(n).

body:
Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E with E FINITE. For events A and B define the DISJOINT OCCURRENCE A box B as the set of configurations omega for which there exist DISJOINT sets of coordinates K and L such that every configuration agreeing with omega on K lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on L lies in B - informally, A and B occur for disjoint reasons. VAN DEN BERG-KESTEN: if A and B are both INCREASING then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B). REIMER: the same inequality holds for ARBITRARY events A and B, with no monotonicity hypothesis. The direction is opposite to Harris-FKG, which is the point: increasing events are positively correlated, but requiring them to occur on disjoint witnesses destroys that correlation and more. The finiteness of E is a genuine hypothesis of the standard statements; infinite index sets are handled by approximation, and the definition of disjoint occurrence itself needs care there. Typical use: bounding the probability of two disjoint open crossings, or of a self-avoiding open path of length n, by a product. [van den Berg and Kesten (1985); Reimer (2000), Combin. Probab. Comput. 9; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.12]
product measure on a FINITE index set

[Proposition prop:sc-diamond of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] The system
(equation eq:sc-linear-1 of the paper)--(equation eq:sc-linear-j of the paper) is
compatible\footnote{That is, for any choice of initial data
$\{\Psi(T^\ell u_0)\}_{\ell \in \mathbb{Z}}$ along a $T$-orbit,
the continuous equation and each $S_j$-recurrence give the
same value for $\partial_1\Psi(S_j u)$, and any two discrete
recurrences give the same value for $\Psi(S_i S_j u)$.}
if and only if two families of conditions hold.  First, for
each $j \geq 2$ and $u \in \mathcal{V}$, the following
semi-discrete diamond equations hold:
\begin{align}
C_1(Tu)C_j(u)
  &= C_j(Tu)C_1(S_j u),
   \\
\Lambda_1(u)\Lambda_j(u)
  &= \Lambda_j(u)\Lambda_1(S_j u)
  + \partial_1\Lambda_j(u),
   \\
C_1(u)\Lambda_j(u)
  + \Lambda_1(Tu)C_j(u)
  &- C_j(u)\Lambda_1(S_j u)
  - \Lambda_j(Tu)C_1(S_j u)
  - \partial_1 C_j(u) = 0.
  
\end{align}
Second, for each pair $i, j \geq 2$ and
$u \in \mathcal{V}$, the fully discrete diamond equations
(equation eq:diamond-C-ij of the paper)--(equation eq:diamond-mixed-ij of the paper) of
Proposition~(prop:CL-gen-system of the paper) hold.

zero entry.  

The vestibule $\V$ consists of the matrices $P>0$
for which $P=QK_{ij}(s)$ for some $Q\in\T$, some $i\neq j$, and some $0 < s <1$. 

The narrow
hall $\NH$ consists of the matrices $P\notin\T\cup\V$ for which
$P=QK_{ij}(s)$ for some $Q\in\V$, some $i\neq j$, and some $0<s<1$.

A measurable real-valued functional $f$ defined on finite simplicial complexes with vertices in $\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{A}$ is called weakly stabilizing if: (i) $f$ is Euclidean translation-invariant, i.e., $f(K + t) = f(K)$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}^d$; and (ii) there exists a real-valued random variable $Z$ such that for every sequence of cubes $(W_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ expanding to $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($W_n \to \mathbb{R}^d$), the difference operator satisfies $\Lambda_{(\mathbf{0}, V, 1, U)} f(\Delta_{W_n}) \xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}} Z$ as $n \to \infty$, where $V \sim \Theta$ and $U \sim \mathbb{Q}$ are independent of $\Psi$.
f is translation invariant

[Thm 3 (Conditional one-point fluctuations) of arXiv:2608.20552, 'One-point fluctuations for exponential last passage percolation under upper-tail condition'] For every $(x,y)\in U_1$ and $\rr\in\R$,
\beq
	\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\prob\left[
		\frac{\LPP(\ac xN,\bc yN)-\mv(x,y)N}{\sdev(x,y)N^{1/3}}
		\le\rr
		\,\bigg|\,
		\LPP(\ac N,\bc N)>\lv N
	\right]
	=F_{\tn{GUE}}(\rr).
\eeq
For every $(x,y)\in U_2$ and $\rr\in\R$,
\beq
	\lim_{N\to\infty}
	\prob\left[
		\frac{\LPP(\ac xN,\bc yN)-\mv(x,y)N}{\sdev(x,y)N^{1/2}}
		\le\rr
		\,\bigg|\,
		\LPP(\ac N,\bc N)>\lv N
	\right]
	=\Phi(\rr).
\eeq (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Conditional one-point fluctuations

[Thm 2 (Spectral radius) of arXiv:2604.13134, '\bf From Gaussian to Gumbel: extreme eigenvalues of complex Ginibre products with exact ra'] Let \(X_n\), \(\alpha\), \(a_n\), \(v_\alpha\), \(q_1(j,\cdot)\), \(q_2(j,\cdot)\), and
\(\Phi_\alpha\) be defined as above. Then the following Berry Esseen bound 
hold for the spectral radius.

\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(\alpha=+\infty\), then
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\big|\mathbb P(X_n\le x)-e^{-e^{-x}}\big|
=\frac{(\log\log \alpha_n)^2}{2e\log \alpha_n}(1+o(1))
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).

\item If \(\alpha=0\), then
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\big|\mathbb P(X_n\le x)-\Phi(x)\big|
=(1+o(1))
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\phi(x)\big|\sqrt{\alpha_n}-\frac{x}{4n}\big|
\]
as \(n\to+\infty\).

\item If \(\alpha\in(0,+\infty)\), then
\[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\big|\mathbb P(X_n\le x)-\Phi_\alpha(x)\big|
\]
\[
=(1+o(1))
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\Phi_\alpha(x)
\big|
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}
\frac{\phi(v_\alpha(j,x))}{\Phi(v_\alpha(j,x))}
\bigl[n^{-1}q_1(j,x)+(\alpha_n-\alpha)q_2(j,x)\bigr]
\big|
\]
whenever \(n\) is sufficiently large.

\item As the tuning parameter \(\alpha\) varies from \(0\) to \(+\infty\), one has
\[
\lim_{\alpha\to0^+}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha}}
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|\Phi_\alpha(x)-\Phi(x)\right|
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}},
\]
and
\[
\lim_{\alpha\to+\infty}
\frac{\log\alpha}{(\log\log\alpha)^2}
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\big|\Phi_\alpha(x)-e^{-e^{-x}}\big|
=\frac{1}{2e}.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Proposition prop:resample-nonsimple of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $\kappa',\kappa,\rho_1,\rho_2,\alpha,\beta$ be as in Theorem~(thm:SLE-duality of the paper). Let $\mu_{\alpha,\beta}$ be the joint law of the curves $(\eta^L,\eta^R)$ in Theorem~(thm:SLE-duality of the paper). Also consider a Markov chain  $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ on pair of non-crossing continuous curves $(\tilde\eta_1,\tilde\eta_2)$ from $0$ to $-i$ in $\mathbb{D}$ such that in each step one uniformly randomly picks $j\in\{1,2\}$, then resamples $\tilde\eta^j$ according to the conditional law of $\eta^j$ given $\eta^{3-j}$ as described in Proposition~(prop:radial-flowline of the paper) where we identify $(1,2)=(L,R)$. Then any invariant $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ of $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ can be written as $\mu = \int_\mathbb{R} \mu_{\alpha\beta}\nu(d\beta)$ where $\nu$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure on $\mathbb{R}$.

[Lemma of arXiv:2411.06827, 'The Exponential Lie Series and a Chen--Strichartz Formula for L{\'e}vy Processes'] The basis change formula expressing the elements of ${\mathbb A}^\ast$ in terms of the elements of $({\mathbb A}^0)^\ast$ in ${\mathbb R} {\langle}{\mathbb A}{\rangle}$ is obtained as
$$
	w=\sum_{(i_1, \ldots, i_\ell)}
	\frac{(-1)^{|w|-\ell}}{i_1\cdots i_\ell} (i_1, \ldots,\, i_\ell)\circ w^0.
$$
where $w^0=a_1^0\cdots a_n^0$. Here we use the same notation as above by setting
\begin{equation*}
	(i_1, \ldots,\, i_\ell)\circ w^0 := 
		[ a_1,\ldots , a_{i_1}]^0
		[ a_{i_1+1}, \ldots , a_{i_1+i_2}]^0\cdots
		[ a_{i_1+\cdots+i_{\ell-1}+1}, \ldots , a_{n}]^0
\end{equation*}
in terms of the concatenation of repeated bracket products of the letters in each subword as indicated. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$h \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}(H_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{M}})$ be a shift satisfying
almost surely $\|D_W h\|_{\mathrm{op}} < 1$ and $\|D_W h\|_{\mathrm{HS}} < \infty$. Then
$W \mapsto W' = W + h(W)$ is almost surely bijective, the laws $\mathcal{L}(W')$
and $\mathcal{L}(W)$ are mutually absolutely continuous, and the Radon--Nikodym
derivative $L = \mathrm{\,d} \mathcal{L}(W')/ \mathrm{\,d} \mathcal{L}(W)$ satisfies
\[
  \log L = \delta(h) - \frac{1}{2}\|h\|_{H_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{M}}}^2 - \log|\det\nolimits_2(I + D_W h)| .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Defn Coulomb gas correlations for a divisor on the Riemann sphere of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let the divisor
$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\sum \sigma_j \cdot z_j,
$$
where $\left\{z_j\right\}_{j=1}^n$ is a finite set of distinct points on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$.
The Coulomb gas correlation $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is a differential of conformal dimension $\lambda_j$ at $z_j$, given by

\begin{equation}
\lambda_j=\lambda_b\left(\sigma_j\right) \equiv \frac{\sigma_j^2}{2}-\sigma_j b ,
\end{equation}

where $\lambda_b(\sigma)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2}-\sigma b \quad(\sigma \in \mathbb{C})$
whose value is given by

\begin{equation}
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] =\prod_{j<k}\left(z_j-z_k\right)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k} ,
\end{equation}
where the product is taken over all finite $z_j$ and $z_k$. 

This defines a holomorphic function of $\boldsymbol{z}$ on the configuration space
\[
\mathbb{C}_{\mathrm{distinct}}^n = \left\{ \boldsymbol{z} = (z_1, \ldots, z_n) \in \mathbb{C}^n \,\middle|\, z_j \neq z_k \text{ for } j \neq k \right\}.
\]
In general, the function is multivalued, and one must choose a single-valued branch for each factor $(z_j-z_k)^{\sigma_j\sigma_k}$, except in special cases where all $\sigma_j$ are integers. If all $\sigma_j$ are even integers, the function becomes single-valued and independent of the ordering of the product. In the special case where $\sigma_j = 1$ for all $j$, the correlation function coincides with the Vandermonde determinant.
title: Coulomb gas correlations for a divisor on the Riemann sphere

[Theorem thm.salem.func.gen of arXiv:2609.01007, 'Global universality of the expected number \\of zeros of non-analytic random signals'] Suppose that the base function $f$ satisfies the condition $\mathbf{(H1)}$ and that the common law of the $(a_k)$ admits a finite third moment. Then, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely, for all $t \in {\rm I\kern-0.16em R}$, we have
\[
\lim_{n\to +\infty} \mathbb{E}_X\left[e^{itf_n(X)}\right]= e^{-\frac{t^2}{2}\langle f,f \rangle}.
\]
In other words, $\mathbb{P}-$almost surely, the sequence of random variables $(f_n(X))_{n\geq 0}$ converges in distribution under $\mathbb{P}_X$ towards a {centered} Gaussian variable {with variance $\langle f,f \rangle$}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def: boundary connectivity event of arXiv:2606.13147, 'Scaling limits of the single-curve interface and outermost loops in the planar random fiel'] Write
$\Sigma_M^c=\{-1,1\}^{\partial\Lambda_M\cup (\Lambda_N\setminus\Lambda_M)}.$

For any $\xi\in \Sigma_M^c$, let
$
\mathcal P=\{x\in \partial \Lambda_M:\xi_x=1\}.
$
Let $\mathcal P_0,\mathcal P_1\subset \mathcal P$ be two disjoint subsets, and let $\mathcal U$ be a collection of mutually disjoint subsets of $\mathcal P$, each of which is also disjoint from $\mathcal P_0\cup \mathcal P_1$.

Define $\mathcal Y^{-}$ to be the event that $\mathcal P_0$ is not plus-connected to $\mathcal P_1$ inside $\Lambda_M$, and define $\mathcal Y^{+}$ to be the event that, for every $U\in \mathcal U$, the set $U$ is plus-connected to $\mathcal P_0$ inside $\Lambda_M$. We then write
$
\mathcal Y=\mathcal Y^{-}\cap \mathcal Y^{+}.
$

Next, let $\mathcal X^{-}$ be the event that there exists a $*$-minus circuit in the annulus
$
\Lambda_{M/2}\setminus \Lambda_{M/4},
$
and let $\mathcal X^{+}$ be the event that there exists a plus circuit in the same annulus which is plus-connected to $\mathcal P_0$. We define
$
\mathcal X=\mathcal X^{+}\cap \mathcal X^{-}.
$

Finally, set
$
\mathcal R=\mathcal Y\setminus \mathcal X,
\mathcal S=\mathcal X\cap \mathcal Y.
$
For simplicity, we use
$
X,X^{+},X^{-},Y,Y^{+},Y^{-},R,S\in\{0,1\}
$
to denote the indicator functions of the events
$
\mathcal X,\mathcal X^{+},\mathcal X^{-},\mathcal Y,\mathcal Y^{+},\mathcal Y^{-},\mathcal R,\mathcal S,
$
respectively.
title: Definition def: boundary connectivity event of arXiv:2606.13147

\E\varphi(X(t))-\E\varphi(X^\eta(t))
\big|
\le
C e^{Ct_L\alpha }\,\eta (t_L+1)\,\max(\eta,\alpha),
\]

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). After the optimism reading was refuted (P20), the gain was located row by row: the per-evaluation-row relative-score gain of the long-only stack over least squares against the bootstrap variance of the least-squares stack at that row. P22 (a) REFUTED at the pre-registered 0.2: the within-cell median Spearman between a row's gain and the least-squares variance load at that row is 0.13 over the 40 EMIT cells (positive in 36 of 40; 0.37 on Y2, 0.01 on Y1); (b) HELD on Y2, REFUTED as an every-group claim: the top-decile-load rows carry 47 pct of Y2's gain (a uniform spread gives 10) but only 11 pct on Y1 (20 on Y3, 32 on Y4); (c) HELD: across the 40 EMIT cells the gain rank-correlates 0.54 with the variance-load share of least squares' error, and 0.65 with the share the constraint removes (least squares minus nn1) - the between-cell statistic that optimism (P20) failed to be; (d) REFUTED as written: the OCO-2 top-decile share reaches 0.40 on sco2, but as the share of a gain of -0.55 pct it is the ratio of two near-zero numbers and does not test the clause; falsifier (within-cell correlation at or below zero) not triggered. Reading: where the gain is large (Y2, +18) it sits where least squares is uncertain - row-level rank correlation 0.37, 47 pct of the gain on the tenth of rows with the largest variance; where it is modest (+5 to +6) it is spread over the rows; between cells the variance-load share of least squares' error predicts the gain (0.54) and the variance the constraint removes predicts it better (0.65). The calibration and evaluation rows share the same target-norm distribution, so this is not a split shift; the gain leans toward the small-norm evaluation rows the reported metric weights most. Cell level: the variance the constraint removes (least squares' bootstrap variance share minus the long-only stack's) predicts the gain within every output group (Spearman 0.79, 0.87, 0.54, 0.43 on Y1-Y4; 0.69 across 40 cells with the group effect removed), while the L1 norm of the least-squares weights does not survive the group adjustment (0.02): the constraint pays what it saves in estimation variance at the rows it is scored on. Fresh-split replication (split C, SPLIT_SEED 11): P23 (a) REFUTED at the per-group 0.5, HELD in the aggregate: on split C the within-group Spearman between the gain and the variance removed is +0.59, +0.49, +0.64, +0.22 on Y1..Y4 and +0.74 across the 40 cells with the group effect removed (split B: +0.69); (b) REFUTED: the split-B variance-removed share predicts the split-C gain only on Y1 and Y2 (+0.72, +0.47; Y3 +0.09, Y4 -0.24; demeaned +0.17), and the split-B gain itself predicts the split-C gain only weakly (Y1 +0.82, Y4 +0.47, Y2 +0.15, Y3 -0.14); (c) HELD: the long-only stack beats least squares on 35 of 40 split-C cells (mean +9.59 against +8.83 on split B); falsifier (any group at or below 0.2, or the demeaned correlation at or below 0.3) not triggered. Fresh-split check of the calibration-side correlates (P32, the P20 driver on split C): P32 (a) HELD: on split C the between-cell Spearman of the gain with the least-squares L1 is +0.55 and with n_eff -0.44; (b) REFUTED: group-demeaned, L1 +0.29 and members kept +0.21; (c) HELD: the nn0 RMSE gain with the smallest relative eigenvalue +0.29 and with the condition number -0.31; falsifier (L1 above +0.3 after the group adjustment) not triggered.

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Finite-second-moment extension of Gaussian product spectral coupling and Target2 comparisons, proof unaudited. Let independent real factor arrays U(N by M),V(P by M) have fixed centered iid unit-variance laws, possibly different, with finite second moments only; P/N->alpha>0 and M/N->beta>0 finite. Ordered product singular profiles of X=UV^T/sqrt(N) and an independent Gaussian-factor reference B satisfy E sum_j(sigma_j(X)-sigma_j(B))^2/(NP)->0. Centered normalized bounded truncations give the exact error E||X-X_K||_F^2/(NP)=2(M/N)(1-c_U,K*c_V,K), where c_A,K=E[A A_K]->1. Apply existing finite-fourth-moment convergence008 at fixed K, then K->infinity. Haar/channel comparison006 gives limsup per-entry MI_X-MI_B<=0 at every fixed s>=0 for ALL positive finite aspect ratios. For P/N->1, the C1 reference limit022 also gives limsup normalized MMSE_X-MMSE_B<=0 at EVERY fixed s>=0, with no exceptional SNR set. Non-unit centered variances follow by rescaling; noncentered or dimension-dependent priors are not asserted. Novelty unestablished.
Independent arrays with fixed centered iid unit-variance real factor laws and finite second moments.
Positive finite limits P/N and M/N; near-square P/N->1 required only for the all-SNR MMSE conclusion.
Independent standard Gaussian channel noise and per-entry Frobenius loss.
Existing finite-fourth-moment spectral coupling008, Haar comparison006 and new reference proof022 remain unaudited dependencies.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:ff286e93f6c37c0dad47334ff8bfca3e8d96473b830ffac93cbb560093e9e5e2","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/ff/ff286e93f6c37c0dad47334ff8bfca3e8d96473b830ffac93cbb560093e9e5e2.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f7ee46a2e3388a11ce13fc89ccd7a2a712259b34ba37615dbe0afe0e0398d634","bundle_entry_key":"finite-variance-product-gaussian-mi-mmse-extremality-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-near-square-c1-and-finite-variance-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:finite-variance-product-gaussian-mi-mmse-extremality-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Finite-variance iid factors: spectral coupling and near-square MMSE comparison

Target 2 partial result, proof draft, unaudited. Novelty is unestablished.
This extends the moment scope of the existing spectral coupling and
uses the new near-square C1 reference limit. It is not an additional
isolated numerical case or a dimension-uniform Target1 expansion.

Let N->infinity, P/N->alpha in (0,infinity), M/N->beta in (0,infinity).
Let U and V be independent real arrays of sizes N by M and P by M.
Each array has iid entries from a fixed centered unit-variance law;
only finite second moments are assumed. The two laws may differ.
Set X=UV^T/sqrt(N), and let B be the same product with independent
standard Gaussian factors. Define ordered-singular-profile distance

 D_N(X,B)^2=E sum_j(sigma_j(X)-sigma_j(B))^2/(NP),

where B is independent of the original arrays. Then

    D_N(X,B)->0.                                    (1)

Consequently, for every fixed s>=0,

 limsup [I(X;sqrt(s)X+G)-I(B;sqrt(s)B+G)]/(NP)<=0.    (2)

If in addition P/N->1, then for every fixed s>=0,

    limsup [mmse_X,N(s)-mmse_B,N(s)]<=0,             (3)

where each Bayes risk uses its own Gaussian observation and Frobenius
loss divided by NP. The Gaussian risk has the explicit limit in
gaussian_reference_near_square_c1.md. This includes N=P=M and all fixed
positive hidden-rank ratios in the near-square aspect. Gaussian factors
maximize the limiting comparison for BOTH MI and product MMSE, with
the latter conclusion here restricted to P/N->1.

## 1. Centered, normalized truncations with exact covariances

For a centered variance-one random variable A define, for sufficiently
large K,

 b_K=E[A 1_(|A|<=K)],
 v_K=E[A^2 1_(|A|<=K)]-b_K^2>0,
 A_K=(A 1_(|A|<=K)-b_K)/sqrt(v_K),
 c_K=E[A A_K]=E[A^2 1_(|A|<=K)]/sqrt(v_K).

Then A_K is bounded, centered and variance one. Finite second moment
gives b_K->0, v_K->1 and c_K->1. Cauchy-Schwarz gives |c_K|<=1; its
displayed numerator shows c_K>=0. Thus 0<=c_K<=1, and
E(A-A_K)^2=2(1-c_K)->0. These facts require no higher moments or tail
decay rate. Thresholds with zero v_K are simply omitted; sufficiently
large thresholds have v_K>0.

Apply this construction separately to the U and V laws, with
covariances c_U,K,c_V,K. Couple every entry with its own normalized
truncation, preserving independence across entries and between arrays.
The resulting U_K,V_K have fixed bounded iid laws, and
X_K=U_K V_K^T/sqrt(N).

For a single product summand, independence between factor arrays gives

 E(U_ia V_ja-(U_K)_ia(V_K)_ja)^2
                  =2(1-c_U,K*c_V,K).

Different hidden indices a have zero cross terms: each difference is
centered and the entry pairs at distinct a are independent. Summing
over the M hidden indices and then the NP entries yields the exact
dimension-independent normalized error

 E||X-X_K||_F^2/(NP)
                  =2(M/N)(1-c_U,K*c_V,K).           (4)

No conditional probabilities or independent error events are multiplied.
The required independence is explicit in this entrywise computation.

## 2. Transfer the bounded-law spectral coupling

Hoffman-Wielandt bounds the ordered singular-value distance between
X and X_K by their Frobenius distance. Fix K. The bounded factor laws
meet every finite-fourth-moment hypothesis of existing unaudited
claim008. With the same independent Gaussian reference B, that claim
gives D_N(X_K,B)->0. Minkowski and the pointwise ordered-profile triangle
therefore give

 limsup_N D_N(X,B)
       <=sqrt(2 beta(1-c_U,K*c_V,K)).                (5)

First take N->infinity with K fixed, then K->infinity. The right side
tends to zero, proving(1). This is a two-limit approximation argument;
no unproved interchange or dimension-dependent truncation law is used.
It also avoids assuming that weak spectral convergence alone implies
expected W2 convergence for the original heavy-tailed factors.

## 3. Information and MMSE consequences

Claim006's finite Haar-mixture comparison and Gaussian information/W2
bound apply under finite second moments, which are present here. The
Gaussian reference is biorthogonally invariant. The spectral coupling(1)
therefore gives the information limsup(2) at every positive fixed s,
without requiring an information limit for the original iid prior.
At s=0 both mutual informations are zero.

For MMSE, Haar-randomizing the signal's left and right frames can only
increase its Bayes risk: revealing those independent frames reduces
the problem to the original Gaussian channel by rotating its noise.
Claim006 also gives two-sided information closeness between the
Haarized signal and B from the shared-frame spectral coupling(1).
When P/N->1, the Gaussian reference has a finite C1 information limit
by the full proof in gaussian_reference_near_square_c1.md. Concave
secant bounds and I-MMSE consequently give the same limiting risk for
the Haarized signal and the Gaussian reference. The original signal's
risk is bounded above by its Haarized risk. This proves(3) for every
s>0, with no exceptional SNR set. At s=0, both product-entry variances
are exactly M/N, proving the zero-SNR comparison directly.

Non-unit positive variances follow by multiplying the signal by the
product of the factor standard deviations and rescaling s accordingly.
The centered zero-variance cases are identically zero. Noncentered or
dimension-dependent prior laws are not asserted here.

## Dependencies and remaining scope

The all-aspect finite-fourth-moment profile convergence in claim008 and
the Haar/channel comparison in claim006 remain unaudited dependencies.
The new near-square reference proof depends on unaudited claims017,
019,020,021 and primary Silverstein/Biane results. None is independently
checked without an exact-version reviewer PASS.

The hardest remaining Target2 piece is pointwise reference regularity
at general rectangular aspect P/N->alpha!=1. Existing averaged and
off-corner statements remain separate. No finite-N Gaussian-factor
extremality is claimed: the old finite-size shrinking-SNR reversal is
compatible with these fixed-SNR dimension-limit conclusions. Target1's
dimension-uniform explicit remainder and Target3's larger-size numerical
correction are not settled by this argument.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:686964a520b560babff49b2d3c712ffe188ecb5df9287b91721884bf39c60f66","revision_digest":"sha256:e3d78694f87f7026224d1fe3fa92818d46f022d5d286d995e6edc50744cfd430","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:finite-variance-product-gaussian-mi-mmse-extremality-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 claim w718-T287-023 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 37 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $p$ is odd, $\chi$ is injective, $m$ is even, and the morphism $X\rightarrow X/G$ is an HKG cover. Let $l_1<\cdots<l_s$ be the lower jumps and let $u_1<\cdots<u_s$ be the upper jumps of the wild cyclic subgroup $H=C_{p^s}$ acting on the completion of the local ring of $X$ at the ramified point. For each $j\in\llbracket0,s\rrbracket$ let $H_{s-j}$ and $Y_j$ be as in Corollary \ref{C4} and, if $j\ge 1$, let 
$$\l_j:=l_j-1.$$ Then the following properties hold. 

\medskip
{\bf (1)} We have $\textup{g}_{Y_0}=0$ and for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ we have
\[
\textup{g}_{Y_i}=\frac{p-1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^i \l_jp^{i-j}.
\]

{\bf (2)} For each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$, $p-1$ divides $\textup{g}_{Y_i}$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Let $\mathcal R_X$ be the $B_0[H]$-module of Proposition \ref{P5}(2). Then we have identities 
$$\frac{\textup{g}_{Y_i}-\textup{g}_{Y_{i-1}}}{p^i-p^{i-1}}=\frac{\l_i+(p-1)\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\l_jp^{i-1-j}}{2p^{i-1}}=\frac{u_i-1}{2}$$
for each $i\in\llbracket1,s\rrbracket$ and hence a $B_0[H]$-linear isomorphism 
$$\mathcal R_X\cong\oplus_{i=1}^s \frac{\l_i+(p-1)\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\l_jp^{i-1-j}}{2p^{i-1}}\mathcal B_i= \oplus_{i=1}^s \frac{u_i-1}{2}\mathcal B_i.$$

{\bf (4)} Let $\mathcal X$ be a smooth projective curve over $\Spec R$ whose reduction modulo $\upsilon$ is $X$ and such that there exists a homomorphism $\varrho:G\rightarrow\Aut(\mathcal X)$ that lifts $\rho$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (4.a) (de Jong)} For each subgroup $\Delta$ of $G$, the quotient curve $\mathcal X/\Delta$ is smooth projective over $\Spec R$ with geometrically connected fibers.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (4.b)} For each subgroup $\Delta$ of $G$, the special fiber $(\mathcal X/\Delta)_k$ of $\mathcal X/\Delta$ is naturally identified with $X/\Delta$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (4.c) (Chinburg--Guralnick--Harbater)} The KGB obstruction for the HKG cover $X\rightarrow X/G$ vanishes.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (4.d)} We have $B[H]$-linear isomorphisms
$$H^0(\mathcal X,\Omega_{\mathcal X})\otimes_R B\cong H^1(\mathcal X,\mathcal O_{\mathcal X})\otimes_R B\cong\oplus_{i=1}^s \frac{u_i-1}{2}\mathcal B_i.$$

[Lem graph-to-weighted-jordan of arXiv:2607.21428, 'Subcritical percolation and network archaeology on random recursive tree substrate network'] Suppose the conclusion of Lemma~(lem:singly-attached-decorations of the paper) holds.
		Write \(X_u:=|D_u|\) for \(u\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}\), and
		\(X(A):=\sum_{u\in A}X_u\).  Put
		\[
		\Delta_n:=\max_{u\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}}|D_u|.
		\]
		Then for every skeleton vertex \(v\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}\),
		\begin{equation}
			
			0
			\leqslant
			\psi_{\mathcal{C}_n^{\operatorname{root}}}(v)
			-
			\psi_{\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}}^X(v)
			\leqslant
			\Delta_n .
		\end{equation}
		Moreover, fix a skeleton vertex \(v_{\mathrm{skel}}\), an integer \(L\geqslant1\), and
		\(\delta>0\).
		If
		\begin{equation}
			
			\Delta_n\leqslant \frac{\delta}{4}X(\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}),
			\qquad
			\psi_{\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}}^X(v_{\mathrm{skel}})
			\leqslant
			(1-\delta)X(\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}),
		\end{equation}
		and
		\begin{equation}
			
			\#\left\{
			v\in\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}:
			\psi_{\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}}^X(v)
			\leqslant
			\psi_{\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}}}^X(v_{\mathrm{skel}})+\delta X(\mathcal{B}_n^{\operatorname{root}})
			\right\}
			\leqslant L,
		\end{equation}
		then \(v_{\mathrm{skel}}\in \operatorname{TopJ}_L(\mathcal{C}_n^{\operatorname{root}})\).

[Proposition preGrera of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $(E, d)$ be Polish. Let $d_{\mathtt{Haus}}$ stand for the Hausdorff distance on $(E,d)$ and  $d_{\mathtt{Pro}}$ for 
the Prokhorov distance on $\mathcal{M}_f(E)$. 
Let $\rho \! \in \!  T$ and $\rho'\! \in \!  T^\prime$ be closed subsets of $E$ such that $(T, d, \rho)$ and that 
$(T'\! , d, \rho^\prime)$ are rooted $\mathbb{R}$-trees. Let $\mu \! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_f (T)$ and $\mu^\prime \! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_f (T^\prime)$ 
(i.e.~$\mu, \mu'\! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_f(E)$ and $\mu(E\backslash T)\! = \!  \mu'(E\backslash T')\! = \!  0$). 
We assume
\begin{equation}

d_{\mathtt{Haus}}(T, T^\prime) < \varepsilon \quad \textrm{and} \quad d_{\mathtt{Pro}} (\mu, \mu^\prime) < \varepsilon 
\end{equation}  
Then for all $h \in (2\varepsilon , \infty)$ we get 
\begin{equation}

\forall h^\prime \in [h-\varepsilon, h+ \varepsilon], \quad 
d_{\mathtt{Haus}} \big( T_{\! \mu, h}, T^\prime_{\! \mu^\prime , h^\prime}\big)\leq 4\varepsilon + d_{\mathtt{Haus}} (T_{\! \mu , h-2\varepsilon},T_{\! \mu , h+2\varepsilon} ) \; .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition preGrera of arXiv:2608.09856

[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2606.01881, '2606.01881'] Let $T$ be an a.s. finite stopping time for $(\mathcal F_n)$, and condition on $\mathcal F_T$.  Let $\mathcal B=\{B_r:r\ge1\}$ be a partition such that, for every $k>K_T$, the block containing $k$ is the singleton $\{k\}$ (since the occupied tables at time $T$ have labels $[K_T]$, this amounts to grouping the tables present at time $T$, while leaving all later labels as singletons).  Put
\[
        M_r^{(T)}:=\sum_{\ell\in B_r}N_\ell^{(T)},
        \qquad r\ge1.
\]
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The aggregated seating sequence after time $T$ is again a Simon-type Chinese restaurant process with parameter $p$, started from the block occupancies $(M_r^{(T)}:r\ge1)$.  Equivalently, for $s\ge T$, an already occupied block $B_r$ is chosen with probability $pM_r^{(s)}/s$, while the next new singleton block is opened with probability $1-p$.
\item Conditionally on the aggregated seating sequence $(C_k^{\mathcal B}:k>T)$, the within-block sequences $C_{B_r}^{(T)}$ over blocks $B_r\subseteq [K_T]$ are independent.  For each such block, $C_{B_r}^{(T)}$ is the fixed-table restaurant on $B_r$ started from the occupancies $(N_\ell^{(T)}:\ell\in B_r)$.
\end{enumerate}

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.17662, 'On the Strong Law of Large Numbers under Sublinear Expectations'] A \textit{sublinear expectation} $\mathbb{E}$ on $\mathcal{H}$ is a functional $\mathbb{E}\colon \mathcal{H} \to \overline{\mathbb{R}} := [-\infty, +\infty]$ satisfying the following properties for all $X, Y \in \mathcal{H}$:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item[(a)] \textit{Monotonicity.} If $X \geq Y$, then $\mathbb{E}[X] \geq \mathbb{E}[Y]$.
			\item[(b)] \textit{Constant preserving.} $\mathbb{E}[c] = c$, $\forall\, c \in \mathbb{R}$.
			\item[(c)] \textit{Positive homogeneity.} $\mathbb{E}[\lambda X] = \lambda\,\mathbb{E}[X]$, $\forall\, \lambda \geq 0$.
			\item[(d)] \textit{Subadditivity.} $\mathbb{E}[X + Y] \leq \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]$, provided that $\mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]$ does not take the form $\infty - \infty$ or $-\infty + \infty$.
		\end{enumerate}

For a vertex a set h=g-2g(a)1_{z=a}, F(z,+1)=g(z), F(z,-1)=h(z), and s_g(a)=#{j:g(a)!=g(a+e_j)}. Then I(F)=m/2+(m+1-2s_g(a))/N; each s=0,...,m is attainable by a character twist of the canonical quadratic bent base. Put R=sqrt(N), K_+=(N+R)/2, K_-=(N-R)/2 and phi(t)=t log_2(1/t), phi(0)=0. H(F)=E_m=K_+phi((R-1)^2/N^2)+K_-phi((R+1)^2/N^2)+Nphi(1/N^2), independent of g and a. At fixed m the sharp class maximum H/I is E_m/[m/2-(m-1)/N], attained by the full-parity twist flipped at zero. At m=4 this example has I=29/16 and H>469/128>2I, so a canonical constant-2 bound does not extend to all bent splices. Every such splice still satisfies H<=3I. These are class results; general FEI is not proved and novelty is not certified.

[Def 39 of arXiv:2609.01389, 'K-stability and birational rigidity of Fano 3-fold weighted complete intersections'] Let $m < n$ be positive integers and $a_1, \dots, a_n, b_1 \dots b_n$ be integers.
Let $R = \mbC [x_1, \dots, x_n]$ be the polynomial ring endowed with a $\mbZ^2$-grading defined by the $2 \times n$ matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
a_1 & \cdots & a_n \\
b_1 & \cdots & b_n 
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This means that the bi-degree of the variable $x_i$ is $(a_i, b_i) \in \mbZ^2$.
We denote by 
\begin{equation} 
\mbT \begin{pNiceArray}{ccc|ccc}[first-row]
x_1 & \dots & x_m & x_{m+1} & \dots & x_n \\
a_1 & \dots & a_m & a_{m+1} & \dots & a_n \\
b_1 & \dots & b_m & b_{m+1} & \dots & b_n
\end{pNiceArray}
\end{equation}
the toric variety whose Cox ring is $R$ and irrelevant ideal is 
\[
I = (x_1, \dots, x_m) \cap (x_{m+1}, \dots, x_n).
\]
In other words, this toric variety is the geometric quotient
\[
(\mbA^n_{x_1, \dots, x_n} \setminus V (I))/(\mbC^*)^2,
\]
where the $(\mbC^*)^2$-action is defined by
\[
(\lambda, \mu) \cdot (x_1, \dots, x_n) = (\lambda^{a_1} \mu^{b_1} x_1, \dots, \lambda^{a_n} \mu^{b_n} x_n).
\]
For a point $\msp$ of the toric variety \eqref{eq:deftoricT}, which we denote by $\mbT$, we pick a point $\msq = (\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_n) \in \mbA^n$ in the preimage of the natural projection $\mbA^n \setminus V (I) \to \mbT$ over $\msp$.
In this case we express $\msp$ as $\msp = (\alpha_1\!:\!\cdots\!:\!\alpha_m;\alpha_{m+1}\!:\!\cdots\!:\!\alpha_n) \in \mbT$.

\begin{align}

[Theorem thm:centrality of arXiv:2606.02472, 'Correlated uniform attachment trees'] Let $T_{n} \sim \mathrm{UA}(n)$ and let $A_{K}(n)$ be the set of the $K$ most central vertices of~$T_{n}$. Fix $c > 1$, $\delta > 0$,
and set 
\[
c^{\prime} := c \left(1 - e^{-1/c} \right) - \delta.
\]
Then there exists a constant $C < \infty$ that depends only on $c$ and $\delta$ such that for every 
$\varepsilon > 0$, 
the following holds for all $K \geq (C/\varepsilon) \log(1/\varepsilon)$ 
and all large enough $n \geq n_{0}(K,\delta, c )$: 
\[
\mathbb{P} \left( \left| A_{\ceil{c K}}(n) \cap \{ 0, 1, \ldots, K-1 \} \right| \geq c^{\prime} \,   K \right) 
\geq 1 - \varepsilon.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:centrality of arXiv:2606.02472

body: [Theorem main_res: local_longtime of arXiv:2504.04792, 'Uniqueness and Longtime Behavior of the Completely Positively Correlated Symbiotic Branchi'] Let $(\phi, \psi) \in C_{\text{tem}}^+ \cap \mathcal{M}$. Assume that $(U^1,U^2)$ is the solution of $((eq: formal of the paper))$ with initial conditions $(U^1_0, U^2_0) = (\phi, \psi)$. Assume without loss of generality that $\overline{\phi} \geq \overline{\psi}$. Then, $\langle U_t^2, g \rangle \xrightarrow[t \to \infty]{P} 0 $ and $\langle U_t^1, g \rangle \xrightarrow[t \to \infty]{P} \left( \overline{\phi} - \overline{\psi} \right) \langle g, \bold{1} \rangle$ for all $g \in C_{\text{exp}}$. In particular, $U^2_t \xrightarrow[t \to \infty]{P} 0$ in $M_{\text{tem}}$ and $U^1_t \xrightarrow[t \to \infty]{P}  \left(\overline{\phi} - \overline{\psi}\right) \bold{1}$ in $M_{\text{tem}}$. That is, local coexistence is impossible. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem main_res: local_longtime of arXiv:2504.04792

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2512.05466, 'Stochastic Flows and Marked Stable Processes'] We call a point $(a, r) \in (0,\infty)\times\bR$ a \textbf{bifurcation point} if $\cS_{r,x}(a) > \cS_{r,x}(a-)$ for some  $x > r$. 
We say that a bifurcation point $(a,r)$ is \textbf{an ancestor of $(b,x)$} if $\cS_{r,x}(a-) \le b <\cS_{r,x}(a)$.

body: FIRES WHEN you are about to prove a convex-order dominance for a Markov-modulated inter-event time by conditioning on the modulating state and calling the result a mixture of exponentials. THE ROUTE: conditionally on the chain's stationary sojourn structure the inter-event time is exponential with a state-dependent rate, and a MIXTURE of exponentials always dominates the matched exponential in the convex order by Jensen applied to t -> E[exp(-lambda t)]. WHERE IT FAILS: only when the chain does NOT move during the inter-event interval. A general MMPP lets it move, and then the law of T is PHASE-TYPE, not a mixture of exponentials, and phase-type laws are not automatically above the exponential in the convex order. MINIMAL WITNESS that the simplest sufficient condition also fails: the source's own four-state example has a NON-MONOTONE hazard rate, so the decreasing-hazard-rate criterion does not apply either. CONDITION OF FAILURE: any modulating transition inside an inter-event interval. The route that worked instead was Palm inversion - see the E0078 result node.

[Proposition 45 (Invariance of frequencies) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $(R_k)_{k=1}^\infty$ be random walk on $X$. Let $Z$ be a closed subset of $X$ such that $\beta(Z)$ exists a.s.~and does not depend on the random walk.
    Then, for every isometry $\tau$ of $(X,d_X)$,
    $$\beta(\tau(Z)) = \beta(Z).$$
    In particular, if $\mathcal{Z}$ is a $G$-invariant enough random closed subset of $X$ which is independent of $(R_k)_k$, then $\beta(\mathcal{Z})$ is an isometry invariant measurable function.

[Theorem thm:main_theorem of arXiv:2605.10911, 'The stochastic block model has the overlap graph property for modularity'] Fix $a>b>0$. Let $p=p(n)=\omega\; a / n$ and $q=q(n)=\omega \; b/n$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $c=c(\varepsilon)$ such that if $\omega>c$ then the following holds with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ provided $n$ is large enough. 

Let $G \in \mathcal{G}(n,k,p,q)$ with the planted partition $\mathcal{P}$. 
For any $d \in \left[0,\frac{1}{k}\right]$, 
let 
$$H(d) = \max_{\mathcal{A}: |\mathcal{A}|\le k} \left\{ q_\mathcal{A}(G) : d - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \le d(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}) \le d + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \right\}.
$$
Then,
\begin{equation*}
\left| H(d)  - \frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b}\cdot h(d) \right| \le \varepsilon,
\end{equation*}
where 
\[h(d)= 1 - \frac {1}{k} - 2d\big (1-d(k-1)\big). \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \bf Maximal modularity at distance at most $1/k$

[Definition 7 (Admissible analytic resolution) of arXiv:2609.01116, 'Vector-Carleson, Calder\'on, and Poisson--Atomic Criteria for\\ Generalized Hilbert Operat'] Let
\[
 I_k=\{n\in\mathbb N:2^k\le n<2^{k+1}\},\qquad k\ge0.
\]
A family of scalar sequences
$\sigma=(\sigma_j)_{j\ge0}$ on $\mathbb N$ is called
$(L,M,p)$-admissible if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
 \item $\sigma_j(n)=0$ for $n\in I_k$ whenever $|j-k|>L$;
 \item $\sum_{j\ge0}\sigma_j(n)=1$ for every $n\ge1$;
 \item for every $|\ell|\le L$, the patched sequence
 \[
  m_\ell(n)=\sigma_{k+\ell}(n)\qquad(n\in I_k),
  \tag{3.8}
 \]
 with $\sigma_j=0$ for $j<0$, is an $H^p$ coefficient multiplier of
 norm at most $M$.
\end{enumerate}
Put
\[
 W_j^\sigma\phi(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_j(n)\widehat\phi(n)z^n,
 \qquad
 \mathscr S_{\phi,p}^{\sigma}a
 =a_{-1}\phi(0)+
  \sum_{j\ge0}a_j2^{-j/p'}W_j^\sigma\phi.
 \tag{3.9}
\]
The hard resolution is $\sigma_j=\mathbf1_{I_j}$ and has $L=0$.

body:
[Dfn 5 (Large deviations principle) of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] The sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ obeys the \textbf{large deviations principle} (`\textbf{LDP}') with \textbf{rate function} $I$ if the following hold:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[i.] (Upper bound) If $x \in \X$ and $a < I(x)$, then there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ such that
		\[\mu_n U \le e^{-an + o(n)}.\]
		\item[ii.] (Lower bound) If $x \in \X$ and $I(x) < a < \infty$, then any neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ satisfies
		\[\mu_n U \ge e^{-a n - o(n)}.\]
		\item[iii.] (Exponential tightness) For every $a > 0$ there is a compact subset $K$ of $\X$ such that
		\[\mu_n (\X\setminus K) \le e^{-an + o(n)}.\]
	\end{itemize}
title: Large deviations principle

[Definition def:drift of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] An $\mathcal F$-predictable process $\overline{\delta}:{\mathbb R}\to{\mathbb R}$ is called a drift function if there exists a deterministic vector $(\delta_i)_{1\le i\le n} \in {\mathbb R}^n$ and $\mathcal F$-stopping times $-\infty=\tilde{t}_1<\tilde{t}_2<\ldots<\tilde{t}_{n+1}=\infty$ such that $\overline{\delta}=\delta_i$ on $A_i:=(\tilde{t}_{i},\tilde{t}_{i+1})$.
    
    
    If $\overline{\delta'}$ is another drift function and $r_1$ is an $\mathcal F$-stopping time, we write $\overline{\delta}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta'}$ for the drift function $\overline{\delta}(x)\mathbbm{1}_{(-\infty,r_1)}(x)+ \overline{\delta'}(x)\mathbbm{1}_{[r_1,\infty)}(x)$.

body:
[Proposition 23 (Conditional Rees face maps) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(S\subset T\subset K\), and set the direction parameters indexed by
\(K\setminus S\) equal to zero before localising those indexed by \(S\).
With the conditional blocks from \eqref{eq:conditional-blocks}, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf W^\rho_{K\to T}f(\boldsymbol u_T)
 =
 \left.
 \exp\!\left(
  \frac{\rho^2}{2}
  \Delta_{C_{K\setminus T\mid T}}^{(\boldsymbol v)}
 \right)
 f\bigl(
  \boldsymbol u_T,
  L_{K\setminus T\mid T}\boldsymbol u_T+\boldsymbol v
 \bigr)
 \right|_{\boldsymbol v=0}.
 
\end{equation}
Then \eqref{eq:conditional-Rees-Wick} induces an isomorphism
\[
 \mathbf W^{\rho,S}_{K\to T}:
 \mathcal L_{K\mid S}
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 \mathcal L_{T\mid S},
 \qquad
 [f\operatorname{vol}_K]
 \longmapsto
 [\mathsf W^\rho_{K\to T}f\operatorname{vol}_T],
\]
where determinant orientation lines are identified as in
\cref{thm:gaussian-face-cube}.  For \(S\subset T\subset K\subset L\), the
polynomial operators satisfy strictly
\begin{equation}
 \mathsf W^\rho_{K\to T}
 \circ\mathsf W^\rho_{L\to K}
 =
 \mathsf W^\rho_{L\to T}.
 
\end{equation}
and, with the determinant-line convention above, so do the induced lattice
maps.  Moreover, after localisation at \(\rho\), these maps intertwine the
cohomological radial connections in the Gaussian-normalised gauge:
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf W^{\rho,S}_{K\to T}
 \nabla_{\rho,K}^{\mathrm{phys}}
 =
 \nabla_{\rho,T}^{\mathrm{phys}}
 \mathbf W^{\rho,S}_{K\to T}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus \eqref{eq:physical-face-horizontality} is an identity from
\(\mathcal L_{K\mid S}[\rho^{-1}]\) to
\(\mathcal L_{T\mid S}[\rho^{-1}]\).  Equivalently, after multiplication
by \(\rho^3\), it is an identity of the unlocalised lattices.
title: Conditional Rees face maps

body:
[Proposition prop:Wishart.integrated.deBruijn of arXiv:2606.04859, 'Stein's method for the Wishart distribution'] Under the assumptions of Proposition~(prop:Wishart.deBruijn of the paper), we have
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Ent}(\mu \, \| \, \xi)
= \int_0^{\infty} J_{\mathcal{W}, \Sigma}(\mu_t \mid \xi) \, \mathrm{d} t
= \int_0^1 \frac{1}{2\tau} J_{\mathcal{W}, \Sigma}(\mu_{\tau} \mid \xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau.
\end{equation}
Assume furthermore that $\mu$ is the law of a random matrix $\mathfrak{X}$ and that this law has Lebesgue density $f_{\mathfrak{X}}$, that is, $\mu(\mathrm{d} X) = f_{\mathfrak{X}}(X) \, \mathrm{d} X$. Equivalently, if $f_{\xi}$ denotes the Lebesgue density of $\xi$, then the initial relative density is $g(X) = f_{\mathfrak{X}}(X)/f_{\xi}(X)$. Assume also that $\mathfrak{X}$ has finite differential entropy
\[
H(\mathfrak{X}) \vcentcolon= -\int_{\mathcal{S}_{++}^d} f_{\mathfrak{X}}(X)\log(f_{\mathfrak{X}}(X)) \, \mathrm{d} X.
\]
If $\mathsf{E}[\mathfrak{X}] = \mathsf{E}[\mathfrak{W}_{\infty}] = \alpha \Sigma$ and $\mathsf{E}[\log(|\mathfrak{X}|)] = \mathsf{E}[\log(|\mathfrak{W}_{\infty}|)]\in \mathbb{R}$ with $\mathfrak{W}_{\infty}\sim \xi$, then
\begin{equation}
H(\mathfrak{W}_{\infty}) - H(\mathfrak{X})
= \int_0^{\infty} J_{\mathcal{W}, \Sigma}(\mu_t \mid \xi) \, \mathrm{d} t
= \int_0^1 \frac{1}{2\tau} J_{\mathcal{W}, \Sigma}(\mu_{\tau} \mid \xi) \, \mathrm{d} \tau.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Integrated De Bruijn identity for the Wishart measure and entropy jump

[Theorem thm:sle of arXiv:2607.18070, 'The Brownian loop-catcher'] For \(\lambda=-c/2\in(0,1]\), let
\(\kappa\in[2,\frac83)\) be in~(equation eq:c-kappa of the paper).  
Let $\eta_-$ and $\eta_+$ be the lower and upper boundaries of \(K_\lambda^{D;a,b}\), respectively (i.e.~$\eta_\pm=\overline{\partial D_K^\pm\setminus \partial^\pm D}$). Then \(\eta_-\) is chordal
\(\SLE_\kappa(\kappa-2)\) in \(D\) from \(a\) to \(b\), with force point
at \(a^+\); conditionally on \(\eta_-\), \(\eta_+\) is chordal \(\SLE_\kappa(\kappa-4)\) in the component adjacent
to \(\partial^+D\),
with force point at \(a^-\).\footnote{At \(\kappa=2\), the law of the second curve
can be viewed as the \(\rho\downarrow-2\) limit of chordal \(\SLE_2(\rho)\) with force
point at \(a^-\); equivalently, $\eta_\pm$ are the two prime-end sides
of a chordal \(\SLE_2\) trace.} As a consequence, we have the following coupling between $\SLE_\kappa$ and Brownian excursion:
\[
 \eta_-\cup\eta_+\subset\gamma_{\mathrm{BE}}^{D;a,b}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2604.20617, 'Structured random perturbations of \\ tridiagonal twisted Toeplitz matrices'] Fix a compact set $K\Subset \C\setminus \Sigma$, where
\[
\Sigma:=\left\{z\in\C:\exists x\in[0,1]\text{ such that }|\xi_1(x,z)|=|\xi_2(x,z)|\right\}
\cup
\left\{z\in\C:\exists x\in[0,1]\text{ such that }\xi_1(x,z)^2=1\right\},
\]
and for each $x\in[0,1]$ the numbers $\xi_1(x,z),\xi_2(x,z)$ are the roots of
\[
\lambda^2-\frac{z-b(x)}{c(x)}\lambda+\frac{d(x)}{c(x)}=0
\]
ordered so that $|\xi_1(x,z)|>|\xi_2(x,z)|$ on $K$.

Then, for every fixed block index $j$ and every $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\prob\!\left(
\left|
\frac{\det(R_{k-1}^{(j)}-zI)}{\det(R_k^{(j)}-zI)}
-\frac{1}{c(jk/n)\,\xi_1(jk/n,z)}
\right|>\varepsilon
\right)=o(1),
\]
and
\[
\prob\!\left(
\left|
\frac{\det(R_k^{(j)'}-zI)}{\det(R_k^{(j)}-zI)}
-\frac{1}{d(jk/n)\,\xi_1(jk/n,z)}
\right|>\varepsilon
\right)=o(1),
\]
uniformly for $z\in K$.

Consequently,
\[
\Theta_k^{(j)}(z):=
\frac{c(jk/n)d(jk/n)\det(R_{k-1}^{(j)}-zI)\det(R_k^{(j+1)'}-zI)}
{\det(R_k^{(j)}-zI)\det(R_k^{(j+1)}-zI)}
\]
satisfies
\[
\Theta_k^{(j)}(z)\longrightarrow
\frac{1}{\xi_1(jk/n,z)^2}
\qquad\text{in probability, uniformly for }z\in K.
\]
In particular, there exists $\delta_K>0$ such that
\[
\prob\!\left(|1-\Theta_k^{(j)}(z)|\ge \delta_K \right)=1-o(1)
\qquad (z\in K).
\]

body:
Let b ∈ C^1(R^n × R; R^n) with sup_{(x,t)} ||D_x b(x,t)|| < ∞, and let g ∈ C^1(R^n). For (x,t) let s ↦ X(s;x,t) be the solution of d/ds X = b(X,s), X(t;x,t) = x; by the global Lipschitz bound in x this flow exists for all s ∈ R and is C^1 in (s,x,t). Then u(x,t) := g( X(0;x,t) ) is the unique C^1 solution of the Cauchy problem u_t + b(x,t)·Du = 0 in R^n × R, u(x,0) = g(x). In particular, for constant b the solution is u(x,t) = g(x - tb), and solutions are constant along the characteristic curves s ↦ X(s;x,t). With a source term, u_t + b·Du = f(x,t) with f continuous, the unique C^1 solution (when it is C^1) is u(x,t) = g(X(0;x,t)) + ∫_0^t f( X(σ;x,t), σ ) dσ.
b ∈ C^1 with globally bounded x-derivative (this gives a globally defined C^1 flow; without a growth restriction characteristics can blow up in finite time and the formula only holds locally)
g ∈ C^1 (a merely continuous g gives the same formula but only a weak/viscosity solution)
the equation is linear in u: the characteristics do not depend on the solution, which is why no shocks form

    =
    e^{-2\pi i a_u2^k\eta}H^{(u)}_{k-m}(\eta),
    \qquad \eta\in G.
\]
Conditional on \(\mathcal F^X_m\), the family
\[
    \{Z_u:|u|=m\}
\]
is independent.  Each \(Z_u\) is independent of \(\mathcal F^X_m\), has the law
of
\[
    \{H_{k-m}(\eta):\eta\in G\}
\]
up to deterministic unimodular phases, and satisfies
\[
    \mathbb{E}[Z_u\mid\mathcal F^X_m]=0
\]
coordinatewise.

[Definition of arXiv:2609.00636, 'Forcing monochromatic subdivisions'] Let $0<\alpha<1$ and $t\ge 1$. A graph $F$ on $q$ vertices is an
$(\alpha,t)$-\emph{expander} if
\[
|N_F(X)|\ge t|X|
\qquad\text{for every }X\subseteq V(F)
\text{ with }|X|\le \frac{\alpha q}{t}.
\]
A graph is $m$-\emph{minor-universal} if it contains every graph with at
most $m$ vertices and at most $m$ edges as a minor.

body: [Defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] If $\mathcal{G}_1$ and $\mathcal{G}_2$ are two foliations on $\mathbb{T}^2$, then say that $\mathcal{G}_1$ has \textbf{lower slope} than $\mathcal{G}_2$ at a point $x\in \mathbb{T}^2$ if positively oriented tangent vectors in $T_x\mathcal{G}_1$ and $T_x\mathcal{G}_2$ combine to form a positively oriented basis of $T_x\mathbb{R}^2$. We say that $\mathcal{G}_1$ has \textbf{pointwise lower slope} than $\mathcal{G}_2$ if $\mathcal{G}_1$ has greater slope than $\mathcal{G}_2$ at every point in $\mathbb{T}^2$. In this case, we write $\mathcal{G}_1 \prec \mathcal{G}_2$. Note that $\prec$ is a partial order when restricted to $\Phi$-horizontal foliations.
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'

[Lemma 39 (Negligibility of integrals compared to the pole) of arXiv:2512.09136, 'On the Green's functions and Martin boundary structure of a planar diffusion in a disconti'] Suppose $x^* \in (0, \M)$. Let $z_0 \in \R^2$, $\alpha_0 \in [0,\alpha^*_+)$, and let $x_c$ be such that $x^* < x_c < \min(x(\alpha_0),\M)$.
