body:
[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2604.26026, 'Stochastic Ordering of Dependent Systems under Transformation Models and Archimedean Copul'] Let $m \ge 1$, let $g:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be $m$ times differentiable, and $h_1,\dots,h_m>0$. Define the iterated forward difference operator by
\[
\Delta_{h_1,\dots,h_m} g(a) :=	(\Delta_{h_m}\circ\cdots\circ\Delta_{h_1})g(a), \qquad	\Delta_h g(a):=g(a+h)-g(a).
\]
Then the following identities hold:
\begin{align}
\Delta_{h_1,\dots,h_m} g(a) &=
   \sum_{L\subseteq\{1,\dots,m\}} (-1)^{m-|L|}\, g\left(a+\sum_{r\in L} h_r\right),  \\[1.5ex]

\end{align}

(Thm 1.4) Let X_1,...,X_n be independent random vectors in R^d, M(.) the essential supremum of the density, and Z_1,...,Z_n independent, Z_i uniform on an origin-symmetric Euclidean ball with M(Z_i) = M(X_i) (Z_i = 0 if M(X_i) = infinity). Then M((T \otimes I_d)X) <= M((T \otimes I_d)Z) for every linear map T: R^n -> R^k. For d = 1: every k-dimensional linear image of a vector with independent coordinates has maximal density at most that of the same image of independent centred uniforms with the same maxima. (Thm 1.1) For P a projection onto a k-dimensional subspace, M((P \otimes I_d)X) <= c(d,k) prod M(X_i)^{gamma_i}, gamma_i in [0,1], sum gamma_i = k, with c(1,k) = min{2^{k/2}, (n/(n-k))^{(n-k)/2}}. For d >= 2: M(sum X_i)^{-2/d} >= Gamma(1+d/2)^{2/d}/(1+d/2) sum M(X_i)^{-2/d}.

Assumes: independent summands or coordinates; M(X_i) finite, or the convention Z_i = 0; linear images only

[Theorem punique of arXiv:2412.02777, 'How to quantify the coherence of a set of beliefs'] Given a credence base $(\mathtt E, \boldsymbol q)$ and a loss function $L$ of the form in ((eqn:lossfunction of the paper)), if there exists a coherent $\boldsymbol p\in C(\mathtt E)$ such that $L(\boldsymbol p, \boldsymbol q)$ is finite, then there exists a unique $\boldsymbol {p^*}$ such that

body:
Every nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. Precisely: let P be any set of partial computable functions that is nontrivial, meaning some partial computable function belongs to P and some does not. Then the index set {encodings of Turing machines M : the partial function computed by M belongs to P} is undecidable. 'Semantic' is essential: the property must depend only on the function computed, not on the machine's text (syntactic properties such as 'has fewer than 100 states' are decidable). Only the two trivial semantic properties (satisfied by all machines, or by none) have decidable index sets. Examples of undecidable questions: does M compute the everywhere-zero function; does M halt on the empty input; is the language accepted by M empty, finite, or regular.
P is a set of partial computable functions
P is nontrivial: neither empty nor all partial computable functions

Reduce halting: given a pair (M, w), effectively construct a machine N(M, w) that on input x behaves as follows - first it simulates M on w, ignoring x; if and when that simulation halts, it runs M_f on x and returns that result. If M halts on w, then N(M, w) computes exactly f, which is in P. If M does not halt on w, then N(M, w) halts on no input, so it computes the nowhere-defined function, which is not in P. The map (M, w) -> N(M, w) is computable. A decider for the index set of P applied to N(M, w) would therefore decide whether M halts on w, contradicting the undecidability of the halting problem. [Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Let $X$ be the CIR process above, take
$A_T=\int_0^T \de s \, X_s$
and fix $0<\theta<\eta$.  With $r_{\beta_\theta}=\frac{\kappa\eta}{\theta}$ and $\beta_\theta
      =\frac{\kappa^2}{2\sigma^2}
        \left(\frac{\eta^2}{\theta^2}-1\right)$,
put
\[
    I_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(\theta)
      =\frac{\kappa^2(\eta-\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2\theta},
    \qquad
    v_\theta
      =\frac{\sigma^2\theta^3}{\kappa^2\eta^2}.
\]
Then, for every fixed $x>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
\begin{split}
    \bbP_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(A_T\leq\theta T+z)
    \sim{}&
    \frac{1}{\beta_\theta\sqrt{2\pi v_\theta T}}
    \left(
       \frac{2r_{\beta_\theta}}
            {\kappa+r_{\beta_\theta}}
    \right)^\alpha
    \exp\!\left(
       -\frac{(r_{\beta_\theta}-\kappa)x}{\sigma^2}
    \right)
    \exp\!\left(
       -I_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(\theta)T+\beta_\theta z
    \right).
\end{split}
\]
On every fixed time interval, the conditioned process converges in total
variation to the CIR process
\[
    \de Y_t
      =r_{\beta_\theta}(\theta-Y_t)\,\de t
       +\sigma\sqrt{Y_t}\,\de B_t,
    \qquad Y_0=x.
\]
Its invariant law is Gamma with shape $\alpha$ and mean $\theta$.

body:
[Corollary 20 of arXiv:2609.01473, 'Keller sequences of exact $\infty$-categories'] Let $i\colon \cal{A} \hookrightarrow \cal{C}$ be a right-special inclusion and $\cal{E}$ some $\infty$-category which admits small colimits. 
Then the square
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = 50pt]
\cal{A} \ar[r,"i"]\ar[d,"j_{\cal{A}}"'] & \cal{C} \ar[d,"j_{\cal{C}}"] \\
\pst(\cal{A}) \ar[r,"\pst(i)"] & \pst(\cal{C}) 
\end{tikzcd}
\]
satisfies the following Beck-Chevalley properties:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item
For every functor $\vphi\colon \C \to \cal{E}$ the Beck-Chevalley transformation
\[ (j_{\cal{A}})_!i^*\vphi \Rightarrow \pst(i)^*(j_{\cal{C}})_!\vphi  \]
is an equivalence, where $(-)^*$ denotes restriction and $(-)_!$ left Kan extension.
\item
For every presheaf $\vphi\colon \pst(\cal{A})^{\op} \to \cal{E}$ the Beck-Chevalley transformation
\[ i_!j_{\cal{A}}^*\vphi \Rightarrow j_{\cal{C}}^*\pst(i)_!\vphi \]
is an equivalence, where by abuse of notation we denoted by $(-)^*$ and $(-)_!$ also restriction and left Kan extension of presheaves.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma LEM:remvit of arXiv:2411.07840, 'Central limit theorem for the focusing $Φ^4$-measure in the infinite volume limit'] Let $g$ be a smooth, compactly supported function with $\textup{dist}(\supp g, x_0)=c_1>0$, where $x_0\in \mathbb{T}_{L}$. Then, we have
\begin{align}
&\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\nu^\perp_{Q, x_0}}  \Big[  e^{i\langle h^\perp, g_L \rangle}(e^{i t^{+}\langle \gamma_L, g \rangle }-1)    e^{\bar {\mathcal{E}}(h^\perp, t^{+}) } e^{c_0(t^+)^2+b(h^\perp)t^+}  , \,D_L, \, B_K  \Big] }{ \mathbb{E}_{\nu^\perp_{Q, x_0}}  \Big[ e^{\bar {\mathcal{E}}(h^\perp, t^{+}) } e^{c_0(t^+)^2+b(h^\perp)t^+}, \, D_L, \, B_K   \Big] }  \\
&=O(e^{-\frac{c_1}{2} L} ),\notag 
\end{align}

\noindent 
uniformly in $x_0\in \mathbb{T}_{L}$ and $\theta \in [0,2\pi]$, where $g_L(x)=L^{-\frac 12}g(L^{-1}x)$.

[Theorem 2 (Lacoin and Tykesson \cite{lt2013}) of arXiv:2605.09459, 'Multipoint connectivity in the branching interlacement process'] Let $d \geq 5$, and $k \geq 3$. Then almost surely, for every $k$ points of the interlacement, there exist $\lceil d(k-1)/2\rceil - (k-2)$ trajectories of the interlacement that connect them.
  Furthermore, almost surely, there exist $k$ points of the interlacement that are not connected by $\lceil d(k-1)/2\rceil - (k-2) -1$ trajectories. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lacoin and Tykesson \cite{lt2013}

body: [Definition defcode of arXiv:2607.06952, 'Universality for cokernels of partially random integral matrices'] Let $X$ be $(\varepsilon,\tau,A)$-balanced and fix $\lambda >1$. Then, we say that $F \in {\mathrm{Hom}}(V,G)$ is a \emph{code for $X$} if for all $\sigma \subset [n]$ with $|\sigma| < \log(n)^\lambda$, then $FA^{-1}(V_{\setminus\sigma \cup \tau}) = G$. For a random matrix $M$ valued in $\M_{n \times (n+u)}(\mathbb{Z}/a\mathbb{Z})$, we say that $F$ is a \emph{code for $M$} if it is a code for all columns of $M$.
title: Definition defcode of arXiv:2607.06952

[Lemma lem:rare-events-changing-Z of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $V_1, V_2, U_1, U_2$ be any domains such that $V_1 \subset V_2$ and $U_1 \subset U_2$. Suppose we have the bounds on the partition functions
		\begin{align}
			&\left|\log {\widehat Z}^n_{V_1, U_1}(A, B) - \log {\widehat Z}^n_{V_1, U_2}(A, B)\right| \leq f_1(A,B)\,, \mbox{ and }\\
			&\left|\log {\widehat Z}^n_{V_1, U_2}(A, B) - \log {\widehat Z}^n_{V_2, U_2}(A, B)\right| \leq f_2(A, B)\,,
		\end{align}
		where we allow the more general form of $\Phi_{U}$ as in (rem:conditions-on-Phi-U of the paper).

		\[{\widehat Z}^n_{V_2, U_2}(A, B \mid \ensuremath{\mathcal E}) \leq p{\widehat Z}^n_{V_2, U_2}(A, B)\,,\]
		we also have
		\[{\widehat Z}^n_{V_1, U_1}(A, B \mid \ensuremath{\mathcal E}) \leq e^{2f_1(A, B) + \tfrac12f_2(A, B)}\sqrt{p}{\widehat Z}^n_{V_1, U_1}(A, B)\,.\]

[Theorem 2 (B\^ocher theorem for $-\Delta+(-\Delta)^s$) of arXiv:2609.01403, '2609.01403'] Let $B_1\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, and $s\in(0,1)$. Assume
$u\in\mathcal L^{2s}(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies $u\ge0$ a.e. in $B_1$ and
\[
    \mathscr{L}_su+cu\ge0
    \qquad
    \text{in }\mathcal D'(B_1\setminus\{0\}),
\]
where $c\in L^\infty(B_1)$. Then there exist $a\ge0$ and a nonnegative
Radon measure $\mu$ in $B_1$, with $\mu(\{0\})=0$, such that
\[
    \mathscr{L}_su+cu
    =
    \mu+a\delta_0
    \qquad
    \text{in }\mathcal D'(B_1).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma 14 (Separated multiscale flows) of arXiv:2609.01143, 'The voter model on the hyperbolic graph'] Fix $\varphi<1$, $\epsilon_0>0$, a sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$ and a sufficiently large fixed $\ell$.  Let $v$ be a prescribed point with
\[
h(v):=R-r_v\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon_0\right)R,
\]
and write $\vartheta(v)$ for its angular coordinate.  Put
\[
J:=\left\lfloor\frac{R-h(v)}{\ell}\right\rfloor, \qquad u_i:=i\ell,\quad 0\leq i\leq J.
\]

For each $i$ and $b\in\{0,1\}$, the construction uses $K_i$ initial half-tiles, where
\begin{equation}
K_i\asymp e^{h(v)/2}e^{-u_i/2}.                              
\end{equation}
There is a fixed $c>0$ such that, uniformly over the choices above, under the Palm law obtained by adding $v$ the construction for $(i,b)$ fails with probability at most $e^{-cK_i}$.  On success, whenever $v\in V(\cG)$, it produces a probability measure $\lambda_i^b$ and a unit flow $g_i^b$ on $\cG$ such that
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{div}g_i^b=\mathbbm{1}_v-\lambda_i^b,\qquad \cE_{\cG}(g_i^b)\leq\frac{C}{P_i},\qquad I_\varphi(\lambda_i^b)\leq\frac{C}{V_i},                         
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
P_i\asymp e^{h(v)/2}e^{-(2\alpha-1)u_i/2}, \qquad V_i\asymp e^{h(v)/2}e^{u_i/2}.                                 
\end{equation}

Let $Q_i^b$ be the support of $\lambda_i^b$, and let $S_i^b$ consist of $v$ and the endpoints of edges carrying nonzero $g_i^b$-flow.  Then $Q_i^b\subset S_i^b\setminus\{v\}$, every vertex in $Q_i^b$ has height $O(1)$ uniformly in $i$ and $b$, and every $x\in S_i^b\setminus\{v\}$ satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb S^1}(\vartheta(x),\vartheta(v))\leq \epsilon,
\]
and
\[
S_i^b\cap S_j^{b'}=\{v\}\qquad\text{whenever }(i,b)\ne(j,b').
\]
title: Separated multiscale flows

body:
[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2603.26303, 'Spectral Gap of Biased Adjacent-Transposition Chains'] Let $P$ and $Q$ be orthogonal projections on a finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$.
Suppose that every non-zero eigenvalue of $P+Q$ is at least $1-p$, where $0\le p<1$.
Then, for every $f\in V$,
\[
\langle Pf,Qf\rangle\ge -p\,\|Pf\|\,\|Qf\|.
\]
In the case of equality, we have $f \!\in\! \bigl(\operatorname{Im}(P) \cap \operatorname{Im}(Q)\bigr)^\perp$, and when $Pf\neq 0\neq Qf$, one has $PQPf = p^2Pf$.

body:
[Cor 6 of arXiv:2511.18861, 'Correlation Decay for Maximum Weight Matchings on Sparse Graphs'] Let $(G_n)$ be a sequence of random graphs and  let $(G_n,o_n)$ converge locally weakly to $(G,o)$ where $o_n$ is  chosen uniformly from $V(G_n)$. Assume  that 
$\sup_n \E \tfrac{|E(G_n)|}{| V(G_n)|} < \infty$ and $\E|w_e|^p<\infty$ for some $p>1$. Further assume that, almost surely under the law of $(G,o)$, the limit graph $G$ satisfies the correlation decay assumption. Then
	\[
	\lim_{n\to\infty} \E \frac{\W_{G_n}}{|V(G_n)|} = \frac{1}{2}\E \left[ \sum_{v: v\sim o}w_{(ov)} \mathbf{1}_{\{(ov) \in \M_G\}} \right],
	\]
    and 
    \[
	\lim_{n\to\infty} \E \frac{|\M_{G_n}|}{|V(G_n)|} = \frac{1}{2}\E \left[ \sum_{v: v\sim o}\mathbf{1}_{\{(ov) \in \M_G\}} \right],
	\]
    where $|\M_{G_n}|$ is the number of edges in the matching $\M_{G_n}$ and the expectation $\E$ is taken over both the randomness in the graph and the edge weights. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Then, $Q_{\varepsilon}(\cdot \mid \mathbf{X})$ majorizes $\mathcal{J}_{\varepsilon}$ globally:

is ordered by the natural order of the integers).

body:
[Lemma 9 (Wick index count for products of traces) of arXiv:2608.04824, 'Strong Convergence for a General Class of Random Matrix Models'] Fix \(h\geq1\) and \(p_1,\ldots,p_h\geq0\).  Expand
\[
 \prod_{a=1}^h\trn_{qn}G_n^{p_a}
\]
using the independent real Ginibre representation from the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:gaussian-limit}.  Consider a monomial containing
\(2e\) centered Gaussian matrix entries and a Wick pairing whose covariance
factors are nonzero.  After all covariance identifications, let \(v\) be the
number of free \(n\)-indices.  Then
\begin{equation}
 v\leq e+h.
\end{equation}
Consequently, the contribution of every fixed nonzero pairing to the product
of normalized traces is \(O(1)\), uniformly in \(n\).

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma le:cle_sle_domain_markov of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Suppose that $\eta$ is an ${\rm SLE}_\kappa$ in $\mathbf{H}$ from $0$ to $\infty$ and (given $\eta$) $\Gamma$ is a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}$ in the component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus \eta$ to the left of $\eta$. Let $W \subseteq \overline{\mathbf{H}}$ be a connected, relatively open set that intersects~$\mathbf{R}_-$, and let $\widetilde{W} \subseteq W$ be the union of connected components of $W \setminus \eta$ that intersect $\mathbf{R}_-$. Let $\Gamma(\widetilde{W})$ be the the collection of loops in $\Gamma$ that intersect $\widetilde{W}$. Let $\widetilde{\eta}$ denote the outer boundary of the union of loops in $\Gamma(\widetilde{W})$ (as seen from $1$, say). Given $\widetilde\eta$ and the set $\widetilde\eta \cap \eta$, pick two points $\eta(\tau), \eta(\sigma) \in \widetilde\eta \cap \eta \setminus \overline{W}$ such that $\eta((\tau,\sigma))$ is a connected component of $\eta \setminus \widetilde{\eta}$. Let $U$ be the component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus (\widetilde{\eta} \cup \eta)$ with $\eta((\tau,\sigma))$ on its right boundary, let $\widetilde{U}$ the component of $\mathbf{H} \setminus (\widetilde{\eta} \cup \eta([0,\tau]) \cup \eta([\sigma,\infty)))$ containing $\eta((\tau,\sigma))$, and let $\Gamma_U$ be the loops of $\Gamma$ that are contained in $\overline{U}$. Then the conditional law of $\eta|_{[\tau,\sigma]}$ given $\Gamma \setminus \Gamma_U$ and $\eta_{[0,\tau]}$, $\eta|_{[\sigma,\infty)}$ is that of an ${\rm SLE}_\kappa$ in $\widetilde{U}$ from $\eta(\tau)$ to $\eta(\sigma)$ and the conditional law of $\Gamma_U$ given $\Gamma \setminus \Gamma_U$ and $\eta$ is that of a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}$ in $U$.

Let G in R^{m x n}, g in R^m and h in R^n have mutually independent standard Gaussian entries. Let S_x in R^n and S_y in R^m be nonempty compact sets and psi:S_x x S_y -> R continuous and deterministic. Define Phi(G)=min_x max_y [y^T G x+psi(x,y)] and phi(g,h)=min_x max_y [||x||_2 g^T y+||y||_2 h^T x+psi(x,y)]. Then for every c in R, P(Phi<c)<=2P(phi<=c). If additionally S_x,S_y are convex and psi is convex in x and concave in y, then for every deterministic mu in R and t>0, P(|Phi-mu|>t)<=2P(|phi-mu|>=t). The offset need not be Gaussian. A random offset may be conditioned on only when the Gaussian matrix and auxiliary vectors retain their stated independent Gaussian laws conditionally.
Nonempty compact index sets
Continuous deterministic offset
Independent standard Gaussian matrix and auxiliary vectors
For the two-sided comparison: compact convex sets and a convex-concave offset

\sup_{\pmark,\qmark\in \vmarkspace}\int_{\emarkspace}|G(\pmark,\qmark,\rmark)|^2\emarklaw(\dd \rmark)<\infty.

body:
[Theorem mainThem of arXiv:2412.04527, 'Critical Drift for Brownian Bees and a Reflected Brownian Motion Invariance Principle'] Let $X^{N,\mu}=(X^{N,\mu}(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be a one dimensional $N$-Brownian bee system with drift $\mu\in \mathbb{R}$, and let $\mu_c^N=v_N$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \underline{Sub-Critical Case}: when $|\mu| < \mu_c^N$, then for any $t_0>0$, the process $(X^{N,\mu}(nt_0))_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is positive Harris recurrent and therefore has a unique stationary probability measure $\pi^{N,\mu}$ on $\mathbb{R}^N$ so that for any $\chi\in \mathbb{R}^N$
    \begin{equation*}
        \lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{C}|\mathbb{P}_{\chi}(X^{N,\mu}(t)\in C)-\pi^{N,\mu}(C)|_{TV}=0.
    \end{equation*}    
    where $|\cdot|_{TV}$ represents the total variation norm, the supremum is taken over all measurable sets, and $\mathbb{P}_\chi(\cdot):=\mathbb{P}(\cdot|X^{N,\mu}(0)=\chi)$.
    \item \underline{Critical Case}: When $|\mu |=\mu_c^N$, there is an invariance principle
    $$  
    \left(m^{-1/2}X^{N,\mu}(mt)\right)_{t\geq 0} \xrightarrow[m\to\infty]{d} \left(\frac{\mu}{|\mu|}\beta^{-1/2}\sigma |B(t)|\underline{1}\right)_{t\geq 0}.
    $$
    in the Skorokhod topology on $\mathcal{D}([0,\infty),\mathbb{R}^N)$, the space of cadlag functions $[0,\infty)\to \mathbb{R}$, where $B$ is a standard Brownian motion, $\underline{1}=(1,\ldots,1)\in \mathbb{R}^N$, and $\beta,\sigma$ are constants which we will define later. 
    \item \underline{Super-Critical Case}: When $|\mu|>\mu_c^N$, $X^{N,\mu}$ is transient in the sense that each particle $X_i^{N,\mu}$ diverges to $\frac{\mu}{|\mu|}\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, and further
    $$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{X^{N,\mu}_1(t)}{t}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{X^{N,\mu}_N(t)}{t} = \left(|\mu| - \mu_c^N\right)\frac{\mu}{|\mu|} \quad \text{a.s.}$$
    where $X_i^{N,\mu}$ denotes the $i$\textsuperscript{th} smallest particle of 
    $X^{N,\mu}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem mainThem of arXiv:2412.04527

[Definition 7 (Supermartingale $C$-monotonicity.) of arXiv:2603.27940, '\Large \bf Stability of supermartingale optimal transport problems'] The Borel set $\Gamma \subset \R \times \Pc_1$ is supermartingale $C$-monotone if and only if there exists $M_0, M_1 \subset \R$, such that for any $N \in \N$, any collection $(x_1, p_1), \cdots, (x_N, p_N) \in \Gamma$ and $q_1, \cdots q_N \in \Pc_1$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i = \sum_{i=1}^{N} q_i$ and 
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_{\R} y p_i(dy)= \int_{\R} y q_i(dy), \ \ \forall i \in \mathcal{I}_1; \\
& \int_{\R} y p_i(dy) \geq \int_{\R} y q_i(dy), \ \ \forall i \in \mathcal{I}_0,
\end{aligned}
$$
 we have
 $$
 \sum_{i=1}^N C(x_i, p_i) \leq  \sum_{i=1}^N C(x_i, q_i).
 $$
where, $\mathcal{I}_0=\{i : x_i \in M_0 \}$, $\mathcal{I}_1=\{i : x_i \in M_1 \}$. In the following, we say a coupling $\pi \in \Pi_S(\mu, \nu)$ is Supermartingale $C$-monotone if there exists a Supermartingale $C$-monotone set $\Gamma$ with 
$$
(x, \pi_x) \in \Gamma \ \ \mbox{for } \mu(dx) \mbox{-almost every }x,
$$ 
with $M_0, M_1$ defined as the martingale region of $\pi$ to the left and right of $x^*$ (recall that $x^*$ is defined in Section \ref{sec:irreducible})  {In addition, a probability measure $\P \in \Pc(\R \times \Pc_1$, which is supported on a martingale $C$-monotone set, is called supermartingale $C$-monotone. }
title: Supermartingale $C$-monotonicity.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2609.01462, 'Parametrized LS category and group actions'] Assume $p\colon X\to B$ is a fibration with a section $s\colon B\to X$ and a path-connected fibre $F$.
Then
\begin{enumerate}[wide, labelwidth=!]
\item $\ev_1\colon P_BX\to X$ is a fibration with fibre $\Omega F$.

\item $\cat_B(X)=\secat(\ev_1).$

\item $\cat(F)\le\cat_B(X)\le \cat(X)$

\item Let $H^*$ denote any cohomology theory, and let $s^*\colon H^*(X)\to H^*(B)$ be the 
homomorphism induced by the section $s\colon B\to X$. Then  
$\cat_B(X)\ge \cl(\Ker s^*)$, 
where $\cl(R)$ of a ring $R$ denotes its cup-length, i.e. the maximal number of factors from $R$
whose product is non-zero.
\end{enumerate}

The algorithmic SDEs (equation e:PHD of the paper) and (equation e:asl-tap-je of the paper) have unique strong solutions such that $\widehat{m}_t \in (-1,1)^n$ for all $t < \infty$ almost-surely.
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\item
There are constants $\lambda,\Lambda>0$ such that 
    for all $m\in (-1,1)^n$,
    \[
        \lambda D(m)^{-1} \preceq \widehat{Q}(m) \preceq \Lambda D(m)^{-1}.
    \]
\item
    For all $t\in [0,T]$, for $m_t$ drawn from \pref{e:HD}, 
    \[
    \mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}\left\Vert {f(m_t)-m_t}\right\Vert_2^2 \leqslant \varepsilon_{\mathrm{drift}}(t)^2,\]
    where $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{drift}}(t)$ is a constant depending only on $\beta$ and $t$ and bounded on $[0,T]$.
\item
\begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists a constant $L$  such that for all $m, w\in (-1,1)^n$,
    \[
    \ve{\widehat{Q}(m) - \widehat{Q}(w)}_F \leqslant L\left\Vert {m-w}\right\Vert_2.
    \]
        \item 
        There exists a constant $L_f$  such that for all $m, w\in (-1,1)^n$, 
    \[
    \left\Vert {f(m) - f(w)}\right\Vert_2 \leqslant L_f\left\Vert {m - w}\right\Vert_2.
    \]
    \end{enumerate}
\item As in  \pref{e:asl-tap-je} and with $\widehat{m}_t$ solving \pref{eq:asl-tap-m}, let 
\[
\widehat{w}_T\ :=\ \frac{1}{2}\int_0^T \left(\mathsf{Tr}\big(\widehat Q(\widehat{m}_t)\big)\;+\;\lpnorm{\widehat{m}_t}^2\right)dt.
\]
Then for all $T \in [0,\infty)$, $\widehat{w}_T$ is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $\lambda^2c_{T_2}C_{\diag}^2T^2/\gamma^8$, i.e. for all $\lambda \in \mathbb R$,
    \[ \mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}_{B}\left[\exp\left(\lambda\widehat{w}_T - \mathop{{}\mathbb{E}}_{B}[\lambda\widehat{w}_T]\right)\right] \leqslant \exp\left(\frac{\lambda^2c_{T_2}C_{\diag}^2T^2}{2\gamma^{8}}\right), \]
    where $c_{T_2}$ is the function of $T$ and $\gamma$ given in \pref{thm:mSDE-path-subgaussian} and $C_{\diag}$ is the constant (for $\beta < 1/2$) in \pref{lem:alg-resolvent-bounds-delta-frob}.
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Thm 3 of arXiv:2607.06242, 'Exponential mixing and Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle for Markov cocycles'] Assume that the coefficients of either \eqref{e.intro.ns} or \eqref{e.intro.sg} satisfy the mild integrability, boundedness, and determining mode controllability conditions stated in Section~\ref{s.060701} or Section~\ref{s.060702}. Then the associated Markov cocycle admits a unique stationary family $\{\mu_\sigma\}_{\sigma\in\Sigma}$, and this family attracts transition probabilities exponentially both in pullback and forward time. Moreover, for the small noise stationary family $\{\mu_\sigma^\varepsilon\}_{\varepsilon\in(0,1]}$, the Freidlin--Wentzell upper bound holds: for $m$-a.e. $\sigma\in\Sigma$ and every closed set $F$ in the corresponding phase space, 
 \[ \limsup_{\varepsilon\to0} \varepsilon\log\mu_\sigma^\varepsilon(F) \leq -\inf_{u\in F}E_{\mathcal A(\sigma)}(u), \] 
 where $E_{\mathcal A(\sigma)}$ is the pullback quasipotential associated with the deterministic limiting equation. If, in addition, the deterministic pullback attractor is a random point, then the matching lower bound holds: for every open set $G$ in the phase space, 
 \[ \liminf_{\varepsilon\to0} \varepsilon\log\mu_\sigma^\varepsilon(G) \geq -\inf_{u\in G}E_{\mathcal A(\sigma)}(u). \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 3 of arXiv:2607.06242

body:
[Definition def:ribbon-majorant of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a ribbon record $\Gamma$, a circuit state $\tau$, and a designated
set $\mathcal E$ of factored endpoint or packet resources.  Expand every
remaining coefficient component in its circuit-anchored projective
presentation and insert every prescribed fixed gate before closing the
original circuit bases.  Define $\mathfrak a_{\Gamma,\tau;\mathcal E}$
to be $|\omega_\Gamma|$ times the sum of the absolute scalar
coefficients multiplied by all remaining positive projective and
trace-class costs.  No endpoint weight or debit in $\mathcal E$ is
included.  In the monomer--dimer applications of (sec:moments of the paper), the
fixed recurrence scalar $(-\gamma)^a$ is also declared a factored
resource: it is not one of the ``scalar coefficients'' in this
definition and is restored exactly once by the resource ledger.
Local fold, transport, and projective-presentation coefficients do remain
inside the majorant.  When $\tau$ and $\mathcal E$ are clear we write
$\mathfrak a_\Gamma$; subscripts such as
$\mathfrak a_{\Gamma,\mathcal C}$ name the part of the record left open.

This is a positive presentation cost, not the possibly cancelling value
of an open contraction.  Consequently it dominates every compatible
partial trace-class contraction obtained from the same atoms.  The
operator-norm estimate needed for the Kac root-open specialization is the
separate, proved statement (lem:root-open-sinfty of the paper); it is not built
into this definition and no replica factorization is assumed.  The later
allocation argument specifies
which carriers are left bare and proves the corresponding Euler bound;
no second copy of this majorant is introduced there.
title: Positive ribbon majorant

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2607.17255, 'Large deviations for long-time occupation measures of stochastic evolution equations with '] Let Hypotheses~\ref{H1} and~\ref{H2} hold, and let
$(\varphi^\eps )_{\eps \in (0,1)} \subset \mathcal{A}_{b,M}$ be a family of
controls.

Let $\bar v^\eps$ denote the unique mild solution of the controlled
equation~\eqref{veps-controlled} corresponding to the control $\varphi^\eps$.
Then there exists some $c>0$ such that 
\begin{equation}

\eps\, \mathbb{E} \sup_{t \in\,[0,1]}  \bigl| \bar v^\eps(t) \bigr|_H^2+\mathbb{E} \int_0^1 \bigl| \bar v^\eps(t) \bigr|_H^2 \, dt\leq c,\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \e \in\,(0,1).

Moreover, there exists $\beta \in (0, \alpha)$ such that

  \sup_{\eps \in (0,1)} \mathbb{E} \int_0^1
    \bigl| (-A)^\beta \bar v^\eps(t) \bigr|_H^2 \, dt
   <  \infty.
\end{equation}

[Thm 16 (Main Formula) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $k$ be a perfect field. Let $K= k(x)$.
    Let $f\in K$ be a nonzero element.
    Let $PFD(\frac{1}{f})=P+L+H$ be its partial fraction decomposition (over $\overline{k}$), see Theorem \ref{thm: PFD}.

    Let $e$ be the degree of $P$. Let $M$ be the highest order of pole in $H$. Let $p$ be a prime number such that $p-1>e$ and $p>M-1$.

    Let $D=f\frac{\partial}{\partial x}$.
    Then we have that
    \begin{equation}
        D^p= \mu D \hspace{1 cm} \text{, where } \mu=f^p\overline{L}=\frac{\overline{L}}{P^p+L^p+H^p}\in K^p
    \end{equation}
    and $\overline{L}=\sum_{i=1}^d \frac{c_i}{x_i^p-a_i^p}$ if ${L}=\sum_{i=1}^d \frac{c_i}{x_i-a_i}$.

[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2609.03243, 'Weighted Ces\`aro type operators on the weighted Bergman spaces in the unit ball'] Let $\alpha>-1$, $\beta>0$ and $1\leq q<\infty$. Set 
\[
    \lambda=\beta+(n+1+\alpha)\Big(1-\frac{1}{q}\Big).
\]
If $\mu$ is a $\lambda$-Carleson measure on $[0,1)$, then $\mathcal{B}_{\mu,\beta,\delta}^{\xi}: L_{\alpha}^1(\mathbb{B}_n)\to L_{\alpha}^q(\mathbb{B}_n)$ is bounded for every $\delta>0$. Consequently, $\mathcal{C}_{\mu,\beta}^{\xi}: A_{\alpha}^1(\mathbb{B}_n)\to A_{\alpha}^q(\mathbb{B}_n)$ is bounded.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Tightness via a Dirichlet-form argument and identification through conformal covariance. Result: The discrete process is a reversible diffusion with respect to the Liouville measure of the regularised field, with Dirichlet form (1/2) integral |grad f|^2 dx (the Dirichlet form is field-independent, only the speed measure depends on the field). Mosco convergence of the speed measures (the Liouville measures converge) gives convergence of the time-changed Brownian motion, i.e. the marginal law of X converges to Liouville Brownian motion; the joint law with the field converges by the same construction because the time change is a measurable functional of the field. But the process in Problem 16.13 is not the time-changed Brownian motion: it has a drift beta grad h_eps (Langevin), whose limit as eps -> 0 is a distribution and not a function, so the drift term does not converge as a process; the joint limit must be defined through an Ito-type renormalisation of the drift, as for the Liouville Brownian motion with drift. I could not find a formulation of the renormalised drift that is closable in eps; the Dirichlet-form route only gives the drift-free limit. Obstruction: The Langevin drift beta grad h_eps diverges; the problem needs a renormalisation scheme which the notes do not specify.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0013-existence-of-the-liouville-langevin-motion-as-a-joint-scaling-limit

body:
Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. Let T_p be a random set, independent of X, containing each coordinate independently with probability p in [0, 1], and J(p) = E over T_p of Var(E[f | X_{T_p}]). Then J(p) = sum over nonempty S of p^|S| w_S = sum_{k=1}^n p^k W_k. Hence J^(k)(0) = k! W_k >= 0 for every k, J(0) = 0, J(1) = Var(f), and J is nondecreasing and convex on [0, 1].

[Prop primi_1 of arXiv:2607.10105, 'The four-dimensional Anderson model: a case study for critical SPDEs'] Fix $1\leq n\lesssim|\log\varepsilon|$, and functions $G_j(z)\in\mathcal E$ satisfying $|G_j(z)|\leq |z|^{-2}$ for $1\leq j\leq 2n-1$. Consider the following expression
\begin{equation}\mathcal J_{2n,\mathrm{prim}}(z-w):=\lambda_\varepsilon^{2n}\sum_{\kappa}\int_{(\mathbb T^4)^{2n-2}}\prod_{j=1}^{2n-1}G_j(x_j-x_{j+1})\prod_{\{i,j\}\in\kappa}\eta_\varepsilon(x_i-x_j)\,\mathrm{d}x_2\cdots\mathrm{d}x_{2n-1},
\end{equation} where $x_1:=z$ and $x_{2n}:=w$, and $\kappa$ runs over all \emph{primitive} full pairings of $[1,2n]$. Then the function $\mathcal J_{2n,\mathrm{prim}}(z)\in\mathcal E$, and satisfies the following estimate
\begin{equation}|\mathcal J_{2n,\mathrm{prim}}(z)|\leq(C\lambda)^{2n}\bigg(\frac{\varepsilon^{-4}}{|\log\varepsilon|}\cdot|z|^{-2}\mathbf{1}_{|z|\lesssim\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{|\log\varepsilon|^2}\cdot(|z|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{-3}\bigg).
\end{equation}
Moreover, if we change $\mathcal J_{2n,\mathrm{prim}}$ into $\widetilde{\mathcal J}_{2n,\mathrm{prim}}$ by inserting an additional factor $\varepsilon^2+\max_{i,j}|x_i-x_j|^2$ in the integrand in ((eq.primi_1 of the paper)), then we have
\begin{equation}|\widetilde{\mathcal J}_{2n,\mathrm{prim}}(z)|\leq(C\lambda)^{2n}\bigg(\frac{\varepsilon^{-2}}{|\log\varepsilon|}\cdot|z|^{-2}\mathbf{1}_{|z|\lesssim\varepsilon}+\frac{1}{|\log\varepsilon|^2}\cdot(|z|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{-2}\bigg).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop primi_1 of arXiv:2607.10105

	\arrow["\cong", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\cong", from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["\cong"', from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["{{\sigma_{\mathcal{J},\PP,\PP,\mathcal{J}}}}"', from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow["\cong"', from=3-3, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]

$\hat{X}^\ell\equiv \hat{X}^{\ell,\eta=0}$, and so on. On the other hand, let $(X^{\ell},M^{\ell},V^{\ell},\dots)_{\ell\leq \ubl}$ be the state evolution limit of our earlier iteration $\IAMP(p,\sigma,b,w,\delta)$, as described around \eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments}. Then
  \[\begin{aligned}
  (\hat{S},\hat{X}^\ell,
    \hat{\prxX}^\ell,
    \hat{M}^\ell,\hat{V}^\ell)_{0\leq \ell\leq \ubl}
  &\stackrel{\textit{d}}{=}
  (S', S' X^{\ell}, S' \prxX^\ell,

  (\hat{R},\hat Y^\ell,\hat{\prxY}^\ell,

  &\stackrel{\textit{d}}{=}(R',R' Y^{\ell},R' \prxY^{\ell}, R' U^{\ell}, R' \bar{G}^{\ell})_{0\leq \ell\leq \ubl}.

where $S'$ and $R'$ are 
symmetric random signs independent of everything else. 
In particular, at $\eta=0$ the constants $\hat{\prxgamma}$, $\hat{\gamma}$ from \eqref{e:gamma.chaotic} are the same as the constants $\prxgamma$, $\gamma$ from \eqref{eq:proxy-C-ell-delta-def}. Additionally $\hat G^{\ell}$ is independent of $(\hat Y^k,\hat\prxY^k,\hat U^k)_{0\leq k\leq \ell-1}$.

body: In statistics, the Neyman–Pearson lemma describes the existence and uniqueness of the likelihood ratio as a uniformly most powerful test in certain contexts. It was introduced by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in a paper in 1933. The Neyman–Pearson lemma is part of the Neyman–Pearson theory of statistical testing, which introduced concepts such as errors of the second kind, power function, and inductive behavior. The previous Fisherian theory of significance testing postulated only one hypothesis. By introducing a competing hypothesis, the Neyman–Pearsonian flavor of statistical testing allows investigating the two types of errors. The trivial cases where one always rejects or fails to reject the null hypothesis are of little interest but it does prove that one must not relinquish control over one type of error while calibrating the other. Neyman and Pearson accordingly proceeded to restrict their attention to the class of all level tests while subsequently minimizing type II error, traditionally denoted by .
title: Neyman–Pearson lemma

body: [Theorem time_exponential_rank_r of arXiv:2411.04795, 'Metastable Distributions of Semi-Markov Processes'] Let $1 \le  r < R, 1 \le  k \le M_r$. For each $t \ge 0, $ $$ \lim \limits_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \mathbb P \left({ \dfrac{T^{r, \varepsilon}(x, S_l^r)}{\tau_k^{r, \varepsilon}} \ge t  }\right) = e^{-t}$$ uniformly in $x \in S_k^r$, for each $1 \le l \le M_r$, provided that $S_k^r \neq S_i $ for every $1 \le i \le M$ (i.e., $S_k^r$ contains more than one subcluster of rank zero)  and  $P_{kl}^{r, \varepsilon}$ is not identically zero. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:BNN_g of arXiv:2510.21186, 'Weingarten Calculus with Virtual Isometries'] Let $X_1,X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent random vectors, where
each $X_k$ is uniformly distributed on the unit sphere of $\mathbb{C}^k$.
For each $1 \le k \le n$, we denote $R_k$ as the corresponding reflection matrix of size $k$, defined similarly to (equation matrixR of the paper),
and define an $n \times n$ matrix $\tilde{R}_k = R_k \oplus I_{n-k}$.
Then, a Haar-distributed unitary matrix $U$ in $\mathrm{U}(n)$ has the same distribution as
the product $\tilde{R}_n \tilde{R}_{n-1} \cdots \tilde{R}_1$.
In particular, the last $k$ columns of $U$ match those of $\tilde{R}_n \tilde{R}_{n-1} \cdots \tilde{R}_{n-k+1}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ be a 2-monoidal category. A \textit{bimonoid} in $\catname{C}$ is a quintuple $(H,\mu,\iota,\Delta,\epsilon)$ where $(H,\mu,\iota)$ is a monoid in $(\C,\square,I)$, $(H,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a comonoid in $(\C,\circ,J)$, and the two structures are compatible in the sense that the following four diagrams commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(H \circ H)\square (H \circ H)} && {(H\square H)\circ (H \square H)} \\
	{H \square H} & H & {H \circ H}
	\arrow["{\zeta_{H,H,H,H}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\mu \circ \mu}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\Delta \square \Delta}", from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["\mu"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\Delta"', from=2-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{H \square H} & {J \square J} && I & H \\
	H & J && {I \circ I} & {H \circ H}
	\arrow["{\epsilon \square \epsilon}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\mu"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\mu_J}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\iota", from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow["{\Delta_I}"', from=1-4, to=2-4]
	\arrow["\Delta", from=1-5, to=2-5]
	\arrow["\epsilon"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\iota \circ \iota}"', from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& H \\
	I && J
	\arrow["\epsilon", from=1-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\iota", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\iota_J = \epsilon_I}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    A morphism of bimonoids is a morphism of the underlying monoids and comonoids. 
    
    The category of bimonoids in $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ is denoted by $\text{Bimon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$.

body:
If a solution of the heat equation attains its maximum over $\overline{U_T}$ at an interior point $(x_0,t_0)\in U_T$, the conclusion is that $u$ is constant on $\overline U\times[0,t_0]$ -- the past of $t_0$ -- and nothing at all is claimed for $t>t_0$. Heat is not time-reversible, and the mean value property over heat balls only looks backwards. Counterexample: on $U=(0,\pi)$, $T=2$, let $h(t)=1$ for $t\le1$ and $h(t)=1-e^{-1/(t-1)}$ for $t>1$ (smooth, $h\le1$, $h<1$ for $t>1$), and let $u$ be the solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ with $u(\cdot,0)\equiv1$ and $u(0,t)=u(\pi,t)=h(t)$. On $[0,1]$, $u\equiv1$ by uniqueness; the weak maximum principle gives $\max_{\overline{U_T}}u=1$, attained at the interior point $(\pi/2,1)\in U_T$; but for $t>1$, $u$ is not constant (its boundary values are $<1$ while, by continuity, $u$ stays near $1$ in the middle). So constancy holds exactly up to $t_0=1$ and fails afterwards. A second load-bearing hypothesis is connectedness of $U$: for $U=(0,1)\cup(2,3)$ the solution equal to $1$ on the first component and to $e^{-\lambda_1t}\phi_1$ on the second attains its maximum at an interior point of the first component and is not constant on $U$. Finally, the interior maximum must be attained in $U_T$, i.e. at a point with $x_0\in U$: a maximum on the lateral boundary says nothing about constancy (that is the Hopf lemma's domain, which asserts instead that the outward normal derivative is strictly positive there).
Conclusion is constancy on the closure of U x [0,t_0] only
U must be connected
The maximum must be attained at a point with x_0 in U and t_0 > 0
title: Pitfall: The Strong Maximum Principle gives constancy only in the past, and needs a connected domain

[Lemma lengtheraprop of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $(T,d,\rho)\! \equiv \! \widetilde{T}\! \in \!   \mathbb{T}^0_{\! c}$ and $h\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+$. 
We recall from ((deflengthera of the paper)) the definition of the $h$-length-erased subtree $R_h(T)$. Then, the following holds true. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$] $d_{\mathtt{Haus}} ( R_h(T), T)\leq h$, and for all $\varepsilon \! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+^*$ we have $N(T, h+ \varepsilon) \leq  N (R_h (T), \varepsilon)$ and $N(R_h (T), h+ \varepsilon) \leq N(T, \varepsilon)$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] If $h\! > \!  0$, then $R_h (T)$ is a compact subtree of $T$ which is of finite type. The isometry class of 
$(R_h (T), d, \rho)$ only depends on $\widetilde{T}$ and we denote it by $R_h (\widetilde{T})$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(iii)$] $R_h \colon \mathbb{T}^0_{\! c} \! \to \! \mathbb{T}^0_{\! c} $ is ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}}$-continuous, and for all $h'\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+$, $R_h \! \circ \! R_{h'}\! = \!  R_{h+h'}$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(iv)$] A $\mathbb{T}^0_{\! c}$-valued sequence $(\widetilde{T}_n)_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}}$-precompact (resp.~${\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}}$-convergent) iff for all $h\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+^*$, $(R_h (\widetilde{T}_n))_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ is ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}}$-precompact (resp.~${\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}}$-convergent). 

\smallskip

\item[$(v)$] Let $\widetilde{\mathbf T}_n$, $n\! \in \!  \mathbb{N}$, be $\mathbb{T}^0_{\! c}$-valued r.v.s. 
Their laws are tight (resp.~converge in law) in $(\mathbb{T}^0_{\! c}, {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}})$ iff for all $h\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+^*$, the laws of $R_h (\widetilde{\mathbf T}_n)$, $n\! \in \!  \mathbb{N}$, are tight (resp.~converge in law) in $(\mathbb{T}^0_{\! c}, {\boldsymbol{\delta}}_{\mathtt{GH}})$. 
\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\]

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: in any uniqueness statement for u_t + H(Du) = 0 the solution must be a VISCOSITY solution (equivalently, for convex superlinear H, a Lipschitz a.e. solution satisfying the one-sided semiconcavity estimate). Satisfying the equation at almost every point plus the initial condition is far too weak. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = p^2, initial datum g ≡ 0. Both u ≡ 0 and v(x,t) := min(0, |x| - t) are Lipschitz on R × [0,∞), vanish at t = 0, and satisfy v_t + v_x^2 = 0 at every point of differentiability: for |x| < t one has v = |x| - t, v_t = -1, v_x = ±1; for |x| > t one has v ≡ 0. Only u ≡ 0 is the viscosity solution (it is also what the Hopf-Lax formula gives, since L(q) = q^2/4 and min_y ( |x-y|^2/(4t) ) = 0). Why v fails: at a point (0,t) with t > 0, v has a local minimum in x with a convex kink, so φ ≡ v(0,t) + c(t'-t) touches from below with φ_x = 0, φ_t = -1, and the supersolution inequality φ_t + φ_x^2 ≥ 0 reads -1 ≥ 0. Equivalently v violates semiconcavity: v(z,t) - 2v(0,t) + v(-z,t) = 2|z|, which is not O(|z|^2). Auditor's check: whenever a proof concludes 'u is the solution' from 'u is Lipschitz and solves the PDE a.e.', the argument is incomplete unless viscosity, semiconcavity, or a variational (Hopf-Lax) representation is verified.
The counterexample uses H(p) = p^2 (smooth, uniformly convex) and zero data, so no exotic Hamiltonian is needed
'Solution a.e.' means Lipschitz plus the equation at points of differentiability
Uniqueness is restored by the viscosity property or, equivalently for convex superlinear H, by the semiconcavity bound of the Hopf-Lax solution
title: Pitfall: Uniqueness for Hamilton-Jacobi Needs the Viscosity (or Semiconcavity) Condition, Not Just 'Solves a.e.'

[Theorem 8 (Necessary Maximum Principle for Games) of arXiv:2604.02998, 'Nonzero-Sum Stochastic Differential Games for Controlled Convection-Diffusion SPDEs'] Let $(\hat u_1,\hat u_2)\in\mathcal U_1\times\mathcal U_2$
be a Nash equilibrium and let $\widehat Y$
be the corresponding state.
For each $i\in\{1,2\}$ let
$(\widehat p^i,\widehat q^i)$ denote the associated adjoint processes.

Then the following are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}

\item For every bounded admissible direction $\beta_i$
such that $\hat u_i+a\beta_i\in\mathcal U_i$
for all sufficiently small $a$,
\[
\left.\frac{d}{da}
J^i(\hat u_i+a\beta_i,\hat u_{-i})
\right|_{a=0}
=
0.
\]

\item (Variational inequality.)
For almost every $t\in[0,T]$, almost surely,
\[
\int_{\R}
\partial_{u_i}H^i
\big(t,x,\widehat Y(t,x),\hat u_1(t),\hat u_2(t),
\widehat p^i(t,x),\widehat q^i(t,x)\big)
(v_i-\hat u_i(t))
\frac{dx}{\rho(x)}
\ge 0,
\quad
\forall v_i\in U_i.
\]

If $U_i$ is open (or $\hat u_i(t)\in\mathrm{int}(U_i)$ a.s.),
this reduces to
\[
\partial_{u_i}H^i
\big(t,x,\widehat Y(t,x),\hat u_1(t),\hat u_2(t),
\widehat p^i(t,x),\widehat q^i(t,x)\big)
=
0.
\]
\end{enumerate}

body:
[Proposition 21 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] The following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item
Assume that \(u_0:\Sigma\to(S,h)\) is an orientation-preserving 
covering map, and let \(Y=(\Sigma,u_0^*h)\) be the unique minimizing point
of the varying-domain energy. Let \(X_t\in\mathcal T(\Sigma)\), \(t\geq0\),
be any unit-speed Teichm\"uller ray and put
\(d_0=d_{\mathrm T}(X_0,Y)\). Then
there exists constant $A_{Y}$ and
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\eta_Y}{2}e^{-2d_0}e^{2t}
  \leq E_{u_0}(X_t)
  \leq A_Ye^{2d_0}e^{2t}
  \qquad (t\geq0).
  
\end{equation}
Consequently, \(E_{u_0}(X_t)\asymp e^{2t}\) and
\(\log E_{u_0}(X_t)=2t+O(1)\). If \(X_0=Y\), one may omit the factors
\(e^{\pm2d_0}\) in \eqref{eq:varying-domain-energy-ray-growth}.

\item
Assume that the varying-target energy \(\mathcal E_{u_0}\) satisfies the
filling hypothesis with filling system
\(\Gamma=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N\}\). Let
\(q\in\mathcal Q^1(X_0)\) be Jenkins--Strebel and let
\(X_t=\gamma_q(t)\), \(t\geq0\), be the associated unit-speed ray. Define
\(\Theta(q,\Gamma)=\sum_{j=1}^N(\sum_{r=1}^m
i(\delta_r,\alpha_j))^2\). Then \(\Theta(q,\Gamma)>0\), and
there exist constants
$A_{\mathfrak F}$ and
$B_{\mathfrak F}$ such that
\begin{equation}
  16
  A_{\mathfrak F}\,
  \Theta(q,\Gamma)
  \leq \frac{\mathcal E_{u_0}(X_t)}{t^2}
  \leq 16
  B_{\mathfrak F}
  \,
  \Theta(q,\Gamma)
    \qquad (t\geq0).

\end{equation}
Consequently, \(\mathcal E_{u_0}(X_t)\asymp t^2\) and
\(\log\mathcal E_{u_0}(X_t)=2\log t+O(1)\).
\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2604.22644, '2604.22644'] For $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, N-1\}$, let
$$G(k;p) = E\left[\left. \sum_{t=0}^{\tau_0 \wedge \tau_N - 1} I(X_t = k) \right| X_0 = 1, Z_1 = p \right].$$
Then $G(k;p)$ is given by:
$$    G(k;p) = \frac{S(N;p) - S(k;p)}{W(k;p) S(N;p)},
$$
where $S(k;p)$ is the scale function defined in Theorem \ref{thm1}, and $W(k;p)$ is defined as follows:
$$    W(k;p) = r^k p \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{1 - r^j p}{r^j p}.$$

[Definition 39 (Levi-Civita connections and associated differential operators) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill

\begin{enumerate}
\item We denote the Levi-Civita connection of $\gfour$ by $\Dfour$. 
\item We denote the Levi-Civita connection of $\gtorus$ by $\newangD$. In particular,
	for $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent tensorfields $\upxi$, we have $\newangD \upxi = \smoothtorusproject \Dfour \upxi$.
\item If $\upxi$ is an $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent one-form, then we define its $\ell_{t,u}$-divergence 
	to be the scalar function
	$\angdiv \upxi \eqdef \mytr_{\gtorus} \angD \upxi =  (\gtorus^{-1})^{AB}\cdot \newangD_A \upxi_B$. Similarly, if $Y$ is an $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent vectorfield, 
	then we define its $\ell_{t,u}$-divergence to be the scalar function $\angdiv Y \eqdef \gtorus^{-1} \cdot \newangD Y_{\flat}$.
	where $Y_{\flat}$ is the $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent one-form that is $\gfour$-dual to $Y$.
\item If $\upxi$ is an $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent one-form, we define its $\ell_{t,u}$-curl to be the scalar function given by $\in^{AB} \angD_A \upxi_B$, where $\in_{AB}$ are the components of the area form element of the Riemannian manifold $(\ell_{t,u},\gtorus)$ relative to an arbitrary frame $e_A$, $A = 2,3$.
\item If $\upxi$ is a symmetric type $\binom{0}{2}$ $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent tensorfield, 
	then we define its $\ell_{t,u}$-divergence 
	to be the $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent one-form with the following $\ell_{t,u}$-components for $A=2,3$:
	$(\angdiv \upxi)_A \eqdef (\gtorus^{-1})^{BC} \cdot \newangDarg{B} \upxi_{CA}$. 
\item We denote the covariant wave operator of $\gfour$ by $\Box_{\gfour} \eqdef \gfour^{-1}\cdot\Dfour^2
	= (\gfour^{-1})^{\alpha \beta} \Dfour_{\alpha} \Dfour_{\beta}
$. 
\item We denote the angular Hessian and angular Laplacian on $\ell_{t,u}$ associated to $\gtorus$ by $\angD^2$ and 
$\angLap \eqdef \gtorus^{-1} \cdot \newangD^2
=
(\gtorus^{-1})^{AB} \angDarg{A} \angDarg{B}
$, respectively.
\end{enumerate}
title: Levi-Civita connections and associated differential operators

body: [Definition def-markov-kernel of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Suppose $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ and $(\Omega', \mathcal{F}')$ are measurable spaces. A function $\Lambda: \Omega \times \mathcal{F}' \to [0,1]$ is a \emph{Markov kernel} if $\Lambda(\omega, \cdot)$ is a probability measure on $(\Omega', \mathcal{F}')$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$, and $\Lambda(\cdot, A)$ is $\mathcal{F}$-measurable for each $A \in \mathcal{F}'$. If $\mu$ is some measure on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ and $(X,Y)$ is a sample from $\Lambda(x, dy) \mu(dx)$, we say the \emph{conditional law} of $Y$ given $X$ is $\Lambda(X, \cdot)$.

Convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}dx$. (a) If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ and $x_jf\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$, then $\partial_{\xi_j}\hat f$ exists everywhere, is continuous, and equals the transform of $-2\pi i x_jf$. Iterating: if $|x|^kf\in L^1$ then $\hat f\in C^k$. (b) If $f\in C^1(\mathbb R^d)$, $f\in L^1$ and $\partial_jf\in L^1$, then $\widehat{\partial_jf}(\xi)=2\pi i\xi_j\hat f(\xi)$. Iterating: if $f\in C^k$ and $\partial^\alpha f\in L^1$ for all $|\alpha|\le k$, then $|\hat f(\xi)|\le C_{d,k}\big(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|\partial^\alpha f\|_1\big)(1+|\xi|)^{-k}$, and by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma $\hat f(\xi)=o(|\xi|^{-k})$. Slogan: decay of $f$ gives smoothness of $\hat f$, smoothness of $f$ gives decay of $\hat f$.
(a): f and x_j f are Lebesgue integrable on R^d
(b): f is continuously differentiable, and f and its partial derivative d_j f are Lebesgue integrable on R^d

body:
[Definition def:RBG of arXiv:2510.13733, 'Internal Diffusion Limited Aggregation \\ with Critical Branching Random Walks'] Let $R_1 < R_2$ be two integer numbers,
set  $H = R_2 - R_1$. 
Let $\eta : \mathbb{Z}^d \to  \mathbb{N}$
be the initial particle configuration
with support in $\partial B_{R_1}$
and number of particles $N_1 = \sum_{z \in 
\partial B_{R_1}} \eta(z)$. 
Let further $Z_1, \ldots Z_{N_1}$ be i.i.d.\  random variables with distribution 
 supported in   $ \{1, \ldots,  H\} $  given by
\begin{equation}
P( Z_i = h) = \frac{ h^{d-1} }{\sum_{r =1 }^H  r^{d-1}},
\end{equation}
The $\{ Z_i\}$ represent the sequence of heights at which the BRWs will probe the space for settlement. 

The RBG consists of a discrete time
Markov chain  $(A_t)_{t \in \mathbb{N}}$
and a sequence of random variables 
$(  \tilde G_t,  \tilde R_t)_{  t \in \mathbb{N}_0  }$,
 defined as follows. 
We set $A_0 =  \emptyset$ 
and label the particles in $\eta$ with integers from $1$ to $N_1$ in some arbitrary order. 
At each step $t \in \{1, \ldots, N_1\}$, 
we start, from the $t$-th particle of $\eta$, an independent BRW
stopped on $\partial B_{ R_1 + Z_t  }$ 
and let $\xi_t$ be the configuration of pioneers  on $\partial B_{ R_1 + Z_t  }$.
We define the aggregate of the step $t$ as 
the union of the aggregate of the step $t-1$ and 
the support of the  pioneers configuration,  namely 
$$
A_t := A_{t-1} \cup \{ z \in \partial  B_{ R_1 + Z_t  } \, \, : \,   \xi_t(z) > 0     \}.
$$
After that we proceed as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)]
For each particle reaching $\partial B_{ R_1 + Z_t  }$ within 
$A_{t-1}$ we start an independent critical branching random walk stopped on
$\partial B_{ R_2  }$  and call $\tilde{G}_t$ the total number of pioneers 
on $\partial B_{ R_2  }$, which we dub \textit{green particles}.
\item[(b)]  
For each vertex 
 $ x \in \partial  B_{ R_1 + Z_t  } \setminus A_{t-1}$
 with $\xi_t(x)>0$,
 we let exactly one of the $\xi_t(x)$ particles at $x$ settle
 and  start 
 $(\xi_t(x) - 1) \1_{ \{ \xi_t(x)>0 \}  }$
  independent critical branching random walks
 stopped on $ B_{ R_2  }$ from $x$, 
 namely one critical Branching Random Walk from each particle which has not settled at $x$. 
 We call $\tilde{R}_t$ 
 be the total number of pioneers on $\partial B_{ R_2  }$,
 which we dub \textit{red particles}.
\end{enumerate}
We then move to the step $t+1$ and iterate the procedure
up to reaching $t = N_1$.
title: \textbf{Random Barrier Growth}

[Corollary 10 of arXiv:2608.29736, '2608.29736'] Let $(M^n,\omega)$ be a compact K\"ahler manifold of complex
 dimension $n\geq 2$. Let $\chi$ be another K\"ahler form.  Suppose that the $J$-semistable condition ~\eqref{topintegralnonnegative}--~\eqref{$J$-semistablecondition} holds. Then the set 
 \[
\operatorname{Dest}_{n-1}(\chi,\omega)
:=
\bigcup_{\substack{
Z\subsetneq M\ \mathrm{irreducible}\\
\dim Z= n-1,\; \int_ZF_{n-1}(\chi)=0
}}Z
\]
is an analytic subvariety of $M$. And there exists a uniform constant $\delta>0$ independent of the prime divisors, such that for any prime divisor $Y$  satisfying $\int_{Y} F_{n-1}(\chi)>0$, we have 
$$\int_{Y} F_{n-1}(\chi)\geq \delta\int_{Y}\omega^{n-1}.$$
title: Corollary 10 of arXiv:2608.29736

[Theorem 33 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Let $\{\Pi_{x}\}$ satisfy condition 1)
and let $\xi^{0}_{\infty}[P,\omega]$
be $\{\Pi_{x}\}$-admissible. Also suppose that
for any $x\in E,P\in\Pi_{x}$, $\tau\in\frT$, $f\in C_{0}$, and $\alpha\geq0$ we have
$$
E^{P}|\xi^{\tau}_{\infty}[P]|<\infty,
$$
$$
E^{P}\Big\{\alpha\xi^{\tau}_{\infty}[P]
+\theta_{\tau}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}f(x_{t})\,dt
\mid \frM_{\tau}\Big\}\leq w_{\alpha}(f,x_{\tau})
\quad P-(a.s.),
$$
$$
E^{P}\Big\{\alpha\xi^{0}_{\tau}[P]
+ \int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-t}f(x_{t})\,dt
+e^{-\tau}w_{\alpha}(f,x_{\tau})\Big\}\leq w_{\alpha}(f,x),
$$
where
$$
w_{\alpha}(f,x):=\sup_{P\in\Pi_{x}}E^{P}
\Big\{\alpha\xi^{\tau}_{\infty}[P]
+ \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}f(x_{t})\,dt\Big\}
$$
(we will see that $w_{\alpha}(f,\cdot)\in\bB(E)$).

Then the system
$$
\big\{P\in\Pi_{x}: E^{P}\xi^{0}_{\infty}[P]
=\sup_{P\in\Pi_{x}}E^{P}\xi^{0}_{\infty}[P]\big\}
$$
is Markovian relative to $(\frT,\frM_{t})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn of arXiv:2606.24385, 'Gradient Mean-Field Dynamics with Measure-Valued States: Well-Posedness, Chaos, and Long-T'] Let $E$ be a generic Banach space, and denote by $\mathscr{B}(E)$ the Borel $\sigma$-field of $E$. A probability measure $\gamma$ on $(E,\mathscr{B}(E))$ is said to be Gaussian if $\gamma \circ f^{-1}$ is Gaussian measure in ${\mathbb R}$ for every $f\in E^{\ast}$ (the topological dual space of $E$ of linear and continuous functionals $f:E\rightarrow {\mathbb R}$). The measure is called centered (or symmetric) if all the measures $\gamma\circ f^{-1}$ are centered.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2605.13512, '2605.13512'] (Hydrodynamic limit)
 For any $n \in \N$, let $z^n$ evolve using a field of independent Poisson processes $\{N^{(n)}_{i,j}\}_{(i,j) \in \Z^2}$ with rates $\{\lambda^n_{i,j}\}_{(i,j) \in \Z^2}$ given by 
\[
        \lambda^n_{i,j}=\tilde c(i/n,j/n)
        = c((i+j)/n,j/n),
\]
and let $\tilde c$ satisfy Assumption \ref{ass:pde-speed}.
Assume \eqref{eq:etaass}, \eqref{eq:in-cur} and \eqref{eq:z0lim} where the limits are assumed either ${\bf P}-$ a.s.~or in ${\bf P}-$probability. 

Then for any $x \in \bR$ and $t \in \bR_+$ we have the existence of a function $v(x,t)$ such that the limit 
\be 
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} z^{n}_{\fl{nx}}(nt) = v(x,t) 
\ee
holds in the same mode of convergence as for $t=0$, i.e. ${\bf P}-$ a.s.~or in ${\bf P}-$probability. 

Moreover, $v(x,t )$ satisfies the following properties
\begin{enumerate}
\item $v(x,t)$ is Lipschitz-1 in the $x$-variable.
\item  $v(x,t)$ is locally Lipschitz, jointly in $(x,t)$. 
\item $v(x,t)$ is differentiable in both $x$ and $t$ for a.e.\ $(x,t)$. 
\end{enumerate}
The a.e. $x$-derivative $\rho(x,t)$ is the density profile for the particle system, as given by the LLN
\be 
\lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = \fl{na}}^{\fl{nb}} \eta^n_i(nt) = \int_{a}^b \rho(x,t) \, dx.
\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 4 of arXiv:2605.13512

[Theorem 4 (Bipartite coefficients) of arXiv:2606.05430, 'On a random matrix proof of\\ a bipartite Harer-Zagier formula'] For all integers $k,M >0$, $g \geq 0$, we have the following identity
    \[\e_g(k,M) = \frac{(-1)^k k!}{kM+1}\sum_{p=0}^{2g} \sfir{kM+1}{p+kM+1-2g}\binom{p+kM+1-2g}{p+k}\ssec{p+k}{k}(-M)^{p+k},\]
    where $\sfir{n}{k}$ and $\ssec{n}{k}$ are, respectively, Stirling numbers of the first and second kind. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For any truncation level b_n > 0, define Y_{n, k} = X_{n, k} \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n, k}| \le b_n\}}. [Satz thm:partialLSITails of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Let $\mu$ be a measure on a product of finite sets satisfying a $\mathfrak{d}\mathrm{-LSI}(\sigma^2)$, and let $f \in L^\infty(\mu)$.
	\begin{enumerate}
	        \item Assuming that $\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(j)} f}_{\mathrm{op},1} \le 1$ for all $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ and $\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(d)} f}_{\mathrm{op},\infty} \le 1$, it holds that
	        \[
	        {\mathbb E} \exp\Big\{c |f(X)|^{2/d} \Big\} \le 2,
	        \]
	        where a possible choice of the constant $c$ is given by
	        \[
	        c = \frac{(\sqrt{2}-1)^2}{16 \kappa e}.
	        \]
	        \item For any $t\ge 0$, it holds that
	        \[
	        {\mathbb P}(|f(X)| \ge t)\le
	        2 \exp\Big\{- \frac{C}{d^2} \min\Big(\min_{j=1, \ldots,d-1} \Big(\frac{t}{\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(j)} f}_{\mathrm{op},1}}\Big)^{2/j}, \Big(\frac{t}{\norm{\mathfrak{h}^{(d)} f}_{\mathrm{op},\infty}}\Big)^{2/d}\Big)\Big\},
	        \]
	        where a possible choice of the constant $C$ is given by
	    	\[
	    	C = \frac{\log(2)}{4 \kappa e^2} > \frac{1}{34}.
	    	\]
	 \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

        \Prob(K_d=k)=\pi_{d,k}\quad(1\le k\le d-1),
        \qquad
        \Prob(K_d=d)=\rho_d,
\]
where
\[
        \rho_d:=\prod_{r=1}^{d-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
\]
is the probability that no one-sided tie-break occurs before simultaneous completion.  Thus the value $K_d=d$ records this exceptional terminal event.  Then
\[
        \frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\Rightarrow X,
        \qquad
        \Prob(X\in \dd x)=2x e^{-x^2}\Ind_{\{x>0\}}\dd x .
\]
In particular,
\[
        K_d\to\infty,
        \qquad
        \frac{K_d}{d}\to0
\]
in probability.  More precisely, for $k=o(d)$,
\[
        \prod_{r=1}^{k-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
        =\exp\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{d}+O\left(\frac{k^4}{d^3}\right)\right),
\]
and there are absolute constants $C,c>0$ such that, for every $R\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge R\sqrt{d\log d}}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C d^{-cR^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
More generally, for every $M\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge M\sqrt d}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C e^{-cM^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $R$ large enough the tail in
\eqref{eq:first-break-tail} is $o(d^{-1})$.

[Lem walkmax of arXiv:2411.12149, 'Airy limit for $\beta$-additions through Dunkl operators'] For $L\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 100}$, take discrete intervals $[\![X,Y]\!]$ contained in $[\![0,L]\!]$ where $Y-X\ge 1$.
Consider three types of random walks $W(t):[\![0,L]\!]\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ as follows. Let $V=W(X)-\min_{[\![X,Y]\!]}W+1$.

(1).    For $H\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, sample the walk  $W(t)$ in $\tilde{\mathcal{W}}(\cdot,H,L;N)$.
Then there exist constants $C>0$, $c>0$, which are uniform in $H,L,N$, such that for all $h\ge 0$, $\tilde{h}\ge 0$,
    $$\mathbb{P}[W\ge 0,\ \max_{t} W(t)-H>h\sqrt{L},\ V>\tilde{h}\sqrt{Y-X}]\le\begin{cases}
         C\exp(-ch^{2})\exp(-c\tilde{h}^{2}),\quad &\text{if}\ \ H>0\\
         \frac{C}{\sqrt{L}}\exp(-ch^{2})\exp(-c\tilde{h}^{2}),\quad &\text{if}\ \ H=0.
    \end{cases}$$

(2). For $H\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$, sample the walk  from $\tilde{\mathcal{W}}(\cdot,H,L,N)$.
Then there exist constants $C>0$, $c>0$, which are uniform in $L,N$, such that for all $h\ge 0$, 
    $$\mathbb{P}[W(0)=0,\ W\ge 0,\ \max_{t} W(t)-H>h\sqrt{L},\ V>\tilde{h}\sqrt{Y-X}]\le\frac{C}{L}\exp(-ch^{2})\exp(-c\tilde{h}^{2}).$$

(3). Sample the walk from $\tilde{\mathcal{W}}(\cdot,0,L,N)$. 
Then there exist constants $C>0$, $c>0$, which are uniform in $L,N$, such that for all $h\ge 0$,
    $$\mathbb{P}[W(0)=0,\ W\ge 0,\ \max_{t} W(t)>h\sqrt{L},\ V>\tilde{h}\sqrt{Y-X}]\le\frac{C}{L^{3/2}}\exp(-ch^{2})\exp(-c\tilde{h}^{2}).$$
title: Lem walkmax of arXiv:2411.12149

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Never-visited density for the planar Poisson greedy walk structural calculation Result: Local finiteness implies a simple but weak path fact: if the infinite greedy walk is well-defined for all steps, then it eventually leaves every bounded ball, since it never revisits a chosen point and a bounded ball contains finitely many Poisson points. This does not imply it visited all those finitely many points before leaving. A deterministic locally finite configuration can have a path going to infinity while leaving an entire bounded subset untouched. Check: The distinction is between eventual departure and exhaustive visitation. The trivial upper bound on never-visited points is the Poisson count, asymptotic pi*r^2 almost surely, but no matching order or limiting density follows from self-avoidance. Obstruction: The finite-window path law is sensitive to points outside the window. Identifying a translation-invariant limit of disjoint doubly infinite greedy paths, or quantitative exploration of missed points, remains the main obstruction.

[Corollary cor:empirical of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_n \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ be i.i.d.\ with
    \[
    \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \coloneqq \E (\mathbf{X}_1 - \E \mathbf{X}_1)^2, 
    \quad
    \lambda_{\max}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) \le \sigma^2,
    \quad
    \norm{\norm{\mathbf{X}_1-\E \mathbf{X}_1}}_{\psi_{\alpha}} \le K.
    \]
    Denote
    \[
    \overline{\mathbf{X}} \coloneqq \frac{1}{n} \sum_i \mathbf{X}_i,
    \quad
    \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} \coloneqq \frac{1}{n} \sum_i (\mathbf{X}_i - \overline{\mathbf{X}})^2,
    \quad
    \hat{\sigma}^2 \coloneqq \lambda_{\max}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}),
    \]
    and define $\hat{z} \coloneqq z(K, \hat{\sigma}; \alpha) \coloneqq \lr{4 \hspace{0.2em}\underline{\log}\hspace{0.2em} \frac{K e}{\hat{\sigma}}}^{1/\alpha}$. Then for any $\mathrm{x} > 0$ such that $n \ge 8 \mathrm{x}$, 
    with probability at least $1 - 3 d e^{-\mathrm{x}}$ holds
    \[
    \norm*{\overline{\mathbf{X}} - \E \mathbf{X}_1} \le \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{2 \frac{\mathrm{x}}{n}} + 15 K \hat{z}\frac{\mathrm{x}}{n}.    
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $X$ be a $d\times r$ matrix with i.i.d. $N(0,1)$ entries and let $z = (XX^\top - rI_d)/\sqrt{2r} \in \mathrm{Sym}_d$, so that $\mathbb{E}\,z=0$ and $\mathbb{E}\langle z,U\rangle^2 = \|U\|_F^2$ for every symmetric $U$ (with the Frobenius inner product). Then for every symmetric $U$ with $\|U\|_F = 1$ and eigenvalues $u_1,\dots,u_d$, the standardized fourth moment of $\langle z,U\rangle$ is exactly
\[ \mathrm{kurt}\,\langle z,U\rangle \;=\; 3 + \frac{12}{r}\,\mathrm{Tr}(U^4) \;=\; 3 + \frac{12}{r}\sum_i u_i^4. \]
In particular $r=1$ (the rank-one form $z=(xx^\top - I)/\sqrt2$, $x\sim N(0,I_d)$) gives $3 + 12\,\mathrm{Tr}(U^4)$: kurtosis $15$ along a pure diagonal coordinate ($\mathrm{Tr}(U^4)=1$), $9$ along a pure off-diagonal coordinate ($\mathrm{Tr}(U^4)=\tfrac12$), and, along a direction $U$ Haar-uniform on the unit Frobenius sphere of $\mathrm{Sym}_d$, $3 + 24/(dr)$ in expectation, since $\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Tr}(U^4) \to 2/d$ (the fourth moment of the semicircle divided by $d$).

[Definition def:sc-dual-dressing of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] Let $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ solve the dual linear and adjoint
linear problems.  A map
$K \colon \mathcal{V} \to \mathrm{End}(H)$ is
\emph{dual dressing compatible} with $(\Psi, \Phi)$ if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*., leftmargin=*]
\item For every $u \in \mathcal V$ and $j \geq 2$,
\begin{align}
K(Tu) - K(u) &= \Psi(Tu)\Phi(Tu),
   \\
\partial_1 K(u) &= \Psi(u)\Lambda_1(u)\Phi(Tu),
   \\
K(S_j u) - K(u)
  &= \Psi(Tu)C_j(u)\Phi(S_j u),
  \qquad j \geq 2.
  
\end{align} 
\item There exists $z \in \mathbb{F}$ such that the resolvent
exists at every vertex:
\[
R(u) \vcentcolon= (I - zK(u))^{-1} \in \mathrm{End}(H),
\qquad u \in \mathcal{V}.
\]
\end{enumerate}

(\bar g,U,\alpha,\mathcal E,\mathcal B,\Psi,\nabla)

\nabla \bar g=0,\qquad \nabla U=0,\qquad \nabla\alpha=0,
\]
\[
\nabla\mathcal E\subset\mathcal E,\qquad \nabla\mathcal B\subset\mathcal B,\qquad \nabla\Psi=0.
\]

body:
Owner draft: independently checked proof within C013 v1. For any finite real c_i in [0,1] with sum_i c_i=m an integer, there is a real orthogonal projection of rank m whose diagonal is c_i. The projection can be chosen Borel measurably in the prescribed diagonal: separate zero/one entries; merge two fractional entries to (s,0) or (1,s-1); recurse; conjugate by a two-coordinate rotation to restore the two original entries. Ordered Gram-Schmidt yields an m-by-n frame B with B^T B=P and BB^T=I_m. This is the finite projection specialization of Schur-Horn, not Schur triangularization. The full general Schur-Horn theorem is not asserted or sourced by this card. Standard fact with a self-contained proof; no novelty claim.
Finite n
c_i in [0,1]
Integer total m with 0<=m<=n

[Prop comparing-Aut of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The maps
    \begin{equation}
        \textup{Aut}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus)\to{\textup{Hom}}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta,\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus)\gets
        \textup{Aut}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta)
    \end{equation}
    induced by $|{\cdot}|$ are monomorphisms, and they have the same image.
    \begin{proof}
        View both $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus$ and $\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta$ as functors $\text{Fin}_*\to\mathbb\Spc_{\textup{Glo}}$ satisfying the Segal condition. Throughout the proof, we will make use of the usual formula [GHN17]*{Proposition~5.1} for mapping spaces in a functor category as the end
        \begin{multline*}
            {\textup{Hom}}(F,G)\simeq\int_{\langle r\rangle\in\text{Fin}_*}{\textup{Hom}}(F(\langle r\rangle),G(\langle r\rangle))\\{}\coloneqq
            \lim\big({\Tw(\text{Fin}_*)\xrightarrow{\;\ev\;} \text{Fin}_*\!\!\!{}^{\textup{op}}\times\text{Fin}_*\xrightarrow{{\textup{Hom}}(F(-),G(-))\;}\Spc}\big),
        \end{multline*}
        where $\Tw$ denotes the twisted arrow category.

        Consider the subfunctor $F_\oplus\colon\Tw(\text{Fin}_*)\to\Spc$ of ${\textup{Hom}}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(-),\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(-))$ given at $\alpha\colon\langle r\rangle \to\langle s\rangle$ by the component of $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(\alpha)\colon\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(\langle r\rangle)\to\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(\langle s\rangle)$. Then the map $\lim F_\oplus\to\lim{\textup{Hom}}\big(\textup{Rep}^\oplus(-),\textup{Rep}^\oplus(-)\big)\simeq{\textup{End}}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus)$ induced by the inclusion is a monomorphism (as a limit of monomorphisms), and its image consists precisely of those natural transformations whose underlying functor is the identity. By Proposition~(prop:Aut-h-Vect of the paper), this image agrees with $\textup{Aut}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus)$. In the same way, Proposition~(prop:Aut-Vect-delta of the paper) identifies $\textup{Aut}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta)$ with the limit of the analogously defined subfunctor $F_\delta\subset{\textup{Hom}}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta(-),\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta(-))$, reducing us to proving that the maps
        \[
            \lim_{\alpha\colon\langle r\rangle\to\langle s\rangle}\hskip0pt minus 15ptF_\oplus(\alpha)\to
            \lim_{\alpha\colon\langle r\rangle\to\langle s\rangle}\hskip0pt minus 15pt{\textup{Hom}}(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta(\langle r\rangle),\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(\langle s\rangle))\gets
            \lim_{\alpha\colon\langle r\rangle\to\langle s\rangle}\hskip0pt minus 15pt F_\delta(\alpha)
        \]
        induced by $|{\cdot}|$ are monomorphisms with the same image. Using once more that limits preserve monomorphisms, it will then suffice to show that for each $\alpha$ the maps
        \begin{equation}
            F_\oplus(\alpha)\to
            {\textup{Hom}}\big(\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta(\langle r\rangle),
            \ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(\langle s\rangle)\big)\gets
            F_\delta(\alpha)
        \end{equation}
        are monomorphisms with the same image. 

        By construction, the image of the first map is the component of $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus(\alpha)\circ|{\cdot}|$, while the image of the second one is the component of $|{\cdot}|\circ\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta(\alpha)$, and these maps are indeed homotopic. To prove that the maps $((eq:monos-without-ends of the paper))$ are monomorphisms, we first note that the Segal conditions for $\ul\textup{Rep}^\amalg_\delta$ and $\ul\textup{Rep}^\oplus$ imply that we have equivalences
        \begin{align*}
            F_\oplus(\alpha)&\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}\prod_{i=1}^s F_\oplus(\chi_i\circ\alpha)\\

[Corollary 20 of arXiv:2607.19873, 'Local limit theorem for the operator norm of products of random matrices'] Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $G$. 
Assume that the action of $G$ on $\wt B$ satisfies the moment condition \eqref{moment-assumption-01} and 
that the action of $G$ on $B$ satisfies the contraction property \eqref{contraction-property-on-B}.  
Suppose that, for every $\wt b \in \wt B$ with $\eta(\wt b) \in \supp \nu$,   we have $\wt b M \subset \overline{\Gamma_{\mu} \wt b}$. 
Fix $\wt b_0 \in \wt B$ with $\eta(\wt b_0) \in \supp \nu$. 
Then, for every character $\chi$ of the group $M/M_0^{\mu}$, the operator $P_{\mu, \chi}$ 
has a unique eigenvalue $\lambda_{\chi}$ of modulus one in the space $W_{\chi}^{0}$. 

Moreover, there exists a unique associated eigenvector $\varphi_{\chi} \in W_{\chi}^{0}$
such that $\varphi_{\chi}(\wt b_0) = 1$ and $\varphi_{\chi}$ is H\"older continuous on $\wt B$.  
Also, the generalized eigenspace associated with the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\chi}$ for the operator $P_{\mu, \chi}$ acting on the space $W_{\chi}^0$ 
is equal to $\bb C \varphi_{\chi}$, that is, this eigenvalue is multiplicity free. 

Finally, the restriction $\varphi_{\chi}|_{\eta^{-1}(\supp \nu)}$ is the unique continuous function on $\eta^{-1}(\supp \nu)$
such that $\varphi_{\chi}(\wt b_0) = 1$ and for every $m \in M$,  $g \in \supp \mu$ and $\wt b \in \eta^{-1}(\supp \nu)$, we have 
\begin{align}
\varphi_{\chi}(\wt b m) = \chi(m)^{-1} \varphi_{\chi}(\wt b)
\quad \mbox{and} \quad
\varphi_{\chi}(g \wt b) = \lambda_{\chi} \varphi_{\chi}(\wt b). 
\end{align}

[Lemma lm:Q_k of arXiv:2602.03058, '\vspace{-3em} Moments of sums of exponentials, beyond CHS'] Let $k$ be a nonnegative integer and let $k < p < k+1$. Define
\[
Q_k(t) = (-1)^{k+1}\left(e^{-t} - \sum_{j=0}^k \frac{(-1)^j}{j!}t^j\right), \qquad t > 0.
\]
Then $Q_k(t) > 0$, the integral
\[
C_p = \int_0^\infty Q_k(t)t^{-p-1}\mathrm{d} t
\]
converges and for $x > 0$, we have
\[
x^p = C_p^{-1}\int_0^\infty Q_k(tx)t^{-p-1}\mathrm{d} t.
\]
title: Lemma lm:Q_k of arXiv:2602.03058

body:
[Proposition prop:poly_limit_scaled of arXiv:2607.27810, 'Perturbed Beta Corners Process'] Let $a_N=\frac{\beta}{2}\mathsf{a}_N$ with $\mathsf{a}_N\ne0$ fixed, let
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=(\mu_1>\cdots>\mu_{N-1})$ be fixed and not depend on $\beta$, and let random
$\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ be obtained from $\boldsymbol{\mu}$
through~(equation eq:random_poly_general of the paper). Then, as $\beta\to\infty$:
\begin{enumerate}[\normalfont(i)]
	\item $N-1$ of the roots stay bounded and converge in probability to the roots of
	\begin{equation}
		
		\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\frac{1}{x-\mu_i}=-\mathsf{a}_N,
		\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad
		D_{\mathsf{a}_N}P_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(x)
		= P_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'(x)+\mathsf{a}_N P_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(x)=0 .
	\end{equation}
	(prop:shifted_derivative of the paper), applied to $P_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$, locates
	these $N-1$ roots: exactly $N-2$ of them interlace with $\boldsymbol{\mu}$,
	one in each gap $(\mu_{i+1},\mu_i)$, and the last lies outside the range of
	$\boldsymbol{\mu}$ --- below $\mu_{N-1}$ if $\mathsf{a}_N>0$, above $\mu_1$
	if $\mathsf{a}_N<0$.
	\item The remaining root escapes on the scale of the perturbation:
	$\dfrac{2}{\beta}\max_j|\lambda_j|\to|\mathsf{a}_N|$,
	the unbounded root having the sign of $\mathsf{a}_N$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:poly_limit_scaled of arXiv:2607.27810

\]
and
\[

    \left(
        \sup_{L>m_{\xi,d,+}}
        \left|
            \widehat F_{\xi,d,n,L}^{\mathrm{post,cap}}
        \right|
        >
        2^{-sn/2}2^{-3\varepsilon n}

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: there is beta > 0 with B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2 for every u in the Hilbert space H. Strict positivity (B[u,u] > 0 for u nonzero) is not enough, and neither is injectivity of the associated operator. Counterexample: H = l^2, B(u,v) = sum_k u_k v_k / k. This form is bounded (|B(u,v)| <= ||u|| ||v||), symmetric and strictly positive, but B(e_k, e_k) = 1/k tends to 0, so it is not coercive. The bounded functional F(v) = sum_k v_k / k is represented by the sequence (1/k) in l^2, yet B(u, .) = F forces u_k = 1 for all k, which is not in l^2: the equation has no solution. PDE instances of the same failure: (i) on H^1_0(Omega) the form B[u,v] = integral (grad u . grad v - lambda_1 u v) satisfies B[u,u] >= 0 with equality exactly on the first eigenfunction, and the Dirichlet problem for -Laplacian - lambda_1 is not solvable for general right-hand sides (the Fredholm orthogonality condition appears); (ii) on H^1(Omega) the Neumann form integral grad u . grad v annihilates constants, and integral f = 0 is necessary for solvability; (iii) on an unbounded Omega the Poincare inequality may fail, so integral (grad u . grad v) is not coercive for the full H^1 norm. Two further points a careful reader should keep straight: coercivity is sufficient but not necessary (for lambda strictly between two Dirichlet eigenvalues the form of -Laplacian - lambda is indefinite, yet the problem is uniquely solvable by the Fredholm alternative), and Lax-Milgram does not require B to be symmetric - symmetry only turns the solution into the minimizer of a quadratic energy (Riesz representation / Dirichlet principle).
title: Pitfall: Lax-Milgram Needs Coercivity, Not Mere Positivity

[Proposition 6 (Enveloping skeleton) of arXiv:2608.06232, 'The mean absolute deviation of the classical discrete distributions:\\ collapse identities'] Let $\Delta:(0,\infty)\to\R$ be continuous with $\Delta(t)<0$ for all $t>0$ and
	$|\Delta(t)|\le Ce^{-ct}$ for some $c>0$.  Put
	\[
		L:=\int_0^\infty\varphi(t)\,\Delta(t)\,dt,
		\qquad
		c_n:=\frac{B_{2n}}{(2n)!}\int_0^\infty t^{2n-2}\,\Delta(t)\,dt\qquad(n\ge1).
	\]
	All the integrals converge absolutely, and for every $M\ge0$
	\begin{equation}
		(-1)^{M+1}\Bigl[L-\sum_{n=1}^{M}c_n\Bigr]\;>\;0 .
	\end{equation}
	Consequently $L$ lies strictly between any two consecutive partial sums of $\sum_nc_n$, and
	$\operatorname{sign}c_n=(-1)^{n}$.

[Proposition 30 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Let $X_t=\gamma_q(t)$ be the Teichm\"uller geodesic determined by
$q\in\mathcal Q^1(X_0)$, let $F_t:X_0\to X_t$ be the associated
Teichm\"uller maps, and set $v_t:=u_{X_t}\circ F_t$ and
$E(t):=\mathcal E(t,v_t)$. Then
\begin{equation}
  E'(t)
  =
  -2e^{-2t}H(v_t)+2e^{2t}V(v_t).
  
\end{equation}
For every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ and every $p>2$, one has
$t\mapsto v_t\in C^2(J,W^{1,p}(X_0,S))$. Let
$W_t:=D_tv_t\in W^{1,p}(X_0,v_t^*TS)$ and define
$\mathcal Q_t:=D_v^2\mathcal E(t,v_t)[W_t,W_t]$. Then
\begin{equation}
  E''(t)=4E(t)-\mathcal Q_t.
  
\end{equation}
Moreover, if
$\widetilde W_t:=W_t\circ F_t^{-1}$, then
$\widetilde W_t\in W^{1,p}(X_t,u_{X_t}^*TS)
\subset W^{1,2}(X_t,u_{X_t}^*TS)$ and
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal Q_t
  =
  I_{u_{X_t}}
  \bigl(
    \widetilde W_t,\widetilde W_t
  \bigr).
  
\end{equation}
In particular, $\mathcal Q_t\ge0$.

body: In calculus and real analysis, the mean value theorem is a theorem about differentiable functions, roughly stating that the average rate of change of such a function over an interval is equal to the instantaneous rate of change at some point in the interval.
