[Lemma lem:ricci-soft-threshold of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Work in the packetless subfiber and suppose the Ricci residual component
has no independently token-bearing hard resource covered by
(lem:ricci-internal-hard of the paper).  Resolve every internal hard
full-centered packet into all-Weyl and mixed children.  The all-Weyl
token-bearing children and, by
(lem:ricci-mixed-closed-hard of the paper), every nonzero mixed child fall
under that lemma.  Thus the retained soft family contains no packet
child.  Let $o$ be the number of unfused
$\mathsf S^\pm$ singleton supernodes and $v$ the total number of
$\mathsf V$ singleton supernodes in all maximal consecutive runs of the
Ricci component.  Put
\[
 \Delta_0=o+\frac v2.
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12n}$}
\]
If $\Delta_0\ge f_R$, where $f_R\in\{1,2\}$ is the number of root-hit
fundamental circuits, then this complete subfiber satisfies the shell
bound on the right of (eq:3.3.1w-12k of the paper).

[Corollary cor:lbm-simple-eigenvalue-response of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $f\in C_c^\infty(D)$,
\begin{equation}
 \partial_f^-\Lambda_n^x
 =\partial_f^+\Lambda_n^x
 =:\partial_f\Lambda_n^x
 =-\gamma\Lambda_n^x\int_Df(\phi_n^x)^2\,dM_x
 =\int_Df\,d\eta_n^x.
 
\end{equation}

body: [Thm higher-dims of arXiv:2411.14336, 'Finding the root in random nearest neighbor trees'] For the $d$-NN model with $d \in \mathbf{N}$, $d \geq 2$, for all $n \in \mathbf{N}$ and all sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a $O(n^2 + n(1/\varepsilon)^{1/(\log \log (1/\varepsilon))})$-time embedded root finding algorithm that returns a confidence set $H(\varepsilon,n)$ of size satisfying $|H(\varepsilon, n)| \leq \exp\bpar{\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\log\log(1/\varepsilon)} + d \log\log(1/\varepsilon)}$. Additionally, there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that it is information-theoretically impossible to provide a confidence set whose size satisfies $|H(\varepsilon, n)| \log \left( {|H(\varepsilon, n)|}{d^{-1/d}}\right) \leq c \log(1/\varepsilon)/d.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm higher-dims of arXiv:2411.14336

body:
[Theorem thm-KTC-ZB of arXiv:2512.17727, 'Stochastic transport equation with L\'evy noise'] Assume that  $(\Omega, \mathscr{F}, \mathbb{P})$ is a  complete probability space,  $X$ is an infinite dimensional vector space and let $\rho$ and $\Vert \cdot \Vert$  be a metric and norm on $X$. The space $X$ endowed with  the metric $\rho$ will be denoted by $E$ and
the space $X$ endowed with  the  norm $\Vert \cdot \Vert$  will be denoted by $B$. We assume that $E$ is separable, $B$ is complete and that the natural embedding
\[
i: B \hookrightarrow E
\]
is continuous. We denote by $\mathscr{B}(E)$ the Borel $\sigma$-field on $E$.

Assume that $D \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$.  Assume that for every $x \in D$, $K(x)$ is an $E$-valued random element, i.e., $K(x):\Omega \to E$ is
$\mathscr{F}/ \mathscr{B}(E)$-measurable. Assume that $p\in (0,\infty)$ and $\delta,\gamma \in (0,1)$, $\delta<\gamma$. \\
Assume that  for all $x,y \in D$, the functions
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\Omega \ni \omega &\mapsto \Vert K(x,\omega)- K(y,\omega) \Vert \in [0,\infty),
\\
\Omega \ni \omega &\mapsto \Vert K(x,\omega) \Vert \in [0,\infty)
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
are $\mathscr{F}/ \mathscr{B}(\mathbb{R})$-measurable.
Assume that there exists $C>0$ such that for all $x,y \in D$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb{E} \Vert K(x)- K(y) \Vert^p \leq C \left[ \vert x-y\vert^{d+\delta}+\vert x-y\vert^{d+\gamma}\right].
\end{equation}
Then, there exists a family $K^\prime(x)$,  $x \in D$, of  $E$-valued random elements, such that
\begin{trivlist}
\item[(i)] $K^\prime$ is a modification of $K$, i.e., for every $x \in D$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(K(x)\not=K^\prime(x))=0;
\]
\item[(ii)] for every $\omega \in \Omega$, the map
\[
D \ni x \mapsto K^\prime(x,\omega) \in B
\]
is continuous.
\end{trivlist}
Moreover, the assertion (ii) can be strengthened as follows. For any $\beta< \frac{\delta}{p}$ and  every $R>0$, the map
\[
D \cap B(0,R) \ni x \mapsto K^\prime(x,\omega) \in B
\]
where $B(0,R)$ is the closed ball of radius $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$,
is $\beta$-H\"older continuous (and hence bounded). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm-KTC-ZB of arXiv:2512.17727

[Proposition prop:highprobindependence of arXiv:2608.11378, 'On the most likely geodesic in last passage percolation'] Carry over the notation from Corollary~(cor:nonintersect of the paper). Write $L = L(u; u + a \1)$ and $L' = L(u'; u' + a' \1)$. Take events $\mathcal{E} \in \sigma(L)$ and $\mathcal{E}' \in \sigma(L')$. There is a constant $c > 0$, uniform in $n$ and across all choices of events $\mathcal{E},\, \mathcal{E}'$, such that
    \[
    \abs[\big]{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E} \cap \mathcal{E}') - \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}')} \le e^{- c n^{3 \alpha - 2}}.
    \]
    That is, the events may be considered as independent, up to an error of $\exp\brac{- c n^{3 \alpha - 2}}$.
\begin{proof}
    Write $\mathcal{T}$ for the tube of width $\lambda n^{\alpha}$ around the line joining $u \to u + a \1$, and $\mathcal{T}'$ for the tube of width $\lambda n^{\alpha}$ around the line $u' \to u' + a' \1$. Choose $\lambda > 0$ small enough that $\mathcal{T} \cap \mathcal{T}' = \emptyset$, which may be done uniformly in the angle $\theta$. Define coupled weights $\tilde{\omega}$ which are equal to $\omega$ on $\mathcal{T}$ and sampled independently elsewhere. Do the same with weights $\tilde{\omega}'$ and $\mathcal{T}'$. Observe that the weights $\tilde{\omega}$ and $\tilde{\omega}'$ are completely independent of one another.
    
    Sample $L = L(u; u + a \1)$ and $L' = L(u'; u' + a' \1)$ according to the usual weights $\omega$. Sample $M$ and $M'$ as passage times between the same points but under weights $\tilde{\omega}$ and $\tilde{\omega}'$, respectively. This choice of $M$ and $M'$ ensures they are independent by construction, and they are of course equal in distribution to their counterparts under weights $\omega$. Moreover, we will have $L = M$ so long as the geodesics defining both remain in $\mathcal{T}$, and the same for $L',\, M'$. Write $I$ for the event that none of the four geodesics leave their corresponding tube and note that $L = M$ and $L' = M'$ conditioned on $I$.
    
    Returning to the claim, choose sets $A,\, A' \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $\mathcal{E} = \set{L \in A}$ and $\mathcal{E}' = \set{L' \in A'}$. We can carry out the following manipulation:
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E} \cap \mathcal{E}') &\le \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E} \cap \mathcal{E}' \mid I)\mathbb{P}(I) + \mathbb{P}(I^c)\\
                       &= \mathbb{P}(L \in A,\, L' \in A' \mid I)\mathbb{P}(I) + \mathbb{P}(I^c)\\
                       &= \mathbb{P}(M \in A,\, M' \in A' \mid I)\mathbb{P}(I) + \mathbb{P}(I^c)\\
                       &= \mathbb{P}(M \in A,\, M' \in A',\, I) + \mathbb{P}(I^c)\\
                       &\le \mathbb{P}(M \in A,\, M' \in A') + \mathbb{P}(I^c)\\
                       &= \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}) \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}') + \mathbb{P}(I^c).
    \end{align*}
    We may estimate $\mathbb{P}(I^c)$ using Proposition~(cor:nonintersect of the paper) and a union bound, and get
    \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E} \cap \mathcal{E}') &\le \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}) \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}') + 4 e^{- c n^{3 \alpha - 2}}.
    \end{align*}
    Reversing the roles of the $L$ and $M$ variables gives the inequality in the other direction.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

STATUS: proof (unaudited); own-work draft. Jointly trained scalar head and factored attention p=kq have open positive-three-dimensional-measure inferior-selection basins for arbitrary n>=2 distinct two-token examples and every fixed eta>0. In the stated sign regions all parameters escape, factors are O(sqrt(log |v|)), loss tends to zero, and actual (v,k,q)-normalized margins are Gamma_-<Gamma_+. The complete finite stationary set is a saddle curve v=0,kq=p_bar, with one zero tangent and opposite-sign normal Hessian eigenvalues.

# Target 1: joint head, key and query training retains open inferior basins

Version 1. Proof unaudited. Own work; global novelty unestablished.

## Statement

Let n>=2, b_i,kappa_i>0 and 0<a_i<b_i. Set
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s),
L(v,k,q)=mean_i log(1+exp(-v h_i(kq))).
Train all three scalar parameters by simultaneous Euclidean GD, at any fixed eta>0.
Write r_min=min_i atanh(-a_i/b_i)/kappa_i<0.
The following nonempty open subsets of R^3 are forward invariant:

 B_-={v<0,k>0,q<0,kq<r_min},
 B_+={v>0,k>0,q>0}.

The simultaneous sign reversal (k,q)->(-k,-q) supplies two more invariant regions.
On B_-: v->-infinity, k->+infinity, q->-infinity, kq->-infinity,
L->0, and (v,k,q)/sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2)->(-1,0,0).
On B_+ the three coordinates tend to +infinity and the normalized limit is
(1,0,0). The normalized minimum signed margins, defined here as
min_i v h_i(kq)/sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2), tend respectively to
Gamma_-=min_i(b_i-a_i) and Gamma_+=min_i(b_i+a_i).
The largest attainable limiting normalized margin is Gamma_+; Gamma_+>Gamma_-.
Consequently the inferior basin has positive three-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
These are invariant-region results, not a classification of all initializations.

The two-token cross-attention and genuine first-token self-attention embeddings
in proofs/004 and 006 remain exact after replacing their attention parameter p
by kq. Thus the claim includes distinct examples and both labels.

## Exact updates and invariance

For s=kq put g_i=1/(1+exp(v h_i(s))),
F=mean g_i h_i(s), G=mean g_i h_i'(s)>0. The exact simultaneous updates are

 v_+=v+eta F, k_+=k+eta vqG, q_+=q+eta vkG.

In B_-, F<0, vq>0 and vk<0. Each sign is therefore preserved and the
product becomes more negative. In B_+ all increments are positive, since
s>0 and h_i(s)>a_i>0. No restriction on eta is needed.

Analyze either branch using positive variables u,w,r. On B_- take
u=-v,w=k,r=-q, x=wr=-s, t_i(x)=b_i tanh(kappa_i x)-a_i.
On B_+ take u=v,w=k,r=q,x=wr=s,t_i(x)=b_i tanh(kappa_i x)+a_i.
Both obey exactly

 Delta u=eta mean g_i t_i, w_+=w+delta r, r_+=r+delta w,
 delta=eta u mean g_i t_i', g_i=(1+exp(u t_i))^-1.

Here x,u,w,r increase, and t_i(x)>=c:=min_i t_i(x_0)>0.
Let H=max_i(a_i+b_i), M=max_i b_i kappa_i, kappa_0=min_i kappa_i.
All t_i<=H and t_i'<=4M exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

## Escape

If u remained bounded, u t_i<=u H would keep every g_i bounded below,
contradicting Delta u>=eta c mean g_i. Hence u->infinity.
If x remained bounded, min_i t_i' would have a positive lower bound d>0.
The exact product update is

 Delta x=delta(w^2+r^2)+delta^2 x.

Using w^2+r^2>=2x_0>0 and
delta/Delta u=u(mean g_i t_i')/(mean g_i t_i)>=u d/H,
we obtain Delta x>=2x_0 d u Delta u/H. The sum of u Delta u diverges
(already u>=u_0>0 and sum Delta u=infinity), contradicting bounded x.
Thus x->infinity, and the loss tends to zero.

## Factor growth is negligible relative to the head

This step is essential: it compares the margin in the actual three parameters,
not the collapsed (v,p) norm. Let D=w-r. The exact relation is
D_+=(1-delta)D. Since g_i<=exp(-c u),
0<delta<=eta M u exp(-c u)->0. Hence eventually delta<=1, and |D| is
bounded by a finite constant D_* (a finite earlier excursion is harmless).
Therefore w^2+r^2=2x+D^2<=2x+D_*^2.
Eventually delta<=1, so

 Delta x<=delta(3x+D_*^2),
 delta<=4 eta M u exp(-c u) exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

The function (3x+D_*^2)exp(-2 kappa_0 x) is bounded for x>=x_0>0.
Consequently Delta x->0, and eventually Delta x<=1. Also

 delta/Delta u<=4M u exp(-2 kappa_0 x)/c.

The mean value theorem now gives

 Delta exp(kappa_0 x)
 <=kappa_0 exp(kappa_0) exp(kappa_0 x) Delta x
 <=C (3x+D_*^2)exp(-kappa_0 x) u Delta u
 <=C' u Delta u.

Summing, using 2u Delta u<=Delta(u^2), yields
exp(kappa_0 x)<=C''(1+u^2). Thus x=O(log u), and
w^2+r^2=O(log u). In particular w/u,r/u->0. Since x->infinity and
|w-r| is bounded, both w,r tend to infinity. This proves every stated
coordinate and normalized limit.

## Margin optimality and positive measure

Endpoint limits give Gamma_+ and Gamma_-. For any parameters, let
N=sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2). If v>=0, choose an index minimizing a_i+b_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_+. If v<0, choose an index minimizing b_i-a_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_-. These inequalities remain valid when that
chosen signed prediction is negative. B_+ attains the larger endpoint
asymptotically. Gamma_+>=Gamma_-+2 min_i a_i>Gamma_-.
B_- is nonempty and open; for example take v=-1,k=R,q=-R with
R^2>-r_min. A sufficiently small ball around that point lies in B_-.

## Finite stationary set (flow stability, separate from the GD basin claim)

The only finite stationary points are v=0, kq=p_bar, where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0. Indeed v!=0 would force k=q=0 from the factor
gradients, but F(v,0)=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0.
At v=0 the remaining condition is exactly the displayed mean root.
It is negative, so k,q are nonzero. Put A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0. The loss Hessian is

 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].

It has one zero tangent eigenvalue and eigenvalues
(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2 of opposite sign. Thus each point
on this critical curve is a saddle with one attracting and one repelling
normal direction for gradient flow. This does not assert a global
stable-manifold classification or small-step GD stability uniformly along
the noncompact curve.

## Prior work and limits

Tarzanagh et al., arXiv:2308.16898, PDF pp.3-4 defines KQ-ERM with
the explicit phrase 'for a fixed head'; Theorem 2 treats the factored
regularization path and nuclear-norm bias. Sheen et al., arXiv:2403.08699,
source sections/preliminariesAr.tex line 17 likewise fixes the linear
prediction head; its main diagonal/general theorems concern gradient flow
and exponential loss. Neither checked scope is this joint-head logistic
arbitrary-step invariant-region statement. This is a bounded comparison,
not a claim that no such result exists elsewhere. Factor-balance identities
and nuclear-norm bias are prior work, not claimed as discoveries here.
The result does not cover matrices, multiple heads, or the full R^3 basin partition.
Average logistic loss of v[a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i kq)], 0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0. Simultaneous Euclidean GD; B_-={v<0,k>0,q<0,kq<min roots}, B_+={v>0,k>0,q>0}, and simultaneous factor-sign reflections. Stability type stated for gradient flow only.

we obtain Delta x>=2x_0 d u Delta u/H. The sum of u Delta u diverges
(already u>=u_0>0 and sum Delta u=infinity), contradicting bounded x.
Thus x->infinity, and the loss tends to zero.

## Factor growth is negligible relative to the head

This step is essential: it compares the margin in the actual three parameters,
not the collapsed (v,p) norm. Let D=w-r. The exact relation is
D_+=(1-delta)D. Since g_i<=exp(-c u),
0<delta<=eta M u exp(-c u)->0. Hence eventually delta<=1, and |D| is
bounded by a finite constant D_* (a finite earlier excursion is harmless).
Therefore w^2+r^2=2x+D^2<=2x+D_*^2.
Eventually delta<=1, so

 Delta x<=delta(3x+D_*^2),
 delta<=4 eta M u exp(-c u) exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

The function (3x+D_*^2)exp(-2 kappa_0 x) is bounded for x>=x_0>0.
Consequently Delta x->0, and eventually Delta x<=1. Also

 delta/Delta u<=4M u exp(-2 kappa_0 x)/c.

The mean value theorem now gives

 Delta exp(kappa_0 x)
 <=kappa_0 exp(kappa_0) exp(kappa_0 x) Delta x
 <=C (3x+D_*^2)exp(-kappa_0 x) u Delta u
 <=C' u Delta u.

Summing, using 2u Delta u<=Delta(u^2), yields
exp(kappa_0 x)<=C''(1+u^2). Thus x=O(log u), and
w^2+r^2=O(log u). In particular w/u,r/u->0. Since x->infinity and
|w-r| is bounded, both w,r tend to infinity. This proves every stated
coordinate and normalized limit.

## Margin optimality and positive measure

Endpoint limits give Gamma_+ and Gamma_-. For any parameters, let
N=sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2). If v>=0, choose an index minimizing a_i+b_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_+. If v<0, choose an index minimizing b_i-a_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_-. These inequalities remain valid when that
chosen signed prediction is negative. B_+ attains the larger endpoint
asymptotically. Gamma_+>=Gamma_-+2 min_i a_i>Gamma_-.
B_- is nonempty and open; for example take v=-1,k=R,q=-R with
R^2>-r_min. A sufficiently small ball around that point lies in B_-.

## Finite stationary set (flow stability, separate from the GD basin claim)

The only finite stationary points are v=0, kq=p_bar, where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0. Indeed v!=0 would force k=q=0 from the factor
gradients, but F(v,0)=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0.
At v=0 the remaining condition is exactly the displayed mean root.
It is negative, so k,q are nonzero. Put A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0. The loss Hessian is

 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].

It has one zero tangent eigenvalue and eigenvalues
(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2 of opposite sign. Thus each point
on this critical curve is a saddle with one attracting and one repelling
normal direction for gradient flow. This does not assert a global
stable-manifold classification or small-step GD stability uniformly along
the noncompact curve.

## Prior work and limits

Tarzanagh et al., arXiv:2308.16898, PDF pp.3-4 defines KQ-ERM with
the explicit phrase 'for a fixed head'; Theorem 2 treats the factored
regularization path and nuclear-norm bias. Sheen et al., arXiv:2403.08699,
source sections/preliminariesAr.tex line 17 likewise fixes the linear
prediction head; its main diagonal/general theorems concern gradient flow
and exponential loss. Neither checked scope is this joint-head logistic
arbitrary-step invariant-region statement. This is a bounded comparison,
not a claim that no such result exists elsewhere. Factor-balance identities
and nuclear-norm bias are prior work, not claimed as discoveries here.
The result does not cover matrices, multiple heads, or the full R^3 basin partition.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:08d8b1d3ef1f36e0eba1beda523151ac4030eeb4090e1c07ba56c128b974fefa","revision_digest":"sha256:eb73c725c1f3d37ce88c91b972496a29abf235066cc0deb1a14e322996a8aaef","source_id":"owner:T328:w698:claim-010:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20 v1; no independent PASS yet","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

\begin{equation}
\lim_{\sigma\to\infty}
\left[
\frac{1}
{\WS{\sigma^2}{a\sigma}{T}\Big(C[0, T]\Big)}

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.14948, 'Graph alignment in sparse inhomogeneous models via self-overlap'] Let $(K_1, K_2)$ be a pair of random graphs, following a joint law $\mu$. The graph alignment problem is the following: a permutation $\sigma^* \in \Sym_n$ is chosen uniformly at random, independently from $K_1, K_2$; from the observation of the graphs $(G, H) = ((\sigma^*)^{-1}(K_1), K_2)$, we wish to recover the matching $\sigma^*$.

    In this setting, we refer to $(G, H)$ as a \textbf{correlated graph system}.

[Lemma lem: colsum of arXiv:2604.10446, 'Least singular values of shifted sparse random combinatorial matrices'] Let $n\geq 2$, $m \geq 1$, $\beta\geq 4$, and $1\leq d\le n/2$.  
      Let $M$ be an $m \times n$ random matrix with entries in $\{0, 1\}$, where each row is independently and uniformly sampled from the set of all vectors in $\{0, 1\}^n$ containing exactly $d$ ones. Given $\tau>0$, consider the event
    \[
    \mathcal{E}_{(lem: colsum of the paper)}=\mathcal{E}_{(lem: colsum of the paper)}(\tau):=\set{M=\{M_{ij}\}_{i \in [m],j \in [n]}: \sum_{i=1}^{m} M_{ij}\le \frac{(1+\tau) md}{n} \ \mbox{ for every } j\le n}.
    \]
    Then for $\tau=\max{\big\{e^2, \frac{\beta n\log m}{md}\big\}}$,
    \[
    \mathbb{P}( \mathcal{E}_{(lem: colsum of the paper)})\ge 1-n\cdot m^{-\beta},
    \]   
and for $0 < \tau < 1$,
    \[
    \mathbb{P}( \mathcal{E}_{(lem: colsum of the paper)})\ge 1-n\exp\left(-\frac{md\tau^2}{3n}\right).
    \]

[Theorem 2 (Spectral zero pattern) of arXiv:2609.02590, 'Directional Optimal Sub-Gamma Scales for Infinitely Divisible Laws'] The directional scales satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \cplus(X)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nu((0,\infty))=0,
 \qquad
 \cminus(X)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nu((-\infty,0))=0.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently, $\cplus(X)=\cminus(X)=0$ if and only if $X$ is Gaussian with
variance $V$.

[Prop 40 of arXiv:2609.01932, 'Essential dimension and faithful rank of finite $p$-gerbes'] Let $\cG/k$ be as above and let $\cE$ be a faithful small vector bundle of
rank $d$.  Let
\[
\pi:\cE\rightarrow \bfE
\]
be its coarse moduli morphism.  Then $\bfE$ is an affine $k$-scheme, the zero
section induces a point $0\in\bfE(k)$, and $(\bfE,0)$ is a $d$-dimensional
tame quotient singularity.  Moreover,
\[
\widehat{\bfE}\simeq \cE,
\quad
\cG\simeq\cG_{(\bfE,0)},
\]
where the second isomorphism is induced by the zero section.

body:
[Theorem 10 (max-domain of attraction of the constructed max-id process) of arXiv:2604.11434, 'Maxima of stationary systems of randomly time-changed L\'evy particles'] Let $\alpha$ be a mass function satisfying Assumption~\ref{asu:alpha},
  let
$(L_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be a L\'evy process
satisfying Assumption~\ref{asu:levy}, and
    let $(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be the time-changed process in the sense of Lemma~\ref{lem:existence_tcp}.
    Consider the max-id process $(Z_t)_{t\ge 0}$ defined by
\begin{align*}
  Z_t
  \ = \
  \max
  \mathfrak{P}_t
  \left(
  (X_t)_{t\ge 0}, \alpha(x)\exp(-x)\mathrm{d}x
  \right)
  \,,
\end{align*}
let
\begin{align*}
    \zeta_n(t)
    \ := \
    \max_{k=1,\ldots,n} Z_t^{(k)} - \log(n)
    \,,
    \qquad n\in\NN
    \,,
  \end{align*}
  where $((Z_t^{(k)})_{t\ge 0})_{k=1,\ldots,n}$ are i.i.d.~copies of $(Z_t)_{t\ge 0}$, and let
\begin{align*}
    \zeta_L(t)
    \ := \
    \max \mathfrak{P}_t((L_t)_{t\ge 0},\exp(-x)\mathrm{d}x)
    \,.
  \end{align*}
  Then $\zeta_n$ converges weakly to $\zeta_L$ in f.d.d.
  If, furthermore, $(L_t)_{t\ge 0}$ has continuous paths,
  then convergence holds in $\mathbb{D}([0,\infty))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: max-domain of attraction of the constructed max-id process

[Prop 17 of arXiv:2603.05174, 'Regularization of the superposition principle: Potential theory meets Fokker-Planck equati'] Let $V\in p\mathcal{B}([0,\infty)\times \mathbb{R}^d)$ and $\delta_V\in(0,\infty)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
    \mu_0(V(0,\cdot))<\infty, \quad P_tV\leq e^{\delta_V t}V,\quad t\geq 0.
\end{equation*}
Then
$
    \mu_t(V(t,\cdot))\leq e^{\delta_Vt}\mu_0(V(0,\cdot)), \quad t\geq 0,
$
and hence assertions (i)-(iii) from \Cref{prop:mu-V} hold.

body:
Let K be a compact Hausdorff space and let A be a subalgebra of C(K, R), the algebra of real-valued continuous functions on K with the supremum norm, such that A contains the constant functions and separates points (for every pair of distinct points x, y in K there is f in A with f(x) different from f(y)). Then A is dense in C(K, R): every continuous real function on K is a uniform limit of elements of A. Complex version: a subalgebra of C(K, C) containing the constants, separating points, and closed under complex conjugation is dense in C(K, C). The classical Weierstrass approximation theorem (polynomials are dense in C([a,b], R)) is the special case A = polynomials on K = [a,b].

For f in B with values in [-M, M], the function t -> |t| is a uniform limit of real polynomials on [-M, M] (this one-variable Weierstrass fact can be proved directly, for example via the iteration p_(n+1)(t) = p_n(t) + (t^2 - p_n(t)^2)/2 converging uniformly to |t| on [-1,1]); composing these polynomials with f gives elements of B converging uniformly to |f|. Hence B is a lattice: max(f, g) = (f + g + |f - g|)/2 and min(f, g) = (f + g - |f - g|)/2 lie in B. Step 2: two-point interpolation. For distinct x, y and prescribed real values a, b, separation plus constants give h in A with h(x) = a, h(y) = b (affinely rescale a separating function). Step 3: let g in C(K, R) and epsilon > 0. Fixing x, the open sets {z : f_(x,y)(z) < g(z) + epsilon}, indexed by y, cover K (y lies in its own set); take a finite subcover and let f_x = min of the corresponding f_(x,y); then f_x < g + epsilon everywhere and f_x(x) = g(x). The open sets {z : f_x(z) > g(z) - epsilon} cover K; a finite subcover and f = max of the corresponding f_x give |f - g| < epsilon with f in B (lattice operations, finitely many). Own-work draft extracted from C010 version 2 section 7; proof (unaudited), not a novelty claim. Let a finite-dimensional parameter space have a norm D dominated by sqrt(3) times a Hilbert norm H. Two adapted recurrences obey theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta_k[G(theta_k)+xi_k], with a common deterministic nonnegative step sequence of total at most T. Both recurrences remain in a domain where D(G(theta)-G(theta'))<=kappa omega(D(theta-theta')), omega(0)=0, omega(s)=s log(e/s) for 0<s<=1, and omega(s)=1 for s>=1. Each noise is centered conditional on the joint past filtration and has conditional H second moment at most G0^2; initializations and any selected relabeling are in that past. Cross-run noise independence is unnecessary if these conditional statements hold. Suppose delta=E[D(theta_0-theta'_0)]+2sqrt(3)G0 sqrt(sum eta_k^2)<=1. Summing the updates first gives accumulated martingales M_n=sum_{k<n}eta_k xi_k with E||M_n||_H<=G0 sqrt(sum eta_k^2). Norm convexity and omega concavity then give e_n<=delta+kappa sum_{k<n}eta_k omega(e_k), where e_n=E D(theta_n-theta'_n). Discrete Bihari comparison yields e_K<=3(1+kappa T)delta^(exp(-kappa T)). This uses the integrated martingale and a concave drift modulus; it requires neither summing expected absolute one-step noises nor a Hilbert Lipschitz bound on G. The source gives this argument on an initialization-measurable good event, where the same proof applies to conditional expectations. Finite martingale checks are validation only, not a quantified theorem certificate or independent audit.
D norm dominated by sqrt(3) times H; all visited states satisfy the displayed common Osgood drift modulus
Joint-past martingale centering and uniform conditional second moments; common deterministic nonnegative steps; finite initial expected D; delta<=1

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given a variable $f:X\to\mathbb R$ which follows the uniform law of $[a,b]$, its even normalized central moments are given by the following formula,
$$M_k''=\frac{3^{k/2}}{k+1}$$
with the small order even normalized central moments being as follows:
$$M_2''=1\quad,\quad 
M_4''=\frac{9}{5}\quad,\quad
M_6''=\frac{27}{7}\quad,\quad\ldots$$
As for the odd normalized central moments, these all vanish.

Vardi, Yehudai and Shamir, Theorem 6.2 (arXiv:2110.03187v1, p.9): Let n>=4, let d,C be positive integers, and let x_1,...,x_n in R^d have Euclidean norms <=r and pairwise Euclidean distances >=delta>0, with labels y_i in {1,...,C}. Use normalized bounds r>=1 and delta<=1. Put R=d*n*C*r/delta and h=log_2 R. For every integer 2<=s<=floor(sqrt(n)), there is a feedforward ReLU network that exactly memorizes all labels, has width O(1), depth O(n*h*sqrt(log_2 s)/s), and at most O(d+n*h*sqrt(log_2 s)/s) nonzero parameters. The bit precision is at most a constant times s*h/sqrt(log_2 s). The parameter s is the tuning parameter called B in the source; it is not the achieved bit budget. Big-O constants are unspecified. Appendix C p.20 prints a weaker precision estimate O(s*sqrt(log_2 s)*h); the theorem display on p.9 and the stage bounds on p.17 give the denominator used here.

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2607.08536, 'Soft edge limit of the Laguerre beta-ensemble at the lower edge'] Suppose that $\zeta_j, 1\le j\le n$ are martingale differences with respect to the filtration $\FF_j, 0\le j\le n$. Assume that $\sigma_j^2, 1\le j\le n$ are non-decreasing positive reals bounded by 1 with
$\ev[\zeta_j^2|\FF_{j-1} ]\le \sigma_j^2$.
Introduce the notations
\begin{align*}
    M(k_1,k_2)=\sum_{j=k_1+1}^{k_2} \zeta_j, \qquad \sigma(k_1,k_2)^2=\sum_{j=k_1+1}^{k_2} \sigma_j^2, \qquad 0\le k_1<k_2\le n. 
\end{align*}
For $x\ge 0$ let 
\[
\gamma(x)=\max(x, x^{1/2}). 
\]
Then for $c$ large enough we have 
\begin{align*}
   & \pr\left(|M(k_1,k_2)|\ge c \cdot \gamma(\sigma(k_1,k_2))
   \log\big(4+\tfrac{\sigma^2(0,k_1)}{\sigma^2(k_1,k_2)}+3|\log\sigma(k_1,k_2)|\big)\text{ for some $0\le k_1<k_2\le n$}\right)\\&\qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \le 2^{-\frac{c}{50}}+\pr(|\zeta_j|> \sigma_j^{1/2} \text{ for some } 1\le j\le n).
\end{align*}
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2607.08536

Let q be a prime power, U uniform on F_q^m, and a_1, ..., a_r in F_q^m. For an index set I, the forms (a_i . U)_{i in I} are uniform on F_q^|I| (equivalently, mutually independent with each a_i . U uniform on F_q) if and only if the indexed family (a_i)_{i in I} is linearly independent, a repeated vector counting as a dependence. Consequently, for every integer k >= 1, the forms are k-wise independent with each form uniform on F_q if and only if every indexed subfamily of at most k coefficient vectors is linearly independent. Without uniformity the criterion is different: (a_i . U)_{i in I} is mutually independent if and only if the nonzero vectors among (a_i)_{i in I} are linearly independent. A zero vector gives the constant 0, independent of everything but not uniform: for q = 2 and m = 1 the rows 0 and 1 give (0, U), which is independent although the rows have rank 1.

the coefficient vectors form an indexed family, repeats allowed

body:
[Definition def:lions_derivative of arXiv:2507.22577, 'A Mean-Field Theory of $\Theta$-Expectations'] A function $U: \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^k) \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to be \textbf{L-differentiable} at a measure $\mu \in \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^k)$ if the following holds:
For any probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ and any random variable $X \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P; \mathbb{R}^k)$ with $\Law(X) = \mu$, the lifted map $\tilde{U}: L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P; \mathbb{R}^k) \to \mathbb{R}$, defined by $\tilde{U}(Y) := U(\Law(Y))$, is Fréchet differentiable at $X$.

The Fréchet derivative $D\tilde{U}(X)$ is a continuous linear functional on $L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P; \mathbb{R}^k)$. By the Riesz representation theorem, there exists a unique random variable $\xi \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P; \mathbb{R}^k)$ such that for all $Y \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P; \mathbb{R}^k)$,
\[ D\tilde{U}(X)[Y] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \scpr{\xi}{Y} \right]. \]
A fundamental result of the theory is that this representing random variable $\xi$ is necessarily measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $X$, i.e., $\xi \in L^2(\Omega, \sigma(X), P; \mathbb{R}^k)$. By the Doob-Dynkin lemma, there exists a Borel-measurable function $\partial_\mu U(\mu, \cdot): \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k$ such that $\xi = \partial_\mu U(\mu, X)$, $P$-a.s. This function $\partial_\mu U(\mu, \cdot)$, which is uniquely defined up to a $\mu$-null set, is called the \textbf{Lions derivative} (or L-derivative) of $U$ at $\mu$.
title: Lions Derivative

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.01419, 'A model of opinion dynamics evolving via a preferential attachment mechanism involving mul'] Consider the stochastic approximation process $\{Z_{n}\}$, with $Z_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, given by
\begin{equation}
Z_{n+1}=Z_{n}+a_{n+1}\left\{F(Z_{n})+\Delta M_{n+1}+\delta_{n}\right\} \text{ for }n\in\mathbb{N}_{0},
\end{equation}
with prescribed $Z_{0}$ and the following assumptions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(B\arabic*), ref=B\arabic*]
\item  the map $F:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is Lipschitz,
\item  the step-size sequence $\{a_{n}\}$, of positive scalars, satisfies $\sum_{n}a_{n}=\infty$ and $\sum_{n}a_{n}^{2}<\infty$,
\item  the sequence $\{\Delta M_{n+1}\}$ is a martingale difference sequence with respect to the filtration $\{\mathcal{F}_{n+1}\}$, where $\mathcal{F}_{n}$ is the $\sigma$-field consisting of all information about the process up to and including epoch $n$, and $\{\delta_{n}\}$ is a sequence of additional error terms adapted to $\{\mathcal{F}_{n}\}$, such that $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_{i+1}(\Delta M_{i+1}+\delta_{i})$ converges almost surely as $n\rightarrow\infty$, 
\item  and $\sup\{||Z_{n}||:n\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\}<\infty$ almost surely, where $||\cdot||$ indicates the usual Euclidean norm in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$.
\end{enumerate}
Then, almost surely, $\{Z_{n}\}$ converges to a (possibly sample path dependent) compact connected internally chain transitive invariant set corresponding to the autonomous ODE $\dot{x}(t)=F(x(t))$ for $t\geqslant 0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.01419

\begin{equation}
h_{\Lambda}T_{\Lambda}(h_{\Lambda})\cdots
T_{\Lambda}^{m-1}(h_{\Lambda})=1.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, the decorated transverse path associated with the concatenation power $\gamma^{*m}$ has trivial signature.

[Proposition prop: hitting time of z and concentration of the stationary measure of arXiv:2509.23069, 'Every cutoff profile is possible'] Let $(k, \boldsymbol{\ell},\boldsymbol{\rho}) \in {\ensuremath{\mathcal P}} $. There exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that the following holds. Let $\varepsilon\in (0,\varepsilon_0)$. Consider the FIT Markov chain with parameters $(k, \boldsymbol{\ell},\boldsymbol{\rho}, \varepsilon)$, and denote its stationary distribution by $\pi_\varepsilon$.
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item We have ${\ensuremath{\mathbb E}} _z \left[ T_z^+ \right] \leq 1+2\varepsilon$.
    \item We have $\pi_\varepsilon(z) \geq 1- 2\varepsilon$.
    \item For any fixed $t\geq 0$, we have ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _z(X_t = z) \geq 1-4\varepsilon$.
    \item For any state $v$, and any times $t_1\leq t_2$, we have ${\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _v(X_{t_2} = z) \geq {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} _v(T_z \leq t_1) - 4\varepsilon$.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Proposition prop: hitting time of z and concentration of the stationary measure of arXiv:2509.23069

[Theorem thm:original version of arXiv:2411.00663, 'Ergodicity and Mixing of invariant capacities and applications'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},V,T)$ be a capacity preserving system, where $V$ is an upper probability. Then $V$ is ergodic with respect to $T$ if and only if for any $f\in B(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$, there exists a unique $c_f\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
	$$
	\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(T^{i} \omega)=c_f \text{ for }V\text{-a.s. }\omega\in\Omega.  
	$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:original version of arXiv:2411.00663

If $G_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt r/(\Gamma\sqrt{1-\beta})\geq1$, then for every $t\geq1$, the learner of~\cref{alg:momentum-muon} achieves
\begin{equation}
  \E[\DReg_t(D)]

  \quad\text{with depth}\quad
  q=\left\lceil\log_A\frac{G_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt r}{\Gamma\sqrt{1-\beta}}\right\rceil.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 4 (Theorem 1.12 in \cite{Zhu2005}) of arXiv:2609.03243, 'Weighted Ces\`aro type operators on the weighted Bergman spaces in the unit ball'] Suppose $\delta>-1$ and $c$ is real. Let
\[
    J_{c,\delta}(z)=\int_{\mathbb{B}_n}\frac{(1-|w|^2)^{\delta}}{|1-\langle z,w\rangle|^{n+1+\delta+c}}{\rm d}v(w),\quad z\in\mathbb{B}_n.
\]
Then the following asymptotic properties hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(1)] If $c<0$, then $J_{c,\delta}$ is bounded in $\mathbb{B}_n$.
\item[(2)] If $c=0$, then
\[
    J_{0,\delta}(z)\simeq \log\frac{1}{1-|z|^2},\quad |z|\to 1^-.
\]
\item[(3)] If $c>0$, then
\[
    J_{c,\delta}(z)\simeq \frac{1}{(1-|z|^2)^c},\quad |z|\to 1^{-}.
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1.12 in \cite{Zhu2005}

[Corollary cor:spectral-bound of arXiv:2606.14687, 'Lehner's operator norm formulas, semidefinite programming, and spiked matrix models'] In the above setting, suppose that there is $\bm S$ such that $\Phi(\bm S) = \lambda_{\max}(\Phi)\bm S$ and having $\bm S \succ \bm 0$.
    Then,
    \[ 2\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Phi)} \leq \Lambda_{\mathsf{sc}}(\bm 0, \bm A_1, \dots, \bm A_n) \leq \left(\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\min}(\bm S)}{\lambda_{\max}(\bm S)}} + \sqrt{\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\bm S)}{\lambda_{\min}(\bm S)}}\right) \sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Phi)}. \]
    Further, when $\Phi(\bm I_d) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \bm A_i^2 = C \bm I_d$ for some $C > 0$, then we may take $\bm S = \bm I_d$ above, in which case both inequalities above are equalities and we obtain the exact formula
    \[ \Lambda_{\mathsf{sc}}(\bm 0, \bm A_1, \dots, \bm A_n) = 2\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\Phi)} = 2\sigma. \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary cor:spectral-bound of arXiv:2606.14687

body:
[Theorem UniformFCLT-general of arXiv:2412.01635, 'On the Weak Convergence of the Function-Indexed Sequential Empirical Process and its Smoot'] (Asymptotic equicontinuity - general case)\\
Let $\nu > 2$ and let $\rho$ be a semimetric on $\mathcal F$. Assume the following conditions to hold: 	
\begin{enumerate}[ref = \arabic*]
\item  There exists $g: \mathbb N \times (0, \infty) \to \mathbb R$ such that for each $n \in \mathbb N$, $\delta > 0$, it holds 
\begin{equation}
\EOuter{ \norm{  S_{n,i,j} }_{\mathcal F_\delta}^\nu } \leq g^{\frac{\nu}{2}}(j-i+1, \delta), ~ \forall ~ 1 \leq i \leq j \leq n,
\end{equation}
and there is a universal index $Q_g \in [1,2^{1-2/\nu})$ such that for each $\delta > 0,$ the pair $(\nu/2, g(.,\delta))$ fulfills condition (equation MSS-ConditionM of the paper) with index $Q_g$. 

\item  There exists $h: \mathbb N \to \mathbb R$ such that for each $n \in \mathbb N$, it holds 
\begin{equation}
\EOuter{ \norm{ S_{n,i,j} }_{\mathcal F}^\nu } \leq h^{\frac{\nu}{2}}(j-i+1), ~ \forall ~ 1 \leq i \leq j \leq n,
\end{equation}
and the pair $(\nu/2, h)$ fulfills condition (equation MSS-ConditionM of the paper) with index $Q_h \in [1,2^{1-2/\nu})$.

\item  It holds $$\lim_{\delta \downarrow 0} \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{g(n,\delta)}{n} = 0.$$	

\item  There exists a constant $C_h \geq 0$ such that for each $0 < \varepsilon  \leq 1,$ it holds $$ \limsup_{n \to \infty}  \frac{h(\left\lfloor n \varepsilon \right\rfloor)}{n}  \leq C_h \varepsilon $$ (with the convention $h(0) = 0$). 
\end{enumerate}
Then (equation DEF:AEC of the paper) holds for $\tau((s,f),(t,g)) = |s-t| + \rho(f,g).$	If, in addition, $(\mathcal F, \rho)$ is totally bounded, then fidi-convergence of $\mathbb Z_n$ implies weak convergence in $\ell^{\infty}([0,1] \times \mathcal F)$.
title: Theorem UniformFCLT-general of arXiv:2412.01635

body: Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.30 is answered NO for every b >= 1. For each b >= 1 and s >= 2b there is a four-state reversible chain X = (Y, V), Y a slow two-state chain whose rare state carries g = b and V a fast sign, with relaxation time tau_2 = 1 and a standardized g with ||g||_inf = b, such that P_pi(S_s <= 0) >= 1 - 4/s. At t = s the Kolmogorov distance of the normalized additive functional from N(0,1) is at least 1/2 - 4/s under any normalization, so no bound psi(b, t/tau_2) -> 0 exists. The normalized sum does tend to 0 in probability; a rare excursion carries its second moment (W^2 is not uniformly integrable). This replaces the 8 Sep claim, which fixed ||g||_inf = 2 and said the normalized sum does not vanish in probability. Posted 13 Oct 2026 as github.com/yspennstate/relaxation-time-normal-approximation 40395f2; outside audit owed.

body: In differential geometry, a Riemannian manifold (or Riemann space) is a geometric space on which many geometric notions such as distance, angles, length, volume, and curvature are defined. Euclidean space, the $n$ -sphere, hyperbolic space, and smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space, such as ellipsoids and paraboloids, are all examples of Riemannian manifolds. Riemannian manifolds take their name from German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, who first conceptualized them in 1854.

[Lemma 174 of arXiv:2605.03236, 'Stochastic It\^o Equations and Parabolic Second-Order Equations with singular Drift'] Let $f(x,\eta)$ be infinitely differentiable and such that
each of its derivatives grows  as $|x|+|\eta|\to\infty$
not faster than polynomially. Let $T\in\bR$. Then

(i) for $t\leq T$, the function
$u(t,x,\eta):=Ef\big((x_{T-t},\eta_{T-t})(t,x,\eta)\big)$
is infinitely differentiable in $(x,\eta)$ and 
each of its derivatives   by absolute
value is bounded on each finite   interval in
$(-\infty,T]$
by a constant times $(1+|x|+|\eta|)^{m}$
for some $m$,

(ii) for each $x,\eta$ the function $u(t,x,\eta)$ is Lipschitz continuous with respect to $t\in[0,T]$, 

(iii) in $(0,T)\times \bR^{2d}$  (a.e.)
$\partial_{t}u(t,x,\eta)$ exists and
$$
0= \partial_{t}u(t,x,\eta)+ (1/2)\sigma^{ik}\sigma^{jk}(t,x)u_{x^{i}x^{j}} (t,x,\eta)
+\sigma^{ik}\sigma_{(\eta)}^{jk}(t,x)u_{x^{i}\eta^{j}} (t,x,\eta)
$$
$$
+(1/2)\sigma_{(\eta)}^{ik} \sigma_{(\eta)}^{jk}(t,x)u_{\eta^{i}\eta^{j}}(t,x,\eta)
+b^{i}(t,x)u_{x^{i}} (t,x,\eta)+b^{i}_{(\eta)}(t,x)u_{\eta^{i}} (t,x,\eta)
$$
\begin{equation}
                          
=:\partial_{t}u(t,x,\eta)+\check \cL(t,x,\eta)u(t,x,\eta).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In algebra, the Wedderburn–Artin theorem is a classification theorem for semisimple rings and semisimple algebras. The theorem states that a(n Artinian) semisimple ring R is isomorphic to the product of finitely many ni-by-ni matrix rings over division rings Di, for some integers ni, both of which are uniquely determined up to permutation of the index i. In particular, any simple left or right Artinian ring is isomorphic to an n-by-n matrix ring over a division ring D, where both n and D are uniquely determined.
title: Wedderburn–Artin theorem

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:1c7affc6c48a11197f6d4790152a6af74d0f0029fd0ceaba35ed8fd8e4bf2d24","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/1c/1c7affc6c48a11197f6d4790152a6af74d0f0029fd0ceaba35ed8fd8e4bf2d24.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:817059dacd03821a365ada579e6a9ad8ceec8af48438472ffcbbfe6e292cea82","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-nonlogarithmic-entrance-finitepart-coefficient","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-nonlogarithmic-entrance-finitepart-021","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks; diffusion weak approximation","draft":"w691/bundle_021.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-nonlogarithmic-entrance-finitepart-coefficient","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Nonlogarithmic critical-tanh correction by entrance matching

20 October 2026. Target3, kind moved. Proof draft, unaudited.
This identifies the coefficient left inside C053's O(1/L), not an
all-orders inverse-width expansion or a numerical rigorous error bound.

## Deterministic entrance constant (C055)

Put f(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, q0=K0>0, q_(r+1)=f(q_r), z_r=1/q_r.
There is a finite constant, depending on K0,

    C0(K0)=lim_(m->infinity) [z_m-2m+(5/6)log m].          (1)

Moreover the error in this limit is O_(K0)(log(m+1)/m).
This is the deterministic matching constant; a Gaussian quadrature
estimate of it is numerical evidence and is not an interval enclosure.

Proof. Tanh(x)^2<x^2 for x!=0, so 0<f(q)<q. Its iterates decrease
to zero (continuity and strict inequality exclude a positive limit).
Gaussian Taylor integration gives

    f(q)=q-2q^2+(17/3)q^3+O(q^4),
    z_(r+1)-z_r=2-5/(3z_r)+O(z_r^-2).                    (2)

Taylor remainder control follows from bounded derivatives of tanh and
finite Gaussian moments, splitting |sqrt(q)Z|<=1 and its Gaussian tail
if necessary. Initially (2) gives z_r/r->2 and then
z_r=2r+O(log(r+1)). For r>=1, the increment of
z_r-2r+(5/6)log r is therefore O(log(r+1)/r^2).
This is absolutely summable, with tail O(log(m+1)/m), proving (1).
There is no stochastic limit or width/depth interchange in this claim.

## Full first correction (C056)

Fix a finite c>0 and positive integer k. Use the exact chain

    K_(r+1)=n^-1 sum_i tanh(sqrt(K_r)Z_(r,i))^2,
    K0>0 fixed, 1<=L<=cn, t=L/n, Y=2L K_L.

The Gaussian rows/layers are independent, zero bias and weight variance
1/n. Let W^(t) start at zero and solve, on 0<=s<=1,

    dW=(2tW+2)ds+sqrt(2t)W dB_s.

Let P_s^t be this semigroup, f_j(w)=(2/w)^j, g_(j,s)=P_(1-s)^t f_j,
m_j(t)=E f_j(W_1), D_j(t)=g_(j,0)'(0)=-(j/2)J_j(t). Explicitly, with
one Brownian path B, put A_t=integral_0^1 exp(tr+sqrt(2t)B_r)dr and
H_t=exp(t+sqrt(2t)B_1). Then m_j(t)=E A_t^-j and
J_j(t)=E[H_t A_t^(-j-1)]. The endpoint factor and exponential
functional are coupled; fixed-time reversal preserves this joint law.
Write

    C^t=(2t^2 w-6t-5/(3w))D
         +(3t^2 w^2-2tw)D^2+(2/3)t^2 w^3 D^3,
    Phi_j(s,t)=E[(C^t g_(j,s))(W_s)],
    I_j(t)=integral_0^1 [Phi_j(s,t)+(5/6)D_j(t)/s] ds,
    R_j(t,K0)=D_j(t) C0(K0)+I_j(t).                       (3)

The integral in (3) is an ordinary absolutely convergent improper
integral of expectations; its displayed subtraction is essential.
For L->infinity, uniformly over integers n with L/n<=c,

    E Y^j=m_j(t)+(5j/12)J_j(t)log L/L
                         +R_j(t,K0)/L+o(1/L), 1<=j<=k.   (4)

Uniform here means there is a function eta_(k,K0,c)(L)->0 bounding
L times the absolute error. A computable numerical rate for eta is
not supplied. In particular (4) makes no claim of a uniform relative
error when L is fixed; C053 covers those finite-L endpoints with O(1/L).

For the moment-cumulant polynomial P_k, put

    R_k^cum(t,K0)=sum_(j=1)^k (partial_j P_k)(m(t)) R_j(t,K0).

Then the same replacement of moments gives

    kappa_k(Y)=F_k(t)+(5/12)G_k(t)log L/L
                               +R_k^cum(t,K0)/L+o(1/L). (5)

No second inverse-width order is asserted. At t=0, (3) reduces exactly
to R_j(0,K0)=-(j/2)C0(K0), as it must for the deterministic chain.

## Proof of matching, including the order of limits

We use C027's uniform positive K moments, C044's uniform inverse-sample
moments, C046's mesoscopic bound and C053's local weak-defect calculation.
C027 is reviewer checked; C044/C046/C053 remain unaudited dependencies.
The hardest step is the entrance overlap, proved explicitly below.

First fix an integer m>=1. The first m chain steps converge in every
fixed inverse/positive moment to the deterministic q_m as n->infinity.
This follows by conditional sample-mean concentration and C044; for
each fixed layer the deterministic q_r is strictly positive, so there
is no inverse singularity at its limit. Taylor expanding the smooth
backward test at (s,w)=(0,0) consequently gives

    L{E g_(j,m/L)(1/(LK_m))-g_(j,0)(0)}
          =D_j(t)(z_m-2m)+o(1),                          (6)

uniformly t<=c, for fixed m. The time derivative at the origin is
-2D_j, by the backward equation, and W0=1/(LK0) is already included
through z_m; adding a second initial-state correction would double-count it.

Telescope from step m onwards. The local operator in C053 and its
remainder bound, divided by 1/L, give

    L{E f_j(W_L)-E g_(j,m/L)(W_m)}
       = L^-1 sum_(r=m)^(L-1)
                     E[(C^t g_(j,(r+1)/L))(W_r)] + e_(m,L),
    limsup_(L->infinity) sup_(n>=L/c) |e_(m,L)| <= C/m.   (7)

Indeed the worst term is sum_(r>=m) E K_r^2<=C/m. The other early
remainders are bounded after this scaling by O(log L/L)+O(L^-1/2).
The late remainders use the terminal inverse-power bounds in C053.
For q>eta (a fixed small activation-variance cutoff), do not Taylor
expand: the scaled total error after m is at most
C sum_(r>=m)P(K_r>eta)<=C/m. On such a step, the exact reciprocal
mean is O(1/L) and the bounded early backward test has bounded derivative;
the singular defect is at most C K_r/L before scaling. Since K_r<=Q,
the same probability estimate controls it. Thus no rare large-q
entrance visit is omitted in (7).

For late large-q visits, (7) needs a sharper version of C053's O(1/L)
bound, rather than reusing that bound unchanged. On s>=1/2,
`1_(q>eta)<= (1/(eta L W_r))^p` for arbitrary p. Exact and reference
tests are bounded in conditional expectation by C W_r^-j, using C044;
all required inverse powers of W_r have uniformly bounded means by
C027. Taking p>=4 makes the total of these late bad-set defects,
after multiplication by L, O(L^(2-p))=o(1). Terms from the explicitly
subtracted defect have extra L^-2 and are smaller, increasing the
moment order if necessary. Thus late large-q visits do not leave an
unidentified order1/L contribution in the matching formula.

We can replace g_((r+1)/L) by g_(r/L) in (7): the early difference
is O(log L/L), and late moment bounds give O(1/L).

Next fix 0<delta<1/2. On [delta,1], convergence of the rescaled chain
to W^t and the same moment bounds imply convergence of the sum in
(7) to integral_delta^1 Phi_j(s,t) ds. The inverse powers at the
terminal test are uniformly integrable by C027 at arbitrarily high
orders. For t converging to a positive value use C026 and its linear
SDE; for t->0 use C046 and the reciprocal martingale estimates
to obtain the deterministic path 2s on [delta,1]. Thus the conclusion
is uniform over 0<=t<=c by the compact-parameter subsequence argument.
Truncate the integrand and its inverse powers first, use path convergence,
then remove truncation by the high moment bounds. This also justifies
Riemann integration of the terminal test and time-dependent derivatives.

Here is the explicit overlap estimate. C046 gives, simultaneously for
m<=r<=delta L,

    sum |E K_r-1/(2r)| <= C(m^-1/2+sqrt(delta)).          (8)

The smooth early backward test satisfies
|g_s'(w)-D_j(t)|<=C(s+w); since K_r W_r=1/L,

    sum_(r=m)^(floor(delta L))
       E[K_r |g_(r/L)'(W_r)-D_j(t)|] <= C delta.        (9)

All nonsingular parts of C^t in this overlap contribute O(delta)
to the scaled defect sum. Combining (8)-(9), its singular part is

    -(5/6)D_j(t) sum_(r=m)^(floor(delta L)) 1/r
          +O(m^-1/2+sqrt(delta)).                       (10)

For the reference diffusion, W_s=2s+O_in_Lp(s^(3/2)) as s->0,
and its inverse moments of order p are O(s^-p), uniformly t<=c,
by the explicit affine solution. Hence
|E(1/W_s)-1/(2s)|<=C s^-1/2: apply Cauchy-Schwarz to
(W_s-2s)/(2s W_s). The same derivative estimate as (9) gives

    Phi_j(s,t)=-(5/6)D_j(t)/s+O(s^-1/2+1).             (11)

This proves absolute integrability in (3). Its finite part over
[0,delta] is O(sqrt(delta)), uniformly t<=c.

Now let L,n->infinity with L/n<=c, keeping m and delta fixed.
Combine (6)-(11), using

    sum_(r=m)^(floor(delta L)) 1/r
          =log L+log delta-H_(m-1)+gamma+o(1).

Then let delta decrease to zero, and only afterwards m increase to
infinity. Since H_(m-1)=log m+gamma+O(1/m), the entrance term is

    D_j(t)[z_m-2m+(5/6)log m] -> D_j(t)C0(K0).

The total remaining overlap error is bounded by
C(m^-1/2+sqrt(delta))+o(1). This establishes (4) and identifies exactly
where both auxiliary cutoffs are removed. The order can equivalently
be recorded as: width/depth joint limit first; continuum overlap cutoff
second; fixed-layer matching cutoff last.

Finally polynomial conversion to cumulants has quadratic error
O(log(L)^2/L^2)=o(1/L), uniformly over the compact t-range, giving (5).

## Reciprocal-mean closed form: a useful independent check

For the linear test f(w)=w the same argument applies, using the
positive reciprocal moments from C045/C046 in place of inverse powers.
Its initial derivative is D=e^(2t), and E W_s=(e^(2ts)-1)/t.
Writing m1(r)=E A_r^-1 gives

    R_w(t,K0)=e^(2t) [ C0(K0)+2t-4(1-e^(-2t))
          -(5/6)integral_0^t [e^(-2r)m1(r)-1]/r dr ].     (12)

At t=0 the integral is zero by continuity and R_w(0)=C0.
Since V=1/(nK)=tW, at L/n=t>0 its nonlogarithmic1/n coefficient is

    c_V(t)=R_w(t,K0)-(5/6)e^(2t)log t,                  (13)

where the logarithmic term is -(5/6)e^(2t)log n/n.
This refines C047 without conflating log L with log n.

These coefficient formulas use the actual ratio t=L/n. If the network
is sampled at L=floor(nt0) for a fixed real t0>0, evaluate (4)-(13) at
t_n=L/n. If the reciprocal leading term is instead written e^(2t0)-1,
its order1/n coefficient includes the lattice correction
`-2e^(2t0)*{nt0}` in addition to c_V(t0). Thus there need not be a
single n-independent coefficient at a fixed nonlattice observation
time unless this fractional-part term is retained. No such correction
is needed in the measured runs L=n.

As an independent check on the nonsingular part of (12), the exact
chi-square control variate below has a_n=n/(n-2) and its small-q mean
innovation begins `2n/[L(n+2)]`. Summing this constant innovation gives
`(n/L)(n-2)/(n+2) * (a_n^L-1)`. Its expansion contributes
`2t e^(2t)-4(e^(2t)-1)` to the order1/L coefficient, exactly the
nonsingular part `e^(2t)[2t-4(1-e^(-2t))]` in (12).
Here the innovation mean uses the exact Gaussian-sphere identity
`E[(n^-1 sum Z_i^4)/(n^-1 sum Z_i^2)^2]=3n/(n+2)`.

The formulas and checks are draft mathematics, not independent audit.
Any Monte Carlo comparison below is numerical evidence only; Gaussian
quadrature and discretized Brownian integrals supply no rigorous bound.

## Exact-mean control variate for the numerical reciprocal check

For each actual network row let M_r=n^-1 sum_i Z_(r,i)^2, using the
SAME Z row as tanh. Conditionally on the history, nM_r is chi-square_n
and E M_r^-1=n/(n-2)=a_n, for n>2. Put

    Delta_r = W_(r+1)-W_r/M_r,
    Z_control = a_n^L W0 + sum_(r=0)^(L-1) a_n^(L-1-r) Delta_r.

Exact telescoping and conditioning give E Z_control=E W_L: the removed
sum consists of martingale differences
`a_n^(L-1-r) W_r(M_r^-1-a_n)`.
All the inverse moments needed are finite for the simulation widths by
C044 and the chi-square moment identity. Independence is only between
the new row and the past; W_(r+1) and M_r are coupled, not independent.
This estimator does not use any discretized diffusion reference. It
therefore distinguishes a source-coefficient error from Brownian mesh
bias, with smaller sampling variance. Its numerical output still has

 	$t\ge i+t_*$, $i\in[0,i_\dagger)$ and $X^-(t)-R\le x\le X^+(t)+R$
 	be  respectively a  super- and  a subsolution of \eqref{moving frame-nonlinear} for $t\ge i+i_\dagger+t_*$, $i\in[0,i_\dagger)$ and $x\in[X^-(t), X^+(t-i)]$, in the sense of Definition \ref{Def_super+sub}.
 	Assume that $\overline v(t,0,x)\ge \underline v(t,0,x)$ for $t\in [ t_*,i_\dagger+t_*]$ and $x\in[X^-(t), X^+(t)]$, and that  $\overline v(t,i,x)\ge\underline v(t,i,x)$ for $t\ge i+t_*$, $i\in[0,i_\dagger)$ and $x\in[X^-(t)-R,X^-(t)]\cup[X^+(t-i),X^+(t)+R]$,  then $\overline v(t,i,x)\ge \underline v(t,i,x)$  for $t\ge i+i_\dagger+t_*$, $i\in[0,i_\dagger)$ and $x\in[X^-(t), X^+(t-i)]$. body:
[Lem 128 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $\tep\ll\lambda\ll 1$, and let $J=J(p,2\tep,\lambda/2)$ as defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. Then there exists a set $\oJ$ such that
$J\subseteq \oJ\subseteq [q_0,1]$,
and $\oJ$ can be expressed as the (not necessarily disjoint) union of at most $L^{O(1)}/\lambda$ open intervals each of width $10\tep$. 
In particular, $\oJ$ has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure
	\[\mu_{\textup{Leb}}(\oJ)
	\leq \frac{L^{O(1)}\tep}{\lambda}
	\ll 1\,.\]

\begin{proof}
Subdivide $[q_0,1]$ into intervals of width $2\tep$. (If $(1-q_0)/(2\tep)$ is not integer-valued, then simply let the last interval have width less than $2\tep$.) For the purposes of this proof let us say an interval is ``bad'' if $p'$ decreases  by more than $\lambda/8$ over the interval; otherwise we say the interval is ``good.'' Since $p'$ is monotone and assumed bounded by $L^{O(1)}$, the total number of bad intervals is at most $L^{O(1)}/\lambda$. Let $B\subseteq[0,1]$ be the union of all the bad intervals, and let $\oJ$ be the $(4\tep)$-neighborhood of $B$. We then claim that $J\subseteq\oJ$: to see this, note that if $x\in \oJ^c$, then the interval $[x-2\tep,x+2\tep]$ is disjoint from the bad intervals $B$, and is covered by at most three good intervals. It follows that $p'$ decreases by at most $3\lambda/8$ over the interval $[x-2\tep,x+2\tep]$, which means $x\in J^c$. This implies the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 93 of arXiv:2608.28200, '\textbf On the Formality of Configuration Spaces of $\aka$'] There exists a quasi-isomorphism of $\Z$-graded CDGAs
$$
\bar \I: \cD(A) \slra \ConfSpaceCohomology
$$
characterized by the relations
$$
\begin{cases}
\bar \I (\VertexDiagram) = p_a^*W & \text{ for $a\in A$} \\
\bar \I (\chorddiagram) = (p_{ab}^*W)\omega_{ab} & \text{ for $a,b$ distinct in $A$} \\
\bar \I (\Gamma)= 0 & \text{for $\Gamma$ with internal vertices}
\end{cases}.
$$

[Theorem thm1 of arXiv:2412.09471, 'On the moderate deviation principles in the sparse multi-type Erd\H{o}s R\'enyi random gra'] Under Assumption (assump1 of the paper), when  the random graph $G_n$ is super-critical $(\Sigma(\kappa,\mu)>1)$, for any sequence $(a_n)$ such that $n^{1/4}\ll a_n\ll \sqrt{n}$ and $|\mu^n-\mu|=O(\frac{1}n)$,  the sequence of random vectors
\[
\frac{1}{a_n\sqrt{n}}\left(\mathcal{C}_{\rm max}^n-(\mu-c)n\right)
\]
satisfies the moderate deviation principle in ${\mathbb R}^d$ with speed $a_n^2$ and the rate function
\[
\mathcal{I}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\left(I-D_c\kappa\right)x,D_v\left(I-D_c\kappa\right)x\right\rangle,
\]
where $D_v$ is the diagonal matrix with the vector
\[
v=\left(\frac{\mu_i}{c_i(\mu_i-c_i)},i\in\mathcal{S}\right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.02699, '\vspace{-0.5 cm}Gauge theory and symplectic structures'] For every even integer $p>0$ and every odd integer $q$ such that
$
|p-q|=1,
$
the degreewise coefficients $H_p$ and $G_q$ satisfy
\[
\mathrm{Re}\left(H_p^{-1}G_q^{-1}\right)>0
\]
Moreover, since there are only finitely many adjacent degree pairs, there is a constant $\kappa_+>0$, depending only on the dimension, such that
\[
\mathrm{Re}\left(H_p^{-1}G_q^{-1}\right)
\geq \kappa_+
\]
for every such pair $(p,q)$.

body:
A SUBADDITIVE PROCESS is a family {X_{m,n} : 0 <= m < n} of integrable random variables satisfying: (K1) X_{0,n} <= X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} for every 0 < m < n; (K2) the joint distributions of the shifted family {X_{m+1,n+1}} are the same as those of {X_{m,n}} - full joint stationarity of the array under the index shift; (K3) E[X_{0,1}] is finite and E[X_{0,n}] >= -c n for every n, for some constant c. Then gamma = lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n exists and is finite, X = lim_n X_{0,n}/n exists almost surely and in L^1 with E[X] = gamma, and if the underlying shift is ERGODIC then X = gamma almost surely. (K3) is what stops the limit from being minus infinity; without the lower linear bound the almost sure limit can be -infinity. (K2) is a strong hypothesis and is exactly what Liggett's version weakens. For i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d the array X_{m,n} = T(m e_1, n e_1) satisfies (K2) directly, because the whole environment is i.i.d. and the shift by e_1 is measure preserving and ergodic; that is why Kingman's original form already delivers the time constant along a coordinate axis. [Kingman (1968), 'The ergodic theory of subadditive stochastic processes', J. Roy. Statist. Soc. B 30]
(K1) subadditivity of the array
(K2) the joint law of the array is invariant under the index shift
(K3) E[X_{0,1}] finite and E[X_{0,n}] >= -cn
ergodicity is needed only for the conclusion that the limit is a constant

Subadditivity chains the block bounds, giving X_{0,n} <= sum over good blocks of (X + eps) times the block length, plus sum over bad steps of X_{j,j+1}, plus a boundary term of at most K steps. Dividing by n and applying Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem to the indicator of the bad set and to the integrable X_{0,1} shows the bad contribution is small, so limsup X_{0,n}/n <= X + eps + (small). Letting eps -> 0 gives limsup <= liminf, hence almost sure convergence. The L^1 convergence follows from uniform integrability of X_{0,n}/n, which is supplied by (K3) together with (K1). body:
Let X >= 0 be a random variable and B an event with q = P(B) > 0, a = E[X 1_B] > 0 and b = E[X^2 1_B] < infinity, and let 0 <= theta <= 1. Then P(X > theta E[X|B] | B) >= (1 - theta)^2 E[X|B]^2 / E[X^2|B], equivalently P(B and X > theta E[X|B]) >= (1 - theta)^2 a^2/b. Applying Paley-Zygmund to X 1_B instead gives P(B and X > theta a) >= (1 - theta)^2 a^2/b. Since E[X|B] = a/q >= a, the conditional form controls the higher threshold with the same right side. The bound is positive for theta < 1; at theta = 1 it is 0 and says nothing, and if E[X|B] = 0 no ratio is defined.
X >= 0
P(B) > 0, E[X 1_B] > 0, E[X^2 1_B] finite
0 <= theta <= 1

AUTHOR-CHECKED CONSEQUENCE; NO NOVELTY CLAIM. Let P be an irreducible transition matrix on a finite state space with stationary probability pi. On the real mean-zero Hilbert space L^2_0(pi), let P* be its adjoint and Z=(I-P)^(-1), extended as zero on constant functions. Then tr[Z^2(P*-P)] >= 0, with equality if and only if P=P* (the chain is reversible). More explicitly, write A=I-P=H+K, H=(A+A*)/2 positive definite, K=(A-A*)/2 skew adjoint, Q=H^(-1/2) K H^(-1/2), and B=Q*Q=-Q^2. The trace equals 4 tr[H^(-1) B (I+B)^(-2)]. This remains valid for periodic chains; Z is the centered inverse, rather than an unqualified convergent power series. The held source gives a direct matrix proof and describes a consequence of established variance-comparison work; external attribution and novelty are not newly certified.

{"claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_006.json","logical_id":"math:probability.markov:known-antisymmetric-perturbation-reversibilization-trace-monotonicity","overlay_schema_version":1,"packet_origin":{"audit_file":"urn:mb-local:701908c65a2119f8","position":37,"quote_kind":"held_author_proof","scope":"Full statement repaired against held source and independently checked mathematics","source_path":"urn:mb-local:c72fabf6859df4b2","source_sha256":"56bc58d488ba1ccf2187de2b19af6ca2fcf53005f6230af27d285825d9862c76"},"proof_status":"reviewed_text_not_formally_verified","proof_text":"# P0249: reversibilization trace inequality ? known-result consequence

Status: author-checked complete argument for a historical conjecture. A later primary theorem implies the result, so this entry is excluded from the current-open target and original-solution count. The direct matrix proof is not independently reviewed here.

Source question: Aldous?Fill, Conjecture 9.22, PDF pages 327?329, asks whether $\operatorname{tr}[Z^2(P^*-P)]\ge0$. Here $P$ is an irreducible finite-state transition matrix, $P^*$ its adjoint in $L^2(\pi)$, and $Z$ the centered fundamental matrix. The centered convention is $Z1=0$ and $Z=(I-P)^{-1}$ on $L^2_0(\pi)$. Adding the constant projection to $Z$ would not change the displayed product.

## Direct matrix proof

Restrict all operators to the finite-dimensional real Hilbert space $L^2_0(\pi)$. Put

$$A=I-P=H+K,\quad H=\frac{A+A^*}{2},\quad K=\frac{A-A^*}{2}.$$

The reversible Dirichlet form shows $H$ is positive definite: its only zero-energy functions on the full space are constants, because the underlying undirected chain is connected. Also $K^*=-K$ and $P^*-P=2K$.

Let $Q=H^{-1/2}KH^{-1/2}$, $B=-Q^2=Q^*Q\succeq0$, and define $F(t)=\operatorname{tr}(H+tK)^{-1}$ for real $t$. All these inverses exist since their symmetric part is positive definite. Using transpose invariance of trace and averaging the inverses with $t$ and $-t$ gives

$$F(t)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}(I+t^2B)^{-1}\right].$$

Indeed $(I+tQ)^{-1}+(I-tQ)^{-1}=2(I-t^2Q^2)^{-1}$. Differentiate the last trace formula:

$$F'(t)=-2t\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}B(I+t^2B)^{-2}\right]\le0\qquad(t\ge0).$$

The product inside the trace need not be symmetric. Its trace is nonnegative because $C=B(I+t^2B)^{-2}$ is positive semidefinite and $\operatorname{tr}(H^{-1}C)=\operatorname{tr}(C^{1/2}H^{-1}C^{1/2})\ge0$. This explicitly avoids an invalid commuting assumption.

Differentiating the original inverse instead gives $F'(1)=-\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}KA^{-1})=-\operatorname{tr}(A^{-2}K)$. Consequently

$$\operatorname{tr}[Z^2(P^*-P)]=-2F'(1)=4\operatorname{tr}\!\left[H^{-1}B(I+B)^{-2}\right]\ge0.$$

In fact equality holds if and only if $B=0$, equivalently $K=0$, equivalently the original chain is reversible. This follows from positive definiteness of $H^{-1}$ and the fact that the positive eigenvalues of $B$ remain positive under $b\mapsto b/(1+b)^2$.

## Independent route through established literature

Huang and Mao, *Variational formulas of asymptotic variance for general discrete-time Markov chains*, arXiv:2012.13895 (December 27, 2020), Theorem 4.3 on PDF page 14, proves that the asymptotic variance for a reversible kernel plus an antisymmetric perturbation is even in the perturbation parameter and decreases with its absolute value. Primary source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.13895 . This is a stronger observable-by-observable statement than the required trace monotonicity.

For finite irreducible chains, first add one-half holding: $R=(I+P)/2$. Every convex mixture of $R$ and $R^*$ is irreducible and aperiodic, so the theorem's spectral-radius assumption on the mean-zero space is satisfied. Apply it to $R_t=(R+R^*)/2+t(R-R^*)/2$, for $-1\le t\le1$.

For an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $L^2_0(\pi)$, the Poisson-equation formula reads

$$\sum_j\widetilde\sigma^2(R_t,e_j)=2\operatorname{tr}(I-R_t)^{-1}-(n-1).$$

Theorem 4.3 therefore gives the same trace monotonicity. Differentiate from the left at $t=1$; analyticity identifies this with the full derivative and yields the conjectured inequality for $R$. Since $Z_R=2Z_P$ and $R^*-R=(P^*-P)/2$, its trace expression is twice that for $P$. The conclusion follows even if $P$ is periodic. The original series definition of $Z$ in the periodic case is interpreted through the centered inverse or Abel limit.

The source does not explicitly name Aldous?Fill Conjecture 9.22 in the checked passage. The implication just proved is the reason for exclusion; no claim of a new resolution is made. [Prop 29 (Purple overlap) of arXiv:2608.26259, 'Cutoff with an $O(1)$ window for Potts Glauber Dynamics\\on lattice at High Temperature'] After decreasing \(\beta_0(d,q)\) if necessary, there exists
\(C<\infty\) such that, at \(T=t_\star+s\), locally uniformly for
\(s\ge0\),
\[
        \mathbb E\left[
        q^{|V_{\mathrm{P}}^{(1)}\cap V_{\mathrm{P}}^{(2)}|}-1
        \right]
        \le
        C|\Lambda|R^{2d}e^{-4(1-m) T}.
\]
Consequently, after decreasing \(\beta_0(d,q)\) so that
\(2(1-m)>1+\kappa\),
\[
        \mathbb E\left[
        q^{|V_{\mathrm{P}}^{(1)}\cap V_{\mathrm{P}}^{(2)}|}-1
        \right]
        =
        o\left(e^{-2(1+\kappa) s}\right)
\]
as \(|\Lambda|\to\infty\), locally uniformly for \(s\ge0\).

[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.25829, 'Topology of low-dimensional generalized Ricci solitons and string backgrounds'] Let $(M^{2n},g, J)$ be a compact BHE with $\pi_1(M)$ free abelian.  Then $M$ is spin.

\begin{proof}
    Since $\pi_1(M)$ is free abelian it follows that $H_1(M)$ is torsion-free, thus the universal coefficient theorem gives $H^2(M) \cong
\operatorname{Hom}\!\left(H_2(M),\mathbb Z\right)$, hence $H^2(M)$ is torsion-free.  Since $M$ is BHE we have $c_1(M; \mathbb R) = 0$, hence $c_1(M; \mathbb Z)=0$.  Since $M$ is complex, $w_2(M)\equiv c_1(M)$ mod $2$, thus $w_2(M) = 0$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition 17 (Eigenvector master equation — Wishart case) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Fix integers $N, T \ge 1$, and let $\{\lambda_i^{(N)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ 
denote the (ordered, positive) eigenvalues of the Wishart matrix 
\(
W^{(N)} := X_{N}^{\!\top} X_{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
\)
Let $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{(N)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ be the associated orthonormal eigenvectors. 
Consider the rank–one extension
\[
X_{N+1} = \big( X_N \;\; g \big),
\qquad g \in \mathbb{R}^{T},
\]
that is, $X_{N+1}$ is obtained by appending the column vector $g$ to $X_N$.
Let $W^{(N+1)} = X_{N+1}^{\!\top} X_{N+1}$, with eigenvalues 
$\{\lambda_i^{(N+1)}\}_{i=1}^{N+1}$ and eigenvectors $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{(N+1)}\}$.
We define
\(
g_i^{(N)} \;=\; \langle v_i^{(N)},\, g \rangle,
\)
where $v_i^{(N)}$ denotes the eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue 
$\lambda_i^{(N)}$ of the matrix $X_N X_N^{\!\top}$.

\smallskip
\noindent
Then the overlap coefficients
\(
\Omega^{(N)}_{ij} := 
\big\langle \mathbf{u}_i^{(N+1)},\, \mathbf{u}_j^{(N)} \big\rangle
\)
satisfy the relation
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Omega^{(N)}_{k j}}{\Omega^{(N)}_{k i}} 
&= 
\frac{g_j^{(N)}}{g_i^{(N)}}
\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_j^{(N)}}{\lambda_i^{(N)}}}
\frac{\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)}}{\Delta_{k,j}^{(N)}},
\qquad 1 \le i,j \le N, \qquad
\frac{\Omega^{(N)}_{k,\,N+1}}{\Omega^{(N)}_{k i}} 
&= 
\frac{\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)}}{g_i^{(N)}}
\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda_i^{(N)}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where
\(
\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)} := \lambda_k^{(N+1)} - \lambda_i^{(N)}.
\)

in $\{1, \dots,t\}$ that is independent of the shuffles $\{\pi_i : i \geq 0\}$. For distinct cards $x, y$ and $z$,
let $T_{xyz}$ be the time of the first
$3$-collision  in the time interval $\{T, \dots, t\}$
that involves either $x, y$ or $z$ (with $T_{xyz}$ undefined if no such collision occurs).
If the collision at time $T_{xyz}$ is a collision of $x, y$ and $z$
then we say that that collision matches $x$ with $y$ and $z$
and define $y$ to be the front match of $x$, written as $M_1(x) = y$, and $z$ to be the back match
of $x$,
written $M_2(x) = z$. Otherwise, define $M_1(x) = M_2(x) = x$. 

Suppose that for every card $k$ wtih $3 \leq k \leq n$ there is a constant
$A_k$ with  $0 \leq A_k \leq 1$
such that 
${ \mathbb P}(M_2(k)=j, M_1(k) < k) \geq \frac{A_k}{k}$ for each $j \in \{1, \dots, k-1\}$.

Let $\mu$ be an arbitrary random permutation that is independent of $\{\pi_i: i \geq 0\}$. Then

\begin{align}
  \nonumber
{\mathbf E}({\rm ENT}(\mu\pi_{(t)}|{\operatorname{sgn}}(\mu\pi_{(t)}))) - {\mathbf E}({\rm ENT}((\mu|{\operatorname{sgn}}(\mu)))) \leq \frac{-C}{\log n} \sum_{k=1}^{n}A_kE_k,

[Lemma lem:angular-moments-comp of arXiv:2609.00698, 'Kinetic Wedge Layers and Diffusive Limit of Neutron Transport in Polygonal Domains'] Let $\phi$ be a smooth scalar function on $\Omega$ and let $q\geq0$ be an integer. Then the angular moments of the directional derivatives of $\phi$ satisfy, pointwise in $\Omega$,
\begin{align}
 \mathbf P\bigl((w\cdot\nabla)^{2q+1}\phi\bigr)
 &=0,
 \\
 \mathbf P\bigl((w\cdot\nabla)^{2q}\phi\bigr)
 &=c_q\Delta^q\phi,
 \qquad
 c_q=\frac{(2q)!}{2^{2q}(q!)^2}.
 
\end{align}
Let now $k\geq0$, let $\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_k$ be smooth and harmonic in $\Omega$, and let $U_0:=\rho_0$ while $U_\ell$ is defined recursively by (equation eq:interior-recursion-comp of the paper) for $1\leq\ell\leq k$. Then the profiles are given explicitly by a finite alternating sum of derivatives of the densities, and their velocity averages obey the solvability identities:
\begin{align}
 U_\ell
 &=
 \sum_{j=0}^{\ell}
 (-1)^j(w\cdot\nabla)^j\rho_{\ell-j},
 \qquad 0\leq\ell\leq k,
 \\
 \pkU_\ell
 &=
 \rho_\ell,
 \qquad
 \mathbf P(w\cdot\nablaU_\ell)=0,
 \qquad 0\leq\ell\leq k.
 
\end{align}
Therefore, the recursively defined profiles satisfy (equation eq:interior-coefficient-equations-comp of the paper), and $\mathbf P(w\cdot\nablaU_k)=0$ is the compatibility condition needed to continue the construction to order $k+1$. Only $\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_{k-1}$ are required to be harmonic for these identities at order $k$, which is the precise sense in which harmonicity is the solvability condition of the next order rather than an ansatz.

[Theorem t:hg of arXiv:2606.11503, 'Percolation on hierarchical lattices'] Let $U, \tilde{U} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ be open sets and consider a diffeomorphism $f:U \to \tilde{U}$. Assume there exists $u_{*} \in U$ such that $f(u_{*}) = u_{*}$ and that the Jacobian matrix $Df(u^{*})$ has no eigenvalue with absolute value one. Then there exist an open neighborhood $V \subset U$ of $u_{*}$, an open neighborhood $\tilde{V} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ of the origin, and a homeomorphism $h: V \to W$ such that $h(u^{*}) = 0$ and
\begin{equation}
f(x) = h^{-1}\Big( Df(u_{*}) h(x) \Big), \qquad \text{for all } x \in V.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, let $\mu$ be its 
Haar probability measure and $Y$ be a random variable on $G$ with density $f_Y \in L^2(G)$. Let $S$ be a set of positive Haar measure and 
write $g_S = \frac{1}{\mu(S)}\mathbb{I}_S$ for the density of the 
random variable $U_S$ having the uniform distribution on $S$ and 
being independent of $Y$. Then,
\begin{equation} 
    \int_{G}(f_Y\ast g_S(x) - 1)^2\, dx \leq \eta_S\int_{G}(f_Y(x)-1)^2\, dx,
\end{equation}
where,
$$\eta_S = \left(\frac{\sin(\pi \mu(S))}{\pi \mu(S)}\right)^2.$$
Equivalently, 
\begin{equation} 
\chi^2(Y+U_S\,\|\,U_{G}) = \chi^2(Y+U_S\,\|\,U_{G} +  U_S)
\le
\eta_S\,\chi^2(Y\,\|\,U_{G}),
\end{equation}
where
$U_{G}$ is uniformly distributed on $G$ and independent of $U_S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.22534

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2607.19873, 'Local limit theorem for the operator norm of products of random matrices'] Assume that $\Gamma_{\mu}$ is strongly irreducible 
and that the image of $\Gamma_{\mu}$ in the projective linear group 
${\rm PGL}(V)$ is not contained in any compact subgroup of ${\rm PGL}(V)$. 
Assume also that $\mu$ admits a finite exponential moment \eqref{Exponential-moment}. 
Then, for any norm $\| \cdot \|$ on $\End (V)$ and any real numbers $a < b$, we have 
\begin{align}
\upsilon_{\mu} \sqrt{2 \pi n} \,  \bb P  \left( \log \|g_n \cdots g_1 \| - n \lambda_{\mu} \in [a, b] \right)
\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}  b-a. 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 (Information descent compatibility) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $R^{\rm raw}:\mathsf U_0\to\mathsf Y$ be a primitive response.  If
$\mathsf Y$ has truncations $\rho_t^{\mathsf Y}$, then $R^{\rm raw}$ is
\emph{$\mathbb I$-compatible} if
\[
 u\sim_{\mathbb I,t}v
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \rho_t^{\mathsf Y}R^{\rm raw}(u)
 =\rho_t^{\mathsf Y}R^{\rm raw}(v)
\]
for every $t$.  For a terminal response the condition is imposed at $T$.  A
constructor is compatible when its output is independent of all information
representatives at the relevant times, and the program is compatible when every
primitive response and declared constructor is compatible.  For a compatible
primitive response, write $R^{\mathbb I}$ for its unique factor through the
global information quotient $q_{\mathbb I}$.
title: Information descent compatibility

[Lemma l.smallkappa.phi of arXiv:2510.07682, 'From tug-of-war to Brownian Boost: \\ explicit ODE solutions for player-funded stochastic-'] Let $(\rho,\beta) \in (0,\infty)^2$ and suppose that $\kappa > 0$ is less than $\min \big\{ \rho^{-2} , (1+\rho)^{-1}/2  \big\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
We have that
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \phi_0(\kappa,\rho,\beta) &= & \beta \;+\; 
     \frac{4\rho\,\beta^{1+\rho}}{(1+\beta^\rho)^2}\,\kappa \;+\; \beta \, \Theta_1(\kappa,\rho,\beta) \kappa^2   \qquad \textrm{and} \\
  \phi_1(\kappa,\rho,\beta) &= & \beta \;-\; 
     \frac{4\rho\,\beta^{1+\rho}}{(1+\beta^\rho)^2}\,\kappa \;+\; \beta \, \Theta_2(\kappa,\rho,\beta) \kappa^2 \, ,
\end{eqnarray*}
where  $\vert \Theta_i(\kappa,\rho,\beta) \vert \, \leq \, 2\rho(1+\rho)$ for $i \in \{1,2\}$.
\item 

We also have that
$$
 s(x) \, = \, x - \frac{8\rho\, x^{1+\rho}}{(1+x^\rho)^2}\,\kappa  \, + \,  x \,  \Theta_3(\kappa,\rho,x) \kappa^2 
$$
with $\vert \Theta_3(\kappa,\rho,x) \vert \leq 52 \rho (1+\rho)^3$. 
\end{enumerate}
Now suppose only that $(\rho,\beta) \in (0,\infty)^2$. 
\begin{enumerate}
    \setcounter{enumi}{2} 
\item For $\xi \in (0,\infty)$ and $\kappa > 0$,
\[
 S_\rho(\xi,\kappa) \,=\, \xi - \frac{8\rho\,\xi^{1+\rho}}{(1+\xi^\rho)^2}\,\kappa \,+\, \xi\,\Theta_4(\kappa,\rho,\xi)\,\kappa^2
\]
with $\vert \Theta_4(\kappa,\rho,\xi)\vert \leq 64 \rho^2 (1+\rho)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma l.smallkappa.phi of arXiv:2510.07682

[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:lacunary}, for sufficiently large $R$ we have
$$
 |\{g\in \mathfrak{B}_n :   0 \notin H(g\lambda_R)\}| =
 2 \sum_{k=1}^n \left( \stirling{n}{k} 2^{n-k} \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{k-1}{j}\right),
$$
where $\stirling{n}{k}$ are the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind defined by the generating function $\sum_{k=0}^n \stirling{n}{k}\, t^k = t(t+1)\cdots(t+n-1)$.
title: Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.16752

[De 3 of arXiv:2607.28078, '2607.28078'] Fix an atomless probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ rich enough to support a random variable with any prescribed
law in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$. A function
$u:\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)\to\mathbb R$ is said to be {\it L-differentiable} at $\mu_0\in\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ if there exists a random variable $X_0$ with law $\mu_0$ such that the lifted function $\tilde{u}$ is Fr\'{e}chet differentiable at $X_0$. The lift of the function $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d)\ni\mu\mapsto u(\mu)$ is the function $\tilde{u}$ defined on the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P};\mathbb{R}^d)$ by $\tilde{u}(X):=u(\mathcal{L}_X)$.
title: Definition 3 of arXiv:2607.28078

[Lemma lem:exp_count of arXiv:2509.15446, 'On the pair correlation function of the $\Sineb$ process'] Suppose that $g : {\mathbb R}\mapsto {\mathbb R}$ is a continuous, strictly increasing deterministic function with $g(0)=0$. Fix $\delta>0$, and let  $\Theta\in[0,2\pi)$ be a random variable with density  (equation eq:Theta of the paper). Consider the process
\[
\Xi=\{\lambda\in {\mathbb R}: g(\lambda)=\Theta \mod 2\pi\}.
\]
Then for $\lambda>0$ the expected number of points of $\Xi$ in $[0,\lambda]$ is given by 
\begin{align}
E[\Xi[0,\lambda]]&=\frac{g(\lambda)}{2\pi}+\frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{k=1}^\infty  \frac{(-\delta)^{\uparrow k}}{(1+ \delta)^{\uparrow k}}\frac{\sin( k g(\lambda))}{k}.
\end{align}

[Theorem thm44 of arXiv:2609.02136, 'Gamma approximation and Poisson--Gaussian invariance principle on Poisson chaos'] Fix an integer $q\geq1$ and $\nu\in(0,\infty)$.  On a suitable
atomless $\sigma$-finite Poisson space, the following assertions hold.

{\rm\bf (a)} For every finite integer $M\geq4$, there is a sequence
$F_n\in\mathcal{C}_q^\eta$ such that $\mathbb{E}[F_n^2]=2\nu$ and
\noindent
\begin{align}
 \mathbb{E}[F_n^r]
 &\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}[Z_\nu^r],
 \quad 1\leq r\leq M,
 \\
 F_n&\xrightarrow{\mathrm d}Y_M,
 \quad
 \mathcal{L}(Y_M)\neq\mathcal{L}(Z_\nu),
 \\
 \mathcal J_4(F_n)&\longrightarrow48q\nu > 0.
 \notag
\end{align}

{\rm\bf (b)} There is a sequence
$R_n\in\mathcal{C}_q^\eta$ such that
\noindent
\begin{align}
& R_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm d}Z_\nu
 \quad{\rm and}\quad
 \mathbb{E}[R_n^r]\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}[Z_\nu^r]
 \quad\text{for every }r\geq1,
 \notag\\
&\text{while}\quad\mathcal J_4(R_n)\longrightarrow48q\nu>0.
 
\end{align}
