For Bernoulli percolation on an arbitrary locally finite transitive infinite graph, the phase transition is SHARP: (a) for every p < p_c the susceptibility is finite, chi(p) = E_p |C(0)| < infinity, and for FINITE-RANGE models the probability of an open path from the origin to distance n decays exponentially in n; (b) for every p > p_c the mean-field lower bound P_p(0 <-> infinity) >= (p - p_c)/p holds. There is therefore no intermediate regime in which the cluster size has a heavy polynomial tail without an infinite cluster - the subcritical decay is exponential right up to p_c. The same paper proves the corresponding statements for the Ising model, with finiteness of the susceptibility below the critical inverse temperature and the mean-field magnetisation bound above it. Historically this recovers the Aizenman-Barsky and Menshikov theorems by a much shorter argument based on a differential inequality for a well-chosen family of finite-volume quantities. The result is about BERNOULLI percolation on a TRANSITIVE graph; the transitivity hypothesis is used and the statement is not asserted here for general graphs. [Duminil-Copin and Tassion (2016), Comm. Math. Phys. 343; arXiv:1502.03050]

[Lem 7 of arXiv:2512.03884, '2512.03884'] Let $\alpha$ be a badly approximable number, and let $1<\theta< \theta'$ be constants. For any $0< \delta \le 1/2$ and any integer $M \ge 1$,
\begin{align}
\sum_{\substack{m=1 \\ \| m \alpha \|<\delta}}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^{\theta}} &\ll \delta^{\theta},  \\
\sum_{\substack{m=1 \\ \| m \alpha \| \ge \delta}}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^{\theta} \| m \alpha \|^{\theta'}} &\ll \frac{1}{\delta^{\theta'-\theta}},  \\
\sum_{\substack{m=M \\ \| m \alpha \| \ge \delta}}^{\infty} \frac{1}{m^{\theta} \| m \alpha \|^{\theta}} &\ll \left\{ \begin{array}{cc} 1+\log \frac{1}{M \delta} & \textrm{if } M \delta \le 1, \\ \frac{1}{(M\delta)^{\theta -1}} & \textrm{if } M \delta >1, \end{array} \right.  \\
\sum_{m=1}^M \frac{1}{m^{\theta} \| m \alpha \|^{\theta}} &\asymp \log M 
\end{align}
with implied constants depending only on $\alpha$, $\theta$ and $\theta'$.

[Theorem thm:HDL weak regime of arXiv:2505.10256, 'Stochastic Oscillators out of equilibrium:\\ scaling limits and correlation estimates'] Let $v_0:\mathbb T\to \mathbb R$ and $e_0:\mathbb T\to (0,\infty)$ be bounded measurable functions.
Let $\{\mu_N\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ be a sequence of probability measures on $\Omega_N$ associated to the pair $(v_0,e_0)$, and assume that $\{\mu_N\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ satisfies Assumption (assump:initial_measure of the paper).  
Moreover, assume $\kappa>1$ where $\kappa$ is the constant appearing in (equation eq:weak_asymmetry of the paper).  
Then, for every $t\in [0,T]$, the sequence of empirical measures $\{(\pi^{v,N}_t, \pi^{e,N}_t)\}_{N\in\mathbb N}$ converges in probability to the absolute continuous measure $(v(t,u)du, e(t,u)du)$, that is, for any $\delta>0$ and for any $G\in C^2(\mathbb{T})$ we have 
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{N\to\infty}
Q^{\sigma,N}_m 
\bigg(\Big|\langle \pi^{\sigma,N}_{t},G\rangle-\int_{\mathbb T} \sigma(t,u)G(u)du \Big|>\delta\bigg) =0 
\end{equation*}
for each $\sigma\in \{e,v\}$ provided $m>5/2$, where recall that the measure $Q^{v,N}_m$ and $Q^{e,N}_m$ were defined for processes taking values on Sobolev space $H^{-m}(\mathbb T)$, see (equation eq:sobolev_empirical_measure_definition of the paper).  
Moreover, the pair $(v(t,u), e(t,u))$ is the unique weal solution of (equation eq:hdl of the paper) under $\alpha=0$ with initial profile $(v_0,e_0)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let~$(\rho_\bullet,\mbbP)$ be any time-homogeneous $\msP$-valued $\mcQ_\pi$-sub-stationary stochastic process adapted to its natural (augmented) filtration with initial distribution~$\mbbP\circ\rho_0^{-1}$ equivalent to~$\mcQ_\pi$.
If any of the conditions~(i:t:DK:1 of the paper)-(i:t:DK:3 of the paper) in Theorem~(t:DK of the paper) is satisfied, then~$(\rho_\bullet,\mbbP)$ is a version of~$\widehat\mcW_\pi$ in~(equation eq:t:TransferP:0 of the paper) up to $\mcQ_\pi$-equivalence.

In particular, for every Borel probability measure~$\mcP$ on~$\msP$ equivalent to~$\mcQ_\pi$, the martingale problems for~$\big({\widehat\mcL_\pi,\msD(\widehat\mcL_\pi),\mcP}\big)$ and~$\tparen{\widehat\mcL,\hCylP{}{0},\mcP}$, the shadow martingale problem~(equation eq:d:ShadowMP:0 of the paper) with initial distribution~$\mcP$, and thus the Dean--Kawasaki-type \emph{\textsc{spde}}~(equation eq:IntroSPDE of the paper) with initial distribution~$\mcP$, are all well-posed in the class of processes~$(\rho_\bullet,\mbbP)$ as above, in the sense of weak existence for~$\widehat\mcE^\pi$-q.e.\ starting point and uniqueness up to $\mcQ_\pi$-equivalence. Let nu be a finite complex measure on a measurable space, |nu| its total variation measure (|nu|(E) = sup over countable measurable partitions of E of sum |nu(E_i)|). There is a measurable function phi with |phi| = 1 everywhere such that nu(E) = int_E phi d|nu| for every measurable E. phi is unique |nu|-almost everywhere and not pointwise: on a |nu|-null set it can take any unit-modulus values. (S. Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis, Theorem 9.41.)

\[
 \Ind_B^A:\mathcal I(B)\longrightarrow\mathcal I(A)
\]
is an order isomorphism, with inverse $\Ind_A^B$.  Hence it is an isomorphism of complete lattices of closed two-sided ideals.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e and total conductance c_G equal to the sum of conductances over all edges, the commute time C(a,b) = E_a[tau_b] + E_b[tau_a] between two vertices a, b satisfies the exact identity C(a,b) = 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), where R_eff(a,b) is the effective resistance in the associated electrical network. The identity is derived by checking that h(x) = P_x(hit a before b) is harmonic away from {a,b} and coincides with the network's voltage function, then relating expected hitting times to the network's energy dissipation. It converts questions about hitting, commute, and cover times of a reversible random walk into purely electrical or combinatorial resistance computations, enabling resistance-based bounds via series-parallel laws, Rayleigh monotonicity, or the Nash-Williams inequality on infinite graphs, on quantities such as cover time and mixing time. It does not directly give the individual one-way hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone, only the symmetrized commute time; and it is specific to reversible chains, since non-reversible walks lack the electrical-network correspondence and require substantially different techniques. Typical failure: Using the commute-time identity to bound a one-directional hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone by simply halving C(a,b), which is valid only under a separate symmetry argument between a and b; in general E_a[tau_b] and E_b[tau_a] can differ substantially even though their sum equals 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), so treating the identity as giving each one-way time individually, without additional justification, is a common overreach. Canonical reference: Chandra, Raghavan, Ruzzo, Smolensky and Tiwari, 1996, Random Structures and Algorithms; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press, Chapter 2.
a finite, irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e
the two states a, b are distinct vertices of the graph
the graph is connected, so hitting and commute times, and R_eff, are all finite
consistent normalization of the total conductance c_G matching the specific convention used for R_eff

[Thm thm-busemann-conv of arXiv:2510.26123, 'Directed distances in bipolar-oriented triangulations:\\ exact exponents and scaling limit'] The following two scaling limit results for the Busemann function $\mathcal X$ introduced in Theorem~(thm-busemann of the paper) hold with respect to the local Skorokhod topology on $\mathbbm R$ (here, all stable processes are strictly stable):
\begin{itemize}
\item
In the LDP case, the re-scaled Busemann function $\{k^{-3/2} \mathcal X( \lfloor k t \rfloor)\}_{t\in\mathbbm R}$ converges in law  to a process $X : \mathbbm R\to\mathbbm R$ such that $-X|_{[0,\infty)}$ is a $2/3$-stable subordinator; and $X(-\cdot)|_{[0,\infty)}$ is a symmetric $2/3$-stable Lévy process independent of $X|_{[0,\infty)}$. 
\item  
In the SDP case, the re-scaled Busemann function $\{k^{-3/4} \mathcal X(\lfloor k t \rfloor)\}_{t\in\mathbbm R}$ converges in law  to a process $X : \mathbbm R\to\mathbbm R$ such that $X|_{[0,\infty)}$ is a $4/3$-stable Lévy process with only upward jumps; and $X(-\cdot)|_{[0,\infty)}$ is a symmetric $4/3$-stable Lévy process independent of $  X|_{[0,\infty)}$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition def:constant-escape of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence~$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$,   
a positive integer~$j$, a non-negative integer~$\tau$,
and a real number $\nu \ge 0$. 
A \emph{constant-escape process} \newsym{E+}{constant-escape process}{E^+} on $[j]$ with 
send sequence~$\overline{p}$,
start time $\tau$, and end-of-step arrival rate \newsym{nu}{end-of-step arrival rate of constant-escape process}{\nu} is a generalised backoff process with send sequence $\overline{p}$, 
start time~$\tau$, the birth distribution~$\mathcal{D}$ that always returns~$0$, and an initial population $\overline{\mathbf{arr}}^{E^+}(\tau)$, that satisfies the following constraints.
\begin{itemize}
\item For all $i>j$ and $t \ge \tau$, $\mathrm{arr}_i^{E^+}(t) = 0$.
\item  For all $i\in [j]$ and $t>\tau$,
$\mathrm{arr}_i^{E^+}(t)$ is a Bernoulli r.v.\ with parameter~$\nu$. These are independent for different~$i$ and for different~$t$.
\item For all $i \in [j-1]$ and $t \ge \tau$, $\mathbf{e}_i^{E^+}(t) = \emptyset$. 
\item For all $i \ge j$ and $t \ge \tau$, $\mathbf{e}_i^{E^+}(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^{E^+}(t)$.
\end{itemize}
title: Definition def:constant-escape of arXiv:2602.21315

Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent audit pending. Let n,d>=1, N even >=8d, K>=2 and beta=r/K with integer 1<=r<K. Of N uniform contexts, N/2 are known arbitrary, N/2-d known systematic, and d have arbitrary binary type labels; the resulting class has VC dimension d. All K candidates are true in a systematic context and a uniform random r-subset is true in an arbitrary context. The target p has context marginal 1/N and is uniform on true candidates within each context. Training supplies n iid uniform contexts and their type labels. A generator g_hv puts mass v uniformly on candidates in h-predicted arbitrary contexts and 1-v uniformly on candidates in its other contexts. Let a be the true arbitrary mass, ahat the predicted mass, eS the mass of true-systematic/predicted-arbitrary contexts, eA the reverse error, and e=eS+eA. For every partition of output-probability levels, including all source bin counts, Mis(g_hv,p)=|v-ahat|. For 0<=c<=1/4 the exact minimum at fixed h is V_h(c)=(1-beta)*(a-c)+(1-beta)*c*L, where L=eS/ahat+eA/(1-ahat), attained at v=ahat-c. The oracle value is (1-beta)*(a-c), and e<=L<=(8/3)e. The minimax expected excess over the oracle, restricted to this generator family, is between (1-beta)*c*R and (8/3)*(1-beta)*c*R, R=d/(2N)*(1-1/N)^n; randomized consistent ERM attains the upper bound. With probability >=1-delta every consistent ERM has e<=min(d/N,(d ln2+ln(1/delta))/n). At c=0 the learning penalty vanishes. These are not claims for unannotated training or unrestricted generators.
N even >=8d; n,d>=1; K>=2; integer 1<=r<K
Factual target has uniform context marginal and is uniform on true candidates within each context
Systematic contexts have all K candidates true; arbitrary contexts have a random r-subset true
Training supplies n iid uniform contexts and their exact partition labels, not ordinary unannotated factual samples
Admissible generators are uniform within each learned block of a classifier in the specified class
Calibration budget c is in [0,1/4]

body: In estimation theory and statistics, the Cramér–Rao bound (CRB) relates to estimation of a deterministic parameter. The result is named in honor of Harald Cramér and Calyampudi Radhakrishna Rao, but has also been derived independently by Maurice Fréchet, Georges Darmois, and by Alexander Aitken and Harold Silverstone. It is also known as Fréchet–Cramér–Rao or Fréchet–Darmois–Cramér–Rao lower bound. It states that the precision of any unbiased estimator is at most the Fisher information; or (equivalently) the reciprocal of the Fisher information is a lower bound on its variance.

where

\nonumber\\

\nonumber
\\
&&
-
\left({\bf Q}^{[N,N]}(\btheta)-s{\bf C}_N\times I(N\in\mathcal{A})\right)^{-1}
\times
\frac{\partial {\bf Q}^{[N,N-1]}(\btheta)}{\partial \btheta},
        
\end{eqnarray}
and for $n=N-1,\ldots,n-k+1$,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}

&= \Big({\bf Q}^{[n,n]}(\btheta)-s{\bf C}_n I(n\in\mathcal{A})

body:
[Proposition 40 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(Z\) be a connected complete normal klt complex space of dimension
\(m+1\), whose regular locus carries a K\"ahler metric \(g_Z\) with
complex structure \(J_Z\).  Let \(f_Z\) be locally Lipschitz on \(Z\),
smooth on \(\Reg Z\), and satisfy
\[
 \Rc(g_Z)+\nabla^2f_Z=\frac12g_Z
 \qquad\text{on }\Reg Z.
\]
Assume the finite-time
tangent-space package used in \cref{thm:singular-product}: its analytic and metric
regular loci agree, \(Z\) is the metric completion of its regular locus,
the restricted distance is intrinsic, the K\"ahler current has bounded
local potentials and the required local ambient lower bound, and the
soliton measure
\[
 d\mathfrak m=(4\pi)^{-(m+1)}e^{-f_Z}\,dV_{g_Z}
 \quad\text{on }\Reg Z,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z\setminus\Reg Z)=0,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z)=1,
\]
is normalized to be a probability measure.  Suppose there is a globally
Lipschitz holomorphic map
\[
 H:Z\longrightarrow\C^m
\]
such that on \(\Reg Z\)
\begin{equation}
 \nabla dH=0,\qquad
 c|a|^2\le |d(a\cdot H)|_{g_Z}^2\le C|a|^2
 \quad(a\in\C^m).
\end{equation}
Then there is a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{GL}(m,\C)\), with no target
translation, such that
\begin{equation}
 Z\cong\C^m\times\Sigma,\qquad LH=\operatorname{pr}_{\C^m},
\end{equation}
where \(\Sigma\) is a complete smooth connected Riemann surface.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 Z\cong\C^{m+1}
 \qquad\text{or}\qquad
 Z\cong\C^m\times\PP^1,
\end{equation}
where the first model is Gaussian and the sphere is round with
\(\Rc=\frac12g\).  In these zero-preserving coordinates,
\((LH)^{-1}(0)\) is respectively \(\C\) or \(\PP^1\).  Define the
normalized Nash entropy by
\[
 \mathcal N(Z):=\int_{\Reg Z}f_Z\,d\mathfrak m-(m+1).
\]
If \(\mathcal N(Z)<0\), only the spherical model occurs.

[Definition def.mul of arXiv:2607.10105, 'The four-dimensional Anderson model: a case study for critical SPDEs'] Consider a Hepp tree $\mathcal T$ with multiplicities $m_\mathfrak l$. We shall divide its leaves into two \emph{types}, \emph{simple} and \emph{compound}, and denote the simple and compound leaf sets by $\mathcal L^S$ and $\mathcal L^C$. Define the quantities
\begin{equation}\gamma_\mathfrak n^2:=\gamma_\mathfrak n+\sum_{\mathfrak l\in\mathcal L^S\cap\mathcal C_\mathfrak n}1+\sum_{\mathfrak l\in\mathcal L^C\cap\mathcal C_\mathfrak n}(m_\mathfrak l-1);\qquad \gamma_\mathfrak n^\infty:=\gamma_\mathfrak n+\sum_{\mathfrak l\in\mathcal L\cap\mathcal C_\mathfrak n}(m_\mathfrak l-1)
\end{equation} (recall $\mathcal C_\mathfrak n$ is the set of children of $\mathfrak n$). In other words, $\gamma_\mathfrak n^2$ is the number of children of $\mathfrak n$ with each simple leaf counted with \emph{multiplicity 2} and each compound leaf counted with full multiplicities $m_\mathfrak l$, while $\gamma_\mathfrak n^\infty$ is the number of children of $\mathfrak n$ with each leaf (simple or compound) counted with full multiplicities $m_\mathfrak l$.

For the initial Hepp tree in Proposition (prop.main_3 of the paper) we take $\mathcal L^C=\varnothing$, so in $\gamma_\mathfrak n^2$ we just count every leaf with multiplicity $2$. Note that in Proposition (prop.main_3 of the paper) the multiplicity $m_\mathfrak l$ is always even; throughout the proof below, we will introduce new leaves whose multiplicity $m_\mathfrak l$ may not be even, but they will always be at least two (Definition (def.hepp of the paper)). In particular, we always have $\gamma_\mathfrak n^2\leq\gamma_\mathfrak n^\infty$ in ((eq.mul_1 of the paper)).

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2609.03061, '2609.03061'] Let the path $M : [a,b] \rightarrow Sp(2n,\mathbb{R})$ be continuous and piecewise smooth.

Let the $n$ eigenvalues of first kind of Gelfand and Lidskii \cite{GL,SZ1,SZ2} of $M(t)$ be $\lambda\#_1(M(t)), \cdots, \lambda\#_n(M(t))$ with  normalized first kind eigenvalues $(\frac{\lambda\#_j(t)}{|\lambda\#_j(t)|})^2
= e^{ i \theta\#_j(t)}$, with $0 \le \theta\#_j(t) < 2 \pi$.
By definition, the Salomon and Zehnder mapping $\rho: Sp(2n,\mathbb{R}) \rightarrow S^1$ \cite{GL,SZ1,SZ2}
is given by
$$
\rho(M(t)) = \prod_{j=1}^n \frac{\lambda\#_j(t)  }{ | \lambda\#_j(t) | }.
$$
 Let $h\#(t)$ be the number
of $j$ with $\lambda\#_j(M(t))^2 = +1$. Then there
is an equality of integers:
$$ \begin{array}{l}
\mu_{HZ}( \{ t \mapsto M(t) \} )
= \int_a^b \ (t \mapsto \rho(M(t))^2))^\star \ (\frac{d \theta}{2\pi})
  + \Sigma_{j=1}^n \ ( \ \frac{\theta\#_j(a)}{2\pi} - \ \frac{\theta\#_j(b)}{2\pi} \ )
  + (h\#(a)-h\#(b))
  \end{array} $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 4 of arXiv:2609.03061

body:
PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. By the cluster-process structure of the DGFF extremal process (Biskup-Louidor), the number of points of the level set at depth t inside A is a Poisson sum over extremal local maxima in A of i.i.d. cluster sizes at the corresponding depths, so its conditional expectation given the extremal measure Z^D equals Z^D(A) times the integral over depth of e^{alpha s} E[cluster size at depth s] ds. Conjecture 16.5 (the count normalised by (1/t) e^{-alpha t} converges to c Z^D(A)) therefore reduces to the existence of lim e^{-alpha h} E_nu(f_h) (Conjecture 16.6) plus (i) uniform integrability of cluster sizes at depth t uniformly in N, to exchange the N and t limits, and (ii) concentration of the Poisson sum, which needs its own argument (a second-moment bound on deep cluster sizes, or truncation under the same uniform integrability): uniform integrability gives no variance bound. Conversely, 16.5 gives the limit in 16.6 by taking expectations only if the normalised counts are uniformly integrable; convergence in probability alone does not move expectations. The open content is thus 16.6 together with the uniform-in-N control of deep clusters, which the concentric decomposition delivers only at bounded depth.
2D DGFF in admissible domains; extremal process with Poisson-cluster structure (Biskup-Louidor)
Exchange of limits requires uniform integrability not currently available

body: [Definition def:steep-level-line of arXiv:2606.06612, 'The limit shape and emergence of the \\ Discrete Gaussian level lines'] We say a $j$ level-line loop $\mathfrak{L}$ in $\lfloor \sigma\rfloor$ is \texttt{steep} if at least $\frac23 |\mathfrak{L}|$ of its bonds $b$ satisfy $|(\nabla \lfloor\sigma\rfloor)_{xy}|\geq 2$, where $xy$ is the edge of $\mathbb Z^2$ dual to $b$. Similarly, we say that a $j$ level-line annulus~${\ensuremath{\mathscr A}}$ in $\lfloor\sigma\rfloor$ is \texttt{steep} if $\frac23|{\ensuremath{\mathscr A}}|$ of the bonds $b$ in ${\ensuremath{\mathscr A}}^{\textsf{in}}\cup {\ensuremath{\mathscr A}}^{\textsf{out}}$ satisfy $|(\nabla \lfloor\sigma\rfloor)_{xy}|\geq 2$ for the $xy$ dual to $b$.

[Defn def-conjugate of arXiv:2411.06301, 'Inverting the operation of conditioning a branching process on extinction'] Let $X = \{X(n) : n\in\mathbbm N\}$ be a subcritical $d$-type branching process such that the $\mathbbm P_k$-extinction probability is one for each $k\in \{1,\dots,d\}$.

[Defn Censored two-source exploration of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Initially,
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_1(0)=\{0\},
 \quad
 \widehat \mathsf{T}_1(0)=0,
 \quad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_2(0)=\{U_n\},
 \quad
 \widehat \mathsf{T}_2(U_n)=0,
\end{align*}
and every other vertex is unlabelled.

Suppose that $q$ is an exploration time immediately after a vertex addition. For $i\in\{1,2\}$, define the active oriented boundary of label $i$ by
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\partial_i(q)
 :=
 \big\{(a,b):
 a\in\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q),\
 b\notin\widehat\mathcal{A}_1(q)\cup\widehat\mathcal{A}_2(q),\
 \{a,b\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}
 \big\}.
\end{align*}
If an unlabelled vertex remains, the next vertex-addition time is
\begin{align*}
 q^+
 :=
 \min_{i\in\{1,2\}}
 \min_{(a,b)\in\widehat\partial_i(q)}
 \big\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_i(a)+\go_{a,b}\big\}.
\end{align*}
On $\Omega_*$, this minimum has a unique minimizing triple $(i,a,b)$.
At time $q^+$, assign label $i$ to $b$ and set
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathsf{T}_i(b):=q^+,
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q^+)
 :=\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q)\cup\{b\},
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_{3-i}(q^+)
 :=\widehat\mathcal{A}_{3-i}(q).
\end{align*}
The labelled sets remain unchanged between successive vertex-addition times.

An edge is called a \emph{bridge} once its endpoints carry different labels. From that time onward, the bridge is censored: its weight is not tested against any further threshold, and the edge is never used for a subsequent vertex addition. The exploration is run without stopping at the first collision. After all vertices are labelled, the process is held fixed.

In rescaled time, define for $s\geqslant0$
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal{C}_i(s):=\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell ),
 \qquad
 N_i(s):=|\mathcal{C}_i(s)|,
 \quad i=1,2,
\end{align*}
and let the bridge set and its cardinality be
\begin{align*}
	\mathcal{B}_s:=\big\{\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}:u\in\mathcal{C}_1(s),\ v\in\mathcal{C}_2(s)\big\},
 \qquad
 B_s:=|\mathcal{B}_s|.
\end{align*}

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2609.03653, 'The derived set of multiple star polylogarithms'] Let $k_1,\ldots,k_r\geq 1$.

$(i)$ The shifted multiple star polylogarithm
\[
\widetilde{\mathrm{Li}}^{\star}_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}(z)
=\sum_{n=0}^{+\infty}A_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}(n)z^n
\]
is the generating function of a completely monotone sequence with $A_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}(0)=1$.  It admits a Hausdorff--Stieltjes representation on $\Lambda$.

$(ii)$ The multiple star polylogarithm $\mathrm{Li}^{\star}_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}$ extends holomorphically to $\Lambda$ and is univalent on $\mathcal{D}$.

$(iii)$ The shifted multiple star polylogarithm $\widetilde{\mathrm{Li}}^{\star}_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}$ extends holomorphically to $\Lambda$ and is univalent on $\mathcal{D}$.

$(iv)$ For every infinite index ${\bf k}=(k_1,k_2,\ldots)\in(\mathbb{Z}^{+})^{\infty}$, the limits
\[
\mathrm{Li}^{\star}_{\bf k}(z)
=\lim_{r\rightarrow+\infty}\mathrm{Li}^{\star}_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}(z),
\qquad
\widetilde{\mathrm{Li}}^{\star}_{\bf k}(z)
=\lim_{r\rightarrow+\infty}\widetilde{\mathrm{Li}}^{\star}_{k_1,\ldots,k_r}(z)
\]
exist locally uniformly on $\mathcal{D}$.  Both limit functions are univalent on $\mathcal{D}$, and the shifted limit has a Hausdorff--Stieltjes representation on $\Lambda$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\Bigg\|\sum_{m=1}^M\sum_{j=1}^{\tau_k-1}\phi(x_h^{m,j},a_h^{m,j})\Bigl[V_{h+1}^{k}(x_{h+1}^{m,j})-\mathbb P_hV_{h+1}^{k}(x_h^{m,j},a_h^{m,j})\Bigr]\Bigg\|_{(\check\Lambda_h^{\tau_k})^{-1}}^2
\le CH^2d^2\chi.
\]
where $\chi = \log(1+(c_\beta+1)dMHT/p)$.
Then, $\mathbb P(\mathcal C) \geq 1-p$.

[Cor 115 (regularity for temporally smoothed coefficients) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $\MAX_N$ from \eqref{e:MAX.N} and Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}.
The coefficients from Definitions~\ref{d:t.smooth} and \ref{d:t.smooth.variant} satisfy the following bounds:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item
Similarly to Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, the coefficients are continuously differentiable in space and time, and satisfy
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big(
	\|\tB^N\|_\infty
    +
    \|\partial_y\tB^N\|_\infty
 + \tep \|\partial_t \tB^N\|_\infty\Big)^2\\
	&\qquad+ \max\bigg\{
    \|\bar{A}\|_\infty
    +\|\partial_y\bar{A}\|_\infty
    + \tep\|\partial_t\bar{A}\|_\infty
    : \bar{A}\in\{ \tV,\tU,\trrr,
	\twww\}^N
    \bigg\} 
	\le 
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2\,.
	
	\end{align}
The analogous bound holds for the coefficients $\{\iB,\iV,\iU,\ir,\iw\}^N$.

\item
Similarly to Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg.SDE}, we have 
\beq
\max\bigg\{
	\bigg\|\frac{\partial}{\partial y}
    \Big[\bar{A}^{1/2}\Big]\bigg\|_\infty
    +\tep
    \bigg\|\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
    \Big[\bar{A}^{1/2}\Big]\bigg\|_\infty
	:\bar{A}\in\{\tF,\twww\}^N\bigg\}
	\le 
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}
		{\sep}
		\bigg)^{O(1)} \MAX_N\,.
	\eeq
The analogous bound holds for $\iF^N$ and $\iw^N$.
\end{enumerate} 

\begin{proof} 
\eqref{c:t.smooth.regularity.N.a}
Recall that the temporally smoothed coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:t.smooth} are obtained by taking the spatially smoothed coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth} and simply convolving with the kernel $\tphi$ in the time coordinate, so they satisfy the same spatial regularity bounds as in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}. As for regularity in the time coordinate, we can calculate for example 
	\begin{align*}
    \bigg|
	\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
	\tB^N(t,y)
    \bigg|
	&= \bigg(\frac{2}{\tep}\bigg)^2
    \bigg|
	\int_{\R}
	(\sphicirc)'\bigg(\frac{2(t-s)}{\tep}-1\bigg)
	\sB^N(s,y)\,ds
    \bigg|\\
	&= \frac{2}{\tep}
    \bigg|
	\int_{\R}
	(\sphicirc)'(u-1)
	\sB^N\bigg(t-\frac{\tep u}{2},y\bigg)\,du
    \bigg|
	\le \frac{2\|(\sphicirc)'\|_1}{\tep} \|\sB^N\|_\infty
	\le \frac{O(1)}{\tep}\|\sB^N\|_\infty\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last term is bounded by Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}. This implies \eqref{e:t.smooth.regularity.N}. To obtain the analogous bound for the ``ideal'' smoothed coefficients, recall the notation $\Num(t,y)$ and $\Den(t,y)$ from the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, and note that for example we can express
	\[
	\iB^N(t,y)
	=\frac{\displaystyle \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)\Num(s,y)\,ds}
	{\displaystyle \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)\Den(s,y)\,ds}
	\equiv \frac{\bar{N}(t,y)}{\bar{D}(t,y)}\,.
	\]
It is easy to conclude that $\iB^N$ satisfies similar spatial regularity bounds as $\sB^N$. Lastly, we have
	\[
	\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \iB^N(t,y)
	= \frac{\partial_t \bar{N}(t,y)}{\bar{D}(t,y)} 
	- \iB(t,y) \frac{\partial_t \bar{D}(t,y)}{\bar{D}(t,y)}\,,
	\]
and from this it is straightforward to conclude that $\iB^N$ satisfies similar temporal regularity bounds as $\tB^N$. This proves \eqref{c:t.smooth.regularity.N.a}.

\eqref{c:t.smooth.regularity.N.b} Recall the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg.SDE}, where we decomposed $\sF=\Num/\Den$. We now again abuse notation by letting $\Num$ stand for the numerator of $\sF$ rather than of $\sB$. Then
	\[\iF(t,y)
	=\frac{ \displaystyle\int_{\R}\tphi(t-s)\Num(s,y)\,ds}
		{ \displaystyle\int_{\R}\tphi(t-s)\Den(s,y)\,ds}
	\equiv \frac{\bar{N}(t,y)}{\bar{D}(t,y)}\,.
	\]
The bound on the spatial derivative of $\iF^{1/2}$ follows by essentially the same argument as in 
Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg.SDE}, so we consider only the time derivative.
Following the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg.SDE}, 
first recall from \eqref{e:denominator.lbd} that $\Den(t,y)\ge 1/\trK^{O(1)}$ for all $|y|\le 5\trK$. Then, similarly to
\eqref{e:sF.quotient.rule}, we have
	\[\bigg|\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \iF(t,y)\bigg|
	\le \trK^{O(1)}
	\bigg|
	\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\bar{N}(t,y)
	- \iF(t,y) 
	\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \bar{D}(t,y)
	\bigg|\,,\]
and w (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Unproved-input proof route for iid Uniform[1,2] undirected nearest-neighbor Z^2 FPP, T_n=T(0,n e1). Refresh every edge independently at rate one. Let C_n(t)=Cov(T_n(W),T_n(W^t)) and H_n(t)=-C_n'(t). Finite-product orthogonality proves H_n>=0, H_n decreasing, Var(T_n)=integral_0^infinity H_n(t)dt and H_n(0)<=2n. If, for every epsilon in (0,1/3) and all large n, H_n(n^(-1/3-epsilon))>=c_epsilon n and C_n(n^(-1/3+epsilon))<=C_epsilon n^(2/3+epsilon), with positive constants independent of n, then c_epsilon n^(2/3-epsilon)<=Var(T_n)<=(2+C_epsilon)n^(2/3+epsilon), yielding variance exponent 1/3. BOTH crossover bounds remain unproved. The conditional implication awaits independent w365 review. Product structure and a linear geodesic-length bound alone only give order n; no parent solution or novelty is claimed.

$$

[Theorem of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let $Z_0^{(1)}$ and $Z_0^{(2)}$ be the zero cells of stationary Poisson hyperplane tessellations with intensity $\gamma$ and directional distributions $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, respectively. Then, for all $\phi_2$ close enough to $\phi_1$ in Wasserstein distance, 
\[W_{\operatorname{dist}}(Z_0^{(1)}, Z_0^{(2)}) 
\leq C_{\operatorname{dist}}(\phi_1) \, \gamma^{-\alpha(\operatorname{dist})} \, W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\beta(\operatorname{dist})} ,\]
where $\operatorname{dist}$ is either the radial metric $\rho_p$ with $p\in[1,\infty)$ or the symmetric-difference volume metric $\Delta$ and where $\alpha(\rho_p)=1$, $\beta(\rho_p) = \frac{1}{p}$, $\alpha(\Delta)=d$ and $\beta(\Delta)=\frac{1}{d}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2607.21062, 'A new probabilistic approach for\\ mean field games of optimal stopping'] Let $\{L^n\}_n\subset\mathcal V$ be a sequence weakly converging in $\mathbb H^2(\mathbb R)$ to some $L\in\mathcal V$. Let $I=\{I_t\}_{0\leq t\leq T}$ be a real-valued It\^o process:
    \[
    I_t = I_0 + \int_0^t F_s ds + \int_0^t G_s dW_s, \qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
    \]
    with $F\colon[0,T]\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb R$, $G\colon[0,T]\times\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb R^m$ being progressively measurable and bounded, and with $I_0$ being a deterministic constant. We set $I_{0^-}:=I_0$. Then, it holds that $\int_{0^-}^T I_tdL_t^n$ converges to $\int_{0^-}^T I_tdL_t$ weakly in $\mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$, that is
    \[
    \mathbb E\bigg[\eta\int_{0^-}^T I_tdL_t^n\bigg] \rightarrow \mathbb E\bigg[\eta\int_{0^-}^T I_tdL_t\bigg],
    \]
    for every real-valued random variable $\eta$ in $\mathcal{L}^2(\mathcal{F}_T)$.

[Corollary cor:SM of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Let $(G_k)$ be a sequence of $\{0,1\}$-valued functions on finite plane
trees, let $(k_n)$ be a sequence of integers, and let $(M_n)$ be a cutoff
sequence. Assume that $(G_k)$ satisfies Assumption (hyp:S of the paper) along $(k_n)$
with respect to $(M_n)$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(G_k)$ satisfies Assumption (hyp:M of the paper) along $(k_n)$ with
respect to $(M_n)$;
\item[(ii)] we have
$
\mathbb{E}\left[
\#\{u\in\mathcal T^n:G_{k_n}(\mathcal T^n_u)=1\}
\right]
\sim
n\P(G_{k_n}(\mathcal T)=1)
$;
\item[(iii)] if $\P(G_{k_n}(\mathcal T)=1)=O(1/n)$, then
$\P(G_{k_n}(\mathcal T^n)=1)\to0$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2607.19176, 'Exponential Convergence of the Sinkhorn Algorithm for the Schrödinger Bridge with Regime S'] Assume that the cost function \(c\) is bounded, with
$
\|c\|_{L^\infty(E\times E)}\le M.
$
Let \(\pi\) be the optimal coupling between \(\rho\) and \(\mu\), and let
\((\varphi,\psi)\) be a pair of optimal Schrödinger potentials. Assume moreover
that, for every \(z_1\in E\) and every \(j\in\mathcal I\), the map
\[
y\longmapsto c\bigl(z_1,(y,j)\bigr)+\psi_j(y)
\]
is \(C^1\) and \(\Lambda\)-semiconcave on \(\mathbb R^d\). Then, for
\(\mu\)-a.e. \(z_2=(y,j)\) and \(z_2'=(y',j')\), one has
\[
H\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid z_2)\mid \pi(\cdot\mid z_2')\bigr)
\le
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\Lambda}{2}|y-y'|^2, & j=j',\\[0.6em]
4M, & j\neq j'.
\end{cases}
\]

body:
[Lemma 9 (Ordering law) of arXiv:2605.26107, 'Radial Extremality for LRU Caching and the Fill--Holst Conjecture'] For every permutation $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_N)$ of $[N]$,
\[
        \Pp(A_{\sigma_1}<A_{\sigma_2}<\cdots<A_{\sigma_N})
        =
        \prod_{r=1}^N
        \frac{\lambda_{\sigma_r}}{\sum_{m=r}^N\lambda_{\sigma_m}}.
\]
Equivalently, the exponential-clock order is generated by repeatedly
choosing the next index from the remaining indices with probability
proportional to its rate.

body: For a first-order quasilinear PDE a(x,y,u) partial u/partial x + b(x,y,u) partial u/partial y = c(x,y,u) for unknown u(x,y), the method of characteristics reduces the PDE to a family of ODEs. Parametrize characteristic curves (x(s),y(s)) together with z(s)=u(x(s),y(s)) along them by dx/ds=a(x,y,z), dy/ds=b(x,y,z), dz/ds=c(x,y,z). Along a solution of this system, u is automatically consistent with the PDE, since the chain rule gives dz/ds = (partial u/partial x)(dx/ds) + (partial u/partial y)(dy/ds) = a(partial u/partial x)+b(partial u/partial y), which equals c(x,y,z) exactly when the PDE holds. Solving the PDE with data prescribed on a noncharacteristic initial curve reduces to solving the characteristic ODEs from each point of that curve and assembling the resulting family into the solution surface, then, where the map from characteristic parameters to (x,y) is invertible, reading off u(x,y). The same idea extends to fully nonlinear first-order PDE F(x,u,Du)=0 via characteristic ODEs derived from F, which also propagate Du along the curves.

[Theorem 1 (Informal) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $D$ be the Riemannian distance on the Stiefel manifold $\mathrm{St}(n,k)$~\footnote{For $1 \le k \le n$, the Stiefel manifold is
$\mathrm{St}(n,k)=\{ X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k} : X^\top X = I_k \}$.} and let $W_D$ be Wasserstein distance with cost $D$. Let $P^T(X)$ denotes the probability distribution induced by running the $k$-column walk for $T$ steps starting with $X \in \mathrm{St}(n,k)$. Then, for every $X,Y\in\mathrm{St}(n,k)$, the Wasserstein distance $W_D\left(P^T(X),P^T(Y)\right)$ is at most $\epsilon$ as long as 
\[
T = \Omega\big(n(k+\log n) \cdot \log (D(X,Y)/\epsilon) \big)~.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 45 (Connected-root deformation retract) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Define
\begin{align*}
 \iota_\rho^0(a)&=a,
 &
 \iota_\rho^1(ae_\rho)&=a\,\mathrm d\log r,\\
 \pi_\rho^0\!\left(\sum_{n\geq0}a_nr^n\right)&=a_0,
 &
 \pi_\rho^1\!\left(
 \sum_{n\geq0}b_nr^n\,\mathrm d\log r
 \right)&=b_0e_\rho.
\end{align*}
These are chain maps and
\(\pi_\rho\iota_\rho=\Id\).  The degree \(-1\) operator
\[
 H_\rho
 \left(
 \sum_{n\geq0}b_nr^n\,\mathrm d\log r
 \right)
 =
 \sum_{n\geq1}\frac{b_n}{n+h}r^n,
 \qquad H_\rho|_{\mathcal A}=0,
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \nabla_{\rho,h}H_\rho+
 H_\rho\nabla_{\rho,h}
 =
 \Id-\iota_\rho\pi_\rho.

\end{equation}
Therefore \(\mathsf K_{\rho,h}^\bullet\) is a strong deformation retract
of \(\widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\rho,h}^\bullet\), and
\[
 H^0(\widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\rho,h})=0,
 \qquad
 H^1(\widehat{\mathsf{DR}}_{\rho,h})\simeq R_0/(h).
\]

body:
[Lemma lem:local-time of arXiv:2604.13968, 'Divisible sandpiles via random walks in random scenery'] Let~$G = (V,E)$ be an infinite, locally finite, connected graph on which the simple random walk $(X_n)_{n\geq 0}$ satisfies the \textbf{spectral dimension bound}
		\begin{equation}
			\sup_{x\in V}\mathbb{P}_x(X_n=x)\leq A\,n^{-d_s/2}\,,
		\end{equation}
		for all $n\geq 1$, for some $d_s>0$ and $A<\infty$.
		Then for every $p \geq 1$ and all $x \in V$ and $n \geq 1$,
		\[
		\sum_{v\in V} \mathbb{E}_x[L_n(v)^p] \leq C_p\begin{cases}
			n^{1+(p-1)(1-d_s/2)} & \text{if } d_s<2,\\[3pt]
			n\,(1+\log n)^{p-1} & \text{if } d_s=2,\\[3pt]
			n & \text{if } d_s>2\,.
		\end{cases}\,
		\]
		Here $C_p<\infty$ depends only on~$p$, $d_s$, and~$A$.

body:
[Theorem 25 (Supercritical shape) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1 / m)$ then $p \, (1-p)^m \,
  (T_{m,p} - m \log{m})$
  converges in law to an exponential distribution with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Recall from Lemma \ref{thm:coupling} that we can
    decompose $p \, (1-p)^m \, (T_{m,p} - m \log{m})$ as
    the sum of independent random variables
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m, 0} - m\log{m})$
    and $p\,(1-p)^m \, (T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$.
    The second random variable~has an exponential limit
    by Theorem~\ref{thm:supercritical}.

    The classical problem has mean
    $\E T_{m, 0} = m\log{m} + O(m)$ and
    variance $\Var(T_{m,0}) = O(m^2)$. Therefore,
    the first random variable's mean is 
    \[
      \E \left[ p\,(1-p)^m\left(T_{m,0} - m\log{m}\right) \right] = p \, (1-p)^m \, O(m) =
      O\left((p\,m) \, e^{-pm}\right) = o(1),
    \]
    and its variance is
    \[
      \Var\left( p\,(1-p)^m\,\left(T_{m, 0} - m\log{m}\right) \right) =
      p^2 \, (1-p)^{2m} \, O(m^2) =
      O\left((p\,m)^2 \, e^{-2pm}\right) = o(1).
    \]
    This implies $p\,(1-p)^m \, (T_{m,0} - m \log{m}) 
    \stackrel{P}{\to} 0$.
    Extend the convergence result using Slutsky's theorem.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:subDiagonal of arXiv:2609.01562, 'Points of maximal traffic on a grid with obstruction'] Let $B=(c,d)\in\mathcal{R}_2(n)$ be such that $c\ge 1$, $d\ge 1$, and $c+d\le n$. Let $a$ be an integer such that $1\le a\le n$. 
\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
\item If $d\ge c+2$, then $f_B(a-1,a)\le f_B(a,a-1) \le f_B(1,0)$.
\item If $c\ge d+2$, then $f_B(a,a-1)\le f_B(a-1,a) \le f_B(0,1)$.
\end{enumerate}

For every integer $n \ge 1$, $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{2n-1}{j}=2^{2n-2}=4^{n-1}$. That is, the first half of the row $\binom{2n-1}{\cdot}$ sums to exactly half the row total. Equivalently $2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{2n-1}{j}=2^{2n-1}$, so the central orthant count $C_{n,2}=2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{2n-1}{j}$ equals $2^{2n-1}$ and the ratio $C_{n,2}/2^{2n}$ is exactly $1/2$ for every $n$, with no dependence on $n$ whatever.

[Definition def:F-function of arXiv:2608.12415, 'Sharp Phase Transition for Ellipsoid Fitting'] Let \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}\) be the semicircle distribution on \([-2,2]\), with
density
\[
    f_{\mathrm{sc}}(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4-x^2}}{2\pi}.
\]
We define
\[
    F(x):=2x_+
    =
    \begin{cases}
        2x, & x\in[0,2],\\
        0,  & x\in[-2,0].
    \end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
    P_j(x):=U_j\left(\frac{x}{2}\right),
\]
where \(U_j\) is the \(j\)-th Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind.  Then
\(\{P_j\}_{j\ge0}\) is an orthonormal basis for
\(L^2([-2,2],\mu_{\mathrm{sc}})\), with \(P_0=1\) and \(P_1=x\).

We write the Chebyshev expansion of \(F\) as
\[
    F(x)=C_F+x+\sum_{j\ge2}b_j \cdot P_j(x),
\]
where
\[
    C_F=b_0=\mathbb E_{X\sim\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}}[F(X)]
    =\frac{8}{3\pi},
    \qquad
    b_1=1,
\]
and, for \(j\ge2\),
\[
    b_j\coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{x\sim \mu_{\mathrm{sc}}}[F(x)]
\]
title: Nonnegative function \(F\) and its Chebyshev expansion

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2606.30364, 'Distributional comparison for non-commutative infinitely divisible probability measures'] Let $\mu = g_{\sigma^2}  \circledast \pi_{\Poiss} \circledast \delta_a$ and $\nu = g_{\zeta^2}  \circledast \pi_{\Delta} \circledast \delta_b$ be infinitely divisible distributions as in Theorem \ref{thm:main_theorm} with triples $(a,\sigma^2,\Poiss)$ and $(b,\zeta^2,\Delta)$, respectively. 

Then
\begin{align}
(x_1 \cdots x_m)^2 (\sigma^2 - \zeta^2)
+
\int_{\R} x^2 (x-x_1)^2  \cdots (x-x_m)^2 \Poiss (dx)
\leq  
	(2 U_{\Delta})^{2m} \, \sum_{n=2}^{2m+2} \abs{ \kappa_n[\mu] - \kappa_n[\nu] },
\end{align}

where $U_\Delta =  \max \{ 1, \abs{x_1} , \ldots, \abs{x_m} \}$.
title: Lemma 17 of arXiv:2606.30364

[Proposition projproj of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $(T,d , \rho)$ be a rooted Polish $\mathbb{R}$-tree with bordification $(T^*\! , d^*\! , \rho)$. For all $n\! \in \! \mathbb{N}$, let $\rho\! \in \! \mathtt{t}_n \! \subseteq \! \mathtt{t}_{n+1} \!\subseteq\!T$ be closed subtrees and let $\mu_n \! \in \! \mathcal{M}_{\! f} (T)$ be such that $\mathtt{P}_{\! \mathtt{t}_n} \mu_{n+1}\! = \!   \mu_n$. Recall the definition of $\mathtt{P}_{\! \mathtt{t}_n}^*$ from Proposition (projdef of the paper) $(vii)$. Then, the following holds. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$] There exists a unique $\mu\! \in \!  \mathcal{M}_{\! f}(T^*)$ whose topological support is contained in the $d^*\! $-closure 
$\mathtt{t}^*$ of $\, \bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \mathtt{t}_n$, and such that $\mathtt{P}_{\! \mathtt{t}_n}^*\mu\! = \!  \mu_n$ for all $n\! \in \!  \mathbb{N}$ and $\mu_n \! \to \! \mu$ weakly on $\mathcal{M}_{\! f} (T^*)$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] Moreover, $\mu(\partial T)\! = \!  0$ iff $ \limsup_{n\to \infty} \mu_n (\mathtt{t}_n \backslash B(\rho, r)) \! \to \! 0$ as $r\! \to \! \infty$. In this case, we view $\mu$ as an element of $\mathcal{M}_f(T)$. Then its topological support in $T$ is included in $T\cap \mathtt{t}^*$ which is the closure of  $\, \bigcup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} \mathtt{t}_n$ in $T$. Moreover, $\mathtt{P}_{\! \mathtt{t}_n} \mu\! = \!  \mu_n$ for all $n\! \in \! \mathbb{N}$ and 
 $\mu_n\! \to \! \mu$ weakly in $\mathcal{M}_{\! f} (T)$. 
\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let independent iid walk increments on Z have P(X=0)=epsilon, P(X=+1)=(1-epsilon)p and P(X=-1)=(1-epsilon)(1-p), with 0<=epsilon<1 and 1/2<=p<=1; let S_0=0 and S_n=sum_{i=1}^n X_i. Independently let C_z be iid fair black/white scenery and Y_i=C_{S_i}. For every n>=1, every deterministic walk record s=(s_1,...,s_n), and every color word y=(y_1,...,y_n), let R(s)=|{s_1,...,s_n}| and call s,y compatible if y_i=y_j whenever s_i=s_j. Then P(S_1^n=s,Y_1^n=y)=P(S_1^n=s)2^(-R(s)) times the compatibility indicator. The range is that of the OBSERVED sites s_1,...,s_n; the origin is included only if it is observed there. Distinct observed sites constrain independent fair scenery variables, while repeated visits impose compatibility. Source: A crossover for the bad configurations of random walk in random scenery, Proposition 2.5, PDF page 7. For two-sided conditioning the corresponding exponent counts the union of the observed site sets, not the sum of their cardinalities.

Own-work draft, proof (unaudited), T326-w697-C06 v1; independent reviewer PASS pending. For the constrained homogeneous linear-attention block model L=(1/2)||[(v/a)Q^TK-I]C^(1/2)||_F^2, every nonzero deterministic PSD C of rank r has global zero-loss Euclidean gradient flow from Q0=K0=alpha I and v0=alpha sqrt(r), provided a,alpha>0 and alpha^3 sqrt(r)/a<1. The selected effective matrix is P+alpha^2 r^(1/3)a^(-2/3)(I-P), with P the range projector of C. Its normalized fresh isotropic Gaussian risk is exactly (1-alpha^2 r^(1/3)a^(-2/3))^2(d-r)/d. For Gaussian finite task pools, alpha=epsilon/sqrt(d), fixed 0<epsilon<1, and either a=1 or a=d, training-time-first limits with M/d->kappa give (1-kappa)_+. The source spectral reduction is prior work; the explicit convergence and finite-pool selector are the own-work corollary submitted here. The written proof derives global boundedness from the active invariant v^2=sum_active u_i^2 and a strict initial loss gap. A positive barrier for each active u_i then yields exponential loss decay for each fixed covariance. The selected scalar is v_infinity=(a r)^(1/3); active Q,K spectral weights tend to sqrt(a/v_infinity) and inactive weights stay alpha. At finite alpha the resulting nullspace term is generally nonzero. Exactly zero initialization is stationary; the small-initialization conclusion takes training to infinity before alpha tends to zero. Published spectral architecture is credited to Kwon et al. [Lemma LemPAIon of arXiv:2508.03577, 'Phase Transitions in a Particle Model\\ for the Self-Adaptive Response to Cancer Dynamics'] The following algorithm samples the steady-state distribution of the (jump-chain) of the model with PAI switched on: start with the zero matrix. Evolve time in discrete steps. At each step, 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item with probability $p/(1+N\lambda_m)$, select a uniformly chosen column to the list of forbidden columns,
        \item with probability $q/(1+N\lambda_m)$, turn the entries of a uniformly selected row into ones, given that the entry is not located in a forbidden row,
        \item with probability $\lambda_m N/(1+N\lambda_m)$, turn a uniformly selected entry of the matrix into a one, given that the entry is not a forbidden column.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

 \operatorname{Cap}_{1,D}(A)=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 M_h(A)=0.
\]
Moreover, for every $u\in H_0^1(D)$,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde u=0\quad M_h\text{-a.e.}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 u=0\quad\mathcal E\text{-q.e. on }D.
\end{equation}
Consequently, $M_h$ is a finite smooth measure for $(\mathcal E,H_0^1(D))$ and has
full $\mathcal E$-quasi-support.

The local lemma survives when independence is replaced by a one-sided condition: each bad event only needs to be no more likely when we condition on any collection of non-neighbouring events not occurring. This covers random permutations and injections, where the events are not independent. Zhao, Theorem 6.5.1 (lopsided local lemma): let A_1, ..., A_n be events and for each i let N(i) ⊆ [n] be such that P(A_i | ∧_{j∈S} Ā_j) ≤ P(A_i) for all S ⊆ [n] \ (N(i) ∪ {i}) (6.1). If there are x_1, ..., x_n ∈ [0,1) with P(A_i) ≤ x_i Π_{j∈N(i)} (1 − x_j) for all i, then P(none of the events A_i occur) ≥ Π_{i=1}^n (1 − x_i). Corollary 6.5.2: if |N(i)| ≤ d and P(A_i) ≤ p for all i, and ep(d+1) ≤ 1, then with positive probability none of the events occur. A graph with these neighbourhoods is called a negative dependency graph; Zhao's example is the random injection model of Lu and Székely (2007).

body: A simple function is a finite linear combination of indicator functions of measurable sets, s = sum c_i 1_{A_i}, with integral sum c_i mu(A_i). Every nonnegative measurable f is an increasing pointwise limit of simple functions, and its Lebesgue integral is defined as integral f dmu = sup { integral s dmu : s simple, 0 <= s <= f }. A general measurable f is integrable if integral |f| < infinity, with integral f = integral f^+ - integral f^-.
title: Simple Function and the Lebesgue Integral

body:
[Thm random coordinate change of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Suppose the driving function $\theta_t$ evolves according to the stochastic differential equation
\begin{equation}
d\theta_t = \sqrt{\kappa}\, dB_t + b\left(\theta_t; \Psi_t(\theta_1), \ldots, \Psi_t(\theta_n)\right)\, dt,
\end{equation}
where $B_t$ is standard Brownian motion, and $\Psi_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}$ is the conformal coordinate change defined as in Theorem~(Loewner coordinate change in angular coordinate of the paper).

Define the transformed driving function
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_t := \Psi_t(\theta_t),
\]
and introduce the reparameterized time
\[
s(t) := \int_0^t |\Psi_u'(\theta_u)|^2 \, du.
\]

Then the process $\widetilde{\theta}_s := \Psi_{t(s)}(\theta_{t(s)})$ satisfies the following SDE:
\begin{equation}

d\widetilde{\theta}_s = \sqrt{\kappa}\, dB_s + \frac{b\left(\theta_s; \Psi_{t(s)}(\theta_1), \ldots, \Psi_{t(s)}(\theta_n)\right)}{\Psi_{t(s)}'(\theta_s)}\, ds + \frac{\kappa - 6}{2} \cdot \frac{\Psi_{t(s)}''(\theta_s)}{[\Psi_{t(s)}'(\theta_s)]^2} \, ds.
\end{equation}
title: Stochastic Loewner chain under coordinate change

body:
[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2506.11707, 'Fluctuations of two-dimensional determinantal processes associated with Berezin--Toeplitz '] Let $A, B$ be bounded self-adjoint operators. 
One has for any $t\ge 0$, 
\[
\| [ e^{itA} , B] \|_\bullet  \le  \|[A,B]\|_\bullet \,  t  . 
\]
In addition, if $ \|[A,B]\| \le \varepsilon$ and $\Delta$ is a trace-class operator satisfying 
$\|\Delta\|_{\tr} \le {\rm C}$ and $\|\Delta (A-B) \|_{\rm tr} \le \varepsilon$,  then for any $t\ge 0$,
\[
\|\Delta(e^{it A} -e^{i t B}) \|_{\rm tr}    \le  \varepsilon t(1+ \tfrac{{\rm C}}{2} t)  . \qedhere
\]

Notation, separate bias corrections and indexing are exactly those of081.
Fix b=9/10, d=999/1000, rho=epsilon/(eta lambda)=1/38,
X=x/eta, M=m/(eta lambda), V=v/(eta lambda)^2, M_0=V_0=0,
X_0 nonzero. Let

 U_t=sqrt(V_(t+1)/(1-d^(t+1))),
 k_t=1/(U_t+rho), a_t=k_t/(1-b^(t+1)), Z_t=X_t+18M_t.

THEOREM. Every such start has exactly one of these alternatives:

* Slow: X_(t+1)/X_t -> -1. There is a sign sigma in {-1,1} with
  t |X_t| -> 1/1444,
  t (-1)^t Z_t -> sigma/27436,
  t (38-k_t) -> 1, and t (38-a_t) -> 1.
* Fast: X_(t+1)/X_t -> -9/10. Then t X_t and t Z_t tend to zero;
  the nonzero exponential amplitude and variance-memory limits are those
  already proved in036. Also t (38-k_t) and t (38-a_t) tend to zero.

In particular lim t(-1)^t Z_t belongs to {0,-1/27436,1/27436},
and equals zero exactly on the fast branch. This is a time-normalized
discriminator, not the raw center limit (which is zero on both branches).
It does not show that either basin is generic or that a fast start exists.

1. VARIANCE AVERAGING ON THE SLOW BRANCH

Audited012 gives X_t ->0;028 gives eventual nonvanishing and the two
ratio alternatives. Assume the slow alternative. Write nu=1-d.
For every r<1 there is a late T with |X_(n+1)| >= r |X_n| for n>=T.
Choose r>sqrt(d). Since b<sqrt(d), this implies

 d^t/X_t^2 ->0, and b^t/|X_t| ->0.                     (1)

The raw variance recursion is exactly

 V_(t+1)=nu sum_(j=0)^t d^j X_(t-j)^2.                (2)

For each fixed j, X_(t-j)^2/X_t^2 ->1. For j<=t-T,
that ratio is at most r^(-2j), so the corresponding summand is bounded
by (d/r^2)^j, a summable geometric sequence. For the finite prefix
t-j<T, its sum after division by X_t^2 is O(d^t/X_t^2), hence tends
to zero by(1). Dominated convergence on the remaining geometric tail
therefore gives V_(t+1)/X_t^2 -> nu/(1-d)=1. Consequently

 U_t/|X_t| ->1.                                     (3)

This is deterministic sequence analysis; it uses no random averaging.

2. EXACT CENTER IDENTITY BECOMES QUADRATIC DAMPING

Since rho=1/38, exact algebra gives

 38-k_t=1444 U_t/(1+38U_t),
 38-a_t=(38-k_t)-k_t b^(t+1)/(1-b^(t+1)).            (4)

Equations(1),(3),(4) imply (38-a_t)/|X_t| ->1444.
In particular this difference is positive eventually, even though its
early sign need not be positive. Also a_t ->38. Momentum elimination
at t>=1 and the slow ratio give

 M_t/X_t=(X_(t-1)/X_t-1)/a_(t-1) -> -1/19,
 Z_t/X_t ->1/19,
 M_(t+1)/X_t=b M_t/X_t+(1-b) ->1/19,
 M_(t+1)/Z_t ->1.                                   (5)

The exact identity from036 is

 Z_(t+1)+Z_t=(38-a_t) M_(t+1).                       (6)

Set W_t=(-1)^t Z_t. By the slow ratio, X eventually alternates in sign;
by(5), Z has the same eventual sign as X. Thus W has a fixed nonzero
sign sigma at all sufficiently late times. Combining(4)-(6),

 W_(t+1)/W_t=1-(38-a_t) M_(t+1)/Z_t
             =1-27436 |W_t| (1+o(1)),               (7)

because |X_t|/|W_t| ->19 and 19*1444=27436.
Put Y_t=|W_t|. Here Y_t>0 eventually and Y_t ->0 by012, so(7) yields

 1/Y_(t+1)-1/Y_t ->27436.

Telescoping and Cesaro averaging imply 1/(t Y_t) ->27436, hence
t Y_t ->1/27436. Equation(5) gives t|X_t| ->1/1444.
Equation(4) then gives both asserted unit sharpness-deficit limits.
These are asymptotic equivalences, with no uniform entry time or
uniform remainder asserted over standard starts.

3. FAST BRANCH AND THE DISCRIMINATOR

Audited036 gives X_t=A(-b)^t+O(q^t), A nonzero, Z_t=O(q^t),
q=8999/10000<b, and V_t=O(d^t). Thus U_t=O(d^(t/2)).
Equation(4) proves all fast limits in the theorem. The two exhaustive
ratio alternatives from028 now prove the discriminator assertion.
It would be incorrect to assume this normalized limit is analytic in
X_0: its three possible values alone do not imply basin regularity.

4. CONDITIONAL TARGET-2 CONSEQUENCE

Fix two positive eigenvalues with theta_l=eta lambda_l/epsilon=38
and theta_h=eta lambda_h/epsilon>38. Assume standard moments, x_l,0
nonzero, the low coordinate is on the slow branch, and x_h,t ->0.
Audited025 supplies |x_h,t|=O(r_h^t) for some r_h<b. By the theorem,
|x_l,t|~eta/(1444 t). Both physical denominators
P_i,t=sqrt(v_i,t+1/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon tend to epsilon.
Let k_i,t=eta lambda_i/P_i,t and let

 omega_h,t=(g_h,t^2/P_h,t)/(g_h,t^2/P_h,t+g_l,t^2/P_l,t).

This is the squared alignment with the high coordinate in the
preconditioned gradient direction. It is O(t^2 r_h^(2t)). The active
curvature convention in the row is

 eta C_active,t=omega_h,t k_h,t+(1-omega_h,t) k_l,t.

Since both k_i,t are bounded, the high contribution is o(1/t). Hence

 eta C_active,t=38-1/t+o(1/t),
 eta S_top,t ->theta_h>38.                           (8)

The alignment angle with the low coordinate is O(t r_h^t).
These conclusions are conditional on high-origin convergence; no
existence or size of its standard-start basin is proved here. The low
slow-branch hypothesis holds on the tiny interval from audited037,
0<|x_l,0|<=10^(-57) eta. At epsilon=eta this applies with lambda_l=38
for every eta>0. It is not a resolution of the p>1 nontracking target.

VALIDATION AND LIMITS

The only inputs beyond the written argument are the exact recurrence,
global critical decay012, ratio dichotomy028, fast-tail refinement036,
supercritical origin rate025, and optional sufficient interval037.
The accompanying exact rational certificate checks the center identity,
constants and reciprocal drift. It is not a finite-run proof of an
infinite-time limit. No numerical asymptotic observation is used.
Literature priority has not been established. In particular the existing
frontier source Fong-Yang2608.20638v2 remains a source lead, not a claim
that this refinement is new. [Lemma lm:preferableevents of arXiv:2411.07125, 'Mixing on the cycle with constant size perturbation'] Consider the following preferable events:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{B}_1 &= \{a_i>\log^2 n,~ i=1,\ldots,2k\}\quad \textrm{--- concerning the graph},\\

\mathcal{B}_2 &=\{\beta(t,s) > -\log^2 n,~ 0\le t<s\le n^2\}\quad \textrm{--- concerning the walk}.
\end{align*}
For these we have $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{B}_1)\geq 1-\lambda_1 \log^2 n/n$ and $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{B}_2)\geq 1-\exp(-\lambda_2\log^2 n)$ for appropriate $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0$ as $n\to\infty$.
In particular, no full arc is backtracked once fully passed and thus $\xi_l, l=0,1,\ldots, L$ asymptotically almost surely (a.a.s.) properly represents the trajectory followed.

body:
[Proposition prop:fouriergap of arXiv:2608.30888, 'Three-term asymptotics for discrete\\ Hardy--Rellich constants in high dimension'] For every fixed $\ell,q\in\mathbb N$, there are constants
$C_{\ell,q}>0$ and $N_{\ell,q}$ and numbers
\[
 0\leq\varepsilon_{\ell,q}(N)
 \leq C_{\ell,q}N^{-1/2},\qquad N\geq N_{\ell,q},
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
 4^\ell\int_{\mathbb T^N}|D^{2\ell}\Psi|^2\omega^\ell
 \geq
 (2q)^\ell N^\ell(1-\varepsilon_{\ell,q}(N))
 \int_{\mathbb T^N}|D^\ell\Psi|^2
\end{equation}
for every smooth $\Psi\in\mathscr F_{q,N}$.

body: [Thm main of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $\rho_0 \in \text{Hit}_n(S)$ and let $\rho\in \mathcal{R}(\lambda)$ be an $n$-pleated representation obtained by bending $\rho_0$ along a maximal geodesic lamination $\lambda$. Then the Hitchin representation $\rho_0$ dominates $\rho$ in the Hilbert length spectrum as well as the translation length spectrum, namely, we have $\ell_\rho(\gamma) \leq \ell_{\rho_0}(\gamma)$ for any  $\gamma \in \pi_1(S)$, where the length function $\ell_\rho(\cdot)$ is either the Hilbert length or the translation length. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition boundary-values1 of arXiv:2504.18739, 'discrete analogues of second-order Riesz transforms'] For all $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $P_t(x)/H_t(x)$ converges as $t\to 0$. Let $\Psi(x)=\lim_{t\to0}P_t(x)/H_t(x)$ and $f\in\ell^p(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ be compactly supported. Define 
\[
    f_\mathrm{ext}(x) := \sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}^d} f(n)\Psi(x-m).
\]
Then, $\|f_{\mathrm{ext}}\|_{L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)} \le\|f\|_{\ell^p(\mathbb{Z}^d)}$ and $f_\mathrm{ext}(n) = f(n)$,  for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}^d$.

[Theorem 40 (representation-level detection criterion) of arXiv:2609.03593, '\textbf{New Homogeneous Einstein Metrics from Detection}'] For the three-factor aligned branch associated with $H/K$, the detector can
be normalized so that
\[
 D(0)>0,\qquad D(1/6)>0,\qquad
 \lim_{u\to+\infty}D(u)=+\infty,
\]
and
\[
 \operatorname{sgn}D(1)=\operatorname{sgn}\Xi(\rho,\sigma).
\]
Consequently
\[
 \Xi(\rho,\sigma)<0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \text{$D$ has a root in $(1/6,1)$ and a root in $(1,\infty)$}.
\]
Thus negativity of $\Xi$ is a sufficient pre-elimination criterion for the
two-root detection pattern.

[Theorem th:skorohod of arXiv:2411.06838, 'Generalized Wasserstein Barycenters'] Let $X$ be a complete, separable, metric space. 	\xi_{\mu_n}(t) \to 	\xi_{\mu}(t)\qquad \text{for almost all }t\in[0,1]
\]
whenever $\mu_n \to \mu$ narrowly in $\mathcal{P}(X)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm 14 of arXiv:2609.03054, 'The classes of bivariate Schur and Herglotz matrix-valued rational functions: realizations'] Let $g(s,p)$ be a polynomial of degree $n$. Then $g(s,p)$ is without roots in $\mathbb{GH}$ if and only if there exists an integer $l \geq 0$ and a contraction $A = \begin{bmatrix} A_1 & A_2 \\ A_2 & A_1 \end{bmatrix}$ such that:
    $$(s+p+1)^l g(s,p) = c \det \left ( (I+2A_1+K) +s(I-K)+p(I-2A_1+K) \right),$$
    where $c$ is a non-zero constant and $K=(A_1+A_2)(A_1-A_2)$.

    In the case that $g(s,p)\in{\mathbb R}[s,p]$, the constant $c$ and the matrices $A_1, A_2$ and $K$ can be chosen to be real.
title: Thm 14 of arXiv:2609.03054

[Definition def:gamble-space-conditions of arXiv:2512.21026, 'Minimax Duality in Game-Theoretic Probability\thanks{Work in progress: mistakes are likely'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{Z})$ be a gamble space.
  We define the following conditions on $\mathcal{Z}$.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item Contains zero: $0\in\mathcal{Z}$.
  \item Arbitrage-free: $Z\in\mathcal{Z} \implies$ $\inf Z \leq 0$.
  \item Normalized: arbitrage-free and contains zero.
  \item Scalable: $Z\in\mathcal{Z}, \alpha\geq 0 \implies \alpha Z\in\mathcal{Z}$;\\
    Downward scalable and upward scalable: $\alpha \in [0,1]$ and $[1,\infty)$, respectively.
  \item Positive-linear: $Z_1,Z_2\in\mathcal{Z}, \alpha_1,\alpha_2 \geq 0 \implies \alpha_1Z_1 + \alpha_2Z_2 \in \mathcal{Z}$.
  \item Bounded-below: $Z\in\mathcal{Z} \implies$ $\inf Z > -\infty$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Conditions on gamble spaces

body:
[Definition 10 (Causal normal geometry) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] A causal normal geometry of step \(N\) consists of a causal evolution
character \(\mathfrak C=(G,\alpha,\Phi)\), a chosen admissible causal lift
\(\widetilde\Phi\) through a transported target extension (the identity
extension is allowed), and a transport-compatible geometric chart
\[
 \widetilde\chi_t:\widetilde G_t^{\rm adm}
 \longrightarrow\mathsf G_{\rm geo}^{\le N}(V_t).
\]
We write
\[
 \mathfrak X=(\mathfrak C;\widetilde\Phi,\widetilde\chi),
 \qquad
 X^{\mathfrak X}_{s,t}
 :=\log_\star\widetilde\chi_t(\widetilde\Phi_{s,t}).
\]
The lift and chart are realization data; the normal filtration itself is the
canonical commutativization filtration of the charted free Lie algebra.  The
geometry is \emph{base-canonical} when the chart is trivial on the
admissible kernel, in which case it descends to \(\Phi\).
title: Causal normal geometry

[Lemma lem-invert of arXiv:2605.15395, 'Equivalence and Separation for Multivariate Matrix-Exponential and Phase-Type Distribution'] Let $\boldsymbol{\upalpha}_{0},\mathbf{U},\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{s})$ be as in Lemma~(lem-diag of the paper). Set $\ell=2q$ and define
\[
  \mathbf{B}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{U}&-\mathbf{I}_{q}\\(\mathbf{U}+\mathbf{I}_{q})^{2}&-\mathbf{U}-2\mathbf{I}_{q}\end{pmatrix} \in\mathbb{R}^{\ell\times \ell}.
\]
Set $\mathbf{T}=\mathbf{B}^{-1}$ and
\[
  \Delta_{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathbf{s}) =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \mathbf{S}(\mathbf{s})&\mathbf{0}_{q\times q}\\ \mathbf{0}_{q\times q}&\mathbf{0}_{q\times q}
  \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Define
\[
  \widehat{\boldsymbol{\upalpha}}=(\boldsymbol{\upalpha}_{0},\;\mathbf{0}_{1\times q}), \qquad \mathbf{b}_{1}=\mathbf{1}_{\ell}=
  \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{1}_{q}\\ \mathbf{1}_{q}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For every \(\mathbf{s}\) such that \(\mathbf{I}_{q}-\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{s})\) is invertible, $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, Hurwitz-stable, and
\[
  \widehat{\boldsymbol{\upalpha}}\bigl(-\mathbf{T}+\Delta_{\mathrm{aug}}(\mathbf{s})\bigr)^{-1}(-\mathbf{T}\mathbf{1}_{\ell}) =\boldsymbol{\upalpha}_{0}(\mathbf{I}_{q}-\mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{s}))^{-1}\mathbf{1}_{q}.
\]

Write Q_t(mu)=sup_f D_nu_t(T_t f)/D_mu(f) over Sobolev functions with positive finite energy. For log-concave mu with finite K=CP(mu), fixed t>0 and Q_t(mu)<=q<1 for every Sobolev f imply K<=t(1+q)/(1-q), by total variance and CP(mu*Gaussian_t)<=K+t. Thus a dimension-uniform strict posterior Dirichlet contraction at some fixed noise level is equivalent to a dimension-free KLS bound. Its nonlinear averaged gap remains unproved in this campaign packet. The unweighted MMSE covariance average cannot be substituted into an energy-weighted expectation.

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2609.00922, 'The Morse Index, Nullity and Jacobi Fields of Constant-Curvature 2-Spheres in Complex Proj'] Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, and put
	$\lambda=n-2k$. Then
	\[
	\Ind(\phi_{\lambda,n})
	=2k(n-k)(n+1)
	=\frac{(n+1)(n^2-\lambda^2)}2,\qquad
	\Nul(\phi_{\lambda,n})=2(n-1)(n+3).
	\]
	Consequently, the holomorphic and anti-holomorphic endpoint maps are
	stable, whereas every non-endpoint member of the Veronese sequence is
	unstable. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
For a centered Gaussian random variable $X \in L^2(\Omega; K)$, its covariance operator $Q_X: K \to K$ is the unique linear, bounded, symmetric, positive semi-definite, trace-class operator satisfying $\langle Q_X u, v \rangle_K = \mathbb{E}[\langle X, u \rangle_K \langle X, v \rangle_K]$ for all $u, v \in K$. In terms of an orthonormal basis $\{k_i\}_{i=1}^\infty$ of $K$, $Q_X = \sum_{i, j = 1}^\infty \mathbb{E}[X_i X_j] (k_j \otimes k_i)$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(Q_X) = \mathbb{E}[\|X\|_K^2] < \infty$.
X is a centered K-valued Gaussian random variable with finite second moment
title: Covariance Operator on Hilbert Space

Let A be an n x n random matrix whose entries are independent, identically distributed, centred, of unit variance and sub-Gaussian (sub-Gaussian norm at most K). Then for every epsilon >= 0, P( s_min(A) <= epsilon n^{-1/2} ) <= C epsilon + c^n, where C > 0 and c in (0,1) depend only on K. So the smallest singular value of a square random matrix is of order n^{-1/2} with high probability - the same order as for the Gaussian case, where Edelman computed the exact law of n s_min(G)^2 - and A is invertible with probability 1 - c^n even for Bernoulli (+-1) entries, for which singularity has positive probability; the c^n term is necessary because two equal rows occur with probability at least 2^{-n} c'. Together with Gordon's bound for tall matrices this settles the invertibility question for the basic random-matrix models.
entries i.i.d., mean zero, variance one, sub-Gaussian with norm at most K
A is square, n x n
C and c depend only on K; the c^n term cannot be removed for discrete entries

Method: Controlled generators, exact finite-state diagnostic, coupling, renewal reward or capacity comparison Result: For the special case where every job needs b servers, put c=floor(s/b). The saturated system is a c-machine list schedule. Its maximum completion time after n jobs is at least total service/c and at most total service/c+(1-1/c)*max_{j<=n}S_j. For iid finite-mean service, total service/n->E[S] and max S_j/n->0 almost surely, so gamma=E[S]/c. Heterogeneous demands break this scalar packing reduction. In the general estimator, a small difference between consecutive sample means does not bound the distance from their limiting value. Check: The list-scheduling upper bound is obtained by looking just before the job that finishes last starts: all c machine loads are at least its start time, and its own service accounts for the remaining gap. Divide by n and use the finite-mean iid maximal-term law. Obstruction: No general finite-sample certificate or computational complexity bound is derived; the equal-demand case is a credited classical scheduling reduction.

body:
Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent, mean-zero, SUB-EXPONENTIAL random variables, and write K_i for the Orlicz norm ||X_i||_{psi_1} = inf{ s > 0 : E exp(|X_i|/s) <= 2 }. Then there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every t >= 0, P( | sum_{i=1}^N X_i | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - c min( t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N K_i^2 , t / max_i K_i ) ). The bound has TWO regimes and that is intrinsic, not an artefact: for small t the tail is Gaussian with variance proxy sum K_i^2, and for large t it is exponential with rate 1/max_i K_i. No almost sure bound on the summands is assumed, which is what distinguishes this from the classical bounded-summand Bernstein inequality; the price is that the sub-Gaussian regime ends at t of order sum K_i^2 / max K_i rather than continuing forever. Squares of sub-Gaussian variables are sub-exponential, which is why this is the inequality behind chi-square tail bounds and the Hanson-Wright inequality. The constant c is absolute and no attempt should be made to read a specific numerical value out of this statement. [standard; e.g. Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 2.8.1]
X_i independent and mean zero
each X_i sub-exponential with finite psi_1 norm K_i
no boundedness and no identical distribution required
c is an absolute constant

[Proposition 25 (weak-strong uniqueness) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $(v,B,p)$ and $X$ be the solution and the volume-preserving map
constructed in \S\ref{ssec:eulerian} on $[0,T_*]$.
If $(\widetilde v,\widetilde B)$ is any other distributional solution with
the same initial data and
\[
 \widetilde v,\ \widetilde B-\Binf\in C([0,T_*],H^s),
\]
then
\[
 \widetilde v=v,\qquad \widetilde B=B
 \quad\text{on }[0,T_*].
\]
The two normalised Riesz pressures also agree. In particular, clause~\textup{(4)} of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} holds.

[Lemma lem:sqrt-rec-lower-slope of arXiv:2608.19050, 'Online Permutation Embedding: \\ Optimal Stopping and Scaling Laws'] For \(x,y\ge0\), set
\[
    \Psi(x,y)
    := \sqrt{G(x^2,y^2)}.
\]
Then, for all \(x,y,h\ge0\),
\[
    \Psi(x+h,y)-\Psi(x,y)\ge \frac{x}{x+1}h,
    \qquad
    \Psi(x,y+h)-\Psi(x,y)\ge \frac{y}{y+1}h .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 75 of arXiv:2604.01685, 'Probability with Measure\footnote{Lecture notes. University of Ljubljana.}'] A probability space is a measure space $(\Omega,\FF,\PP)$ where $\PP$ is a probability measure; let $(\Omega,\FF,\PP)$ be so. $\Omega$ is called the sample space and to the elements of $\FF$ one refers to as events.  $A$ is $\PP$-almost sure (abbreviated $\PP$-a.s.) \deff $A\in \FF$ and $\PP(A)=1$. For a measurable space $(E,\EE)$, elements of $\FF/\EE$ are called $(E,\EE)$-valued random elements; in the particular case when $(E,\EE)=(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$ they are called random variables. 
	For a random element $X$: $X\sim_\PP \QQ$ \deff $X$ has law $\QQ$ under $\PP$. Two random elements  valued in the same measurable space (and possibly defined on different probability spaces) are identically distributed \deff they have the same law. The distribution function of a random variable $X$ is the map $F_X:\mathbb{R}\to [0,1]$ given by $F_X(u):=\PP(X\leq u)$ for $u\in \mathbb{R}$. A random variable $X$ is said to be discrete (resp. absolutely continuous, continuous (also, diffuse)) \deff there is a countable $C\subset \mathbb{R}$ such that $\PP(X\in C)=1$ (resp. \deff $\PP_X\ll \leb$, \deff $F_X$ is continuous). A bivariate random vector is an element $(X,Y)$ of $\FF/\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}^2}$ (a general random vector is defined analogously), absolutely continuous \deff  $\PP_{(X,Y)}\ll \leb^2$, and so on.
title: Definition 75 of arXiv:2604.01685

body: In mathematics, concentration of measure is a principle that is applied in measure theory, probability and combinatorics, and has consequences for other fields such as Banach space theory. Informally, it states that "A random variable that depends in a Lipschitz way on many independent variables is essentially constant".

[Proposition 145 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] \cite[Theorem 2.4]{Johansson}

Assume $\theta$ and $\kappa$ positive. Let $f$ be an analytic test function and keep the notations $\sigma(z)$ and $\beta$ of \eqref{sigmasqbeta}. The random variable
\[
\sum_{i = 1}^{N} f(\lambda_i) - N \int_{-\beta}^{\beta} f(x)\dd \mu(x)
\]
is approximated in the sense of moments as $N \rightarrow \infty$ by a Gaussian random variable, with mean
\[
\textnormal{\textsf{Mean}}[f] = \frac{\theta -1}{2\theta}\left(\frac{f(-\beta) + f(\beta)}{2} - \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\beta}^{\beta} \frac{f(x) \dd x}{|\sigma(x)|} \right),
\]
and covariance like in Proposition~\ref{CLTGAUSSIANWEIGHT}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 24 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let $\mathbf X \in G\Omega_p(V)$. For each $N\in\mathbb N$ and each $1\le i\le d$, let
\(
A_i^N:\Omega\to\mathfrak h_N
\)
be a Hermitian random matrix defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. Assume that the following hold.

First, for every $k\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{1\le i\le d}\sup_{1\le m,l\le N}
\mathbb E\big[|A_i^N(m,l)|^k\big]\le c_A(k)<\infty,
\]
and moreover
\[
\mathbb E[A_i^N(m,l)]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[|A_i^N(m,l)|^2]=1.
\]

Second, there exists $K>0$ such that, for every $r\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{0\le s<t\le T}
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{1}{N^{r/2}}\|A_i^N(m,l)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^r\right]
\le K^r\Gamma\!\left(\frac{r}{2p}+1\right).
\]

Finally, assume that the sigma-algebras
\[
\bigvee_{i=1}^d \sigma(A_i^N(m,l)),
\qquad 1\le m\le l\le N,
\]
are independent, and that
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[A_i^N(m,l)A_j^N(m,l)\right]=0,
\qquad i\ne j.
\]

Define
\[
M^N\in\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb R^d,\mathfrak h_N),
\qquad
M^N(\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^d A_i^N\,\eta^{(i)}.
\]
Let $Z^N(\mathbf X)\in\mathcal D^p([0,T],U(N;\mathbb C))$ denote the solution of
\begin{equation} 
dZ^N(s,t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt N}M^N(d\mathbf X_t)\,Z^N(s,t),
\qquad
Z^N(s,s)=I_N.
\end{equation}

Then, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$ and for $\xi_N \in \mathcal{P}(\mathfrak{h}^d_N)$ denoting the law of the hermitian matrices $A^N_i$, the limit
\[
K(s,t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\,
\mathbb E_{\xi_N}\!\left[\operatorname{Tr}(Z^N(s,t))\right]
\]
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
K(s,t)=\sum_{|L|=0}^\infty i^{|L|}\varphi(L)\,S^{(L)}(\mathbf X)_{s,t}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, \(K\) solves the two-parameter RDE
\begin{equation}
K(s,t)=1-\int_s^t\int_s^r f(K(s,u),K(u,r))\,d\mathbf X_u\,d\mathbf X_r,
\end{equation}
where
\[
f:\mathbb R^2\to \mathrm{Hom}(V\boxtimes V, \mathbb{R}),
\qquad
f(z_1,z_2)[\eta,\xi]=z_1z_2\langle \eta,\xi\rangle_V.
\]
title: Theorem 24 of arXiv:2605.08844

body:
[Definition 13 (Projective-plane incidence class) of arXiv:2608.26516, '2608.26516'] For every integer $m\ge2$, let
\[
    q_m:=2^{m+10},
    \qquad
    N_m:=q_m^2+q_m+1,
    \qquad
    d_m:=q_m+1.
\]
Since $q_m$ is a prime power, a projective plane of order $q_m$ exists.

Take three disjoint vertex sets $V_0^{(m)},V_1^{(m)},V_2^{(m)}$, each of cardinality $N_m$. For every $r\in\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$, place an oriented copy of the point-line incidence graph from $V_r^{(m)}$ to $V_{r+1}^{(m)}$. For $v\in V_r^{(m)}$, write $\Gamma^+(v)\subseteq V_{r+1}^{(m)}$ for its outgoing neighborhood and put $\mathsf S(v):=\{v\}\cup\Gamma^+(v)$. The projective-plane axioms imply
\begin{equation}

    |\mathsf S(v)\cap\mathsf S(w)|
    \le 1
    \qquad
    \text{for every pair of distinct vertices }v,w.
\end{equation}
Indeed, two vertices in the same part have exactly one common outgoing neighbor, whereas the cyclic supports of vertices in different parts permit at most one intersection.

For every vertex $v$, create the Boolean-cube block $Z_v:=\{0,1\}^{\Gamma^+(v)}$. The $m$th incidence component and the full domain are
\[
    \CX_m^{\mathrm I}
    :=
    \bigsqcup_{v\in V_0^{(m)}\sqcup V_1^{(m)}\sqcup V_2^{(m)}} Z_v,
    \qquad
    \CX^{\mathrm I}
    :=
    \bigsqcup_{m\ge2}\CX_m^{\mathrm I}.
\]
Introduce a private label $\tau_u$ for every vertex $u$, with all such labels distinct across components. For a vertex $u$ in the $m$th component, define $g_u$ on that component by
\begin{equation}

    g_u(v,z)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \starlabel,
            & u=v,\\
        \starlabel,
            & u\in\Gamma^+(v)\text{ and }z_u=0,\\
        \tau_u,
            & \text{otherwise},
    \end{cases}
    \qquad
    (v,z)\in\CX_m^{\mathrm I},
\end{equation}
and extend $g_u$ by $\dollarlabel$ outside its component. Let $h_{\dollarlabel}$ be the all-$\dollarlabel$ hypothesis, and set
\[
    \Hinc
    :=
    \{h_{\dollarlabel}\}
    \cup
    \{g_u:u\text{ is a vertex in some incidence component}\}.
\]
We call $\Hinc$ the \edefn{projective-plane incidence class}.
title: Projective-plane incidence class

body:
Let A_n and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, with no assumption relating their domains. (a) If A_n -> A in the NORM resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) in operator norm for every continuous f : R -> C vanishing at infinity. (b) If A_n -> A in the STRONG resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) strongly for every BOUNDED CONTINUOUS f : R -> C, where f(A) is given by the functional calculus of the spectral theorem. In particular exp(i t A_n) -> exp(i t A) strongly for every real t, and for a fixed vector the convergence is uniform for t in compact sets. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) 'bounded continuous' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded Borel'. On H = C take A_n = multiplication by 1/n and A = 0 (convergence in every sense) and f the indicator of (0, infinity): then f(A_n) = 1 for every n while f(A) = 0. Convergence of spectral projections therefore needs a separate hypothesis - typically that the endpoints of the interval carry no spectral mass for A - and even then it is only strong convergence. (ii) In (b) one gets strong, never norm, convergence, because strong resolvent convergence does not imply norm resolvent convergence: on l^2 let P_n be the orthogonal projection onto the coordinates with index at least n and set A_n = P_n, A = 0; then A_n -> 0 strongly and in the strong resolvent sense, while the resolvent difference has constant operator norm. (iii) Unbounded f is outside the theorem and the natural statement is false: strong resolvent convergence does not give A_n psi -> A psi, even for psi in every domain (rank-one examples with growing coefficients show this). (iv) Nothing is assumed about domains - that is exactly why the hypothesis is phrased through resolvents rather than as pointwise convergence of the operators.
A_n and A are self-adjoint on a common Hilbert space H
the mode of convergence (strong or norm resolvent) is as in the definition of resolvent convergence
in (a) the function f is continuous and vanishes at infinity
in (b) the function f is continuous and bounded on R
f(A) means the bounded functional calculus supplied by the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators

The hypothesis is that r_z(A_n) -> r_z(A) strongly (respectively in norm) for the functions r_z(x) = (x - z)^(-1) with z non-real. STEP 2, the algebra they generate. The star-algebra generated by the family { r_z : z non-real } consists of continuous functions vanishing at infinity, separates the points of R, is closed under complex conjugation and vanishes nowhere, so by the Stone-Weierstrass theorem it is uniformly dense in C_infinity(R), the continuous functions vanishing at infinity. Strong convergence is preserved by sums and by products of uniformly bounded operators, and if f_k -> f uniformly on R then the operator norm of f_k(B) - f(B) is at most the supremum of |f_k - f| for any self-adjoint B; hence the set of f for which f(A_n) -> f(A) strongly is closed under uniform limits, and contains all of C_infinity(R). STEP 3, from C_infinity to bounded continuous. Let f be bounded continuous, psi in H and eps > 0. Choose g in C_infinity(R) with 0 <= g <= 1 and with the integral of (1 - g^2) against the spectral measure of psi for A small. Since 0 <= g <= 1 implies (1 - g)^2 <= 1 - g^2, the spectral theorem gives the norm squared of (1 - g)(A_n) psi bounded by the inner product of psi with (I - g^2(A_n)) psi; as g^2 lies in C_infinity, step 2 gives g^2(A_n) -> g^2(A) strongly, so the limsup over n of that quantity is at most the inner product of psi with (I - g^2(A)) psi, which is small by the choice of g. Now split f = f g + f (1 - g). The product f g belongs to C_infinity, so (f g)(A_n) psi -> (f g)(A) psi by step 2, while the norm of (f (1 - g))(A_n) psi is at most sup |f| times the norm of (1 - g)(A_n) psi, eventually small, and likewise for A. Combining the three estimates gives f(A_n) psi -> f(A) psi. [Definition 14 of arXiv:2606.01832, 'MA(1) processes with uniform innovations conditioned to stay positive in the non-expanding'] For any $\theta\in \R$ and $a>-1$, we define  $q_0^a(\theta)\coloneqq1$, $q_0^{a,y}(\theta)\coloneqq1$ and, for $n\geq 1$,
    $$
    q_n^a(\theta)\coloneqq\P(\theta X_1\geq  X_2,\dots,\theta X_n\geq X_{n+1}),\qquad q_n^{a,y}(\theta)\coloneqq\P(\theta y\geq  X_2,\dots,\theta X_n\geq X_{n+1}).
    $$ 
    
    The respective generating functions are denoted by
    $$\hat{Q}_{a,\theta}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} q_n^{a}(\theta)z^n ~~\text{ and }~~\hat{Q}_{a,y,\theta}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} q_n^{a,y}(\theta)z^n.$$
title: Definition 14 of arXiv:2606.01832
